#1 — Highly Innovative (80)

SWE-Proof: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World Issues with Machine-Checked Proofs?

G Ma, B Mikek, H Li, F Erata, Y Zhang, Z Shui… · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BENCHPROOFER, a pipeline that converts coding tasks with known ground-truth patches into formally verified benchmark instances, and uses it to build SWE-PROOF — 500 SWE-Bench Verified tasks (plus 242 of 266 Python SWE-Bench Pro tasks) each carrying a formal specification, a verifying reference implementation, and a machine-checked proof under three backends (Nagini, Velvet, pure Lean) plus a structured-natural-language control (EARS). - Why it's important: Held-out test suites, the standard oracle for agentic coding benchmarks, are incomplete and increasingly gameable, so reported resolution rates overstate real correctness; a verification oracle certifies behavior on the entire specified input domain rather than sampled inputs. - How it does it: The pipeline axiomatizes unchanged callees to keep verification tractable, and admits an instance only after thirteen gates agree — mechanical checks (verification, discrimination against a pre-fix twin, mutation, conformance via 187.6M differential inputs, leakage screens) plus blind adversarial LLM auditors whose attacks are adjudicated by execution rather than opinion. - The good: The measurement is large and multi-pronged: 26.8% of patches that pass every hidden test are overturned by adversarial audit, and a correct supplied specification lifts resolution from 85.0% to 95.0–96.2% under strict joint scoring, isolating specification synthesis as the bottleneck (only 46.0–61.4% of model-written specifications pass the audit, with faithfulness failing on 37.2–52.2%). - The missing: All headline evaluation uses a single model (Claude Opus 4.8) on a single agent scaffold, so it is unknown whether the specification-synthesis bottleneck generalizes across models or is an artifact of one system; the core "verify ⇒ resolve" claim also rests on two audited but unproven trust points (axiom soundness, refinement fidelity), which the authors acknowledge. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on code-agent evaluation or verified generation — the benchmark and the faithfulness-gap finding will shape follow-up work — but skip it if you only need another SWE-Bench leaderboard, since the evaluation grid covers one frontier model.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. This is the cluster's strongest paper: Novelty (82) is high — the first benchmark attaching a machine-checked verification oracle to real-world repository-level issue resolution, with the axiomatization-plus-adversarial-admission pipeline as a genuine methodological contribution and the quantified 26.8% test-incompleteness / faithfulness-bottleneck findings as real empirical discoveries. Rigor (85) is unusually thorough (four backends, nine one-factor-varied evaluation settings, out-of-corpus audit calibration with κ≈0.86, 187.6M differential inputs, versioned admission outcomes), trimmed slightly because it is a preprint, all headline numbers come from one frontier model, and no error bars accompany small deltas like +0.6. Non-Obviousness (76) is solid — the EARS control cleanly separating 'better description' from 'checkable description' was not predicted by prior work. Completeness (80) and Resilience (72) benefit from the paper's direct confrontation of its trust chain (axiom soundness, refinement fidelity), but Resilience is capped by the single-model evaluation grid and the LLM-mediated correspondence that bounds the 'verify ⇒ resolve' claim. Practical Impact (80) reflects a large released-to-be artifact (3,064 bundles with evidence records), though it is a benchmark, not a verification tool. Weighted composite: 0.20*82 + 0.25*85 + 0.15*76 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*80 = 80.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building LLM coding agents need a correctness oracle they can trust. Test-suite-based benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified credit patches that pass hidden tests, but finite test suites cannot certify behavior on unexercised inputs, and prior audits (Aleithan et al. 2024; Zhong et al. 2025) document test-passing-but-wrong solutions at scale. Formal verification solves this in principle, but existing verified-generation work (VERINA, DafnyBench, CLEVER, CLOVER) targets small curated exercises or standalone tasks where the formal specification is given as input. Real GitHub issues, by contrast, state intent in vague natural language and require edits inside large repositories with dependencies — no existing benchmark attaches a sound verification oracle to such tasks. The gap: nobody has both a verification-grade oracle and real-world issue-resolution tasks. Key Idea: The core trick is environment axiomatization combined with adversarial admission. Instead of verifying new code in the context of an entire repository — intractable — the pipeline models only the new or modified code and summarizes each unchanged callee with an over-approximative axiom stating just the properties the fix relies on, validated by fuzzing against the real callee and by whether the proof closes. Correctness of the resulting instance is then secured not by any single check but by a gate suite that forces the specification to be both achievable (correct code verifies) and discriminating (the pre-fix implementation and mutants fail to verify), with LLM auditors used only to generate attacks that are adjudicated mechanically. The second half of the idea is the discipline of the EARS control: a structured natural-language specification backend that separates "giving the agent a precise intent statement" from "giving it a machine-checkable one." Methodology: BENCHPROOFER runs in four stages. (1) Modeling: a construction agent that sees the gold patch, repository, and tests writes the specification module, a reference implementation that must verify, and a pre-fix twin that must fail verification, plus a correspondence map and provenance record linking formal artifacts to repository entities. (2) Proof (Lean backend only): an agent searches for a kernel-checked proof term. (3) Attack: four blind adversarial auditors (fidelity, strength, faithfulness, disclosure) that do not see the gold patch produce concrete artifacts — counterexample inputs, wrong implementations that verify, patch reconstructions — each adjudicated by running the verifier or repository. (4) Admission: thirteen recorded checks (verification, discrimination, mutation with an 80% per-bundle kill floor, hygiene, axiom soundness, conformance, soundness/completeness, property-based falsification, equivalence, leakage). Evaluation instantiates an agent in nine settings differing in what is provided (verifier tool, edit localization, specification view) and what a pass requires (hidden tests only, or tests + verification + majority auditor agreement on implementation-patch correspondence). The formal guarantee is Claim 1 (verify ⇒ resolve), which is explicitly a hypothesis-laden trust chain, not a theorem: it holds modulo axiom soundness and the audited equivalence between the verified implementation and the executed Python patch. Critical design decisions: construction agents see the gold patch while auditors do not (justified as necessary for specification strength calibration); the 80% mutation floor rather than 100% (well-justified — some survivors are genuinely unconstrained behavior); requiring discrimination against pre-fix twins (well-justified, prevents vacuous specifications). Key Results: On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances with Claude Opus 4.8: unaided baseline resolves 85.0%; under adversarial audit of patch-patch equivalence, 26.8% of test-passing patches are overturned, quantifying test-suite incompleteness. End-to-end self-specification gives no gain (85.6% Nagini, 85.0% Velvet, 83.8% Lean). Providing the ground-truth specification plus localization raises resolution to 96.2%/94.0%/95.2%, and the stricter verified-from-specification setting retains 95.0%/94.0%/93.6% — a +9.0 to +11.0 point gain over the agent writing its own specification. The EARS natural-language control does not close the gap (80.0% verified from specification; 17.8 points of its pass rate come from patches still distinguishable from ground truth). Specification synthesis passes the five-property audit only 46.0% (Nagini), 60.0% (Velvet), 61.4% (Lean) of the time, with faithfulness the dominant failure (42.5% average). Specification quality tracks outcome: specifications from unresolved instances fail the audit 92.3% of the time versus 50.5% for resolved ones. Construction scale: 2,000 green bundles on SWE-Bench Verified (100%), 996/1,064 on SWE-Bench Pro; 23,482 property-test cases all producing their labeled verdict, 25,163/25,457 mutants killed, 187.6M differential inputs with zero disagreements, 25.7M axiom-probe observations. Baselines are current (SWE-Bench Verified official harness, frontier model), and the benchmark itself is the contribution rather than a leaderboard win. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (SWE-PROOF is, per the authors' own accounting and the related-work comparison, the first benchmark attaching a verification oracle to real-world repository-level issue resolution), NEW METHOD (the BENCHPROOFER gate pipeline, particularly the axiomatization-plus-adversarial-admission recipe and the five-property specification audit including the faithfulness criterion), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the quantified faithfulness gap as the bottleneck for verified code generation). The verifiers themselves (Nagini, Lean, Velvet), the agent scaffold, and iterative refinement loops are existing components; the genuine novelty is the benchmark construction discipline and the finding, not any new verification algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: four backends isolate formal-checking value from specification-as-description value; nine evaluation settings vary one factor at a time; the audit is calibrated out-of-corpus with Fleiss κ of 0.861 (faithfulness) and 0.871 (overall verdict) among independent ballots, and specification-audit verdicts are associated with independent resolution outcomes (Mantel–Haenszel odds ratio 13.5, 95% CI [7.96, 22.93]). Mutation survivors are individually reviewed and the 80% floor is defended rather than hidden. Every admission outcome is versioned and recomputed; per-instance evidence (axiom probes, property suites, gate records) ships with the corpus, and a reproducibility statement commits to releasing both BENCHPROOFER and SWE-PROOF (no URL given in the provided text). Concerns: (a) only one frontier model is evaluated, so findings may not transfer; (b) the adversarial auditors are the same class of LLM that could be attacked, so audit soundness is calibrated statistically, not guaranteed — the authors state this; (c) construction agents see the gold patch, so constructed specifications could be subtly shaped by it (mitigated by the disclosure gate, but not eliminated); (d) the 76 bundles with documented disclosure relaxations slightly weaken evaluation on those instances. No significance tests or multiple seeds are reported for the headline pass-rate deltas, though all numbers cover the full 500 instances. This is a preprint under review. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a constructed benchmark and a model evaluation; no deployment of the method itself as a product). - Practical: Yes — verification runs on commodity hardware (mean 6.0–25.8 s per bundle check, max 288.6 s), though construction and auditing require frontier LLM API access at scale (12,000 audit ballots, 87.0 hours of prover time for property suites). - Efficient: Verification of released bundles is cheap (~8.4 serial prover-hours total); the expensive part is construction, dominated by refutation (property suites cost 10× the verification cost), and evaluation requires a full agent episode per setting. - Effective: The evidence shows the oracle works as claimed — every gold patch resolves in the official harness, every pre-fix twin fails, and the differential harness finds zero disagreements across 187.6M inputs — but the pipeline cannot build verified twins for ~8% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks whose graded tests discriminate on non-value properties (renames, signatures, side effects). - Scalable: Tested at 10× patch size (SWE-Bench Pro: mean 145.5 vs 14.3 changed lines) with verification cost actually dropping under Lean backends; beyond that only claimed — the authors assert extensibility to any task with a value-observable change but test only two corpora. The work delivers a concrete artifact: a benchmark corpus of 3,064 bundles with per-instance evidence records and the construction pipeline, committed for release; it does not deliver a verification tool for practitioners' own code. Strengths: (1) The gate-suite design — mechanical adjudication of adversarial attacks, pre-fix twins that must fail, property suites as reusable refutation evidence — is a genuine methodological contribution to benchmark construction, not just competent plumbing. (2) The EARS control is a smart experimental design move: it cleanly separates "the agent got a better problem description" from "the agent got a checkable one," and the result (EARS fails where formal specs succeed) is the paper's sharpest finding. (3) The faithfulness-failure analysis is a real empirical discovery with a concrete diagnosis (specifications correct on modeled functions but covering too few of them), corroborated by independent work the authors cite (CodeSpecBench's 20.2% repository-scale specification pass rate). (4) The honesty infrastructure — versioned outcomes, released attack records, calibration statistics, explicit trust-point boundaries — exceeds the norm for benchmark papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive. They explicitly state that verify ⇒ resolve is not a proof and rests on two audited trust points (axiom soundness, refinement fidelity); that backend expressiveness forced manual modeling on some instances (e.g., an import-timing side effect partial-correctness logic cannot express); that a minority of bundles (76, e.g., scikit-learn-26194) relax the no-leakage property because a faithful specification necessarily names a discriminator absent from the public issue text; and that the LLM specification audit is evidence rather than proof. They also honestly report that the near-zero finding rate on released bundles is by construction and therefore uninformative about audit quality — hence the out-of-corpus calibration. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single-model evaluation: every headline finding comes from Claude Opus 4.8; the claim that specification synthesis is the bottleneck would be far stronger with a second, weaker or stronger model showing the same faithfulness-dominated failure profile. (2) The trust chain is longer than the framing suggests: axiom soundness is checked by fuzzing plus LLM audit, and refinement fidelity for Lean/Velvet backends runs against an agent-written Python "transliteration" the authors themselves call the weakest link — so the 26.8% test-incompleteness figure and the verified pass rates are bounded by unproven LLM-mediated correspondence, not by the Lean kernel alone. (3) The constructed specifications may inherit subtle bias from construction agents seeing the gold patch; the disclosure gate catches lexical and semantic leakage of the fix, but not subtler calibration of specification strength to the known solution's shape. (4) No error bars or repeated runs are reported for the evaluation grid (Appendix F.4 mentions repetition accounting but the provided text is truncated), so deltas like +0.6 points (Row 2 vs Row 0) are within plausible run-to-run noise. (5) The evaluation is confined to Python repositories and SWE-Bench-family tasks; generalization beyond this distribution is asserted via the pipeline's design, not measured. Bottom Line: A practitioner in code-agent evaluation or verified generation should read this: the benchmark, the gate methodology, and the quantified faithfulness gap are genuinely new and immediately usable, and no existing alternative attaches a verification oracle to real-world issues at this scale — but the single-model evaluation and LLM-mediated trust chain mean its headline numbers should be treated as one strong data point, not settled science.

#2 — Highly Innovative (78)

BI-Agent and BI-Bench: Towards Automating End-to-End Business Intelligence (12 ▲ )

Chuxuan Hu, Yeye He, Penny Zhou, Wee Hyong Tok, Daniel Kang, Surajit Chaudhuri · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BI-Bench, a 100-case benchmark of real end-to-end BI tasks extracted from crawled Power BI projects, and BI-Agent, a tool-augmented LLM agent plus a trajectory-synthesis post-training framework (SFT and GRPO-based RL) that lifts Qwen3-8B from 5.2% to 35.0% SQL accuracy on it. - Why it's important: Enterprise BI tools still require non-technical users to manually identify tables, reshape non-relational data, and define joins before analysis; this paper quantifies that even frontier LLMs and top NL2SQL systems fail on over half of such end-to-end tasks, exposing a gap that NL2SQL benchmarks like BIRD and Spider 2.0 do not capture. - How it does it: The core move is offloading the hardest data-management steps (table relationalization, join prediction over snowflake schemas, table search) to specialized algorithms exposed as agentic tools, then post-training the orchestrator LLM on synthetic trajectories generated by materializing joined wide tables (which simplifies code generation) and re-scattering the data into raw, sometimes non-relational, input tables. - The good: Evaluation is unusually rigorous for an agent paper — 10 runs per setting, paired t-tests with 95% bootstrap CIs, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control over 36 comparisons, a project-level robustness re-analysis, and an out-of-domain test on Spider 2.0 where gains transfer (Qwen3-8B: 0.8% to 16.4% on Spider 2.0-lite SQL with tools). - The missing: The benchmark has only 100 manually curated test cases built and evaluated by the same team that designed the system, the RL stage trains only on tasks a teacher model could already solve, and the automated error taxonomy (classified by GPT-5.2) is not human-validated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building LLM agents over messy multi-table enterprise data or designing domain-specific post-training pipelines; skippable if you only care about clean-schema NL2SQL, where existing benchmarks already cover the ground.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with a systems component). Rigor (80) is the standout dimension: 10 runs per setting, paired t-tests with bootstrap CIs, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control across 36 comparisons, project-level re-analysis, informative reward and tool-count ablations, and released code/data/checkpoints — docked for same-team benchmark construction, no human-validated error taxonomy, and preprint status. Novelty (78) is strong: a first-of-kind end-to-end BI benchmark plus the wide-table-then-re-scatter trajectory synthesis trick, though built from existing components. Non-Obviousness (75) is earned by the division-of-labor insight and the demonstration that BIRD/Spider leaders collapse to 6-26%, pinpointing data preparation as the bottleneck. Completeness (78) benefits from directly confronting scope limits and residual failure modes; Resilience (72) is solid given out-of-domain Spider 2.0 transfer, though the missing strong-prompt baseline caps it. Impact (85) is high — released artifact, $0.19/query 8B model, under-$200 training. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*80 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*85 = 78.

Problem & Motivation: Non-technical enterprise users of Power BI and Tableau must complete a multi-stage workflow — selecting relevant tables from large projects, performing table-reshaping transformations (pivot/unpivot/transpose) in vendor DSLs, and defining join relationships across star/snowflake schemas — before any analysis is possible. Prior benchmarks do not test this pipeline: NL2SQL benchmarks (BIRD, Spider) hand models clean, pre-joined, analysis-ready tables, and data-science benchmarks (DSBench, DA-Code, KramaBench) come from notebooks or scientific papers rather than BI workflows with messy spreadsheet-derived data. The authors target one-off, low-tail analysis over raw tables where no curated data model exists — a regime they position as complementary to, not a replacement for, enterprise BI. Key Idea: The central insight is a division of labor: LLMs are good at analysis-style code generation but unreliable at recognizing when a pivot table needs relationalizing or at predicting joins over large cryptic-keyed schemas, whereas classical data-management algorithms (Auto-Tables-style transformation prediction, Auto-BI-style global join prediction over schema graphs) handle these well when given full-table statistics. The second insight is a training-data trick: because the crawled BI projects contain user-defined joins, one can materialize a joined wide table W, have an LLM write a query and code c over W to get R = c(W) (easy, since search and join are pre-solved), then re-mix relevant and irrelevant tables and apply inverse reshaping operators to reconstruct a hard raw-table task (q, T, R) with a verified answer — yielding 7,985 synthesized queries for SFT and RL without manual labeling. Methodology: BI-Bench construction: crawl ~3K .pbix files; extract raw tables, user-defined transformations, join relationships, and dashboards via DAX Studio and Power Automate RPA; sample visualizations with unambiguous titles; paraphrase the visualization intent into a natural-language query (adding implicit filters found in the visualization DSL); export the underlying result table as ground truth; verify via manual review plus an LLM-assisted check where two frontier models with full hints attempting 10 times flag suspicious cases (23.1% triggered re-review; 14.4% repaired, 5.2% discarded, 3.5% retained as genuinely hard); augment ground truths with semantically valid alternative schemas. BI-Agent: an LLM orchestrator in a reasoning/tool-call loop with four tools — a generic code executor (Python or SQL against SQLite), a transform tool wrapping reshaping-prediction algorithms, a join tool wrapping schema-graph-based join prediction, and a search tool that uses an LLM to conservatively prune irrelevant tables. Post-training: GPT-4o generates teacher trajectories retained only if execution exactly reproduces R, split into turn-level SFT examples (19K–43K turns per configuration across {Python, SQL} × {tool, no-tool}); RL uses GRPO with a verifiable table-match reward (+1 − 0.1n for correct, −0.5 − 0.1n for non-empty incorrect, −1 − 0.1n for empty, where n counts syntax-error iterations), gradients restricted to tool-call blocks. Critical design decisions: (1) wide-table-first synthesis to make code generation tractable — well justified; (2) partial-credit reward shaping — validated by ablations (removing either reward term drops RL-Tool accuracy below the SFT initialization); (3) keeping RL tasks to those GPT-4o solved — pragmatic but introduces teacher-solvable bias, only briefly justified. Key Results: On BI-Bench (100 tasks from 82 projects; average 10.6 tables, 80,464 rows, 12.75 joins per project), the best vanilla model is o4-mini at 48.2% SQL accuracy without tools; GPT-5.5 gets 46.7%. Adding BI-Agent's tools improves accuracy by 14 points on average for SQL and 11 for Python, significant in 19 of 20 cases; the largest jump is GPT-OSS-120B, from 5.3% to 45.3% SQL (+40.0 points). Post-trained Qwen3-8B reaches 35.0% SQL with tools (SFT+RL), up 29.8 points from the 5.2% base, beating GPT-4o (37.7% with tools is higher, but 27.1% without) and 4 of 5 large open-source models in their no-tools settings, at ~54× lower per-query cost ($0.19 vs. >$10 for some frontier models; total training cost under $200 on 2×H100). Top BIRD-leaderboard models (Kwai-AutoSQL-32B, Infly-RL-SQL-32B, XiYanSQL-QwenCoder-32B), which exceed 70% on BIRD, score 6.0–17.3% on BI-Bench; the two best Spider 2.0-lite agents (ktx with Codex/GPT-5.5, Databao Agent) drop to 23.8–26.3%. On the out-of-domain Spider 2.0-lite, Qwen3-8B-RL-Tool reaches 16.4% SQL versus 0.8% for the base model. Error analysis (GPT-5.2-classified traces) shows tools cut transform errors by 54.2% and table-selection errors by 40.9%; "missing information" remains the most common unresolved error type. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (BI-Bench is the first end-to-end BI benchmark built from real user dashboards), NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (BI-Agent), and NEW METHOD (the wide-table-then-re-scatter trajectory synthesis pipeline with leakage quantification), plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (frontier LLMs and SOTA NL2SQL systems collapse on end-to-end BI). The individual components — ReAct-style tool loops, GRPO/RLVR, Auto-Tables and Auto-BI algorithms, SFT-then-RL post-training — are existing ideas; the genuinely novel parts are the benchmark construction methodology and the synthetic-trajectory pipeline that converts user-defined joins into self-supervised training signal. The authors themselves state BI-Agent's novelty lies in system-level co-design rather than new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: tool-count sensitivity (monotonically increasing gains, 1→2→3 tools), complexity-stratified gains, reward-design ablations (all three reward variants underperform the SFT checkpoint), and error-type distributions. Statistical hygiene is above the bar for this area: 10 repeated runs, paired t-tests, paired-bootstrap 95% CIs, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control across 36 comparisons, and a project-level re-analysis confirming task-level significance findings. Code and data are released at https://github.com/Hu-Chuxuan/bi-agent. Concerns: the benchmark is small (100 tasks, though comparable to peers like KramaBench's 104 and REPRO-Bench's 112); the benchmark and system come from the same team, so the benchmark's difficulty profile may implicitly favor BI-Agent's specific tool decomposition (the authors partially mitigate this by showing tools help 10 vanilla models and that gains transfer to Spider 2.0); the automated error classifier is not validated against human labels; and per the arXiv posting this is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — a released agent and benchmark). Practical: Yes — runs via commercial LLM APIs or a single 8B open-weights model; training used only 2×80GB H100s for under $200. Efficient: Post-trained Qwen3-8B costs $0.19–0.31 per query versus $3–$15 for frontier models at comparable or better accuracy; tools also cut output tokens by 16–25% and interaction rounds. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated raw-table-to-answer-table problem on the authors' benchmark and partially on Spider 2.0, but absolute accuracy (35% best SQL) means the problem is far from solved — this is demonstrated improvement, not a deployed solution. Scalable: Not tested beyond the benchmark's maximum (52 tables, 7M rows in one project); behavior on projects an order of magnitude larger is unclaimed and unmeasured. The work delivers a software artifact (agent code, benchmark, and post-trained Qwen3-8B checkpoints), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The benchmark fills a real, well-argued hole — the empirical collapse of BIRD/Spider leaders on BI-Bench (70%+ to 6–26%) is the paper's most convincing evidence that data preparation, not analysis, is the bottleneck. (2) The trajectory-synthesis pipeline is a genuinely clever self-supervision scheme: it exploits user-defined joins in real projects to manufacture verified hard training tasks at scale, with quantified train/test separation (99.72% query-level, 99.27% transform-level dissimilarity). (3) The demonstration that an 8B model post-trained for under $200 matches much larger frontier models at 54× lower inference cost is a practically important result. (4) Statistical rigor (FDR control, project-level clustering, multi-run averaging) is well beyond the norm for agentic-system papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly scope the work to one-off, low-touch analysis over raw tables rather than full enterprise BI deployments with curated data models, and they exclude visualization generation since ground truth for visual form is non-unique. They acknowledge that "missing information" errors remain the most common failure mode and that their tool set is explicitly non-exhaustive and extensible. They confront these boundaries directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Query construction depends on visualization titles and annotator paraphrasing — the benchmark measures whether a model can reproduce a dashboard's result table from a human-written description of that dashboard's intent, which is a slightly easier task than inferring intent cold; inter-annotator agreement statistics for the query-writing process are not reported. (2) The RL training set is restricted to tasks GPT-4o could already solve, so the RL model never trains on the hardest task types; the paper does not measure how this caps capability. (3) The LLM-assisted benchmark verification uses model failure as a review trigger — while the authors carefully report that 3.5% of model-failing cases were retained, the process still risks a residual correlation between benchmark content and frontier-model behavior. (4) The error taxonomy is produced by GPT-5.2 without human validation of the classifications. (5) Cost comparisons use list API pricing from a single point in time and one execution per query, ignoring retries and caching effects in production. (6) There is no comparison against a simple strong baseline of "give the vanilla model a better system prompt describing BI best practices," so some of the tool gain could conceivably be recovered for free. Bottom Line: This is the most credible and useful piece of work to date on LLM-driven end-to-end BI — the benchmark exposes a real, quantified gap that NL2SQL work has been ignoring, and the synthesis-plus-tools recipe is directly reusable — so practitioners building agents over messy enterprise data should read it, while pure NL2SQL researchers can safely rely on the headline finding that their benchmarks under-represent data preparation.

RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents

S Bai, J Deng, S Fan, Y Fu, C Gao, X Hu, M Huang… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RECREATIONWORLD, a five-platform (Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android, Web) framework where hybrid computer-use agents must reconstruct a running reference application from scratch, plus RECREATIONBENCH, a 250-task held-out benchmark with frozen programmatic and visual test suites, and shows that SFT on 35,000 verified recreation trajectories transfers to five out-of-distribution benchmarks (gains up to +17.9 pp). - Why it's important: Real digital work interleaves GUI operation with coding, but existing benchmarks measure one modality at a time, leaving the autonomous explore–implement–verify loop — and its self-grounding, verifiable reward — unmeasured and untrained. - How it does it: The running reference application acts as an executable oracle from which hidden behavioral test suites (accessibility-tree assertions plus VLM-judged visual assertions) are generated, validated on the reference, human-reviewed, and frozen, providing implementation-agnostic, automatically scorable reward. - The good: The benchmark is rigorous and transparent about its own integrity: tests are validated against the reference before freezing, ~94% of cases check action-conditioned outcomes, isolation is probed under the agent's exact identity, and contamination audits show median exact-line overlap below 0.09%. - The missing: Main benchmark results use one rollout per model-task with no error bars or significance tests, the VLM judge is the authors' own in-house Qwen3.7-Plus, and the transfer claim rests on exploratory single-trial checkpoint sweeps the authors themselves label non-causal. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build agent environments, RL/SFT reward pipelines for CUAs, or agent benchmarks; skippable if you only care about model leaderboard numbers, which occupy a small fraction of the paper.

Problem & Motivation: Computer-use agents have developed along two disconnected lines: GUI agents that operate applications they cannot build, and terminal/coding agents that build software they cannot see. Real software-intensive work requires interleaving both — observation shapes implementation, and running the implementation reshapes what to observe — yet existing benchmarks (OSWorld 2.0 for GUI, ProgramBench for code) measure one interaction mode, under-measuring long-horizon autonomous coordination. Practitioners training general agents lack both an environment that generates verifiable experience for this fused loop and a benchmark that scores it. Key Idea: Recreation as a task formulation: because the specification exists only inside a running reference application and the deliverable is code that must build and run, the explore–implement–verify hybrid loop is forced rather than optional; and because the reference is executable, it doubles as an oracle for deriving a frozen, implementation-agnostic behavioral test suite — exploiting the "asymmetry of verification" so that generating/validating tasks is hard once (with human review) but scoring is automatic forever. Methodology: Three components. (1) Environment infrastructure: versioned, task-isolated workers per platform (native GUI automation via qwen-cua-driver/mobile-mcp/Playwright MCP, build toolchains, Android emulator, headless Chromium) scheduled on a horizontally scaled VM pool with 20-hour per-rollout budgets; agents submit source under a per-platform build/launch contract (e.g., Gradle→APK on Android, self-contained index.html on Web) without architecture constraints. (2) Test construction: an orchestrator builds a behavior inventory from source inspection plus live probing; specialized subagent generators author fixture + trigger + assertion cases (programmatic via AT-SPI/AXUIElement/UI Automation/UiAutomator/DOM-ARIA, and visual via screenshot + natural-language assertion judged by a temperature-zero Qwen3.7-Plus judge); every case is replayed on the reference, filtered for instability/discriminativeness, human-reviewed, then frozen. Coverage audit: 77.2% of cases leave the start surface, 24.1% cross 2+ surfaces, 94.2% check action outcomes, 40.7% require exact values. (3) Training: rejection-sampled high-scoring Qwen3.8-Max rollouts on open-source apps, 7,000 per platform (35,000 total), balanced SFT on two initializations (Qwen3.7-Plus, Qwen-Flash-CPT). Key design decisions: source-blind reference withholding on desktop/Android (justified; Web inherently cannot be), action+outcome coupling of assertions (justified via coverage audit), and equal platform weighting in scoring. A separate study replaces per-call direct MCP with a persistent Node.js REPL/SDK for composability. Key Results: On RECREATIONBENCH (10 frontier models, 250 tasks), GPT-6 Astra leads at 58.06% average (Prog 58.19%, VLM 57.92%), followed by Claude Opus 5 at 44.16% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 42.06%; Qwen3.7-Plus trails at 9.15%. Full programmatic-suite passes are rare even for the leader: 2.8% of applications at 100% Prog and 17.6% at ≥90%. Training transfer: both SFT arms finish above their first checkpoint on all five OOD benchmarks — e.g., WeaveBench 35.7→48.2 (Qwen3.7-Plus) and 30.6→47.6 (Qwen-Flash-CPT), ProgramBench partial 41.9→44.6 and 18→24, with up to +17.9 pp on GameCraft-Bench. The programmable-SDK study (Windows, 50 apps, Claude Opus 4.8, one rollout per task) shows similar quality with input tokens −40.7%, tool-result text −65.5%, wall-clock 4.12→3.04 h/task, estimated cost $90.50→$41.58/task. Diagnostic findings: recreations reproduce static structure better than button/computation/interaction tests (trailing by 9.1–34.4 points); median recreation-to-reference LOC ratio is 16.9% with 89.4% of recreations smaller than their references; only 23.6–47.5% of trajectories complete a strict final edit–relaunch–inspect sequence. Baselines are current frontier models with their native scaffolds (Codex, Claude Code), which is strong, though scaffold and model identity co-vary. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (RECREATIONBENCH, five platforms, reference-derived frozen suites) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (multi-platform recreation environments with verifiable reward), plus a NEW FORMULATION of hybrid CUA capability as autonomous interleaving of explore–implement–verify rather than stacked modalities. The individual ingredients — rejection-sampling SFT, accessibility-tree assertions, VLM judges, sandboxed rollouts — are standard; the genuine novelty is using an executable reference as both a specification to discover by interaction and an oracle for behaviorally grounded reward, and the systematic test-generation/validation pipeline behind it. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the coverage audit (Table 2) and the direct-MCP vs. REPL comparison probe design choices, but there is no ablation isolating which training-data components drive transfer. Error bars appear only in trajectory analyses (95% bootstrap intervals); the headline benchmark table and transfer sweeps report single rollouts with no variance or significance testing. The authors repeatedly and explicitly flag their own correlational limits ("descriptive comparisons do not establish that these behaviors cause higher scores"). Code, environments, dataset, and test suites are released (GitHub, Hugging Face, ModelScope, project website). Integrity work is unusually thorough: preflight isolation probes per identity, per-platform network controls, a four-class evaluation-hacking audit (GLM-5.3 shows the most attempts; attempts, not successes), and a contamination audit with noise-filtered exact-line overlap medians of 0.014–0.088%. Methodological concerns: the VLM judge is the authors' own Qwen3.7-Plus (potential self-favoring bias, unquantified judge validity); one trial per model-task limits score reliability on 50-task platforms; and the transfer evaluation uses differing budgets/harnesses across benchmarks, acknowledged as exploratory. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS with a strong EMPIRICAL component (a built, released infrastructure evaluated by deployment and by experiments). - Practical: Requires substantial infrastructure — VM pools, per-platform GUI runtimes, macOS/Windows licensing — beyond typical academic labs, though the agent-facing contract is standard MCP/tools; consumer hardware is insufficient to reproduce the full pipeline. - Efficient: Rollouts are expensive (23–259M cumulative input tokens, 191–741 assistant turns, up to ~$200+/trajectory estimated API cost on Claude Opus 5); the REPL runtime cuts cost roughly in half versus direct MCP. - Effective: Evidence supports measuring and training the hybrid loop; OOD transfer gains are consistent across two arms and five benchmarks, but single-trial, non-causal designs mean effect sizes are uncertain. - Scalable: Only claimed via design (open-source app pool, VM pool scaling); training data is fixed at 35,000 trajectories and no scaling experiment beyond that is run; long-horizon stability is demonstrated at 20-hour budgets, not 10–100× beyond. The work delivers a real software artifact: harness, platform runners, evaluation code, benchmark dataset, and hidden test suites, all publicly released. Strengths: - The reference-as-oracle reward design converts a hard, human bottleneck (behavioral specification writing) into a validated, frozen, automatic evaluator — the cleanest instantiation of verifiable reward for GUI+code agents to date. - Evaluation integrity is treated as a first-class contribution: source-blind boundaries probed under the agent's identity, hacking-attempt telemetry by category, and a contamination audit that quantifies (rather than assumes away) pretraining leakage risk. - The failure-mode analysis is genuinely diagnostic, not decorative: the static-structure vs. action-conditioned gap, the ~17% controlled-input-variation rate, the <50% final-loop-closure rate, and the PhotoCollage/Plus Plus Battery case studies give the community concrete, actionable improvement targets. - Honest statistical hygiene throughout: the paper distinguishes structural benchmark comparisons from controlled comparisons, separates claims from measurements in nearly every analysis paragraph, and reports residual risks (e.g., Android packet-level egress not attested). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that pinned reproducible environments exclude live services, changing external state, and multi-user workflows; that finite hidden suites cannot establish equivalence across all states and paths; that public references may appear in pretraining data and source-overlap screening cannot rule out non-verbatim memorization; and that scores measure fidelity only within the specified environments and frozen suites. They also repeatedly caveat that trajectory correlations are non-causal and that transfer curves are not uniformly monotonic. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-rollout benchmark protocol: with 50 tasks per platform, per-platform score differences of a few points (e.g., mid-table models) are within plausible rollout noise; no seeds/repeats or CIs are reported for Table 3. - Judge validity is unexamined: no human-agreement study for the Qwen3.7-Plus visual judge, and no analysis of whether the in-house judge favors in-house models (Qwen3.7-Plus is also the OOD-evaluation judge in Vision2Web/OSWorld/WeaveBench settings via GPT judges — those are third-party, but the RECREATIONBENCH VLM channel is not). - The transfer baseline is "first evaluated checkpoint," not a matched-control SFT on an alternative data source (e.g., generic coding trajectories of equal size), so the claim that recreation supervision specifically drives transfer is not isolated. - Android's APK-recoverable reference risk and Web's non-source-blind setting are noted as residual risks but not quantified (e.g., no experiment testing whether an agent that extracts the APK scores higher). - The per-application task count (50/platform) limits coverage of rare-but-important behaviors (multi-window, long persistence chains), and the benchmark's difficulty ceiling is set by the test suites' finite coverage — agents could score highly while missing large uncovered behavior, which the authors acknowledge but do not estimate. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating computer-use agents, this is a substantive and unusually self-critical benchmark/environment contribution that defines and measures hybrid GUI+code capability better than any prior work cited, and it is worth reading in full despite single-rollout scoring and an in-house visual judge that warrant independent replication.

The Tasteful Agent: Measuring and Improving Taste in Long-Horizon Tasks (111 ▲ )

Wenbo Pan, Zhichao Liu, Shujie Liu, Jingying Zeng, Chin-Yew Lin, Xianfeng Tang, Yan Lu, Qi He, Xiaohua Jia · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 23 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Taste-Bench, a 502-question benchmark that measures an LLM agent's "taste" — the ability to pick the better direction at a decision fork in a long-horizon engineering or research trajectory — with labels assigned automatically from the recorded outcomes of the trajectory branches, and shows that distilling this judgment into a 27B model improves end-to-end task success. - Why it's important: Existing agent benchmarks score only end-to-end task completion, so a run that wastes most of its budget on a plausible-looking but wrong direction looks identical to a well-run one; a cheap, scalable measure of mid-trajectory decision quality targets a capability gap that grows as agents take on longer autonomous work. - How it does it: The core move is hindsight mining: freeze real agent trajectories at points where parallel attempts (or a self-corrected detour) diverged, hide everything after the fork, and label the better direction using which branch actually passed tests or hit its experimental objective — no human annotation needed. - The good: The label quality is credibly validated — a 100-question human review shows 98.8% agreement with mined labels (Cohen's κ = 0.973 between reviewers), and every released question was confirmed unanimously by four held-out judge models reading the full record. - The missing: The end-to-end claim rests on only 41 SWE-bench Pro tasks with a single 27B executor, and the distillation is tested only on engineering-domain questions, so transfer of the training result to research tasks and to larger or different executors is unevaluated. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate agentic systems and care about step-level decision quality rather than pass/fail scores; skip it if you need research-domain taste results or large-scale end-to-end evidence — both are thin here.

Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (82) is the anchor — a NEW PROBLEM (mid-trajectory decision quality) plus a NEW BENCHMARK whose hindsight-parallel-trajectory labeling scheme converts trajectory archives into validated expert-quality supervision without annotators. Rigor (80) is unusually strong for a benchmark paper: 95% item-bootstrap CIs, exact McNemar testing, human validation at κ = 0.973, dual-order scoring to neutralize position bias, task-disjoint distillation folds, and a released dataset and codebase. Non-Obviousness (78) is backed by the well-powered negative result on reasoning budget and the horizon effect; Impact (78) follows from a usable, released artifact. Completeness (70) and Resilience (72) are held back by the thin 41-task, single-executor end-to-end evidence, the self-fulfilling detour labels, and the missing limitations section. Problem & Motivation Agent systems increasingly run multi-hour, multi-step engineering and research tasks (repository-scale software work, ML experimentation), where early decisions — which hypothesis to test, which implementation strategy to build on — determine whether the whole run succeeds. A wrong early decision often looks locally reasonable, and its cost surfaces only much later. Existing benchmarks (SWE-bench, SWE-bench Pro, RE-Bench, AgentBench, HCAST) report only whether the agent finishes the task; none measures the quality of the intermediate direction choices, and direct human evaluation of those choices requires domain expertise that does not scale. The paper targets teams developing and selecting agent models who currently cannot decompose end-to-end failure into "bad execution" versus "bad judgment." Key Idea Treat later trajectory content as free hindsight supervision: when two attempts at the same task share an equivalent prefix and diverge into different directions, the recorded outcomes of the two branches isolate the causal effect of the decision, so the better direction can be labeled mechanically (y = argmax_i U(E_i)). This converts trajectory archives — which agent systems already produce at scale — into labeled tests of long-horizon judgment, sidestepping both the expert-annotation cost and the confound that a single trajectory's outcome mixes decision quality with execution quality and environment luck. Methodology The pipeline has three stages: (1) Mining — a generator model (GPT-5.6 Sol at high reasoning effort) reads trajectories from two pools (2,677 GPT-5.4/5.5 rollouts on 517 SWE-bench Pro tasks collected by the authors; 1,132 METR MALT runs on 47 RE-Bench/HCAST research tasks) and extracts forks of two kinds: parallel forks (independent attempts diverge at comparable points) and detour forks (the agent commits to a direction, observes a hard failure such as a non-zero exit code, and recovers; the fork is placed just before the commitment). Mechanical checks require verbatim evidence excerpts in mandatory order. (2) Filtering — a four-judge panel (Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, Llama 4 Maverick, Mistral Large 3, disjoint from the generator) discards "trivial" questions (all judges answer correctly from candidate wording alone) and "undecidable" questions (any judge disagrees with the label given the full record); 4,657 candidates yield 502 released questions (10.8% survival). (3) Evaluation — each question presents task + prefix + two candidates; each is scored under two candidate orderings, and a question counts correct only if both orders are answered correctly, making chance 25%. The distillation phase trains Qwen3.6-27B (LoRA, rank 16, 79.7M trainable params) with an SDPO-style forward-KL token distillation on teacher reasoning: the teacher is the same base model given a privileged context containing the supported candidate, so its freely generated reasoning reliably reaches the correct choice; the student context omits the hint. Training uses task-disjoint folds, followed by a light calibration pass. The design decision to distill teacher reasoning rather than fit binary labels is well-justified (label fitting is shown to risk memorization, and task-disjoint folds verify it); the decision to compute KL on teacher-sampled rather than student-sampled continuations is argued but less standard; the detour construction's assumption that the agent's own abandonment marks the mistake is plausible but is the weaker of the two label sources. Key Results - Taste is scarce: the best of 14 frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol) scores 59.7% Average accuracy under the both-orders-correct protocol (chance = 25%), with GPT-5.5 at 59.5% and dispersion down to 15.7% (Grok 4.20 Reasoning, partly due to 459/1,004 unparsable responses). Datasets: the released 502 questions (390 engineering, 112 research). - Horizon effect: mean accuracy over 14 models falls from 62.3% (decisive evidence in prefix) to 21.0% (requires substantial later work) — below chance at the hardest level. - Reasoning budget does not help: GPT-5.6 Sol changes by −0.2 points and GPT-5.6 Luna by +2.2 points from lowest to highest effort (95% CIs spanning zero), across 6,024 responses; both models spend the most reasoning tokens on the level where they score lowest. - Partial decorrelation from end-to-end skill: Pearson r = +0.63 with SWE-bench Verified (R² = 0.39, n = 11 models, CI [+0.04, +0.89]); the engineering subset correlates at only r = +0.37, and the top four SWE-bench models, within 4.0 points of each other there, span 10.7 points on Taste-Bench. - Distillation transfers: on 390 held-out engineering questions, the student reaches 47.9% vs 30.0% for the base model (both-orders protocol), placing it between GPT-5.6 Terra (50.0%) and Claude Opus 5 (46.7%) in the frontier ranking. - End-to-end gains: on 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks (98 forks), a fixed Qwen3.6-27B SWE-agent executor improves from 14.6% to 33.7% success with student advice, against a 39.0% upper bound with always-correct advice (McNemar p ≤ 0.004 for the correct-advice comparison). Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM (measuring mid-trajectory decision quality rather than end-to-end success), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (Taste-Bench with outcome-labeled forks), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (horizon effect; reasoning budget invariance), and a training result. The genuinely novel elements are the hindsight-from-parallel-trajectories labeling scheme and the demonstration that mined forks constitute trainable supervision. The distillation recipe itself is a competent adaptation of existing techniques (context distillation, SDPO-style forward KL, LoRA, advisor-model steering) applied to the new supervision source; the detour construction overlaps conceptually with failure-attribution work (Who&When, AgenTracer) but differs in labeling the better direction rather than attributing failure. Rigor & Reproducibility Strong for a benchmark paper. Ablations are present at the benchmark level (construction × domain 2×2 design with per-cell yields; time-horizon stratification), and the distillation uses task-disjoint folds with leakage controls. Uncertainty is reported throughout: 95% item-bootstrap intervals (4,000 draws) on headline accuracies, bootstrap CIs on reasoning-budget differences, logistic interaction tests (p = 0.80/0.82), exact McNemar for the end-to-end gain, and human inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.973). Code and dataset are publicly released (github.com/wbopan/tastebench; huggingface.co/datasets/wenbopan/taste-bench), with prompts, hyperparameters, and per-cell counts in appendices. Concerns: (1) the benchmark questions are mined from SWE-bench Pro tasks and the end-to-end evaluation uses SWE-bench Pro tasks from which those forks were mined — task-disjoint within the distillation, but the advice pipeline's value is only demonstrated on tasks that already have mined forks; (2) the detour labels are self-fulfilling by construction (the agent's own abandonment defines the mistake), partially mitigated by the hindsight-nameability rejection rubric; (3) the time-horizon annotation uses a single judge model (GPT-5.5) without human validation of that specific annotation; (4) the reasoning-budget null result rests on only two models. The paper is a preprint and has not, per the text, undergone peer review. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark construction plus controlled training/deployment experiments actually run by the authors). - Practical: Yes — evaluation is API calls under a uniform prompt and 65,536-token budget; distillation trains on one A100 80GB in ~2 hours per fold with LoRA. - Efficient: Benchmarking a model costs ~1,004 presentations; the advisor adds a 27B forward pass per fork; no cost is reported for the trajectory mining pipeline itself, which consumed thousands of full agent rollouts (though many are reused public MALT transcripts). - Effective: The benchmark demonstrably measures something partly orthogonal to SWE-bench Verified (r = +0.63 overall but r = +0.37 on the engineering subset), and the distilled advisor recovers 19.1 of the 24.4-point upper-bound gain on held-out tasks — though on a narrow 41-task, single-executor slice. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the current 502 questions; the paper claims the benchmark scales with trajectory volume but mining yield (10.8% survival) and generator dependence on a frontier model (GPT-5.6 Sol) at scale are unverified. Deliverables: released dataset, evaluation code, and recorded results of all 14 models; the distilled student weights are not stated as released. Strengths - The parallel-trajectory labeling scheme is a real conceptual contribution: it converts the confound-prone question "was this judgment good?" into a controlled comparison where everything but the judgment is held fixed, yielding expert-quality labels without expert annotators (validated at 98.8% agreement, κ = 0.973). - The dual-order, both-must-be-correct scoring protocol cleanly neutralizes position bias — a failure mode most LLM-judge benchmarks ignore — and the resulting 25% chance floor is properly used as the reference in interpretation. - The negative result on reasoning budget is a genuinely useful, well-powered finding (6,024 responses, per-level analysis, models reasoning longest exactly where they fail), which rules out the obvious alternative explanation of the horizon effect. - The construction/filtering pipeline is unusually transparent: 4,657 → 1,809 → 729 → 502 with per-cell counts, worked examples of rejected questions, and full generator/judge prompts published. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper has no dedicated limitations section, but it acknowledges inline: the 95% CI on the SWE-bench Verified correlation is wide ([+0.04, +0.89] overall; [−0.30, +0.79] on the engineering subset) and reasoning-effort settings are not matched between the two evaluations; only 13 questions at the highest horizon level forced a merge; Grok 4.20 Reasoning's 45.7% unparsable rate complicates its 15.7% score; and three models were excluded from the correlation analysis for >9% unparsable responses. It confronts these directly rather than minimizing them. It does not explicitly flag the small size of the end-to-end evaluation or the self-labeling nature of detour forks. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The end-to-end result (41 tasks, 98 forks, one 27B executor, one scaffolding) is the weakest link relative to the paper's headline claim that "taste can be trained" to improve agents; no variance estimate per task, no second executor, and no frontier-model executor are reported. - The advice format embeds task-specific "decision trap" notes derived from prior runs on the exact same task — this is a distributional hint that a strong executor could partially exploit through the advice text itself (e.g., the embedded submission-verification contract), and no ablation separates the student's judgment from the structured advice format's generic scaffolding. - The detour construction's labels are determined by the acting agent's own abandonment, so the benchmark partially measures "avoid what this particular agent got wrong," and the generator writing both candidates is also the source of potential wording leakage; the trivial filter mitigates but cannot eliminate this. - Distillation is evaluated only on engineering questions; whether taste transfers to the research domain — the paper's more compelling motivation — is untested. - Fork availability is a hard dependency: the advisor framework requires that forks were previously mined on a task, so its applicability to genuinely novel tasks (no prior runs, no forks) is undefined. Bottom Line This is the strongest attempt I have seen to operationalize mid-trajectory decision quality for agents, with a genuinely reusable labeling mechanism and unusually careful measurement — practitioners building or selecting agent models should read it and use the benchmark, but treat the distillation and end-to-end results as an early proof of concept on 41 tasks rather than an established training recipe.

RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses (154 ▲ )

Peng Xia, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Yanfei Chen, Yufan Zhuang, Yoonho Lee, Chengsong Huang, Han Yu, Zhongying CuiZhu, Yifei Ming, Huaxiu Yao, Burak Gokturk, Tomas Pfister, Chen-Yu Lee · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 22 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RRSI, a framework that regularizes both the proposal and selection steps of automated agent-harness evolution so that measured self-improvement gains transfer to out-of-distribution benchmarks instead of overfitting the evolve set. - Why it's important: Automated harness evolution (recursive self-improvement at the agent-system level) currently shows large gains on the split it optimizes against that shrink or vanish on unseen tasks, wasting compute on benchmark-specific fitting; fixing this determines whether self-improving agents are practically useful. - How it does it: It constrains the evolution loop with an annealed edit-cardinality budget (L0-style), full-history credit assignment, structured exploration, an LLM leakage critic, a noise-adjusted acceptance floor, a gain-dependent token-cost rule (Ridge analogy), and structural pruning of unproductive components (Lasso analogy). - The good: Across eight benchmarks in three domains, RRSI is the only evolved harness whose OOD average clears the unevolved baseline meaningfully (43.6 vs. 39.7 OOD avg. on agentic workspace) while using 2.42M policy tokens/trial versus 3.80M for unregularized evolution, and it improves all six held-out splits including under a second policy family (Gemini 3.5 Flash: +14.1 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, +2.2 on SWE-bench Verified). - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; all headline comparisons rest on single runs whose differences (e.g., +1.8 on SWE-bench Verified) may be within the very evaluation noise the method itself tries to model. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building agent-scaffold optimization loops — it is the most credible treatment of evolve-set overfitting in this line of work — but skim the method if you only want the regularization recipe and skip if you work outside agent systems.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents are frozen backbone models wrapped in a "harness" of prompts, control flow, tool interfaces, memory, and context management; recent methods automate harness engineering by iteratively proposing and selecting edits using feedback from a finite evolve set — a practical form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). Because the same evolve set is reused adaptively across rounds, the search can overfit: it encodes benchmark-specific patterns, chases evaluation noise, and accumulates complexity, producing in-distribution gains that do not transfer (the paper cites prior work reporting exactly this failure). The problem is who pays for it: anyone deploying self-evolving agents gets harnesses tuned to one suite that regress on the next one. The gap closed is that prior harness-evolution methods (Meta-Harness, AHE, TTHE, HarnessX) optimize evolve-set score with no generalization term. Key Idea: Treat classical regularization (sparsity, shrinkage, pruning) as constraints on the search trajectory of harness evolution rather than on the harness representation: cap how many edits a candidate can bundle (annealed over rounds), refuse to permanently accept improvements that are small relative to an empirically calibrated noise band or that increase token cost without proportional score gain, and delete components with no recent measured contribution — leaving the edit space Ω(H) fully open. Methodology: The method instantiates the standard harness-evolution loop (execute current harness H_t on Devolve, summarize trajectories into feedback F_t, propose candidates, evaluate, select incumbent) with regularized proposal and selection operators. Proposal side: (1) an annealed edit budget b_t = b_min + (b_max − b_min)·½(1 + cos(πt/T)) bounds the number of independently attributable atomic edits per candidate (‖z_t‖₀ ≤ b_t); (2) evidence-aware credit assignment logs every evaluated edit with its component tag, hypothesis, diff, score/cost deltas, and acceptance outcome, and the proposer conditions on this history; (3) when progress over a stall window w stays within noise band δ, a reserved slot of proposals targets unexercised component types (from a 9-type vocabulary). Selection side: (1) an LLM critic screens candidate diffs pre-evaluation for benchmark-specific leakage; (2) candidates must clear a noise-adjusted floor Ŝ(H′) ≥ S★ − δ, where δ is calibrated from repeated runs of the unchanged base harness; (3) gain-dependent cost rule ΔC ≤ β₀ + β₁ΔS (Ridge analogy); (4) components with no positive measured gain over a pruning window are reported as deletion targets (Lasso analogy); a shaped within-band rule (w_sΔS − w_cΔC + w_nν > 0) handles candidates inside the noise band. All thresholds are tuned on the evolve set only and fixed for transfer evaluation. Critical design decisions: the critic runs before scoring (prevents leaking candidates from ever earning an inflated score — well justified); δ is calibrated empirically rather than assumed (good); the policy token count is used as the sole proxy for complexity footprint (convenient but arguably narrow). The L0/L1/L2 terminology is explicitly qualitative analogy, not penalized objectives — the paper is honest about this. Key Results: Evolution runs on three suites — Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 coding tasks), Harvey LAB (120 evolve / 40 in-distribution held-out legal tasks), EngDesign (61 design tasks with frozen simulators) — with transfer evaluated on SWE-bench Verified, JobBench, GDPval, APEX-Agents, and Frontier-Eng, all under a frozen Claude Opus 4.8 policy. Evolve-set gains: +6.0 (Terminal-Bench 74.2→80.2), +1.1 (Harvey LAB 89.4→90.5), +4.9 (EngDesign 50.0→54.9). OOD gains: +1.8 SWE-bench Verified (82.0→83.8), +4.7 JobBench (36.0→40.7), +3.5 GDPval (48.8→52.3), +3.7 APEX-Agents (34.2→37.9), +4.3 Medal points on Frontier-Eng (17.7→22.0, +24.3% relative). Against four same-budget baselines on agentic workspace: RRSI posts the smallest evolve-set gain (90.5 vs. 93.0 for Meta-Harness) but the only OOD average above H₀+1 (43.6 vs. 40.3 for unregularized evolution; Meta-Harness +0.9, HarnessX ≈ H₀, AHE and TTHE below H₀). Ablations show removing both regularizer groups yields the highest evolve score (92.8) but OOD 40.3 at 3.80M tokens/trial vs. RRSI's 2.42M (57% more tokens for 3.3 fewer OOD points). Cross-policy: the coding run with Gemini 3.5 Flash gains +14.1 evolve / +2.2 OOD, and the evolved harness transfers to the unseen Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite (11.2→14.6 on Terminal-Bench). Baselines are current (2026-era harness-evolution methods) and run under matched budgets, which is stronger than typical comparisons; scale is standard-benchmark, not stress-scale; the deterministically graded engineering suites rule out judge-gaming as the explanation for transfer. Surprising finding: the arm with the highest evolve score is the one that transfers least — the regularizers deliberately trade in-distribution score for transfer. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel move is framing harness-evolution overfitting as an adaptive-data-analysis problem (citing Dwork et al., 2015) and translating classical regularization principles into constraints on an LLM-driven search loop's proposal and acceptance dynamics; concurrent work (HarnessCompass, quality-diversity archives) targets the same generalization problem differently, so the problem is not exclusively theirs. The individual mechanisms (noise floors, cost-gain trade-offs, pruning, annealed budgets) are standard ideas re-instantiated for harness search, and the paper's own L0/L1/L2 analogies are qualitative rather than formal — the honest contribution is the system-level synthesis plus the transfer evidence, not any single new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed: proposal-side and acceptance-side regularizers are removed separately and together, each showing the predicted signature (higher evolve score, lower OOD, higher token cost), which supports the claim that both constraint groups matter. Policy-robustness is checked across two model families and cross-model harness transfer is tested with a smaller unseen backbone — unusually thorough for this area. However: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported for any headline number, despite the method's core premise being that evaluation noise is large enough to corrupt selection (δ is estimated per-domain, e.g., δ = 0.004 for agentic workspace, yet +1.8-point SWE-bench and 0.3-point ID differences are discussed without uncertainty). The project page (regularized-rsi.com) and GitHub (github.com/google-research/rrsi) are listed as releasing round-by-round trajectories and diffs; whether the full code is runnable is not confirmed in the text. Concerns: hyperparameters (δ, β₀, β₁, weights) are tuned on the evolve set — legitimate, but RRSI's small evolve-set margin over baselines could partly reflect tuning effort; the leakage critic is Claude Opus 4.8, the same model as the policy and proposer, so critic blind spots are correlated with proposer blind spots; baseline comparison depth (Table 1) is shown only for the agentic workspace domain. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method run at benchmark scale with ablations and cross-policy checks; a systems artifact exists but is evaluated empirically). - Practical: Yes — it runs on commercial frontier-model APIs (Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash) with no weight training; harnesses are editable programs. - Efficient: Evolution itself is expensive (20–40 rounds × candidate evaluations × k trials), but the output harness is cheaper than unregularized alternatives (2.42M vs. 3.80M policy tokens/trial, 26.3 vs. 27.3–34.6 steps), though still ~55% costlier than the unevolved H₀ (1.56M tokens). - Effective: The evidence supports transfer to unseen benchmarks (improves all six held-out splits, survives deterministic grading), so it addresses the stated problem beyond a proxy — but at modest absolute magnitude for coding (+1.8 SWE-bench). - Scalable: Not tested beyond single-suite-per-domain evolution and 20–40 rounds; the authors themselves flag longer-running self-improvement as unvalidated, and adaptive-overfitting risk should grow with more rounds, not shrink. Deliverable: a released code repository and project website with full evolution trajectories and harness diffs, plus the method as described in the paper; no trained model weights (by design, the backbone is frozen). Strengths: - The problem framing is the right one: it imports the adaptive-data-analysis view (reusing a finite evolve set adaptively = adaptive holdout reuse) into agent self-improvement, which prior harness-evolution papers ignore entirely. - The evaluation is designed to disambiguate the mechanism: the engineering-design suites use deterministic simulators, so the OOD gains cannot be judge-model gaming — a control most agent papers lack. - The ablation cleanly demonstrates the central trade-off: the unconstrained arm wins evolve-set score (92.8 vs. 90.5) and loses OOD (40.3 vs. 43.6) while spending 57% more tokens — direct evidence that the regularizers, not the search itself, produce transfer. - Cross-policy results (two model families, plus transfer to a smaller unseen backbone) show the evolved harness encodes reusable mechanisms rather than policy-specific artifacts. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) only frozen-backbone harness-level RSI is addressed, not weight-updating evolution; (2) RRSI still relies on a finite evolve set and several regularization hyperparameters, so effectiveness may depend on feedback quality and search budget; (3) broader validation is needed for different agent architectures, tool ecosystems, and longer-running self-improvement processes. These are stated directly and non-defensively in a Limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical uncertainty anywhere: single runs, no seeds, no significance tests, despite the method's own thesis that evaluation noise is large; several headline deltas (e.g., +1.8 SWE-bench, +0.3 ID held-out over Meta-Harness) plausibly sit within the noise band the paper itself calibrates. - The leakage critic, proposer, analyst, and policy are all Claude Opus 4.8 — self-critique by the same model family raises correlated-failure risk that is not discussed or ablated (e.g., a different critic model). - Baseline-vs-RRSI comparison is fully tabulated only for the agentic workspace domain; coding and engineering comparisons are only against H₀, so the claim "consistently outperforms baselines on all held-out datasets" is measured in one of three domains. - Hyperparameter asymmetry: RRSI's thresholds are carefully calibrated on the evolve set, while the fairness of comparing against baselines given equal candidate budget (but not equal tuning effort) is unexamined. - Cost confound: part of RRSI's transfer advantage may come simply from rejecting expensive edits (cheaper harnesses may generalize differently), which is not separated from the mechanism-quality explanation. - OOD benchmarks partially overlap the evolve domain type (SWE-bench vs. Terminal-Bench are both coding; JobBench/GDPval/APEX are all judge-graded workspace tasks), so "distribution shift" is moderate rather than extreme; the deterministically graded Frontier-Eng is the strongest test and contributes only one split. Bottom Line: For anyone building automated agent-scaffold or harness-optimization loops, this is currently the most rigorous and honest treatment of the evolve-set-overfitting failure mode and is worth reading in full; for readers outside agent systems it is an instructive but domain-specific application of classical regularization intuition with modest absolute gains and no uncertainty quantification, so skimming the framing and ablations suffices.

#6 — Highly Innovative (75)

Coding Agents for Generalized Task and Motion Planning Problems (6 ▲ )

Matteo Merler, Bowen Li, Josh Roy, Yichao Liang, Qianwei Wang, Yixuan Huang, Tom Silver · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents AgenticGenPlan, a large-scale empirical study (98,000 evaluation episodes across 28 simulated TAMP environments) showing that off-the-shelf coding agents can synthesize frozen, LLM-free programmatic policies that generalize across TAMP problem instances and outperform hand-engineered planners. - Why it's important: Generalized TAMP has historically required substantial hand-designed predicates, operators, samplers, and skills; if coding agents can do this automatically, it removes much of the domain-specific engineering bottleneck in robotic manipulation planning. - How it does it: Each agent receives only a task description and simulator access (reset/step) inside a sandboxed Docker container with a $20 synthesis budget; it probes the simulator, writes and tests a policy program, and the final program is frozen and evaluated on 100 unseen instances with no LLM at test time. - The good: All three agent backends beat the hand-engineered planners on the 16 environments where a planner exists (56–95% vs. 47% mean success), while spending an order of magnitude less per-instance compute (e.g., 0.5–2.1 s vs. 29 s), and qualitative log analysis shows genuinely new strategies (non-prehensile sweeps, tool regrasping, self-calibrated kinematic models) unlikely to be memorized solutions. - The missing: The evaluation relies on benchmarks (KinDER) authored by overlapping researchers, training-data contamination by the closed models cannot be excluded, and there is no comparison against learned generalized-TAMP methods (learned samplers, heuristics, abstractions) — only symbolic planners and one LLM baseline. - Read it or not: Worth reading for TAMP/robotics researchers and anyone evaluating coding agents on physical reasoning; skippable if you only care about the practical takeaway, which is already in the abstract: coding agents are now a strong generalized-TAMP baseline.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (80) is the top contributor — 98,000 episodes, hidden evaluation seeds verified unused, red-teamed sandbox isolation, per-run ranges, and released code, prompts, and logs put this well above the field's floor. Novelty (72) reflects a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING rather than a new algorithm: the surprising, controlled demonstration that frozen, LLM-free programs from off-the-shelf coding agents beat official hand-engineered TAMP planners at ~10× less test-time compute. Non-Obviousness (75) is supported by checkable emergent behaviors (self-calibrated kinematics, tool regrasping) and the distillation insight. Completeness (78) benefits from honest failure reporting and direct confrontation of contamination risk, though the missing learned-generalized-TAMP baselines and the author-overlap benchmark temper it; Resilience (75) and Impact (75, released reusable harness) round out a strong but not groundbreaking profile.
