Problem & Motivation: VLA policies (π0, OpenVLA, π0.5, Octo) condition each policy call on the current observation, robot state, and instruction, discarding information from earlier in the episode. This causes temporal state aliasing: identical current observations can demand different actions depending on past events invisible in the present frame (e.g., which pad a block originally occupied, or which battery orientations were already tried). Existing fixes each pay a cost—appending past observations grows context, memory, and latency unboundedly; compressed-history token methods (HAMLET, NativeMEM) still enlarge the context; recurrent-token methods (µVLA) carry information only implicitly; and memory-bank/retrieval/language-scratchpad methods (SAM2Act, MemoryVLA, MAP-VLA, Notes-to-Self) add auxiliary pipelines or objectives. The gap is a memory that updates online, stays fixed in size regardless of episode length, and is retrievable according to the policy's current state, trained end-to-end with only the native action loss. Key Idea: Treat episode history as a fast-weight associative memory: per action-expert layer, a rank-128 matrix is written with a gated delta rule (retention gate α, write gate β) whose value encodes the transition—the executed action chunk concatenated with the pooled post-execution visual observation—rather than an isolated frame; retrieval via a query from the layer's input state is injected as contextual content into a dedicated memory token before self-attention, complemented by a fixed, pooled 4×4-per-camera anchor of the first observation queried by the current state through rank-64 cross-attention. The delayed-write schedule (read → act → observe consequence → write) lets the memory store action-outcome associations causally, and sequence-level backpropagation through the memory operations trains everything with the standard flow-matching action objective—no auxiliary memory loss. Methodology: The pipeline per policy call: (1) read the associative matrices S(l)_{t-1} with queries derived from layer-input hidden states and inject gated readouts (scaled by α_mem/r = 2) into a non-persistent memory token; (2) condition action tokens on an anchor readout c_t obtained by robot-state queries attending to the current observation, which cross-attends to the fixed anchor A built by average-pooling the first observation's 16×16 patch grids to 4×4 per camera; (3) generate a 50-step action chunk via flow-matching (10 denoising steps); (4) after execution, construct the write value from the pooled next-observation encoding (robot-state-attended, gradient-stopped at patch tokens) concatenated with the action-chunk summary, and update each layer's matrix with the gated delta rule S_t = Diag(α)S_{t-1} + Diag(β)(v_t − Diag(α)S_{t-1}k_t)k_t^T. Training samples sequences of N observation-action pairs (length 8–18 depending on task) with gradient flow through the full sequence, LoRA adaptation of both PaliGemma backbone (rank 16) and action expert (rank 32), 10,000 steps, batch size 8. Critical design decisions, each ablated: (a) memory-token injection vs attention steering (37.6% vs 20.8% mean success) and vs an LSTM-like hierarchical variant (23.2%)—justified empirically; (b) the separate anchor pathway (+12.4 points over anchor-free, though it hurts Block Ranking by 10 points)—justified with the acknowledged caveat; (c) writing action+vision vs vision-only vs action-only values (46.7% vs 42.7% vs 34.7% three-task mean)—well justified. LIBERO experiments use a different recipe (full fine-tuning, batch 32, 30,000 steps) with a round-robin ten-slot memory to reconcile the 50-step write interval with 5-step replanning—a somewhat awkward but disclosed compromise. Key Results: On five RMBench tasks (three M(1), two M(n); 50 rollouts each), MemBodied scores 50.0% mean success vs 6.4% for π0-Stateless, 14.8% for π0-FrameStack (4 frames), 16.8% for a locally adapted vanilla recurrent memory, 38.4% for NativeMEM, and 12.4% for full-fine-tuned π0.5; on the π0.5 backbone MemBodied reaches 48.0% (3.87× the baseline), with Rearrange Blocks jumping 13.0% → 94.0%. On LIBERO (2,000 rollouts per checkpoint), MemBodied averages 95.1% vs π0's 94.2%, with the gain concentrated on LIBERO-Long (90.6% vs 85.2%, +5.4 points) while Spatial (−0.6) and Object (−1.0) dip slightly. Inference profiling on A100 GPUs over ~2,550 policy cycles: 129.2 ms vs NativeMEM's 1593.7 ms per cycle (91.9% lower) and 18.61 vs 20.57 GiB peak memory, with 40M added parameters (1.26% of π0) vs NativeMEM's 415M. Real-robot experiments on a bimanual AgileX PiPER platform (3 tasks, 20 rollouts each, 41–50 retained demonstrations per task) improve mean success from 3.33% to 26.67%. Notable non-dominance finding: NativeMEM beats MemBodied on Put Back Block (70% vs 40%) and Swap Blocks, and combining the two (45.2%) still trails standalone MemBodied. The paired-rollout analysis is unusually careful: stateless wrong-pad returns drop from 37/50 to 13/50 (p < 10^-4), premature swap completion from 41/50 to 19/50, with Holm-corrected McNemar/Fisher tests and Wilson CIs. Memory-rank ablations (32/64/128) show monotonic gains, and carrying memory across episodes reduces mean success from 50.0% to 36.8%—a useful negative result. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (primary) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the adaptation of fast-weight gated delta-rule associative memory (Schmidhuber 1992; Gated DeltaNet; δ-MEM for LLMs) to continuous robot control with transition-conditioned writes (action + observed consequence) and a delayed causal write schedule, plus the systematic comparison of three readout interfaces showing memory-token injection beats attention steering—directly relevant since δ-MEM used attention corrections. The anchor pathway and the training recipe are competent combinations of standard components (pooling, cross-attention, LoRA); the empirical finding that fixed-size associative memory dominates both in-context and compressed histories on memory benchmarks, without the Markovian regression one might fear, is itself a contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: three readout variants, anchor on/off, write-value composition (vision/action/both), memory rank sweep, anchor-vs-first-frame-in-prefix, and cross-episode memory carryover. Statistical treatment is stronger than typical for robotics: paired seed-matched rollouts, Holm-corrected p-values, Wilson CIs. However: (1) a single training seed (42) for all runs—no multi-seed variance on training, only evaluation-rollout uncertainty; (2) the π0-µ-VLA baseline at 0.0% on all tasks is a red flag that the shared training recipe disadvantages that baseline, which the authors acknowledge but cannot rule out; (3) NativeMEM was trained with a different staged procedure (50,000 tokenizer steps + 20,000 policy steps) than the LoRA-based locals, so the efficiency and quality comparison is not compute-matched; (4) LIBERO uses full fine-tuning while RMBench uses LoRA, so cross-benchmark recipes are inconsistent (disclosed); (5) latency profiling covers model-side computation only. Code is released (github.com/declare-lab/MemBodied) with a project website. No evidence of benchmark gaming; the benchmark (RMBench) is third-party (Chen et al., 2026), not the authors' own, and published baseline numbers are quoted from that source. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a real-robot systems component). Practical: Runs on a single 80 GB A100 in bfloat16 on top of open π0/π0.5 backbones with LoRA, plus a modest bimanual arm setup for the physical experiments. Efficient: 40M added parameters and 129.2 ms per policy call—dramatically cheaper than the NativeMEM alternative (415M, 1593.7 ms) and cheaper than any growing-context approach at long horizons. Effective: The evidence (simulation + real robot + localized failure-mode analysis) shows it solves the stated history-dependence problem, not just a proxy, though absolute real-robot success (26.67%) remains low. Scalable: Episode-length independence of memory size is structural, but M(n) tasks with long search (Block Ranking, 22%) still degrade—the paper has not tested episodes much longer than ~18 policy calls, and the 10-slot round-robin LIBERO workaround hints at friction when write cadence and replanning cadence diverge. Delivers a software artifact: code repository and trained-recipe configuration; no released model weights are stated. Strengths: (1) A well-chosen transfer of fast-weight associative memory into VLA control, with the transition-conditioned write value (action summary + observed consequence) being a genuinely apt design for manipulation, where what matters is what an action did, not what a frame showed. (2) The interface study (attention steering vs hierarchical vs memory-token injection) answers a question the δ-MEM LLM literature leaves open and could guide future memory designs. (3) The paired-rollout, statistically corrected behavioral analysis that localizes gains to aliased decisions rather than general motor competence is a model of evaluation practice rare in this field. (4) The negative results reported candidly—cross-episode carryover hurts (50.0% → 36.8%), the anchor hurts one task, NativeMEM wins two tasks—increase trust in the positive claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that no single method dominates at task level (NativeMEM wins Put Back Block and Swap Blocks), that combining compressed history with associative memory is unresolved future work, that the anchor is task-dependent (reducing Block Ranking from 32.0% to 22.0%), that π0-µ-VLA's 0.0% reflects their adaptation rather than µVLA generally, that π0-Hint is a privileged-information reference not an upper bound, that residual failures involve motor execution (stalling, dropped batteries, missed presses) and longer-term tracking, and that the AI-assisted manuscript was manually verified. They confront limitations directly—this is a credibility positive—though they do not flag the single-training-seed issue or baseline compute-matching concerns. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single training seed everywhere; with 50 rollouts per task, several reported gaps (e.g., 40.0% vs 38.4% task-level differences) are within plausible seed-to-seed and binomial noise, so the 1.30× claim over NativeMEM rests partly on the five-task mean. (2) FrameStack is limited to 4 frames spaced 50 steps apart—a fairly weak in-context baseline; a sliding-window of recent frames, which is what practitioners would actually deploy, is missing. (3) The latency comparison excludes any wall-clock cost of the delayed write outside the timed window and compares against only one memory baseline (NativeMEM) with a differently structured training pipeline. (4) All five RMBench tasks come from one benchmark family with one simulator's visual style; no cross-embodiment or cross-scene generalization test of the memory components. (5) The LIBERO ten-slot round-robin memory introduces a train/test cadence mismatch (training writes at 50-step intervals with summaries of actions beyond those executed) whose effect is not isolated. (6) The claim that associative memory is a 'practical alternative to expanding the policy context' is extrapolated from ≤18-call sequences; behavior at hundreds of calls—where delta-rule interference and anchor staleness could compound—is untested. Bottom Line: For anyone building memory-augmented or long-horizon VLA policies, this is currently the most convincing evidence that fixed-size delta-rule associative memory beats growing-context and compressed-history alternatives at a fraction of the latency cost, and it is worth reading despite single-seed training and narrow-benchmark caveats that invite but do not invalidate the conclusions.

no inference-latency/compute overhead is quantified, and no code, data, or model weights release URL is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agent scaffolds, process verifiers, or world models for LLM agents — the reframe from observation simulation to state editing is a genuinely useful design insight — but practitioners seeking a deployable artifact should note it is a preprint with no released weights.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents handling long-horizon tasks (deep search, terminal operation, repository construction) degrade because errors in their interpretation of partial observations — treating guesses as facts, keeping outdated plans, mistaking partial progress for completion — persist in the interaction history and steer later decisions. Existing "language world models" learn by predicting action-conditioned next observations (tool responses, search results, execution outputs), but these are high-entropy and execution-dependent, so reconstructing them is both hard and of limited value when the real tool can be called. The paper targets the gap: what should a world model for task-oriented agents predict, given that agents need grounded feedback, not simulated environments? The affected population is anyone deploying LLM agents on multi-step, tool-using tasks where a single bad decision propagates. Key Idea: Replace observation prediction with agent-state editing: predict the effect type of a proposed decision (CRITICAL = on a compact solution path, EXPLORATORY = usefully reduces uncertainty, NOISY = unproductive) from the pre-execution state, and when NOISY, generate a replacement reasoning–action pair from the same history — so the world model's output is an edited state fed into real execution, not a simulated observation. Formally, conventional world models map st → b̂ot while AEWM maps st → est = ht ⊕ (ẽrt, êat). The secondary insight is that these corrected trajectories, verified by real execution, can be distilled back into the agent (AEWM-RFT) so the editing capability transfers without the world model at inference. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Data synthesis: successful verified trajectories are decomposed into turns and labeled by an annotation agent (DeepSeek-V4-Pro/GLM-5 rollouts, three annotations per decision, majority/unanimous filtering, GPT-5.6-Sol review) with strictly prefix-grounded rationales; State Revision data is built by a proposal agent (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), an Action-Judge checkpoint flagging NOISY proposals, and a revision agent (DeepSeek-V4-Pro), retaining samples only where the executed replacement made verified progress. (2) Two-stage training of a single Qwen3.5-35B-A3B AEWM: mid-training on ~52.16B tokens (20.56B AJ, 25.01B SR, 6.59B raw trajectories) followed by SFT on 120K examples (60K AJ + 60K SR, 40K per domain), trained with verl/Megatron, lr 1e-5, up to 262K context. (3) Inference (EditAct): the agent proposes (r̂t, ât); Action Judge labels it; CRITICAL/EXPLORATORY proposals pass through unchanged, NOISY ones are replaced by State Revision; the selected action executes in the real environment and the history updates. AEWM-RFT then fine-tunes the agent on verified EditAct rollouts (4,000/7,095/1,456 trajectories per domain) versus Self-RFT on agent-only rollouts as a controlled comparison. Critical design decisions: the explicit EXPLORATORY class (preserves information gathering — justified via class-level F1 and label-distribution analysis); joint reasoning+action editing rather than either alone (justified by ablation: 48.3 vs. 30.7/39.3 on TB2 variants); and executing revisions in the real environment rather than trusting edits (justified as grounding, though it makes SR-sample retention dependent on downstream success). No explicit loss function beyond standard next-token SFT objectives is given. Key Results: On the authors' 3,000-decision Action Judge benchmark, AEWM reaches 70.5% macro-F1 overall (Search 60.9, Terminal 72.1, SWE 77.8) versus DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 59.9%, GPT-5.5 at 55.3, Qwen3.7-Max at 54.9, GLM-5.2 at 53.2, Gemini-3-Pro at 45.1; class-level, NOISY F1 is 81.1 while EXPLORATORY is 62.3. In agent experiments, EditAct beats ReAct, step-level Best@3, and trajectory-level Best@3 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro verifier) on all six benchmarks — BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, Terminal-Bench 2.0, Doc2Repo, NL2Repo, SWE-Bench Pro — with average gains of 6.7, 5.2, and 3.2 points over the strongest baseline for Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B (e.g., 4B: 41.8 avg vs. 35.1; 35B: Terminal-Bench 2.0 48.3 vs. 44.9). Qwen3.5-9B+EditAct (44.1) exceeds 35B+ReAct (42.2). AEWM-RFT beats Self-RFT by 2.2–2.6 points on BrowseComp (45.4 vs. 43.2), Terminal-Bench 2.0 (43.4 vs. 40.8), and Doc2Repo (48.6 vs. 46.1) with ReAct-only inference, and cuts turns by up to 30% on the first two. Ablations show learned judgment beats random gating at matched intervention rates (e.g., BC 48.1 vs. 44.1) and a separately trained model beats both Self-WM and DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the world model. Scale is standard-to-large (52B-token mid-training; benchmarks up to 1,266 tasks) but not stress-scale; gains shrink as agent scale grows and nearly vanish with Qwen3.5-Plus on Terminal/SWE. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD — the genuinely novel move is redefining what a language world model predicts for agents (decision effects plus state edits, rather than observations), instantiated through the Action Judge taxonomy and pre-execution state replacement, plus the AEWM-RFT distillation loop. The components are standard: three-way step classification resembles process reward models, revision resembles Self-Refine/Agent-R, and RFT is conventional — the novelty lies in the formulation, grounding labels in real executed outcomes, and the cross-domain unified training, not in any single algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for this area: nine inference variants (random gate, agent resampling, hint-only, action-only/reasoning-only revision, Self-WM, frontier-model WM) and training-stage ablations (SFT-only, mid-only, full), each isolating a specific claim. Three evaluation runs per benchmark with mean reporting are stated, but no error bars, seeds variance, or significance tests are reported. No code, data, or model weights release URL is stated (only the third-party AweAgent framework is referenced on GitHub). Methodological concerns: (a) the Action Judge benchmark is constructed by the authors from the same annotation pipeline as the training data, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro — the strongest baseline — is also the primary annotator, creating potential label-distribution bias favoring the trained AEWM; (b) four of six benchmarks are in-distribution relative to training domains and scaffolds partially authored by the same group (CalibForge, SearchSWE, DeNovoSWE), though DeepSearchQA and SWE-Bench Pro are held out; (c) SR training retention is conditioned on downstream task success, which may confound edit quality with task easiness. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained model plus an inference-time intervention loop, evaluated on benchmarks). - Practical: Requires a 35B-class MoE world model (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) in addition to the agent, plus environment containers (e.g., 32 cores/48 GiB per Terminal task) — feasible for well-resourced labs, not consumer hardware. - Efficient: Adds at least one extra LLM call per step (8K-token AJ generation) plus revision calls on NOISY steps; the paper reports turn reductions (16.7–30% on two benchmarks) but no wall-clock latency, token-cost, or FLOP overhead, so the cost side is unquantified. - Effective: Evidence covers task success on six benchmarks including two held-out ones, plus behavioral metrics (longer evidence-gathering breadth, fewer repetitive search sequences), supporting effectiveness on the stated problem rather than a pure proxy. - Scalable: Not tested — gains shrink monotonically with agent scale (6.7 → 3.2 points from 4B to 35B, and limited gains with Qwen3.5-Plus), and 10–100× longer horizons or larger backbones are unexamined; scalability is claimed only implicitly. Deliverable status: paper form only as far as the text states; no released artifact is mentioned. Strengths: (1) A clear conceptual contribution: identifying observation reconstruction as the wrong objective for language world models in tool-grounded settings and substituting decision-effect prediction with state intervention — a reframe that a reader can immediately reuse. (2) Disciplined data construction: prefix-grounded rationales with explicit future-leakage filtering, unanimous/majority annotation tiers, and semantic rubrics distinguishing plausible wording from grounded decision quality. (3) The ablation suite directly tests the paper's core claims — direct editing > resampling > hints, learned gating > random gating, trained WM > frontier WM — rather than only the full system. (4) The AEWM-RFT result is a well-controlled demonstration (identical filtering and hyperparameters, only rollout source differs) that editor-corrected trajectories transfer supervision the agent cannot generate alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that gains with a stronger agent (Qwen3.5-Plus) are limited on Terminal and SWE, attributing this to the capacity gap between AEWM and the stronger agent; they note Search is the most challenging judgment domain (60.9 macro-F1); the appendix candidly concedes that each annotation describes one observed continuation rather than an action's value across possible futures, and that retrospective labels are only outcome-based supervision for prospective prediction. They confront these directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Benchmark circularity: the Action Judge benchmark's gold labels come from DeepSeek-V4-Pro/GPT-5.6-Sol annotation, the same sources and rubrics generating AEWM's training data, so the 10.6-point margin over DeepSeek-V4-Pro conflates judgment quality with fit to a self-defined label distribution; no human-annotated or externally validated gold set is reported. (2) No inference-overhead accounting: EditAct's latency and token cost relative to ReAct and Best@3 (which also pays verifier calls) is unmeasured, so the efficiency trade-off is unknown. (3) NOISY-label risk: false-positive NOISY judgments trigger state replacement, and the paper does not measure how often AEWM wrongly discards productive actions (only aggregate outcomes). (4) The related-work competitor SRR-Judge and process-reward-model baselines are discussed but not empirically compared. (5) Only one AEWM backbone (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) is trained, so the interaction between world-model and agent scale is probed only from the agent side. (6) The latency-relevant effect of RFT on Doc2Repo (turns increase from 76.3 to 89.8 while score improves) is reported but not analyzed. Bottom Line: For researchers designing verifiers, scaffolds, or world models for LLM agents, this preprint offers a genuinely useful reframe backed by the most complete ablation suite I have seen in this sub-area — but the self-constructed judgment benchmark, unquantified inference overhead, and absence of released artifacts mean its headline numbers should be treated as promising rather than settled, and no existing work covers the state-editing formulation comparably well.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Geometry-Native Autoencoder (GAE), a learned codec that compresses the four-level feature hierarchy of a frozen geometry foundation model (DA3-GIANT) into a single 64–128-channel latent that is jointly decodable to RGB, depth, camera rays, and point maps, and then trains a standard conditional flow model in that latent for camera-controlled, reference-conditioned, and text-to-image generation. - Why it's important: Video generators produce photorealistic frames whose recovered 3D geometry and camera trajectories drift, which blocks their use as world models; GAE argues and shows the root cause is the appearance-centric latent, not the generator. - How it does it: A bottleneck is trained between the frozen DA3 encoder and its frozen DPT geometry head (so geometry must stay readable through the original interface), with two representation-shaping losses — token alignment to C-RADIO and pairwise-similarity matching to DINOv2 — that organize the latent for smooth flow transport. - The good: A matched-protocol comparison (same flow backbone, data, budget, sampler) shows GAE-64 reduces FVD by 12.7% on RealEstate10K and 23.1% on DL3DV versus the strongest competing latent, while halving VGGT-measured camera-trajectory error (ATE 0.0034 vs. 0.0072 for the best pixel-VAE baseline) on RealEstate10K. - The missing: The controlled evaluation uses only 64 held-out scenes per dataset at 252×252 with no seed variance or significance testing, and the compelling 81-view, 672×378 rollout results are qualitative and excluded from the comparison. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on latent-space design for visual generation or geometry-consistent world models — it is the clearest controlled evidence to date that the latent, not the denoiser, drives 3D consistency; skip it if you only need text-to-image or video quality results at production scale.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building camera-controlled video generators and world models need generated frames to describe one persistent 3D scene with a camera that follows the requested trajectory. Geometry foundation models (DUSt3R/VGGT/DA3 lineage) can read such geometry from real views, but generators trained on appearance-centric pixel VAEs or semantic representation autoencoders produce frames whose recovered geometry drifts and whose cameras deviate from the prescribed path. Prior remedies bolt geometry onto an appearance-native state via camera conditioning, feature alignment, or geometry-reward post-training. The paper targets the upstream representation question: no existing latent simultaneously preserves geometry, decodes appearance, and is well-conditioned for generative transport. Its diagnostic motivation is concrete — raw DA3 levels span ~11 effective dimensions out of 3,072 channels with condition numbers from 10^8 to 10^16, and no single level retains the semantic, spatial, and cross-view structure a generator needs. Key Idea: Reparameterize the geometry foundation model's feature hierarchy, not its outputs: learn a compact bottleneck between the frozen DA3 encoder and the frozen DA3 geometry head, so the latent must remain natively decodable to depth/rays/point maps through the untouched perception interface, while a separate learned head decodes RGB from the same state — then shape that latent's organization (token-wise C-RADIO alignment plus DINOv2 pairwise-similarity matching) so a single standard flow model can transport it, replacing the level-wise cascades that prior geometry-feature generators (GLD) require. Methodology: Two stages. Stage 1 (codec): the frozen DA3 encoder produces four per-view token levels; each level is per-channel normalized, reshaped, and channel-concatenated into a fused tensor X (fixed operator P). A convolutional encoder with spatial self-attention maps X to a variational latent z of C_z ∈ {64, 128} channels on the DA3 patch grid (18×18); a decoder reconstructs all four levels, which the frozen DPT head reads as depth, rays, and point maps, while a learned RGB head renders appearance from z. The codec loss is L_feat + λ_kl·L_kl + L_rgb + L_geo + L_repr, where geometry targets are pseudo-targets from the frozen DA3 head on original features. L_repr = 0.25·(L_tok + 8.0·L_struct): L_tok aligns posterior tokens to co-located C-RADIO features (cosine), L_struct matches pairwise cosine similarities to DINOv2 in the posterior space. The paper shows a failure-mode progression (Table 1): token alignment improves transport smoothness (ρ 0.820→0.700) and LNC@5 but collapses relational structure (LDS 0.240→0.020), which L_struct restores (LDS 0.444, SRSS 0.553). Stage 2 (generation): the codec is frozen; a DDT-style DiT (~0.93B parameters, 28 encoder blocks width 768, 6 decoder blocks width 2048) is trained with conditional flow matching on the standardized posterior means, linear path, clean-latent prediction with t_ε = 0.05, timestep-shared across views. Conditioning: clean reference latents (encoded using only observed references as context, assigned t=0, attending but never evolved by the ODE — avoiding a train/test mismatch from set-conditioned geometry encoders), metric Plücker-ray embeddings modulating QK self-attention (with a log-scale channel preserving metric translation), and frozen Qwen3-0.6B text features via cross-attention; condition dropout (0.10/0.05/0.05) enables one checkpoint for text-only, camera-controlled, and reference-conditioned modes. Critical design decisions: (1) freezing the DPT head so the codec cannot adapt around lost information — well justified by the ablation-backed argument; (2) keeping reference evidence as clean tokens outside the ODE state — ablated, point-cloud gap 0.1016 → 0.0318; (3) metric rather than per-scene-normalized pose — ablated, SE(3) ATE 0.0346 → 0.0093 and FVD 350.7 → 225.7. All three are empirically supported. Key Results: Controlled comparison on RealEstate10K and DL3DV (64 held-out scenes each, 9 views at 252×252, one reference, 50 Euler steps, CFG 2) with matched flow models for SD-VAE, WAN2.1 VAE, RAEv2, raw DA3 L0/L3, and GAE-64/128; GLD and Gen3R reported as external system references. GAE-64 achieves FVD 225.7 (RealEstate10K) and 287.0 (DL3DV) vs. 258.6/373.2 for the best pixel VAE — the stated 12.7%/23.1% reductions. VGGT-measured camera ATE: 0.0034 (GAE-64) vs. 0.0072 (best pixel baseline), a 52.8% reduction on RealEstate10K; MEt3R 0.1208 (best on RealEstate10K). Geometry generation (Table 7, against Pi3 on real frames and dataset poses): GAE-64 AbsRel 0.134 and ATE 0.010 on RealEstate10K, leading all six geometry metrics on DL3DV; both GAE variants beat raw DA3 L0 and the external GLD/Gen3R on most geometry metrics. Codec reconstruction: GAE-128 matches raw 3,072-channel L0 on RGB (PSNR 28.76 vs 28.64, rFID 5.4 vs 5.5) with 24× fewer channels. Ablations (Table 8) confirm L_repr, clean reference tokens, metric pose, and T2I co-training (FVD 472.9 → 225.7) each contribute. The 81-view 672×378 long-rollout and text-conditioned results are qualitative capability demonstrations from a separately trained model on a larger multi-domain mixture, explicitly excluded from the quantitative ranking. Baselines are current and the controlled protocol is unusually careful, though the evaluation pool is small. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the placement of a learned generative state between a frozen geometry foundation encoder and its frozen geometry head, yielding one compact latent that is natively geometry-decodable and appearance-decodable, replacing the level-wise feature cascades of GLD and the product-manifold flow of Weijler et al. The flow-matching backbone, REPA-style alignment losses, RAE-style representation autoencoding, and Plücker-ray conditioning are competent applications of existing techniques; the novelty lies in the latent reparameterization and in the controlled demonstration that the latent, not the generator, governs 3D consistency. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted (representation shaping, codec width/backbone, reference conditioning, pose scale, T2I co-training), each tied to a specific metric. The evaluation design is a strength: 3D consistency is measured with VGGT (independent of the DA3 backbone used to build GAE) and Pi3 on real frames, with DA3-GIANT included only as a labeled backbone-overlap cross-check, and geometry references come from Pi3/dataset poses rather than the generator's own outputs. Weaknesses: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; the quantitative evaluation uses only 64 scenes per dataset at 252×252; the final showcase model trains on "several internally curated datasets" that are not public. No code, weights, or project URL is stated in the provided text (a "Project Page" link appears in Figure 1 but no repository is given). This is an arXiv preprint (2609.24981), not peer-reviewed. No Goodhart violation is apparent given the independent evaluators, though the geometry codec is trained on DA3 pseudo-targets, so absolute geometry quality is bounded by DA3 itself. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained and evaluated systems with quantitative benchmarks). - Practical: Yes — a 0.93B-parameter flow transformer plus frozen DA3-GIANT and text encoder trains on 8 GPUs (controlled) and 80 GPUs (final model), all commodity accelerators. - Efficient: The compact 64–128-channel latent permits a single flow model without GLD-style cascades; inference is 50 Euler steps; frozen DA3-GIANT encoding at generation time is an additional cost not itemized. - Effective: The evidence shows genuine 3D-consistent generation at 9 views/252² against independent evaluators; generation of truly novel, geometrically valid content beyond RealEstate10K/DL3DV-style indoor scenes is shown only qualitatively. - Scalable: 10–100× scale is claimed, not measured — the 81-view 672×378 rollout is a single-scene qualitative showcase from a separately trained model, with no benchmark at that scale. The work delivers a method and (implicitly) a project page; no public library, weights, or dataset artifact is stated. Strengths: - The frozen-head bottleneck design is a genuinely sharp idea: keeping DA3's DPT head frozen forces the compressed latent to remain readable through the original perception interface, making "geometry-native" a testable constraint rather than a slogan. - The latent-space diagnostic study (Table 2: ρ, condition number, effective rank, LNC@5, LDS, SRSS, cross-view xLNC*) is itself a contribution — it exposes the ill-conditioning of raw geometry features (κ up to 6.6×10^16, effective rank ~11) and demonstrates the token-alignment-vs-relational-structure trade-off that motivates L_struct. - The controlled latent-swap protocol (identical flow backbone, data, budget, sampler across seven latent families) cleanly isolates the representation as the causal variable, which most geometry-aware generation papers do not do. - Evaluation hygiene: independent VGGT/Pi3 references, explicit flagging of the DA3 backbone-overlap cross-check, and exclusion of external pipelines from the controlled ranking. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly separate the controlled comparison (9 views, 252×252, RealEstate10K/DL3DV) from the final qualitative model (81 views, 672×378, larger mixture including internal data), stating the latter "are qualitative and are not part of the comparison" — a credibility positive. They acknowledge the text-to-image results are "a qualitative capability check rather than a standalone text-to-image benchmark." They acknowledge the backbone-overlap concern by labeling DA3-GIANT results as a cross-check. They do not, in the provided text, discuss compute cost of the frozen backbone at inference, failure modes on out-of-distribution scenes, dynamic scenes, or the pseudo-target circularity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical robustness: 64 scenes per dataset with no seed variance or confidence intervals — several margins (e.g., MEt3R 0.1208 vs 0.1213 between GAE variants) are within plausible noise. (2) The geometry codec trains on DA3 pseudo-targets, so no configuration can exceed DA3's geometry quality; the paper does not discuss this ceiling. (3) All quantitative evaluation is on static, camera-trajectory-driven indoor/outdoor scene datasets; dynamic scenes, object-centric generation, and genuinely novel content are untested quantitatively. (4) The final model's training mixture includes "several internally curated datasets," limiting reproducibility of the showcase results. (5) Baselines are strong within the latent-swap frame, but no comparison to geometry-reward post-training (VGGRPO) or feature-alignment-at-the-denoiser (REPA applied to a pixel VAE) alternatives that attack the same problem from the generator side. (6) The cost of encoding every conditioning reference through frozen DA3-GIANT at inference is never reported. Bottom Line: For anyone designing latents for visual generation or chasing 3D-consistent world models, this is one of the most rigorous and conceptually clarifying papers in its lane — the frozen-head bottleneck and the matched latent-swap protocol are worth adopting regardless of whether GAE itself remains the best instantiation — but the small evaluation pool, preprint status, and scale of the quantitative evidence mean the headline results deserve replication before being treated as settled.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SchrodingerRepo, an evaluation framework that renders semantically equivalent, seed-conditioned transformed views of SWE-bench repositories at evaluation time to measure whether coding-agent performance reflects reasoning or memorization of canonical repository cues. - Why it's important: SWE-bench Verified scores are the de facto standard for claiming frontier coding capability, but the benchmark's instances are drawn from public repositories likely present in training data, so high scores may conflate capability with familiarity — a validity problem for every leaderboard built on it. - How it does it: It applies four semantics-preserving transformations (problem-statement reconstruction, seeded invertible namespace remapping, AST-based intra-file reordering via randomized topological sort, and functionality-preserving LLM rewrites validated by pass-to-pass/fail-to-pass test gates) through a bidirectional translator that keeps execution grounded in the original repository. - The good: Full transformation drops Pass@1 by 6.0–14.4 points across four models (p < 0.05), while on temporally held-out SWE-rebench instances Pass@1 is unchanged (17.27%) — evidence the degradation comes from eroded familiarity, not harder tasks. - The missing: Levels 3 and 4 are applied only to golden-patch-related files for computational feasibility, and the held-out disambiguation experiment (RQ4) covers only one model on a 110-instance split with a 17.27% baseline, leaving the hardest confound — transformation-induced difficulty — only partially ruled out. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or interpreting coding-agent evaluations or leaderboards, since it quantifies a memorization tax on the field's central benchmark; model developers chasing SWE-bench points can skip it without losing methods.

Problem & Motivation: Repository-level coding benchmarks, above all SWE-bench Verified (500 manually curated instances from public GitHub repositories), are the primary yardstick for coding agents. Because these repositories, issues, and discussions appear in training corpora, each task is exposed through a single canonical repository presentation that models may have repeatedly seen. The paper's motivation experiment — human experts progressively reveal issue-semantic units to each LLM and check whether outputs contain unseen task-specific content — reports that over 65% of SWE-bench Verified instances show leakage evidence per model and over 18% are recalled at patch/test level. Existing remedies (SWE-bench Live, SWE-rebench, SWE-bench Pro) add post-release instances but sacrifice coverage and scale; the paper instead targets the representation itself. The open question: does strong benchmark performance reflect robust repository reasoning or memorized surface cues (naming conventions, file layouts, implementation patterns)? Key Idea: Treat the test repository as an evaluation-time latent variable: construct a seeded, invertible mapping between the canonical repository and an agent-facing view that is instantiated only when the agent enters the environment, so that executable behavior and test-defined correctness are preserved while every familiar repository-side cue is erased — and no fixed transformed artifact can itself be memorized, since fresh views are generated per run from random seeds. This is the genuinely non-obvious move; the individual transformations (paraphrasing, identifier renaming, definition reordering, behavior-preserving rewriting) are known techniques, but the invertible observation-layer translation that keeps execution on the pristine original repository is the trick that makes the framework sound. Methodology: SchrodingerRepo applies four transformation levels, usable jointly or in isolation. Level 1 uses a generator–verifier LLM pair to reconstruct the problem statement while preserving task-defining constraints. Level 2 extracts repository-internal identifiers from ASTs (filtering builtins, keywords, and third-party symbols), decomposes them into subword tokens, and maps them to plausible alternatives under naming-convention constraints (CamelCase, snake_case, shared-token coherence), instantiated as a bidirectional translator: observations are translated into the virtual namespace, agent actions are translated back before execution — the physical repository is never modified. Level 3 builds a definition-time dependency graph over reorderable definitions within contiguous runs and samples valid orderings via randomized topological sort. Level 4 uses a constrained rewriting agent to produce unified diffs that restate issue-relevant implementations in behaviorally equivalent form, retained only if Pass-to-Pass = 1 and Fail-to-Pass = 0 in the official SWE-bench environment. Human reviewers validated 100 sampled instances per level. Final submissions are recovered from repository states (diffs of changed files against the original), unifying evaluation across levels. Critical design decisions: (1) the invertible observation-layer translation for Level 2 — well justified, as it guarantees executability; (2) restricting Levels 3–4 to golden-patch-related files — justified only by preprocessing/runtime cost, and it weakens the claim that these levels fully erode implementation-pattern cues; (3) three seed-conditioned views per instance averaged into results — good practice for measuring representation robustness rather than a single perturbation. Evaluation uses mini-swe-agent (temperature 0, max 250 actions) with GPT 5.1, GPT-5.4-mini, DeepSeek-v4-Flash, and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-QA, and the March 2026 SWE-rebench split. Key Results: On SWE-bench Verified, the full setting reduces Pass@1 from 46.8% to 35.6% (GPT-5.4-mini, −11.2), 72.8% to 66.8% (DeepSeek-v4-Flash, −6.0), 44.6% to 36.2% (GPT 5.1, −8.4), and 56.7% to 42.3% (Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, −14.4, on the 300 instances with strongest leakage evidence). Level 2 (Namespace Mapping) is the dominant factor: −7.4/−6.4/−6.0 points with actions up 63.3%/32.6%/112.4% and input tokens up 162.3%/108.2%/218.3% (all p < 0.01); Level 1 is nearly inert (0 to −2.0 points); Levels 3–4 cost 0.8–3.4 points. Trajectory analysis shows 81.6–83.6% of additional actions go to navigate/search/read/probe (DeepSeek favors probing at 31.4%, GPT-5.4-mini static reading at 41.8%). On SWE-QA (144 instances across three repositories), scores drop up to 4.64 points (GPT-5.4-mini) but only 0.75 for DeepSeek, with actions up 18.15–43.02%. On the 110-instance temporally held-out SWE-rebench split (post-release issues), GPT-5.4-mini's Pass@1 is identical at 17.27% while actions rise 8.15% and input tokens 22.01%. A case study on a Django issue shows the same fix reached in 37 actions on the canonical view versus 217 on the transformed view. Baselines are the models' own untransformed performance on the current standard benchmark — appropriate for the research question. Testing is at standard benchmark scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the evaluation-time, seed-conditioned instantiation of repository representations (as opposed to static perturbations like SWE-Bench Illusion, PoorCodeSumEval, or RepoMirage, which the authors themselves note can be re-absorbed into training corpora) and the first systematic quantification of repository-representation sensitivity in coding-agent evaluation. The individual transformations are standard techniques; the contribution is their composition under an invertible execution-grounded translation layer plus the causal disambiguation via temporally held-out instances. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and central — each transformation level is evaluated in isolation, cleanly attributing the effect to namespace cues. Statistical significance is reported (p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 markers across tables), and three seed-conditioned views per instance are averaged, which partially addresses run-to-run variance, though no per-seed error bars are shown. The motivation experiment relies on human expert judgment with no reported inter-annotator agreement. Code and data are released at https://github.com/cslsolow/Schrodinger-Repo. Methodological concerns: (1) Levels 3–4 are confined to golden-patch regions, so their measured effects (small) underestimate what full-repository transformation would show — the authors' framing of Levels 3–4 as "removing additional cues" leans on this restricted application; (2) Level 4's rewrites are LLM-generated and could subtly alter local difficulty despite test gating (test gates cannot detect semantic-easiness changes); (3) the RQ4 disambiguation experiment uses one model, one scaffold, the full setting only, and a 110-instance split with a 17.27% baseline, so the "familiarity, not difficulty" conclusion rests on a narrow evidentiary base; (4) the human-judged leakage evidence (Fig. 1) is self-reported without validation of the judging protocol. This is a preprint (arXiv 2609.27891) and has not, as far as the text states, undergone peer review. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement framework and study, with a released tool). - Practical: Yes — it wraps existing SWE-bench execution environments and command-line agent scaffolds on standard infrastructure, with no special hardware. - Efficient: Transformation adds offline preprocessing and validation cost; for agents, the transformed views more than double input tokens in the worst configurations (e.g., 255.4% increase for GPT-5.4-mini), so evaluation under SchrodingerRepo is roughly 2–3.5× more expensive per run than canonical evaluation. - Effective: It demonstrates the problem it targets — quantified, statistically significant performance dependence on repository representation — though it does not (and does not claim to) produce a memorization-free benchmark score. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 500-instance SWE-bench Verified; repository-wide Levels 3–4 were explicitly deferred for cost, and scaling to larger corpora or richer tool interfaces (IDE, language-server) is future work. The work delivers a software artifact (framework, transformations, and data on GitHub) suitable for reuse in agent evaluation pipelines. Strengths: - The evaluation-time latent-variable design closes a real loophole in prior perturbation work: because views are seed-conditioned per run, the perturbed instances themselves cannot be memorized, which static benchmarks (SWE-Bench Illusion, RepoMirage, Saving SWE-Bench) cannot guarantee. - The invertible observation-layer translation for Level 2 is a clean architectural contribution — the agent lives entirely in the virtual namespace while execution stays grounded in the pristine repository, eliminating a whole class of validity confounds. - The RQ4 held-out design is the right experiment: identical Pass@1 (17.27%) with higher interaction cost on post-release instances is strong, direct evidence that the degradation mechanism is cue-removal rather than task-hardening — a counter-intuitive and consequential finding. - The behavioral decomposition (RQ2) moves beyond aggregate scores to a mechanism, showing the cost is concentrated in exploration/localization (81.6–83.6% of extra actions) and revealing a consistent exploration-strategy taxonomy across models. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two threats explicitly: external validity (evaluation is Python-only, open-source, SWE-bench-style, so generalization to other languages and ecosystems is open) and internal validity (the implementation targets command-line interaction only; agents using IDE APIs, language-server queries, or AST-level navigation may break the consistency of transformed views, and extending support is future work). They also acknowledge in the implementation section that Levels 3–4 were restricted to golden-patch files for cost. This is a reasonably direct confrontation of limitations, though the difficulty-confound caveat for the RQ4 experiment is not stated with matching force. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single scaffold: all results use mini-swe-agent; the paper's claim about "current coding agents" broadly is untested against other scaffolds (e.g., OpenHands, SWE-agent with richer interfaces) — precisely the agents the authors admit may need adaptation. - RQ4's evidence is thin: one proprietary model, full-setting only, 110 instances, and a very low 17.27% baseline where floor effects could mask a Pass@1 difference; no per-level or per-model held-out analysis. - The Level-2 effect is potentially confounded by context length: input tokens rise 108–218% under namespace mapping, and longer, noisier contexts alone degrade LLM performance independent of memorization; the paper does not run a length-matched control (e.g., padding canonical observations to equivalent length). - The motivation experiment's human-judged leakage taxonomy lacks inter-rater reliability, model-probing details, or a control probing a model on genuinely unseen repositories. - Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite is evaluated on a different instance subset (300 highest-leakage instances), making its −14.4 drop not directly comparable to the other models' full-500 numbers, yet it is quoted in the headline range. - No open-weight frontier models beyond DeepSeek-v4-Flash, and no analysis of whether memorization correlates with pretraining-data presence of specific repositories. Bottom Line: For anyone who builds, cites, or funds SWE-bench leaderboard results, this paper is required reading — it delivers the cleanest demonstration yet that a meaningful slice of reported coding-agent performance is representation memorization, and its evaluation-time transformation framework is a practical instrument the field should adopt; the gaps above narrow the precision of its estimates but do not overturn its central finding.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper reports a measured operating profile of a proprietary decision-only judge (TypeSafe JEV 1.13) against sixteen generative-LLM and reward-model judges, and shows that JEV's native confidence signal supports a frozen accept-or-escalate cascade that retains 99% of a frontier LLM judge's accuracy at 47-57% of its fee. - Why it's important: Judge inference cost becomes part of the cost of building and operating LLM systems, and overconfident LLM self-reports make cheap judging unreliable; a validated cheap-first-pass-plus-escalation recipe directly reduces evaluation bills for teams running large-scale or repeated judging. - How it does it: JEV returns a verdict and a full label-probability distribution (no rationale); the maximum label probability q is used as a selective-prediction gate that accepts confident verdicts and routes uncertain pairs to a stronger LLM, with two-order presentation and probability averaging for pairwise tasks. - The good: A pre-registered blinded human adjudication of 183 disputed items confirms the headline gaps are judge quality, not label noise (e.g., on JudgeBench the human sides with GPT-6 on 57 of 69 disagreements, human-adjudicated gap -16.0 points [−20.0, −12.3]), while also exposing HaluEval label noise that flattered both judges. - The missing: JEV is proprietary and unexplained, so the mechanism behind its calibration is unknowable and version-dependent; the cascade is never compared against a cheap generative first stage (e.g., GPT-4.1 mini at $0.39/1,000 with its own confidence) under the same gate. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building judge pipelines or LLM-cascade cost policies who wants a concrete, honestly-measured template including failure modes (style-adversarial pairs, reference-free prose, threshold-transfer failures); skippable for readers seeking a new method, since the contribution is an empirical audit, not an algorithm.

Problem & Motivation: Teams that use LLM-as-a-judge at scale face two coupled constraints: generative judges with long chains of thought are expensive and slow when evaluation is repeated across many responses and model revisions, and LLM confidence reports are unreliable, so it is unclear when a cheap verdict can be trusted. The paper addresses the gap between inexpensive judging and trustworthy judging: when is a decision-only, probability-exposing judge sufficient, when does a stronger judge earn its fee, and can the judge's own confidence decide between the two? The audience is practitioners operating evaluation and reward pipelines, not judge designers. Key Idea: Treat judging cost as a selective-prediction problem: a decision-only judge whose label probabilities are well-ordered against correctness can serve as the first stage of a frozen cascade — accept when q (max label probability) exceeds a workload-validated threshold, escalate otherwise — and the empirical question is whether JEV's confidence actually orders its errors and where that property breaks. The core insight, validated empirically, is that JEV's errors concentrate in its low-confidence region (pooled accuracy 47.7% at q<0.6 vs 99.1% at q=1, while GPT-6 moves only 78.5%→99.1% on the same items), so confidence captures roughly half the oracle escalation gain. There is no new algorithm here; the paper's contribution is the empirical demonstration and its boundary conditions. Methodology: The study evaluates seventeen judge configurations (JEV 1.13; GPT-4.1 mini through GPT-6 Astra; GPT-OSS 120B; Qwen3/3.5/3.6/3.8; Claude Sonnet 5; Gemini 3 Flash and 3.1 Pro; local PairRM and Skywork-Reward-V2-8B) under a shared output contract: generative baselines receive the same instructions and are asked for a verdict plus verbalized label probabilities without a rationale, with JSON schema constraints and temperature zero or low reasoning effort. Tasks span pairwise preference (RewardBench 400 pairs; RewardBench 2 four-way 100), evidence-grounded factuality (HaluEval 240), final-answer adjudication (150 existing replies), hard style-adversarial selection (RM-Bench 480 per condition), plus saturated positive controls (108 reference-correct GSM8K trajectory replies, 64 synthetic evidence judgments) and natural-prose samples (80 grounded summaries, 80 reference-free responses). The 642-item pilot was frozen before inference (40/60 selection/test split); temperatures and cascade thresholds were fit only on the selection set; the 670-item extension was frozen before pilot accuracy was inspected. Metrics: accuracy with invalid outputs counted as errors, macro-F1, Brier, clipped NLL, 10-bin ECE, error-detection AUROC, paired differences via 2,000 source-question cluster bootstrap resamples, and separate latency/fee measurement on a frozen 120-decision isolated panel with collection-time prices. The cascade gate (Eq. 1) averages aligned probabilities over both candidate orders; frozen two-order policies select the threshold on 96 pilot pairs to maximize coverage within two points of the fallback's accuracy. Three critical design decisions: (1) invalid outputs count as accuracy errors — well justified, it prevents availability from masquerading as quality; (2) blinded human adjudication of every disagreement item — well justified and pre-registered; (3) frozen-threshold policies evaluated on held-out extension data — well justified, and the paper honestly reports that thresholds did not always transfer (GPT-5.6 policy lost 2.35 points, beyond its 2-point tolerance). Key Results: On RewardBench JEV scores 92.2% vs GPT-6's 93.5% (−1.25 [−3.8, 1.5]); on HaluEval 87.5% vs 86.7% (+0.83 [−1.25, 2.92]); on the 150 existing labels 94.0% vs 96.7%. The gap opens on hard tasks: JudgeBench 78.6% vs 93.1% (−14.6 [−18.9, −10.3]; widest in reasoning 68.4% vs 95.9%), RM-Bench style-adversarial pairs 74.8% vs 94.6% (−19.8 [−27.7, −12.7]), while Skywork drops even harder on hard pairs (69.6%). On reference-free prose all judges are near chance (JEV 52.5%, GPT-5.4 55.0%) yet highly confident (mean max probability 0.90-0.96; JEV Brier 0.815, AUROC 0.518). Cost: JEV median latency 0.152 s and $0.044 per 1,000 judgments vs GPT-6's 1.885 s and $12.182 — about 9× and 277× cheaper (the abstract's 0.36% figure matches this workload). Calibration: JEV Brier 0.111/0.297/0.176 vs GPT-6's 0.104/0.095/0.245 — JEV is better calibrated on HaluEval while GPT-6 is better on JudgeBench, showing accuracy and uncertainty ranking dissociate. Cascade: the frozen GPT-6 two-order policy accepts 53.7% of 510 extension pairs at 92.5% vs 93.1% (−0.59 [−1.78, 0.59]) at 56.8% of the fee; single-order post-hoc simulations retain 99.6% of GPT-6 accuracy pooled at 47% of fee; random escalation at the same budget reaches only 88.1% vs the 94.4% oracle. On RM-Bench hard pairs the cascade breaks down (AUROC of q falls to 0.770; τ=0.9 retains only 96.5% of GPT-6's accuracy), and no threshold helps on reference-free prose. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with an element of NEW SYSTEM/TOOL evaluation (a hosted decision-only judge's operating profile); the cascade mechanism itself is a standard application of selective classification and LLM cascading (Geifman & El-Yaniv 2017; FrugalGPT; Jung et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2025) to a new setting. Genuinely novel: the first measured account of a typed decision-only judge with native probabilities against current generative judges at reported fees, plus the demonstration that JEV's confidence and GPT-6's strength are complementary (oracle union 95.7% on JudgeBench). Not novel: the accept-when-confident policy, temperature scaling, order-reversal diagnostics, and the benchmark suite. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is well above the norm for this genre: pre-frozen pilot/extension splits, pre-registered cascade policies and adjudication protocol, source-cluster bootstrap intervals on every headline difference, invalid outputs counted as errors with three failure mechanisms (provider/contract/transport) separated, saturation controls to catch elementary failures, blinded adjudication of all disagreement items, and explicit logging of collection windows and post-hoc analyses. Weaknesses: no code-matching compute baselines (the authors concede this is not compute-matched), a 120-item latency panel with poor tail resolution, fee estimates from collection-time prices rather than invoices, and all post-hoc single-order cascades scored on the items that defined their thresholds (the authors flag this themselves). A reproducibility package is supplied: anonymous supplementary ZIP with exact inputs, rubrics, decision-level outcomes, archived pricing pages with retrieval hashes, adjudication sheets, and executable code needing no GPU or API calls; no model weights or new dataset are released. JEV's implementation is proprietary, so the key mechanism behind the main result cannot be independently examined. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs measurements; it builds no tool). Practical: Yes — everything runs through hosted APIs or a single H100/V100, and reproducing public results needs no GPU. Efficient: The core selling point — $0.044 per 1,000 judgments at 0.152 s median versus $12.182 and 1.885 s for GPT-6 on the same workload, with cascade fee ratios measured under both reported-usage and conservative bounds. Effective: Evidence supports the stated role within the envelope (preference, evidence-grounded factuality, final-answer adjudication) but shows it fails outside it (style-adversarial pairs, reference-free prose), so effectiveness is workload-conditional and honestly mapped. Scalable: Untested beyond ~1,300 judgments per judge plus follow-up samples; cascade fees are offline simulations with no live sequential-latency measurement, and fee ratios at 10-100× scale depend on pricing and cache behavior the paper cannot control. The work delivers a reproducibility artifact and a reusable measurement template, not a software library or trained model. Strengths: - The blinded human adjudication converts a benchmark-label fight into a defensible finding: it confirms the JudgeBench gap is real (−16.0 human-adjudicated) while simultaneously exposing HaluEval label noise (24 of 26 both-judge "misses" have labels the evidence does not support), which the authors report even though it complicates their own tie claim. - The dissociation findings are genuinely useful: accuracy ranking and uncertainty ranking disagree across judges (GPT-6 better calibrated on JudgeBench, JEV on HaluEval; GPT-6 better at ranking HaluEval errors despite worse Brier), and directional bias, reversal instability, and style sensitivity are separated rather than conflated. - Failure-mode honesty as a contribution: the paper maps exactly where the cheap judge's confidence signal degrades (AUROC 0.918 on easy RM-Bench pairs vs 0.770 on hard pairs; 0.518 on reference-free prose) and shows frozen thresholds failing to transfer, which is more actionable than a uniformly positive result. - Measurement hygiene: separating provider failures, contract violations, and transport errors; counting invalid outputs as errors in primary accuracy; conservative fee reservations where usage is missing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length. They acknowledge: one proprietary JEV version with unknown training overlap and benchmark contamination; no compute-matched architectural comparison; decision-only prompts excluding explanations and extended deliberation; the expansion being exploratory after results were seen; small calibration sets and no isolated superiority claim; incomplete provenance of existing annotations and easy synthetic controls; the adjudication being one author-annotator with an LLM second pass (a recorded protocol deviation), not a random audit or consensus at scale; untested professional domains; latency from one client location and window with no invoices, energy measurements, or API-equivalent local prices; simulated cascade fees with no live latency; and post-hoc single-order cascade thresholds. This is unusually candid and adds credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The missing cascade baseline: a first stage of GPT-4.1 mini ($0.39/1,000, 0.548 s) using its own verbalized confidence, gated to GPT-6, is never run. Without it, the claim that JEV is the right cheap first stage is untested against the obvious alternative — the same architecture question the paper raises for reward models. - All headline quality and cost claims rest on a single proprietary, versioned service whose internals are unpublished; the calibration result could be an artifact of the provider's training or serving stack, and version drift would invalidate the thresholds the paper recommends validating locally. The paper notes version dependence but does not treat non-replicability of the judge itself as a limitation of the contribution. - The human adjudication's second pass was an LLM (Claude) that may share failure modes with the judges under study — acknowledged, but the resulting κ of 0.29 on RewardBench means the adjudicated preference differences there rest on thin ground. - Verbalized probabilities from generative baselines are known to be a weak elicitation channel; the paper acknowledges miscalibration is an empirical question but does not test a stronger baseline elicitation (e.g., sampling-based or logit-based confidence for open-weight models), so the probability-quality comparison may structurally favor JEV. - Follow-up benchmarks (RewardBench 2, RM-Bench) were designed after primary results with GPT-6 added in a later window; the authors label these exploratory, but the operating-envelope table presents them alongside pre-registered results without visual distinction. Bottom Line: Practitioners building or paying for judge pipelines should read this for its measured cost-quality-calibration envelope and its failure-mode checklist — it is the most honest empirical audit of a cheap judge I have seen in this area — while method researchers can skip it, since the cascade is known and the deepest limitation (a proprietary, unexamined judge) caps what the finding can teach.

Just-in-Time Memory: Learning to Curate Task-Adaptive Memory for LLM Agents (33 ▲ )

Yefan Zhou, Yang Li, Zeyu Leo Liu, Semih Yavuz, Shafiq Joty · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces JITMEM, a memory system for LLM agents that stores raw trajectories losslessly and defers curation to read time, where an LLM curator (optionally trained with GRPO) synthesizes a compact, task-conditioned payload for the current task. - Why it's important: Dominant agentic memory systems distill trajectories into fixed artifacts before the future query is known, irreversibly discarding information, and learned write-time curators suffer long-horizon credit assignment that forces artificial task grouping. - How it does it: Because the curated payload is consumed on the very task it was built for, the curator's reward is the immediate task success, collapsing credit assignment to a single step; GRPO trains a frozen-executor curator on this zero-delay signal over a fixed pre-built training bank. - The good: The untrained read-time curator already matches or beats RL-trained write-time baselines (e.g., 61.0 vs. 41.0 SR on WebShop with Gemini-2.5-Pro as both curator and executor vs. SkillOS), cleanly isolating read-time task adaptivity — not curator capacity — as the source of the gain. - The missing: No code, data, or trained-curator release is mentioned, and evaluation is limited to three benchmarks of modest size (140–500 test tasks) where the strongest baseline (SkillOS) is a concurrent/arXiv-only method whose settings the authors had to partially reverse-engineer. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building persistent agent memory or RL-trained context curation, since the write-time vs. read-time framing is a genuinely useful design axis; skippable if you only need a mature system, as the artifact is not released and results are preprint-grade.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying LLM agents over streaming task sequences want memory that improves future task success, but nearly all prior memory designs — Reflexion-style reflections, ReasoningBank strategies, skill libraries, learned memory operations — curate at write time: they commit to a query-independent distilled artifact the moment a task ends. This causes two costs: irreversible information loss (details discarded at write time cannot serve a later query that needs them) and one-size-fits-all summaries (the same trajectory is useful in different ways for different downstream tasks). Learning a write-time curator is additionally hard because a storage decision's value materializes only when a matching future query arrives, requiring delayed-return machinery or task grouping (as in SkillOS). The gap is a memory design where the timing of curation itself is treated as the central design choice. Key Idea: Move curation from write time to read time: keep the memory bank as a passive store of raw trajectories, and, once the current task is known, condition a curator on (task, retrieved raw trajectories) to synthesize a payload consumed on that same task. This makes the curator's learning signal the immediate task reward — the temporal gap between the curator's action and its reward is zero — eliminating delayed credit assignment, and makes memory outputs task-adaptive, since the same trajectory yields different payloads for different tasks. The paper explicitly links this to the cognitive-science view of memory as reconstructive rather than replayed. Methodology: JITMEM is a four-step pipeline over a streaming task stream: (1) Retrieve top-k (k=3) raw trajectories via BM25 over task descriptions; (2) Curate: the trainable curator πϕ takes the current task plus the k raw trajectories and emits a natural-language payload (relevant experiences, extracted strategies, task-specific guidance); (3) Execute: a frozen executor (Qwen3-8B, Gemini-2.5-Pro, or GPT-5.4) solves the task with the payload prepended to its prompt; (4) Update: the executor doubles as an LLM-as-judge quality gate, and only trajectories it deems successful are appended to the bank. Only the curator is trained, via GRPO (group size 8, batch 32, LR 1e-6, 100 steps, KL coeff 1e-3, no std. normalization, no value network) with the benchmark's native reward (binary SR on ALFWorld/τ²-bench, continuous score on WebShop). To stabilize training, a fixed training bank of base-executor successful trajectories (labeled by ground truth) is pre-built, accepting a mild train/test distribution shift the authors quantify with a staged bank-refresh experiment. Critical design decisions: (a) storing raw rather than distilled trajectories — well justified by an ablation showing write-time distillation drops SR up to 8.2 on WebShop; (b) quality-filtered (success-only) storage — justified by an ablation against label-annotated full storage; (c) BM25 over task descriptions only — a convenience choice kept for baseline consistency, acknowledged as a potential bottleneck, not ablated against dense retrievers. Key Results: Across ALFWorld (140 test tasks), WebShop (500 test instances), and τ²-bench, with three executors and 3–4 random task orderings per cell: RL-trained JITMEM with Qwen3-8B as both curator and executor reaches 77.4 vs. 61.2 SR (+16.2) over SkillOS on ALFWorld and 32.8 vs. 16.5 SR (+16.3) on WebShop; with GPT-5.4 as executor, JITMEM-gpt reaches 75.6 macro SR on τ²-bench (+3.9 over the best baseline). The untrained JITMEM-base (Qwen3-8B curator, GPT-5.4 executor) already hits 79.3 SR on ALFWorld, beating ReasoningBank and SkillOS-gpt that use GPT-5.4 as curator, isolating curation timing as the driver. The Qwen3-8B-trained curator transfers to GPT-5.4 within 1.4 SR of a directly trained curator. Efficiency: JITMEM uses 9.8K input tokens and 11.6 steps per ALFWorld task vs. 22.4K/16.9 for SkillOS-base and 9.0K/17.8 for no-memory. Baselines are recent (ReasoningBank, MemP, SkillOS — ICLR 2026 and concurrent arXiv work), and the authors conservatively reproduced the no-memory baseline at or below SkillOS's reported numbers. Notably, τ²-bench gains concentrate in Telecom (+11.0) with no improvement over no-memory on Airline/Retail beyond variance. Ablations confirm all three design choices contribute independently, and forcing empty retrieval (−14.8 SR on ALFWorld) shows the RL-trained curator distills retrieved experience rather than emitting parametric hints. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel move is the formulation: reframing memory curation as a read-time, task-conditioned synthesis problem with an immediate single-step reward, which converts a hard delayed-credit-assignment RL problem into a simple one. The components — raw trajectory storage, BM25 retrieval, GRPO on a Qwen3-8B curator, LLM-as-judge gating — are individually standard; MemHarness (concurrent work) also curates at read time with GRPO, though it entangles curator and executor in one model, which JITMEM's decoupled design avoids and empirically enables cross-executor transfer. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough and targeted: task-adaptivity removal, success-filtering removal, raw-trajectory removal, empty-retrieval, k∈{3,5} retrieval sensitivity, staged bank refresh, and test-bank warm-starting, each reported per-executor with mean±std over 3–4 orderings. The baseline reproduction study (Table 6) is a credibility positive — they calibrate settings so the reproduced no-memory baseline is at or below SkillOS's reported numbers, avoiding inflated gains. Two methodological concerns: (1) the fixed training bank is built from base-executor successes on the training split while evaluation is on the test split of the same benchmarks — not Goodhart's-law contamination per se, but the curator's training reward is the benchmark metric; (2) the JITMEM-base score on ALFWorld with Qwen3-8B (32.5) is below the no-memory baseline (33.3), an inconsistency in the reported table the authors do not discuss. No public release of code, data, or trained curators is stated anywhere in the text. Training cost is non-trivial: ~21–27 hours on 8×H200 per benchmark. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built system). Practical: Yes — the curator is a Qwen3-8B and executors are commercially available (Qwen3-8B, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5.4), served with vLLM on a single 8×H200 node. Efficient: Favorable on executor-side cost (50.3%–56.3% fewer input tokens and 28.4%–31.4% fewer steps than write-time baselines) but adds an extra LLM curator call per task and requires ~1 day of 8-GPU RL training per benchmark. Effective: Strong evidence on ALFWorld/WebShop (immediate task success is the true metric); τ²-bench gains are mixed, with no improvement over no-memory on two of three domains, so effectiveness is demonstrated on procedural-synthesis tasks but not fact-retrieval or policy-heavy dialogue uniformly. Scalable: Untested beyond 500-instance banks; the authors themselves flag that BM25 over task descriptions may become a bottleneck as the bank grows, and no experiment stresses bank size beyond these benchmarks. Delivers no released software artifact — the work stops at paper form despite giving full prompts and hyperparameters. Strengths: - The read-time curation framing is a real conceptual contribution: recasting memory curation timing as the key design axis and showing that read-time adaptivity alone (untrained curator) accounts for most of the gain over RL-trained write-time baselines is a genuinely surprising, well-isolated finding. - The cross-executor transfer result (trained-on-Qwen3-8B curator within 1.4 SR of trained-on-GPT-5.4) directly validates the modular curator/executor decoupling and gives it a practical payoff (one curator serving many executors). - The ablation that empties the retriever is exactly the right control: it shows RL-trained curators learn to distill retrieved experience rather than smuggling in parametric knowledge, ruling out a common confound in memory papers. - Conservative baseline handling — reproducing no-memory numbers at or below the prior work's reported values and stating where they could not fully reproduce — is rigorous and unusual. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion names three: the BM25 retriever may bottleneck as the bank grows large and diverse; the curator adds an extra LLM call per task; and the payload format is fixed and hand-designed per benchmark. The authors confront limitations directly and concisely (a credibility positive), and also transparently report the train/test bank distribution shift and the cold-start effect, testing both empirically. They do not, however, flag the τ²-bench Airline/Retail null results as a scope boundary on read-time curation itself, even though the results section admits it. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No dense or learned retriever baseline; the entire retrieval layer is a 2009-vintage BM25 over task descriptions, so the interaction between retrieval quality and read-time curation is unmeasured — curation may be partially compensating for retrieval, or could do much better with it. - The untrained JITMEM-base on ALFWorld/Qwen3-8B (32.5) underperforms no-memory (33.3), unremarked in the text; this suggests read-time curation can hurt weaker executors in some regimes, which a deployment decision needs to know. - All three benchmarks have short, intra-domain task streams where task similarity is high; nothing tests memory growth to thousands of trajectories, cross-domain transfer of stored traces, or bank maintenance/eviction — the stated streaming setting is largely unexercised. - SkillOS, the strongest baseline and the closest competitor, is concurrent arXiv work whose inference settings the authors partially had to guess (thinking vs. non-thinking mode), so the headline +16.2/+16.3 margins carry baseline-reproduction uncertainty. - The curator sees only k=3 raw trajectories in full, so its effective context is a tiny slice of the bank; how curation quality degrades with retrieval noise or long horizons of accumulated (possibly conflicting) successful traces is not evaluated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building persistent agent memory should read this for the write-time-vs-read-time framing and the ablation discipline, which together convincingly establish that curation timing matters more than curator model strength — but should treat the absolute numbers with caution given the un-released artifact, unpublished closest baseline, and narrow benchmark scale.
