onPanda: Efficient Annotation of On-Policy Alignment Data for LLMs and Agents via Token-Level Correction (27 ▲ )

Lei Yang, Mengyin Liu, Jia Wang, Hangyu Guo, Liang Zhao, Zheng Ge, Kang An, Binxing Jiao, Qi Han, Daxin Jiang, Siqi Shen, Xiangyu Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 22 Sep 2026
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces onPanda, an interactive annotation tool that produces LLM alignment data and agent trajectories through a locate-correct-continue loop at the token level, and releases the Panda-CVL dataset with a token-level-correction benchmark. - Why it's important: Alignment data annotation is a central cost bottleneck, and existing pipelines force a trade-off between annotation cost, on-policy fidelity (data staying close to the rollout model's distribution), and supervision granularity. - How it does it: The annotator finds the first bad token, replaces it from the model's top-k candidates or by free-form typing, and the system truncates and continues generation from the corrected prefix, so ~97-99% of final tokens remain model-generated. - The good: A Latin-square controlled study (3 annotators, 21 prompts) shows a 51.5% median time reduction over manual post-editing (330s vs 681s) while post-editing inflates response PPL by 36.3% relative to the rollout model and onPanda keeps it within 0.9%. - The missing: No training experiments: the claimed downstream benefit of the token-level correction supervision signal (for PRM, DPO-style, or token-level reward training) is entirely unverified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building annotation infrastructure or studying fine-grained alignment supervision, and skimmable for anyone only interested in validated training recipes, since the tool and data are real but the training payoff is future work.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Impact (82) leads: an open-source tool, Python library, released 7,491-session dataset, and a token-level correction benchmark, backed by production deployment across 130K+ sessions — a complete, reusable artifact chain, which is exactly what the Practical Impact dimension rewards. Completeness (75) is strong due to unusually candid limitations, though the central claim that token-level correction data improves post-training is never tested by any learning experiment. Novelty (68) is a solid interaction-paradigm composition (correct-and-continue from iMT transplanted to alignment and agent trajectories), while Rigor (62) is limited by a 21-prompt, 3-annotator controlled study without significance tests, in-house annotators, and the near-nil efficiency win over Argilla. Non-Obviousness (62) and Resilience (65) are moderate. Weighted composite: 0.15*68 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*62 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.30*82 = 71.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building aligned LLMs and agents face a three-way tension in data annotation. Writing responses from scratch or post-editing rollouts is expensive and produces off-policy data whose distribution diverges from the model being trained. Preference ranking is cheaper but gives only response-level supervision and fails when the model cannot sample a good response at all. Annotating agent trajectories is harder still, since corrections must actually execute tools in a live environment before generation continues. The paper targets annotation practitioners and alignment researchers who need SFT and preference data that is cheap, on-policy, and fine-grained. Key Idea: Treat the annotator's job as minimal token-level intervention rather than text editing: because the human touches only a few positions and the model regenerates everything after each correction, the data stays near the rollout model's distribution by construction, and every correction is automatically logged as a position-precise, naturally paired positive-negative supervision triple. This is the correct-and-continue pattern from interactive machine translation (Green et al. 2014; INMT 2019) transplanted into alignment annotation with model logprobs exposed to the annotator. Methodology: The system is a componentized front-end requiring only two inference-API capabilities: assistant-prefix continuation and top-k logprobs (plus prompt_logprobs for probability refresh). The pipeline: (1) streaming generation renders each token color-coded by probability; (2) the annotator clicks a candidate substitute or double-clicks for free-form editing at the first bad token; (3) the system truncates and requests native continuation from the corrected prefix; (4) sessions are serialized as annotation trees in .panda.json with full operation logs, from which the onpanda Python library exports SFT samples (is_good=Y nodes), response-level preference pairs (ancestor-descendant node pairs), and token-level correction triples (negative sample, rejected token, chosen token). For agents, a response-template mechanism bidirectionally converts structured messages (reasoning, content, tool_calls) to/from the native token stream so special tokens and tool-call arguments are correctable; tools connect via MCP, with harnesses like Claude Code wrapped as MCP servers, and rejected tool calls are kept as negatives. Design decisions: candidate-first correction (preserves on-policy fidelity, with free-form editing as a distribution-perturbing fallback), ancestor-based preference pairing (guarantees prefix-sharing pairs), and a tokenizer-agnostic span-match evaluation protocol — the first two are well-motivated, the third is a reasonable but lossy approximation. Key Results: In the controlled study (3 annotators × 21 image-description prompts, Latin-square, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B rollouts, vs POTATO post-editing and Argilla 4-way ranking): median time 330s for onPanda vs 681s (POTATO) and 336s (Argilla); GPT-5.5-judged pairwise win rate 66.7% (vs 54.8% POTATO, 28.6% Argilla); response PPL under the rollout model 1.181 (+0.86% vs re-sampling baseline 1.171) for onPanda vs 1.596 (+36.31%) for POTATO; SFT coverage 100% by design for editing paradigms vs 52% for ranking; 7.43 preference pairs per prompt vs 0.95 (POTATO) and 6.00 (Argilla). NASA-TLX workload: onPanda 3.1 vs Argilla 5.4 and POTATO 6.8. Production deployment reports 25,596 vision, 105,143 audio, and 1,257 agentic sessions yielding ~388K token-level corrections; 97.0% of final tokens are model-generated, 2.1% candidate-selected, 0.9% typed. On the released benchmark (2,126 instances from 652 test conversations), the best model reaches only 17.09% F1 (GPT-5.5; 53.37% GoodAcc, 10.18% Corr.-NG), showing token-level correction is far from solved for current frontier models. The study is standard-scale for a tool paper but small; there is no controlled agent-annotation study. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, with a genuine interaction-paradigm contribution: candidate-token-click correction with prefix continuation applied to general alignment data, multimodal inputs, and structured agent trajectories. The core correct-and-continue mechanism is borrowed from interactive MT, and the underlying components (logprob visualization, MCP tool access, prefix continuation) are standard; the novelty lies in their composition into an annotation workflow that jointly yields on-policy SFT, preference, and token-level correction supervision, which prior tools (POTATO, Argilla, Reptile) do not provide. Rigor & Reproducibility: The controlled study uses a sensible Latin-square design balancing prompt difficulty, annotator proficiency, and ordering effects, with non-developer annotators and warm-up tasks — better methodology than typical tool papers. Ablations are absent in the sense that the authors themselves note gains over POTATO may conflate interface, paradigm, and continuation effects; they cannot disentangle these by design. No error bars or significance tests are reported; sample size (21 prompts) is too small for the differences to be statistically solid. Quality is judged primarily by GPT-5.5 as LLM-judge with only a small human comparison (54.8% preference for onPanda over POTATO). Annotation agreement is analyzed on a 21-prompt multi-reference subset: human first-correction-position agreement is 30.95% exact (44.44% within 4 tokens) vs a ~0.2% chance baseline, and replacement-token agreement is 69.44% conditional on identical positions — supporting reference reliability but showing meaningful annotator variance. The paper is transparent that it does not compare head-to-head with Reptile, the closest system. Code, the Panda-CVL dataset (7,491 sessions), and the benchmark are released at on-panda.github.io/research with a GitHub repo; the multi-reference subset appears at github.com/on-panda/Panda-MultiRef-21. Benchmark evaluation is on the authors' own dataset, and the baselines (POTATO, Argilla) are current and appropriately configured. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated by controlled study and production deployment). Practical: Yes — runs as a static-hosted web app with no database, requiring only prefix-continuation and logprobs from any Chat Completions API, supported by vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, and ollama. Efficient: The tool itself is lightweight; the annotation workflow cuts median human time by ~52% vs post-editing in the study, though mean time (515.6s) shows the gain shrinks on hard prompts. Effective: Evidence covers annotation efficiency, data quality proxies (win rate, PPL, coverage), and workload — but not whether downstream training on the produced data actually improves models. Scalable: Production statistics across 130K+ sessions and 98 annotators demonstrate operational scale, but the controlled evidence is 21 prompts and the on-policy advantage is relative to annotation-time weights and decays as training proceeds (acknowledged). The work delivers a software artifact (open-source tool + Python library), a released dataset, and a benchmark, not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The observation that ancestor-paired corrections yield position-aligned, naturally balanced positive-negative token pairs at the same position is a genuinely useful framing for fine-grained supervision that emerges for free from the annotation process, unlike synthetic perturbation schemes (e.g., TLDR) or step-level human labels (PRM800K). (2) The evaluation honestly measures the right property — PPL under the rollout model — quantifying the off-policy cost of post-editing (+36.31%) that the field usually leaves anecdotal. (3) The response-template mechanism making special tokens correctable uniformly across reasoning, content, and tool-call arguments is a clean engineering solution to a real obstacle in structured-agent annotation. (4) The released benchmark shows token-level correction is hard for frontier models (best F1 17.09%), establishing headroom and a testbed for the proposed follow-up research direction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually candid: they state the dependence on two API capabilities that some proprietary providers do not expose; the sparse-error premise (advantages collapse when corrections are dense); the relativity of on-policy fidelity to annotation-time weights; the small controlled study (3 annotators × 21 prompts, one rollout model, in-house annotators); reliance on LLM-as-judge with position-bias mitigation only; absence of a controlled agent study; and, most importantly, that no training experiments verify the downstream benefit of token-level correction data. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged issues: (1) the efficiency win over Argilla (330s vs 336s median) is essentially nil — the headline 52% claim holds only against POTATO post-editing, so the efficiency advantage over the cheaper mainstream paradigm is unproven and the paper's framing slightly obscures this; (2) all controlled-study annotators and the NASA-TLX participants come from the authors' own annotation team, so familiarity with in-house workflows could bias against the external POTATO/Argilla setups; (3) win-rate evaluation by GPT-5.5, a vendor-judged metric on the vendor's own tool, plus only 21 prompts, leaves quality claims statistically fragile; (4) the token-level correction triple data is defined and motivated but never consumed by any learning algorithm in the paper, so its advertised granularity advantage is purely a structural argument; (5) the benchmark's tokenizer-agnostic span-matching protocol could systematically favor or penalize certain tokenizers in unexamined ways, and single-reference exact-match scoring sits on annotator agreement (31% exact location agreement) that bounds achievable Corr.-NG scores; (6) agentic evidence is limited to deployment counts — no comparison of trajectory data quality or annotation time against any alternative for the agent setting, where the tool's claims are arguably most valuable. Bottom Line: This is a well-executed, honestly evaluated systems contribution that will genuinely help teams building alignment-data pipelines and gives researchers a new benchmark and data format to attack, but its central scientific claim — that token-level correction supervision improves post-training — remains an untested hypothesis, so read it as infrastructure and a research agenda, not as a validated training method.

Your Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once: Evidence of Linear Superposition in LLMs (55 ▲ )

Pavel Tikhonov, Anton Korznikov, Matvey Mikhalchuk, Nikita Dragunov, Temurbek Rahmatullaev, Polina Druzhinina, Anton Razzhigaev, Ivan Oseledets, Elena Tutubalina · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that off-the-shelf LLMs, when fed a token-wise average of embeddings from two unrelated texts, produce next-token distributions that approximate the superposition of the two independent distributions, and that a lightweight self-distillation finetune plus a contrastive guided decoder can partially disentangle the two streams. - Why it's important: If two text streams can be processed in one forward pass, inference throughput could double and KV-cache footprint per stream could halve — a direct cost lever for high-volume LLM serving. - How it does it: The core move is element-wise averaging of input embeddings through an unmodified backbone, quantified with rank-survival and divergence metrics against the ½(P_A + P_B) target, then a KL self-distillation objective against a frozen teacher copy of the same model. - The good: The frequency-baseline control (cross-stream ground-truth tokens land in the top-10 only 2.63% of the time vs. 30–40% under actual mixing) and the Pythia checkpoint trajectory showing linearity is highest at initialization and degrades with training together make the core finding genuinely hard to explain away. - The missing: No code or model release is mentioned, and the headline 2× throughput is measured against sequential decoding — batched independent inference achieves the same throughput at far better quality, so the practical win over the obvious baseline is never demonstrated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for mechanistic-interpretability and inference-efficiency researchers interested in residual-stream linearity and multiplexing; practitioners seeking a drop-in 2× serving speedup should skip it, since the decoding quality gap (LAMBADA 0.43 superposed vs. 0.64 single-stream on Llama-3.2-3B) is not closed.

Completeness (78) is high — the paper confronts the distillation quality tax and decoding gap directly rather than minimizing them. Problem & Motivation: LLM inference is expensive, and the standard paradigm treats each request as a separate forward pass because attention and MLP non-linearities are assumed to destroy any signal from linearly combined inputs. Prior multiplexing work (DataMUX, RevMUX, MIMONets, Superposed Decoding) engineers superposition via added adapters, binding keys, or mux/demux layers. The gap this paper targets is whether superposition is already present in unmodified pretrained Transformers as an input–output property — and if so, whether it can be amplified enough to become a parallel-inference primitive. The motivating stakeholders are inference-serving systems where throughput and KV-cache memory dominate cost. Key Idea: The Superposition Linearity Hypothesis: for a decoder-only Transformer, M(½(E(x)+E(y))) ≈ ½(M(x)+M(y)) at the distribution level — the end-to-end input–output map, not just layer-to-layer transitions (as in Razzhigaev et al. 2024), is approximately linear with respect to embedding superposition. The second key observation is the geometric-mean obstruction: since averaging logits yields probabilities proportional to √(P_A·P_B), tokens probable in one stream but improbable in the other are suppressed, which is why decoding two coherent streams is strictly harder than fitting the mixed distribution. Methodology: Four phases. (1) Analysis: mix embeddings of random FineWeb/TinyStories pairs token-wise, run the frozen backbone, and measure (a) the rank of each stream's argmax token in the mixed distribution, and (b) KL/JS/Wasserstein divergence between the mixed output and the ½(P_A+P_B) target, normalized by the Superposition Approximation Ratio R_D = D(P_target‖P_mix)/D(P_A‖P_B). (2) Training-dynamics study: a hidden-state additivity error (Eq. 8, mean-centered, ℓ2-normalized) computed across Pythia checkpoints from 10² to 10⁵ steps. (3) Attention-patching: donor patching (substitute another text's post-softmax attention weights, preserving attention shape) vs. permutation patching (destroy structure, preserve row weight multisets), stratified by predictable vs. content token positions. (4) Restoration: self-distillation minimizing KL(P_target‖M_student(z)) for ~200k steps on FineWeb (114–132 hours on 2×A100 for 3B models), plus a Joint Contrastive decoder with a small guide model per stream (ℓ̃(A) = ℓ_large(z) + αℓ_small(A) − βℓ_small(B)). Critical design decisions: token-wise embedding averaging as the mixing operator (justified as the minimal linear composition, and validated against a frequency-only baseline); the normalized ratio R_D to make divergences comparable across models (reasonable but benchmark-relative rather than absolute); and per-layer mean-centering in the additivity metric (sensible, though it removes information about raw-scale interference). The paper is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. Key Results: On unmodified models (Pythia 160M–6.9B, Llama-3.1-8B/3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, Gemma, OLMo), the single-stream argmax token lands in the mixed distribution's top-10 in 30–40% of cases and top-100 in 60–65% (vs. 2.63%/10.41% for the frequency control), with R_KL = 0.34–0.42 (below the 1.0 random-relation baseline) at context lengths 32 and 512; N=3 mixing degrades ratios by only +0.04 to +0.10. Hidden-state additivity error is lowest at Pythia initialization and grows monotonically through training, supporting the claim that superposition is architectural, not learned. Self-distillation drops Pythia-2.8B mean KL from 1.86 to 0.27 and R_KL from 0.42 to 0.06, and raises top-5 rank survival from ~30% to >60% — critically, on hard content tokens median rank falls from 284 to 5 with top-1 agreement rising to 22.8%. The cost: single-stream LAMBADA accuracy drops (Pythia-2.8B 0.544→0.357; Qwen2.5-3B 0.602→0.460; tuned-distillation FineWeb PPL rises from 12.44 to 65.52 on Qwen). Joint Contrastive decoding lifts superposed LAMBADA from 0.065–0.182 to 0.110–0.430, still well below the single-stream baseline (0.50–0.64). Throughput: fused "Separate" decoding matches batch-2 independent inference within 3% (109.6 vs. 113.1 tok/s on Pythia-2.8B) and roughly 2× sequential decoding, with 95% CIs over n=100 runs. Tested scale is standard (≤8B parameters, contexts ≤512 tokens); baselines are current model families and the controls (frequency baseline, permutation patching, donor patching) are well chosen. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (input–output superposition exists in unmodified pretrained LLMs, is highest at initialization, and degrades during pretraining) plus NEW METHOD (self-distillation to restore it; Joint Contrastive guided decoding). The measurement apparatus adapts the known layer-wise linearity score of Razzhigaev et al. 2024, and the decoding methods are combinations of standard distillation and contrastive-decoding ideas; the genuinely novel element is the demonstration that no mux/demux machinery is needed for superposition to appear, and the honest characterization of the geometric-mean obstruction that separates distribution-fitting from decodability. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually strong for this kind of paper: the frequency-baseline control rules out Zipf-prior explanations; donor vs. permutation patching dissociates the frequency prior from attention structure; the predictable/content token stratification exposes that aggregate metrics are dominated by predictable positions (median rank 6 vs. 284 on content tokens in the base model); and the training-trajectory analysis spans six Pythia sizes. Some error bars exist (±s.e. bands on Fig. 2, 95% CIs on throughput), but the rank CDFs and distributional-divergence tables report no seed variance or significance tests, and the LLM-as-judge evaluations (GPT-5.2 grading TinyStories stories) have no inter-rater reliability. No code, data split, or model checkpoints are stated as released — a significant reproducibility gap given how implementation-sensitive the mixing protocol likely is. No Goodhart concern arises for the phenomenon itself (it is measured, not optimized on a benchmark), but the decoding evaluation relies on only 200 LAMBADA prompts and the authors' own FineWeb generations. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent decoding benchmark). Practical: Yes — all experiments run on 1–2 A100 80GB GPUs, well within commercial hardware. Efficient: The distillation is cheap relative to pretraining (<0.025% of pretraining data), but the fused approach adds memory over single-stream (7.15 vs. 6.34 GB on Pythia-2.8B) and guided decoding needs a resident auxiliary model (12.93 GB peak for Llama-3B+1B); more importantly, throughput parity with ordinary batch-2 inference means the efficiency advantage over the standard baseline is unproven. Effective: Only partially — distribution-level superposition fidelity is convincingly demonstrated, but coherent two-stream generation remains a proof of concept at 0.11–0.43 LAMBADA vs. 0.50–0.64 single-stream. Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B parameters and 512-token contexts; the 2× claim at 100× scale (production serving with continuous batching, where batching already saturates GPUs) is unexamined and arguably moot. Deliverable: currently paper-only; no library, CLI, or checkpoints are mentioned. Strengths: (1) The training-trajectory finding — that superposition fidelity peaks at initialization and decays under the LM objective — is a genuinely surprising, falsifiable claim about what pretraining does to residual-stream geometry, supported across six model sizes. (2) The attention-patching section is a model control study: donor vs. permutation patching cleanly dissociates frequency prior, attention shape, and content-specific signal, and the predictable/content stratification preempts the most obvious objection to the aggregate rank numbers. (3) The paper distinguishes claims from evidence unusually honestly: it explicitly reports the single-stream quality cost of distillation (LAMBADA 0.544→0.357; PPL 12.44→65.52), states the geometric-mean obstruction as the reason decoding remains open, and labels the decoder a proof of concept rather than a solution. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section states that evaluations use short contexts (L ≤ 128 for analysis, 512 for distributional metrics), predominantly monolingual corpora, and text-only models, with multimodal extension unexplored. The authors also confront the finetuning quality tax directly (Sec. 4 and Table 8) and the residual gap to single-stream decoding (Sec. 5). This is direct confrontation, not minimization — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The 2× throughput and halved KV-cache framing compares only against sequential decoding; against batch-2 independent inference — the actual standard — throughput is equal within 3% and quality is far worse, so the deployed value proposition is overstated in the abstract and conclusion. (2) The architectural-intrinsic claim rests on the Pythia checkpoint trajectory alone; no equivalent analysis for Llama/Qwen/Gemma training runs is provided, and "maximal at initialization" could partly reflect untrained-embedding idiosyncrasies. (3) No seed variance or significance testing for the rank CDFs and divergence metrics, and only 200 LAMBADA prompts for the decoding evaluation. (4) No code or checkpoint release is stated. (5) The N=3 result is presented as evidence of generality but receives no decoding or content-token analysis. (6) All mixing is pairwise token-position-aligned averaging of unrelated texts; robustness to length mismatch, different tokenizers' alignment, or adversarial stream pairs is untouched. Bottom Line: A rigorous and unusually honest empirical study that convincingly establishes an underappreciated phenomenon — intrinsic input–output superposition in vanilla Transformers, degrading with pretraining and restorable by cheap distillation — but the parallel-inference payoff remains speculative until someone shows it beating ordinary batched inference, so interpretability researchers should read it closely and serving engineers should wait for the follow-up that closes the geometric-mean decoding gap.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper proves that three regularity conditions (Completeness, Prefix Consistency, Neutrality) uniquely determine token-level credit as martingale differences of conditional reward predictions, then uses this characterization to derive PACT, an actor-critic training procedure that aligns the critic with the updated policy via importance-corrected targets and a BCE critic objective. - Why it's important: Token-level credit assignment in LLM RL lacks a mathematical definition, and actor-critic methods like PPO with GAE empirically underperform critic-free methods on long-horizon agentic tasks; a principled account could explain why and fix the training signal. - How it does it: The core move is a martingale argument — accumulated credit under the three axioms must be a martingale with terminal value R − E[R|F0], hence is uniquely the increment sequence of E[R|F_t] — which then shows OPD teachers are implicit critics, RLOO is gradient-unbiased, GAE with λ=1 cancels intermediate critic error, and motivates retraining the critic after the actor update using current-token importance ratios ρ·R as BCE targets. - The good: The ablation directly isolates the paper's central mechanism: importance-corrected critic training improves average math accuracy from 67.74% to 72.87% (+5.13 points across all four benchmarks), and fixed-policy critic pretraining shows BCE critics converge faster and separate positive/negative trajectories better than MSE critics at both 4B and 35B-A3B scales. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, the math results come from a single run configuration (Qwen3.5-4B, 3,200 DAPO-Math-17k problems), and the headline +8.80/+13.16 point margins on math shrink to +2.0/+2.4 points on SWE-bench Verified, where noise is unquantified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for RL-for-LLM researchers working on actor-critic methods, credit assignment, or on-policy distillation — the uniqueness theorem and its algorithmic consequences are genuinely useful — but practitioners just seeking a better recipe can likely get the essence from the method section and ablation table.

Problem & Motivation: In LLM post-training with reinforcement learning, the training signal is typically a single scalar outcome reward revealed after a trajectory completes, while updates are applied per token; how to attribute the outcome to individual tokens (credit assignment) has no generally accepted mathematical definition, and different algorithms (RLOO, GRPO, GAE/PPO, on-policy distillation) operationalize it through incompatible quantities. This matters to anyone training reasoning or coding agents on long, multi-turn trajectories, where a coarse or misaligned signal plausibly causes PPO-style training collapse. Prior work either treats the token-level MDP formulation as sufficient (it is not — Markovness does not say how reward information should be distributed across tokens) or derives credit forms under specific objectives; the paper closes the gap of a defn-independent characterization. Key Idea: Token-level credit, if it must (i) telescope to R − E[R|F0], (ii) be a function of the realized prefix, and (iii) have zero conditional expectation given the prefix, is uniquely C_i = E[R|F_i] − E[R|F_{i−1}] — the increments of the conditional reward prediction, a martingale difference sequence. The proof is a one-page martingale argument (Prefix Consistency ⇒ adaptedness, Neutrality ⇒ martingale property, Completeness ⇒ terminal value pins down the whole martingale). Everything else — OPD-as-implicit-critic, RLOO gradient equivalence, credit sparsity (E[Σ C_i²|F0] = Var(R|F0) ≤ 1/4 for R∈[0,1]), the GAE error analysis, and PACT — is derived from this representation. Methodology: Theoretical pipeline: (1) formalize reward information flow as a filtration F_i over prompt, tokens, and environment observations, with V_i = E[R|F_i]; (2) state three axioms and prove Theorem 1 (uniqueness, with a Rademacher counterexample construction in Appendix C.2.3 showing all three axioms are necessary); (3) derive corollaries — Theorem 2 (an ideal KL-regularized teacher yields OPD gradients equal to (1/β)E[Z_t C_t|F_{t−1}]), Theorem 3 (RLOO's response-level leave-one-out signal gives the same expected token-level policy gradient), Theorem 4 (credit sparsity via Var(R|F0) ≤ 1/4), and a GAE decomposition showing λ<1 retains critic error terms that can dominate the sparse credit signal, while λ=1 reduces the advantage to R − V̂_{t−1}. The algorithmic output, PACT, reorders the PPO loop to Actor-then-Critic: after actor updates, one extra forward pass over the same rollouts yields pre/post-update log-probabilities; a current-token importance ratio ρ_t (masks outside [0,6]) multiplies the reward target, and the critic trains on BCE(σ(z), ρ_t·R) instead of MSE. Key design decisions: (a) λ=1 GAE, justified by the error-cancellation analysis and consistent with DeepSeek-R1's empirical finding; (b) BCE critic, justified by an equivalence argument (BCE and MSE share the conditional-mean optimum on [0,1]) plus a controlled pretraining ablation; (c) current-token instead of full continuation importance ratio, justified by a hybrid-policy identity and an O(L·ε) bias bound (Proposition 2). Decisions (a) and (c) are approximations whose residual gaps are characterized but not empirically isolated. Key Results: Mathematical reasoning (Qwen3.5-4B, agentic OpenCode harness, 3,200-problem DAPO-Math-17k subset, Avg@16): PACT averages 72.87% across AIME 2025 (83.12), AIME 2026 (85.21), BeyondAIME (51.69), and HMMT Nov. 2025 (71.46), versus GRPO with Clip-Higher 64.07, PPO λ=1.0 59.71, SAO 51.14, base 41.01. PPO λ=0.95 collapses (26.31), which the authors present as consistent with their GAE error analysis. SWE-bench Verified (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Codex agent, pass@1): PACT 67.4 vs GRPO 65.4, PPO λ=1.0 65.0, SAO 63.6, base 60.8. Baselines are current and relevant (GRPO with Clip-Higher, SAO, PPO at the λ=1 setting the paper itself argues for), but each is a single configuration; the ablations show IS correction adds +5.13 points average (67.74→72.87) on all four math benchmarks, and BCE critics beat MSE critics on BCE loss, MSE loss, and value separation Δ± at both scales. No seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported for any comparison. Scale is standard-to-large (4B and 35B-A3B MoE models, 128k context, 512 trajectories per rollout), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW THEOREM (axiomatic unique characterization of token-level credit as conditional-reward-prediction increments, with necessity of each axiom) plus NEW METHOD (PACT's Actor-then-Critic order with importance-corrected BCE critic targets). The individual mathematical tools — martingale convergence, change of measure, BCE-as-conditional-mean (cited from Farebrother et al.'s classification-based value learning) — are standard; the novelty lies in the axiomatic framing and in using it to derive both interpretive results (OPD/RLOO equivalences, GAE error analysis) and a concrete algorithm, rather than in any single component of PACT itself. Rigor & Reproducibility: The proofs in Appendices C.1–C.7 are complete and self-contained, including a necessity construction for each axiom and explicit bias bounds for the one-step importance surrogate — this is above-average theoretical hygiene. Ablations exist and are well-targeted: BCE vs MSE critic pretraining under a fixed rollout policy (the cleanest possible comparison), and PACT w/o IS retaining all other components. However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; single runs underlie all headline numbers; the one-step IS surrogate (Proposition 2) is characterized theoretically but not ablated against the exact continuation ratio; and Appendix E.4 reveals PACT additionally uses token-level importance sampling on the actor side ([0,2] ratio range) that PPO/GRPO/SAO baselines do not, a confound not isolated by any ablation. Code is stated to be released at github.com/AllSpark-Research/PACT (URL given; release completeness not verifiable from the text). No Goodhart-style benchmark development concern for math (training on DAPO-Math-17k, evaluating on AIME/HMMT/BeyondAIME), and SWE-bench Verified is a held-out external benchmark, but the near-identical training/eval domain (agentic tool-use math) means the math gains partly measure harness fit. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a theoretical core). - Practical: Yes — PACT requires one additional forward pass per iteration over existing rollouts plus a critic head; it runs on standard RL training infrastructure (the authors' Dressage framework on slime), and the 35B-A3B result shows MoE-scale feasibility. - Efficient: Critic training costs one extra forward pass and critic gradient steps per iteration; no additional rollouts, so overhead is modest relative to generation-dominated RL, though a learned critic adds memory and the BCE/λ=1 choices add no cost. - Effective: Evidence supports effectiveness on the tested agentic math and coding tasks with consistent ablation support, but the +2.0 to +3.8 point SWE-bench margins without variance estimates leave real-world effectiveness on coding agents less certain than the math results suggest. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 35B-A3B / 512-trajectory rollouts; the O(L·ε) bias of the one-step IS surrogate grows with response length (already 64k-token generations), so the paper claims rather than demonstrates behavior at longer horizons or larger models. The work delivers a described algorithm and a stated code release; no trained model weights are mentioned. Strengths: - The uniqueness theorem is a genuine conceptual contribution: it converts a folklore notion into three checkable axioms, proves necessity of each via explicit counterexamples, and recovers turn-level credit by aggregation — this gives the field a shared target quantity. - The interpretive results have real explanatory power: the OPD-teacher-as-implicit-critic theorem and the RLOO gradient-equivalence theorem unify seemingly unrelated algorithms, and the credit-sparsity result provides the first clean account of why GAE with λ<1 fails in long-horizon LLM RL while λ=1 survives. - The theory-to-algorithm chain is unusually tight: every PACT design choice (λ=1, BCE, IS-corrected critic targets, Actor-then-Critic order) traces to a specific theorem or proposition rather than to tuning folklore. - The PACT w/o IS ablation (+5.13 points, uniform across benchmarks) directly validates the paper's central mechanism rather than a bundled system, and the λ=0.95 PPO collapse observed in their own runs matches the theory's prediction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Appendix F) three limitations directly and honestly: (1) uniqueness is conditional on the three proposed axioms — different axioms would yield different but internally consistent credit notions (the Euclid's-postulate analogy); (2) the credit notion is statistical, not causal — it does not characterize counterfactual effects of replacing a token; (3) the work characterizes what credit is but does not solve its exact estimation in practice. This is a credibility positive: the limitations section confronts the framework's scope rather than minimizing it. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting of any kind: with Avg@16 and pass@1 on 500 SWE-bench problems, the 2.0–3.8 point coding margins could plausibly fall within run-to-run noise; the paper cannot rule this out. - The actor-side token importance sampling ([0,2] range) used by PACT but not by baselines (per Appendix E.4) is a confound: part of the math gain may come from the actor correction, not the critic alignment, and no ablation separates them. - The one-step IS surrogate is validated only in aggregate (PACT vs PACT w/o IS), not against exact or first-order continuation corrections, despite Proposition 2 quantifying its O(L·ε) bias at 64k-token generations. - All results use Qwen-family models and a single training mixture; no second model family, and the math evaluation suite (AIME/HMMT/BeyondAIME) is homogeneous competition math, so generalization of the critic-alignment benefit to other reward structures (process rewards, preference rewards, multi-objective RLHF) is untested. - The 'ideal teacher' theorem assumes full support and a bounded reward with an exact KL-regularized argmax teacher; the gap between this idealization and real distilled teachers is not quantified empirically. - PPO and GRPO hyperparameters are reported but there is no tuned critic-pretraining baseline (e.g., VC-PPO-style value pretraining), which the related-work section itself identifies as the strongest critic-based competitor. Bottom Line: This is one of the more intellectually substantive RL-for-LLM papers of its cycle — the uniqueness theorem and its consequences are worth internalizing regardless of whether one adopts PACT — but the empirical case for PACT over strong baselines rests on single runs without variance estimates, so a practitioner should treat the method as a promising, theory-motivated recipe to verify on their own workloads rather than a settled improvement.

skip it if you want quantitative head-to-head comparisons — it contains none.

Problem & Motivation: AR video generation (discrete-token models like VideoPoet and Emu3, and continuous chunk-wise AR diffusion like Causal Forcing and MAGI-1) factorizes video generation into causal steps, but practical generators operate under a bounded local context Cn of W recent units because self-attention cost, KV-cache storage, and accelerator memory grow with the rollout. Information that leaves this window — an entity's identity, a scene's layout, a door opened three minutes ago — becomes unavailable exactly when it may still determine correct output. The paper documents the resulting failure modes: entity forgetting, appearance drift, spatial inconsistency, dynamics degradation, semantic drift, and causal/state inconsistency (e.g., an opened door reverting to closed). Prior surveys on video diffusion and world models treat memory only in passing (retrieval or long-context conditioning); no existing work systematizes memory as the central design problem of causal AR rollouts, and terminology across papers is fragmented, obscuring shared design principles. The intended audience is researchers building long-horizon generative video systems and interactive world models. Key Idea: The single core insight is an operational, carrier-agnostic definition of memory: any state Mn functions as memory if its removal or modification would change later outputs after the corresponding evidence is no longer locally accessible — the distinction between memory and long context depends on how history is managed (selected, compressed, indexed, revised), not on window size, module name, or carrier type. Everything else follows from this: heterogeneous mechanisms (FIFO latent queues, sink KV caches, Mamba states, 3D point maps, LoRA fast weights) become commensurable instantiations of a shared lifecycle, formalized as pθ(yn | Cn, Mn, c) with operators for query formation, reading, integration, writing, updating, and budget-constrained management. Methodology: This is a survey, so the "method" is a formal framing plus a literature synthesis. Section 2 derives the formal setting: AR factorization over generic visual units (tokens, latents, frames, chunks), separating the outer causal rollout from the inner generator (next-token prediction for discrete models; a denoising/flow ODE dy(τ)n/dτ = fθ(y(τ)n, τ, y<n, c) for continuous ones), the bounded-context approximation, and the memory-conditioned generalization with an explicit lifecycle of six operators (Qθ, Rβ, Iη, Wα, Uφ, Gγ with budget B). Sections 3–7 then organize roughly 90+ systems along five axes: Forms (visual memory in pixel/VAE space; implicit states via KV caches, recurrent/SSM states, encoded histories; explicit entity- and geometry-typed states; adaptive parametric memory via TTT/fast weights and LoRA modules), Functions (identity, spatial, dynamic, semantic, causal preservation, plus coupled functions), Operations (writing policies from exhaustive admission to transition-triggered and address-bound writing; reading; updating; management; integration), Learning (output-level, memory-state, and memory-dynamics objectives; memory-state distributions under teacher forcing, history augmentation, and self-rollout), and Evaluation (a hierarchy of memory evidence, memory-revealing setups, validity controls). Three critical design decisions: (1) the operational memory/context boundary — well-justified and consistently applied (e.g., static prompts excluded, camera trajectories included only when persisted); (2) treating rollout-reliability training methods (Self Forcing, Causal Forcing family) as cross-cutting supports rather than a sixth preservation function — a defensible but arguable call; (3) defining explicit state by declared meaning rather than update mechanism, which cleanly separates pose-indexed retrieval from opaque learned features. Key Results: Not evaluated — the paper reports no experiments, measurements, or quantitative comparisons, which is appropriate for a survey but must be stated plainly. Its "results" are structural: a working formalization (Equations 1–15), a carrier taxonomy with per-method annotations of storage growth (fixed/bounded/linear/scene-scaled), unit structure, access key, interpretability, editability, and model coupling (Tables 2–3); a function taxonomy mapping failure modes to preservation responsibilities (Tables 4–5); and an operation taxonomy with per-method write/read/update/manage/integrate codes, schedules, and rule-based vs. learned policy labels (Tables 6–7). The qualitative cross-cutting conclusion — that effective memory is not about capacity but about retained states remaining accurate, accessible, and causally influential — is supported by mechanism analysis throughout, not by measurement. The identified open problems are composable and resource-aware memory, trustworthy state updating, self-rollout learning, interactive/causal memory, and standardized evaluation protocols. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW TAXONOMY (survey contribution, not NEW METHOD). Genuinely novel is the operational memory definition and the five-perspective decomposition applied specifically to AR video generation — no prior survey treats memory as the central design problem of causal visual rollouts. What is a competent combination of existing ideas: the individual mechanisms surveyed (KV-cache management descends from StreamingLLM, recurrent state from RMT/Compressive Transformer, parametric memory from TTT/Titans, explicit states from SLAM-style world modeling); the survey's value is unification, not invention. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests apply — no experiments were run. The synthesis itself is rigorous in coverage and consistency: notation is unified across ~90 methods, scope boundaries are explicit (short-video generation without persistent cross-step memory excluded; world-action models covered selectively), and the paper repeatedly flags that similar failure modes can arise from non-memory causes, deferring attribution to its evaluation section. The repository (https://github.com/HaroldChen19/Awesome-AR-Video-Memory) is a literature index, not a software artifact. Methodological concerns: (1) the function and setting labels in Tables 4–5 are author-assigned judgments based on papers' claims, not verified capabilities — a survey-grade Goodhart risk if readers treat the labels as evidence; (2) the paper's own diagnosis — that no standardized memory-revealing evaluation exists — means the taxonomy cannot yet be validated empirically by anyone; (3) as a rapidly-dated preprint (September 2026 arXiv v1) in a fast-moving area, coverage may already lag. Deployability: Profile: none of the three cleanly fits — this is a survey/synthesis paper with no primary experiments (EMPIRICAL), no proofs (THEORETICAL), and no built tool (SYSTEMS). I evaluated it as a scholarly synthesis. Practical: Not applicable — no artifact to deploy; the deliverable is a conceptual framework and literature index. Efficient: Not applicable. Effective: The framework is effective as an organizing tool — the failure-mode-to-function mapping and lifecycle operators genuinely clarify design trade-offs (omission vs. contamination vs. misbinding at write time; capacity vs. accessibility at read time). Scalable: Not applicable, though the taxonomy's storage-growth column (fixed/bounded/linear/scene-scaled) is directly relevant to scaling decisions. The work stops at paper form plus a GitHub reading list. Strengths: - The operational memory definition is a real conceptual contribution: it dissolves the sterile "memory vs. long context" and "cache vs. memory" terminology disputes by tying memory to counterfactual influence (removal changes output after evidence leaves local access), making ~90 heterogeneous systems commensurable. - The six failure modes mapped onto five preservation functions (§2.5 + §4) gives the field its first shared diagnostic vocabulary — e.g., distinguishing dynamic preservation (autonomous state evolution under occlusion) from causal preservation (intervention-induced state that must not revert), a distinction most world-model papers conflate. - The recurring "selective invariance" principle (preserve what should be invariant, allow legitimate change) and the write-time risk triad (omission / contamination / misbinding) are actionable design heuristics, not just labels. - Honest scoping: the paper explicitly notes when taxonomy labels rest on claimed rather than demonstrated capability, and the evaluation section distinguishes memory-revealing evidence from generic video-quality metrics — a standard the survey itself necessarily cannot meet, but states openly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: (1) failure modes like entity forgetting can also stem from imperfect dynamics modeling or rendering, not only memory loss, with attribution deferred to §7; (2) the memory/context boundary is operational rather than architectural, so some classifications (e.g., recent-frame retention) are deliberately fuzzy; (3) coverage of world-action models is selective rather than comprehensive; (4) the field lacks comparable evaluation protocols, making cross-method claims provisional; (5) the field evolves rapidly and the survey invites corrections for overlooked work. This is a credibility positive — limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, particularly the evaluation-gap admission, which the paper elevates to a first-class open problem (§8.6). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The taxonomy's function labels (Tables 4–5) inherit the claims of the surveyed papers without experimental verification; a multi-label "✓" for, say, causal preservation in Khora or WorldCraft reflects the source paper's assertion, and the survey does not flag which labels are well-evidenced versus self-reported — precisely the vendor-style inflation the paper's own evaluation section warns about. - No quantitative synthesis is attempted anywhere: storage growth, latency overhead, or consistency metrics are never tabulated numerically across methods, so a reader cannot answer "which carrier family buys the most persistence per GB/FLOP" from this survey. - The carrier taxonomy has borderline cases that cut against its own operational definition (e.g., whether a noised VAE latent carried one chunk forward is "memory" or "active context" depends on judgment), and the paper resolves these by fiat rather than a testable criterion. - The survey advocates memory-revealing evaluation but does not propose even a minimal concrete protocol or benchmark, leaving the field's most urgent gap (its own §8.6) unaddressed by the paper best positioned to address it. - Single-blind risk: with 26 authors across 15+ institutions, several surveyed systems likely originate from the authors' own communities; no self-citation or conflict analysis is provided. Bottom Line: For anyone building long-horizon AR video generators or interactive world models, this survey is currently the definitive map of the memory design space and worth reading in full; for anyone seeking empirical guidance on which memory mechanism to adopt, it offers vocabulary and structure but no data, so it complements rather than replaces reading the primary papers.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agent performance depends on both the model and its harness (tools, middleware, skills, memory that mediate environment interaction). Automated harness optimization (e.g., meta-harness-style evolution) improves the scaffolding but not the model, so the gains evaporate if the harness is removed, and the best harness varies across domains, instances, and base models. A general-purpose agent must therefore either ship a shared harness that forfeits specialized gains or maintain and route among a growing collection of specialized harnesses, with recurring context, latency, and orchestration costs. The paper targets the gap of moving harness-discovered improvements into model parameters — a concern supported by cited controlled evidence that changing the evaluation harness affects coding-agent performance more than the training method. The beneficiaries are agent builders who want domain-optimized behavior under one fixed, minimal deployment harness. Key Idea: The core trick is "agent-as-harness": because the evolved harness h and the target harness h differ in action space and available information (trajectories from h cannot be directly imitated under h), a separate harnessing agent wraps the student at its response boundary, reads a privately adapted reference harness K (tools become action recipes, middleware becomes review-time triggers, skills/memory become review guidance), and re-expresses h's guidance as the minimal coherent correction to each student proposal — written as a complete, executable response in h's action space, grounded only in student-visible evidence. The accepted responses form an SFT dataset that internalizes h's induced behaviors into the weights, after which h*, K, and the harnessing agent are discarded. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Evolve & adapt: a skill-guided three-round evolution loop (failure analysis by a swarm of subagents, bank consolidation, re-evaluation on failed tasks) produces h per domain, built on the DeepAgents abstraction; a (possibly automated) adaptation step rewrites h into K relative to h, changing each component's audience and enforcement point. (2) Agent-as-harness trajectory collection: formally, the student samples y_t ~ π_S(·|c_t) under h; a harnessing policy π_H receives (c_t, y_t, K, r_<t) and emits a decision d_t ∈ {PASS, REPLACE} plus a complete replacement z_t when replacing; the accepted ỹ_t is executed through h and only it enters the student-visible trajectory, while rejected proposals and review context stay private. The harnessing agent cannot inspect the sandbox, hidden solutions, or verifier feedback, must make minimal coherent corrections, and has a per-trial REPLACE budget (1–5). (3) Train & deploy: SFT (Eq. 4) on accepted responses, with reviewer-perspective reasoning masked from the loss and privacy-violating trajectories filtered; deployment is (π_θ̂, h) alone. Critical design decisions: (a) restricting interventions to full-response replacement in the student's action space — well-justified by the action-space-mismatch failure of teacher-under-h* distillation (3% vs. 30%); (b) same underlying model playing student and harnessing agent in the inference-time comparison — well-justified, it rules out a stronger-teacher confound; (c) retaining all USPTO trials (not only successes) for the ablation — reasonable for controlled comparison but creates an inconsistency with the success-only filtering used for SpreadsheetBench/AppWorld that is noted but not ablated. Key Results: On three benchmarks — SpreadsheetBench Verified (100 held-out tasks), AppWorld (56 scenarios, 168 tasks), and USPTO Retrosynthesis (100 tasks), all run in the Harbor framework — with h as a mini-SWE-agent harness with a single Bash tool: (1) Inference-time, frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, DeepSeek-V4-Pro), same model as student and harnessing agent: agent-as-harness with adapted K averages 81.1% vs. 78.1% for code-as-harness (meta-harness) and 68.6% for mini-SWE-agent alone across six benchmark–model settings; empty-K review averages only 69.2%, so review alone explains little. The advantage of agent-as-harness over meta-harness correlates with model capability and turns negative on weaker models (−12.0% on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). (2) Distillation on Qwen3.5-9B: macro-average success rises from 23.3% (base under h) to 44.3% (distilled under h), exceeding the 41.7% of the base model with h still attached; per-benchmark: SpreadsheetBench 44.0%, AppWorld 58.9%, USPTO 30.0% — USPTO trails the 38.0% achieved with h attached, attributed to deep chemical priors and executable validation tooling that SFT does not fully absorb. General-purpose harnesses (DeepAgents 20.5%, Claude Code 15.9%) hurt the 9B base model. (3) Supervision-source ablation on USPTO: teacher rollouts → 12%, teacher under h → 3%, student under h → 12%, empty-K review → 11%, oracle-answer review (98.6% collection success) → 15%, HARNESS-ZERO (59.4% collection success) → 30% — collection success does not predict distillation value. (4) Behavioral internalization: 82.3% average recovery across 28 harness-exclusive patterns (18 SpreadsheetBench, 6 USPTO, 4 AppWorld), each with author-built deterministic trajectory detectors. Baselines are current and appropriate for the setting. Scale is modest: a 9B student, ~280–500 trajectories per domain, 100-task test sets, single-run pass@1. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD. The formulation of "agent harness distillation" — transferring an evolved harness's induced behaviors into weights so they survive under a fixed minimal harness — is a genuinely new framing, and the response-boundary review mechanism that bridges harness action-space mismatch is a new algorithmic move. The ingredients (SFT on corrected rollouts, harness/prompt evolution, privileged-guidance distillation, draft–verify style review) are each established; the contribution is their specific composition and the empirical demonstration that review-based, student-anchored correction is the load-bearing component. The distinction from prior co-evolution and harness-internalization work (EvoHarness-RL, OPHSD) — distilling a complete tool-using harness into a model that runs harness-free under a minimal target — is real but incremental relative to those adjacent systems. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a clear strength: the supervision-source comparison (Table 3) varies rollout generator, harness availability, and harnessing-agent context, and the four-condition Table 1 isolates harness availability from delivery mechanism. The weaker-model analysis (Appendix F, four capability tiers) honestly charts where the method breaks. However: all results are single-run pass@1 with one training seed (42); no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; 100-task test splits make the 2.6-point macro-average margin over h*-attached (44.3% vs. 41.7%) fragile. A GitHub repo is provided (https://github.com/metaevo-ai/harness-zero), with detailed prompts, evolution skills, component inventories, and filtering rules in the appendix — unusually good procedural transparency. Methodological concerns: the 28 behavior-recovery detectors are designed by the authors and matched semantically, so recovery rates partly measure detector coverage; the harness evolution and distillation occur on the same domains later evaluated (held-out task splits exist, but no cross-domain transfer is tested); SpreadsheetBench/AppWorld filter to successful trajectories while USPTO retains all, a policy inconsistency acknowledged but not ablated; and the privacy filtering relies on string-pattern masking of reviewer-voice reasoning, whose completeness is not verified. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs the full pipeline: evolution, collection, SFT, evaluation). - Practical: Yes — API-accessed frontier models, LoRA SFT (rank 32) on A100s via the Tinker recipe, and a one-tool mini-SWE-agent target harness; nothing requires exotic hardware. - Efficient: Collection is expensive — reviewing every proposal roughly doubles model calls and raises mean USPTO trial latency to 2.4× (237.2 s vs. 100.1 s) — but this cost is training-time only; deployment is a 9B model under a minimal harness. - Effective: Strong proxy evidence on three benchmarks including a behavioral-internalization analysis, but the deployed artifact is only validated on the same three domains used for harness evolution, and USPTO shows the method under-delivers when h* encodes deep domain knowledge. - Scalable: Not tested — only a 9B student, ~500 tasks per domain, and three domains; the authors only claim (not show) that a minimal harness will increasingly suffice as distillation improves, and the dependence on a capable harnessing model caps where the method applies today. The work delivers a software artifact (GitHub repo with evolution skill, adaptation examples, prompts, and training configuration) plus reusable LoRA checkpoints implied but not stated as released; no trained model weights are explicitly mentioned as public. Strengths: - The supervision-source ablation is the paper's best contribution: demonstrating that oracle-answer review (98.6% collection success) produces worse students (15%) than answer-free procedural review (30%) is a non-obvious, transferable insight about distillation data design. - The same-model student/harnessing-agent design in the inference-time comparison cleanly removes the stronger-teacher confound that plagues most distillation evaluations. - The behavioral-internalization analysis (28 mined harness-exclusive patterns with deterministic detectors, base model scoring 0% by construction) goes beyond benchmark scores to show what was learned, and per-pattern results honestly expose weak spots (e.g., 40% on AppWorld pagination). - The action-space-mismatch diagnosis — teacher trajectories collected under h* actively hurt distillation (3%) because the student attempts unavailable harness tools — is a concrete, well-evidenced failure mode that generalizes to any cross-scaffolding distillation effort. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the method requires a sufficiently capable harnessing model (review becomes net harmful on weak models, with the capability threshold charted in Appendix F); review of every proposal raises collection latency to 2.4× on USPTO; SFT fails to fully internalize deep domain knowledge (USPTO trails h*); some harness mechanisms (e.g., context management) are not expressible as student responses, so a harness is still needed at deployment, just a more minimal one. The future-work section candidly identifies the harnessing agent's counterfactual prediction problem, the coarse PASS/REPLACE control, and the discarded preference signal between rejected and accepted responses. These limitations are confronted directly and quantified — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical rigor: single seed, single run, 100-task test splits; the headline claim that the distilled model surpasses the h*-attached baseline (44.3% vs. 41.7%) rests on a margin well within plausible run-to-run variance and should be treated as unproven. - No cross-domain or cross-harness transfer test: each h* is evolved, adapted, and distilled on the same domain it is evaluated on; whether the distilled behaviors generalize to a related-but-different domain is untested, which matters for the "harness development as scalable training signal" vision. - The recovery-rate metric depends on author-designed semantic detectors; no human validation of detector precision is reported, and patterns requiring ≥10 support tasks skew the measurement toward frequent behaviors. - The filtering-policy asymmetry across benchmarks (success-only for two domains, all-trials for USPTO) is a confound in cross-domain comparison of distillation efficiency. - Missing comparison to preference-learning alternatives (DPO-style on the rejected/accepted pairs the method already generates) and to on-policy RL under h — both are deferred to future work, so the claim that response-level SFT is the right trainer for this signal is unexamined. - Only one student model (Qwen3.5-9B) and one harnessing model (GPT-5.6 Sol) are tested for distillation; the interaction between student capability and distillable harness content is unexplored below the frontier-harnessing regime. - Note: this is an arXiv preprint (2609.24974) citing numerous contemporaneous preprints; results are not peer-reviewed. Bottom Line: A practitioner building self-improving or scaffold-heavy agent systems should read this for the problem formulation and the striking ablation showing that on-policy, action-space-compatible review beats stronger demonstrations and even oracle answers for distillation — but should not yet trust the headline distillation numbers given single-run evaluation on small test sets, and no existing alternative squarely covers the same ground, making this the current reference point for harness distillation.

Zipbench: Low-Cost Framework for Compressing Comprehensive Benchmarks of Large Language Models

Z Huang, J Li, G Ling, Y Lin, S Zhong, H Wu · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ZipBench, a benchmark-compression method that builds compact LLM benchmark proxies using only six real anchor-LLM evaluations plus synthesized pseudo evaluation logs, and ships ZipBench Zoo, compact proxies for 100+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks with mean absolute score error of 0.002–0.02 and average Spearman rank correlation of ~0.98 against the full benchmarks. - Why it's important: Existing strong compression methods require item-level evaluation logs from tens to thousands of LLMs (up to 152M+ records), making them impractical for newly released benchmarks and locking the technique behind already-collected public resources; cheap compression lowers the evaluation bottleneck for compute-constrained labs. - How it does it: Six anchor LLMs spanning a wide accuracy range are evaluated once; virtual 'pseudo LLMs' are generated by majority-vote over k-subsets of anchors and accepted via rejection sampling into uniform accuracy buckets, then a 2-parameter item response theory (IRT) model learns per-sample fingerprints from the augmented response matrix, and K-means clustering picks one representative per cluster. - The good: The evaluation is unusually broad and honest for this literature — 100+ benchmarks with per-benchmark build costs in dollars, 100-seed stability runs (ZipBench beats random subsampling at p<0.001 on most benchmarks), an OOD extrapolation test where the proxy is built from a 75% accuracy window and evaluated outside it (mean MAE 0.0309 vs 0.0381 for tinyBenchmarks), and theory that correctly predicts the observed failure mode of clustered anchors. - The missing: Several per-benchmark fidelity numbers rest on very few held-out test LLMs (6–10 for SciCode, Arena-hard, OCRBench v2, SWE-bench Multilingual), so Spearman correlations of 0.99+ on those rows carry wide confidence intervals that are never quantified, and no comparison against existing BCMs at their full-log budgets is reported — only under the artificially constrained 6-record setting. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or maintain LLM evaluation suites or need cheap proxies for a new benchmark; skip it if you want a fundamentally new selection algorithm — the IRT-plus-clustering core is inherited from tinyBenchmarks, and the contribution is the log-free construction recipe and the released zoo.

Problem & Motivation: LLM developers and researchers run models on benchmark suites of thousands to tens of thousands of items, yet prior work (tinyBenchmarks, MiniLongBench) shows <20% of samples often preserve full-benchmark ranking fidelity. Existing benchmark compression methods (BCMs) close this gap but depend on large collections of per-item evaluation logs — tinyBenchmarks uses 30–395 LLMs and ~17.4M logs, metabench ≥5,000 LLMs and ≥152M logs, SparseEval ≥4,800 LLMs and ~137M logs. Where public logs exist these methods work; for a newly released benchmark, collecting such logs costs as much as the evaluation the compression was meant to avoid. The paper targets the construction-cost bottleneck: how to compress a benchmark reliably when almost no historical evaluation data exists. The intended beneficiaries are compute-constrained research groups and anyone wanting to compress benchmarks outside the handful with public logs, including multimodal and agentic suites that prior BCMs largely ignore. Key Idea: Replace massive real evaluation-log collections with a small, deliberately uniform synthetic anchor pool: treat each k-subset of the six real anchor LLMs as a 'virtual LLM' whose responses are majority votes over the subset, use rejection sampling to accept virtual LLMs only when their accuracy lands in an empty bucket of the [κmin, κmax] range, and feed the augmented response matrix into standard IRT fingerprint learning. The theoretical motivation is that a density-bounded (ideally uniform) spread of anchor accuracies both minimizes the leading constant in the Spearman rank-preservation guarantee and keeps the Fisher information matrix of sample fingerprints well-conditioned (Proposition 1 shows collapsed accuracies make it rank-one). Methodology: Three-stage pipeline. (1) Initial evaluation: pick N1=6 anchor LLMs with broadly separated accuracies, evaluate each on all m benchmark items, producing a binary response matrix Y (continuous metrics like F1 are discretized via a threshold chosen to match the mean of the normalized continuous scores). (2) Pseudo-log synthesis: enumerate k-subsets of anchors (k=1..6), compute majority-vote responses, and accept a virtual anchor if its accuracy fills an empty equal-width bucket of the accuracy range; this yields N2=6 synthetic logs at zero additional inference cost. (3) Representation and compression: fit a 2PL-style IRT model, P(y=1)=σ(aᵢ⊤bⱼ), by minimizing Bernoulli negative log-likelihood (latent dimension d=5, lr 0.1, 2000 epochs), then run K-means on sample fingerprints {bⱼ} and select one representative per cluster, weighting clusters by size when scoring. Theoretical support: Theorem 1 bounds per-LLM score error by δw = Aϵ/4 (fingerprint norm × max cluster radius, via a sigmoid-Lipschitz argument); Theorem 2 lower-bounds expected Spearman correlation as 1 − 96c²δw² − O(cδw/N) under a density bound c on anchor accuracies; Proposition 1 shows the Fisher information of fingerprints degenerates when anchor accuracies collapse. Critical design decisions: (a) uniformity of the anchor accuracy distribution — well-justified both by the theory and by ablation (uniform beats normal and clustered placements); (b) majority-vote synthesis — plausible but the synthesized logs are deterministic functions of the six real response vectors, so their information content is bounded, a point the paper does not analyze directly; (c) fixed hyperparameters (d=5, no per-benchmark tuning) — a deliberate reproducibility choice, ablated in Appendix B.2. Key Results: ZipBench Zoo ships small (~50% reduction on average, MAE 0.008, Spearman 0.99) and tiny (~77.5% reduction, MAE 0.015, Spearman 0.98) proxies for 100+ benchmarks, reducing evaluation cost to 20–40% of full-benchmark cost. Representative numbers: MMLU compressed from 14,042 to 767 samples (MAE 0.010, SP 1.00); MMLU-Pro from 12,032 to 388 (MAE 0.012, SP 0.99); SWE-bench Verified from 500 to 188 (MAE 0.016, SP 0.99); worst tiny-version rank fidelity is MuSR at SP 0.92. Build costs range from $0 (public logs available) to $670.7 (LongBench v2). Ablations: compression quality saturates beyond ~20–30 anchors, consistent with the 1/N term in Theorem 2; ZipBench beats random subsampling with p<0.001 (Welch's t-test) on most of 100-seed stability runs; uniform anchor placement beats clustered and Gaussian placements, matching Proposition 1; optimal synthesis budget is N2≈N1 (both set to 6). Under a constrained 6-real-record construction setting, ZipBench attains lower MAE with smaller variance than tinyBenchmarks, SUBLIME, EssenceBench, Anchor Points, and SparseEval variants. In OOD extrapolation (proxies built from a 75% accuracy window, tested outside it), ZipBench achieves mean MAE 0.0309 vs 0.0381 (tinyBenchmarks), 0.0336 (SUBLIME), and 0.2231 (SparseEval-Linear). Baselines are recent and venue-published (ICML'24 through ICML'26), though the head-to-head is only run in the low-record regime the authors choose. This is a preprint (arXiv:2609.12475), not peer-reviewed at submission. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the anchor-plus-synthetic-pseudo-log recipe with uniformity-driven rejection sampling for benchmark compression) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (ZipBench Zoo, 100+ compressed proxies spanning text, multimodal, and agentic tasks — a scope no prior BCM covers). The IRT fingerprint learning and K-means selection are standard, inherited from tinyBenchmarks and psychometrics; the genuinely novel pieces are the majority-vote virtual-LLM synthesis, the explicit connection between anchor uniformity and fingerprint identifiability via Fisher-information conditioning, and the demonstration that this works at 110-benchmark scale with six real models. Theorems 1–2 are competent but straightforward consequences of sigmoid Lipschitzness and a density-bounded rank-perturbation argument. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative — anchor count, anchor distribution (clustered/normal/uniform), synthesis budget N2, fingerprint dimension d, and initial anchor accuracy range are each isolated, and the theory predicts the ablation outcomes (clustered anchors fail as Proposition 1 predicts), which is a strong internal-consistency check. Stability is assessed with 100 random seeds and Welch's t-tests; a one-sided Spearman significance test is run per benchmark. Code is stated as released on GitHub, though no URL appears in the provided text, and anchor/test LLM identities are deferred to the released code. Methodological concerns: (1) held-out test sets are small for many benchmarks (6–10 LLMs for SciCode, OCRBench v2, SWE-bench Multilingual, Terminal-Bench 2.0 has 67 but Arena-hard has 9), making per-row Spearman values noisy — no confidence intervals are given; (2) the comparison against competing BCMs is conducted only under the 6-record constraint that favors ZipBench by construction; no full-budget head-to-head is shown; (3) evaluation fidelity is measured against full-benchmark scores on mainstream commercial models (GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemini), which is a sensible but self-curated population, and the paper acknowledges excluding heterogeneous leaderboard submissions; (4) the i.i.d. assumption in Theorem 2's proof is flagged by the authors themselves as an idealization, with an exchangeability fallback sketched. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL with a SYSTEMS artifact (the released Zoo of proxies and pipeline). - Practical: Yes — construction requires evaluating six anchor LLMs on the target benchmark plus lightweight IRT fitting and K-means on CPU-scale data; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: Strongly — build costs range from $0 (recycled public logs) to ~$671 (LongBench v2), and the tiny proxies cut inference cost to ~20–25% of full-benchmark cost, so three repeated runs on the tiny proxy are cheaper than one full run. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated goal (preserving aggregate scores and rankings on held-out mainstream LLMs, MAE ≤0.02, SP ≈0.98), but this is fidelity to a proxy target, not evidence that compact benchmarks detect subtle capability differences that full suites would catch — tail behaviors and per-item diagnostics are necessarily discarded. - Scalable: Tested at 110 benchmarks and up to 14K-item benchmarks; the pipeline itself does not obviously bottleneck at larger scales, but the paper has not demonstrated compression of very large agentic suites where anchor evaluation cost dominates (their own agent builds cost $34–$81 each, and the anchor cost scales with benchmark size). The deliverable is a software artifact: the ZipBench pipeline plus the ZipBench Zoo proxy collection. Strengths: - The scale and breadth of the artifact is the real contribution: 100+ compressed proxies across three modalities with per-benchmark dollar-denominated build costs, which no prior BCM (each covering 1–13 benchmarks) approaches. - The theory is not decorative: Proposition 1's prediction that clustered anchors destroy fingerprint identifiability is directly confirmed in the ablation (Fig. 1c, Fig. 9), giving the paper an unusually tight theory-to-practice loop. - The OOD extrapolation test (build from a 75% accuracy window, evaluate outside it) probes a real deployment failure mode — compressing with weak models, predicting strong ones — that almost no prior BCM evaluates. - Honest cost accounting, including nonzero dollar figures for expensive builds and an explicit acknowledgment that six anchors must still run the full benchmark, resists the overclaiming common in this subfield. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) compression inevitably introduces approximation error, though they argue it is well controlled; (2) construction is not free — six anchors must be fully evaluated, which is non-negligible for expensive agent benchmarks (corroborated by their own $670.7 LongBench v2 build cost); (3) completely removing performance records is unlikely to yield reliable compression, bounding how cheap the method can get. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, including quantifying when tiny-proxy repetitions beat a single full run. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical fragility of per-benchmark rank correlations: with 6–10 held-out LLMs on roughly a dozen benchmarks, a Spearman of 0.99 is compatible with meaningful rank instability; no confidence intervals or bootstrap over the test set are reported, and the pooled 0.98 average hides this heterogeneity. - The pseudo-logs add no information beyond the six real response vectors — every virtual anchor's response is a deterministic majority vote over subsets — yet the framing suggests 'broadened coverage.' An ablation of synthesis against simply weighting the six real anchors (or against logistic-regression-based augmentation on the same six responses) is absent, so the specific value of the synthesis step versus any other way of regularizing a 6-row response matrix is not isolated. - The comparison with prior BCMs is run only under a 6-record budget that disadvantages log-hungry methods by design; the natural experiment — does ZipBench still match tinyBenchmarks or SparseEval when both get their preferred data budgets? — is not reported. - IRT unidimensionality is verified empirically on four text benchmarks only, while the zoo includes 100+ heterogeneous benchmarks; the authors' own remark concedes multi-skill benchmarks violate the assumption, and only multi-metric cases (OmniDocBench) are handled explicitly. - The 'reduces evaluation cost to 20–40%' headline counts proxy inference only; adding amortized construction cost changes the calculus for small labs evaluating few models, which is precisely the stated target audience. Bottom Line: For anyone who needs to evaluate LLMs (or VLMs/agents) on a benchmark that lacks public item-level logs, ZipBench is currently the most practical and best-validated compression recipe available, and the Zoo alone justifies a skim — but read the appendix cost tables and small test-set caveats before trusting individual per-benchmark numbers over a standard log-rich method where logs already exist.
