RewardVerse: Rubric-Guided Policy Optimization for Video Reward Modeling (20 ▲ )

Zhenchen Tang, Yang Li, Songlin Yang, Bo Peng, Xiaotong Zhao, Shuai Li, Haotian Fan, Alan Zhao, Jing Dong · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RewardVerse, a video reward model that inserts a dynamically generated, query-conditioned rubric as an intermediate representation between the evaluation prompt and the scorer, trained via a two-stage GRPO-style algorithm (RGPO) to mitigate score-range collapse and context-sensitive score drift in pointwise video evaluation. - Why it's important: Unstable scalar rewards make reinforcement learning fine-tuning of video generation models unreliable — collapsed or drifting score scales yield near-flat gradients and noisy RL signals, so a stable, data-efficient reward model directly improves downstream video generation quality. - How it does it: A shared MLLM policy plays two roles: a rubric generator that emits query-adaptive themes/weights/tips without seeing the video, and a scorer that produces per-theme scores via soft-logit expectations over rating tokens (1–5), with the generator optimized by rubric-level GRPO rewards and the scorer by a human-margin calibration loss. - The good: The paper shows the method reaches macro-averaged PLCC 0.554 across 16 EvalVerse dimensions (next-best baseline Q-Scorer: 0.467) while training on only 480 preference pairs, with clean 2×2 ablations (rubric × readout format) that isolate which design choice fixes which drift symptom. - The missing: All main results come from a single 7B backbone, a single seed (no error bars or significance tests reported), and an EvalVerse-derived test set curated by overlapping authors, so generalization beyond this taxonomy and beyond 7B is unverified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building video reward models or doing RLHF-style post-training of video generators, since the scalar-drift diagnosis and the rubric+soft-logits protocol are directly actionable; skippable for readers focused on LLM reward modeling, where rubric-as-reward ideas already exist.
Why this rank

Rigor (68) is supported by well-targeted 2×2 ablations, bootstrap CIs on diagnostics, and released code/weights, but reduced by single-seed headline results and an author-associated evaluation taxonomy. Non-Obviousness (60): the asymmetric generator/scorer optimization is thoughtful, but rubric anchoring is intuitive. Completeness (70) is high — the authors' limitations section is specific and direct, including negative diagnostics. Resilience (63) suffers from the EvalVerse overlap and zero-shot baseline remapping. Practical Impact (78) is strong: 480-pair data efficiency, released weights, and a downstream RL demonstration. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Video generation models are increasingly aligned via RL, which requires a reliable scalar reward model (RM). Existing video RMs — both discriminative regression heads (VideoScore, VideoReward) and generative MLLM scorers (UnifiedReward, VideoScore2) — map a video directly to a score without explicit evaluation criteria. The authors name and characterize the resulting failure mode as "scalar drift": (i) score-range collapse, where pointwise scores concentrate in a narrow band (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B zero-shot σ = 0.203 on a [1,5] scale), producing near-flat preference gaps for RL, and (ii) high variance under context shift (paraphrased instructions, pair-order swaps — an 79.2% flip rate in pairwise A/B without rubrics). They motivate the fix from professional human annotation practice: annotators decompose tasks into explicit criteria before scoring, providing a stable semantic anchor. Key Idea: Insert a rubric — a structured set of themes, weights, and scoring tips generated from the query alone (candidate-independent) — as a learnable intermediate representation, and read scores as continuous soft-logit expectations over the rating-token vocabulary rather than parsed natural-language integers. The rubric anchors the scoring scale (mitigating collapse and context sensitivity), the soft-logits readout decompresses the scale and guarantees 0% parse failure, and GRPO-style joint optimization with asymmetric signals (generator gets preference + alignment rewards; scorer gets a human-margin calibration loss) calibrates the pipeline to human ratings from as few as 30 preference pairs per dimension. Methodology: The pipeline has two modules sharing a Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, distinguished by role prompts. Module 1 (generator π_gen) maps query q = (dimension d, prompt p) to a rubric R̂q = {(t_k, w_k, T_k)}, k = 1..K (K = 5), with weights summing to 1, without video access. Module 2 (scorer π_sco) emits per-theme scores c_k(y|R) as the softmax-weighted expectation over tokens "1"–"5", aggregated as S(y|R) = Σ w_k·c_k. Training (RGPO) is two-stage: Stage 1 builds static seed rubrics R*_d offline via a self-evolving loop (propose → verify → revise) with Gemini-3.1-Pro over 30 preference pairs per dimension, deduplicated by two-level Jaccard filtering and reduced to 5 entries via an MCR2 sampler; the scorer is warmed up with GRPO on a pairwise preference reward r_pref = σ(S(y_w) − S(y_l)) plus format rewards, plus an L1 margin-calibration loss |(S(y_w) − S(y_l))/4 − Δŝ_w,l| against human score margins. Stage 2 jointly optimizes the generator via rubric-level GRPO (reward = preference separation + format validity + cosine similarity of BGE-M3 theme embeddings to seed themes) while continuing scorer calibration on the fixed generated-rubric text (no gradient through the rubric), with a scheduled scorer-loss coefficient. Key design decisions: candidate-independent rubric generation (justified as preventing video-lenient/strict rubric bias), asymmetric optimization signals to prevent the scorer from gaming reward magnitude (well-motivated), and soft-logits over integer parsing (justified by measured 46.7–53.3% parse-failure rates for text formats). Training: 1 epoch per stage (~60 steps), G = 8 rollouts, lr 2e-6, on 8×H20 GPUs. Key Results: On a curated EvalVerse pointwise test set (n = 994 across 16 dimensions), RewardVerse attains the best PLCC in 14 of 16 dimensions (e.g., Logic 0.750 vs. next-best 0.593; Action 0.566 vs. 0.390) with macro-avg PLCC 0.554 / SRCC 0.446, versus Q-Scorer (0.467/0.354), VisionReward (0.408/0.351), VideoReward (0.384/0.399), VideoScore2 (0.433/0.427), UnifiedReward (0.334/0.328), VideoScore-v1.1 (−0.033/0.132). Baselines are recent and reasonably strong, though they are evaluated zero-shot with coarse native outputs mapped to dimensions (per Table 12). On VGRB (26.5K pairs), RewardVerse achieves the best non-oracle results on both splits: Text Alignment (unseen dimension) 0.471/0.623 accuracy with/without ties, Visual Quality (seen) 0.545/0.660, beating VisionReward by ~7 points on the seen split and approaching the oracle VideoReward (which defined VGRB's training set). Ablations under the same 480-pair budget show the full pipeline at 0.530/0.416 macro PLCC/SRCC vs. 0.431/0.355 without Stage 1, 0.456/0.364 without Stage 2, 0.497/0.398 with flat rubrics, and 0.439/0.351 for direct rubric-free pointwise training. Post-RGPO calibration diagnostics on a 240-video hold-out show bias dropping from +0.610 to +0.164 and normalized prompt-perturbation variance from 0.206 to 0.085. Downstream GRPO of Wan-2.2-A14B improves Imaging Quality 0.640 → 0.653 and VBench-Text 0.428 → 0.446 while preserving VBench-Quality (0.808 → 0.809), whereas VideoReward as reward degrades VBench-Text to 0.392. Inference cost: ~2.0 s/video vs. 1.7 s rubric-free, on one H20. Scale of testing: standard research scale (7B RM, 14B generator, 1K-sample test set), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (rubric-as-reward applied to video reward modeling with a learned, dynamic, candidate-independent rubric intermediate plus joint GRPO optimization) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the systematic characterization of "scalar drift" — collapse and context-shift variance — across video RMs). The rubric-as-reward concept itself is established in LLM alignment (RaR, OpenRubrics, RLCF) and image generation (AlphaGRPO, EditR1), so the genuinely novel element is the video-specific instantiation: query-conditioned rubric generation without video access, soft-logits readout for scale decompression, and the asymmetric two-role GRPO scheme — a competent, non-obvious transfer and extension rather than a fundamentally new paradigm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-targeted: the 2×2 rubric × readout study isolates each design choice's effect on each drift symptom, and the three-way ablation (no Stage 1 / no Stage 2 / flat rubric / rubric-free) quantifies each component's contribution (0.074–0.099 PLCC deltas). Diagnostics include bootstrap 95% CIs for bias (+0.771, CI [+0.64, +0.90]) and per-dimension bias breakdowns. However, no multi-seed runs, error bars, or significance tests are reported for the headline EvalVerse/VGRB results, and single-run PLCC gaps of ~0.05–0.09 over Q-Scorer could be within run-to-run variance. Code and models are released at https://github.com/2kxx/RewardVerse. Methodological concerns: (1) the pointwise test set is curated from EvalVerse, whose paper shares an author (Songlin Yang) — evaluation on an author-associated taxonomy with training pairs drawn from the same taxonomy risks favorable dimension alignment; (2) baseline scoring protocols require remapping coarse native outputs to the 16 dimensions, which may understate baselines; (3) VGRB's defining model (VideoReward) is correctly excluded as an oracle, which is a credibility positive. No Goodhart-style train/test leakage is apparent, but the field's reliance on human-labeled correlation as the sole validation metric is inherent. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained reward model with experiments and a downstream RL demonstration). - Practical: Yes — runs on a 7B open backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) with released code/weights; training needed 8×H20, inference fits a single H20 at ~2.0 s/video. - Efficient: Modest overhead vs. direct scoring (+18% latency over rubric-free soft-logits), and rubric reuse across candidate videos amortizes cost; data efficiency is a standout at 480 preference pairs total with no SFT. - Effective: Evidence supports improved pointwise correlation, pairwise transfer, and downstream RL quality on the target dimension, but "solves scalar drift" is demonstrated only as reduced bias/variance on curated test sets, not as drift-freedom in long-horizon RL rollouts. - Scalable: Not tested — the authors explicitly flag that 7B backbone, 30 pairs/dimension, and one 14B generator are the evaluated envelope; behavior with stronger backbones or RL on multiple generator models is claimed, not shown. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: released code, model weights, and a project page. Strengths: - The scalar-drift diagnostic study is the paper's most transferable contribution: the 2×2 rubric × readout ablation with matched backbones cleanly separates which intervention fixes score collapse (rubric anchoring, +82.6% σ expansion) versus which fixes parse fragility and scale anchoring (soft-logits), and the cross-backbone bias analysis (Qwen overestimates, Gemini underestimates) is genuinely informative for practitioners. - The asymmetric optimization design — generator driven by rubric-level preference rewards, scorer driven only by margin calibration with rubrics treated as fixed context — is a thoughtful solution to a real gaming vector (scorers inflating score gaps), and is explicitly reasoned rather than incidental. - Extreme data efficiency (480 preference pairs, no SFT, one epoch per stage) with credible headline numbers and strong zero-shot transfer to an unseen VGRB dimension. - Honest internal reporting: the paper publishes its own negative diagnostics (residual 56.2% pairwise flip rate even with rubrics, +0.77 pooled bias pre-RGPO, PR4's lower decided-pair accuracy than PR1) before arguing why the deployed configuration is still the right one. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly (Appendix A.6): (1) backbone capacity — RGPO can only align existing perceptual ability, not recover details a 7B backbone cannot see; (2) theme-level calibration is unsupervised, so individual rubric-theme scores can remain biased even when aggregate margins align; (3) scaling — results cover one 7B reward backbone, 30 pairs/dimension, and one 14B generator, and larger-scale consistency is unverified; (4) relation to CoT-based scoring — the rubric defines criteria pre-video while CoT summarizes evidence, so the two are complementary but untested in combination. This direct, specific treatment of limitations is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No multi-seed variance or significance testing for the headline comparisons; several margins (e.g., 0.530 vs. 0.497 for the flat-rubric ablation, 0.554 vs. 0.467 over Q-Scorer) are single-run numbers where seed noise is unquantified. - The pointwise evaluation taxonomy and the training pairs both derive from EvalVerse, and EvalVerse's paper shares an author with this work; independent-taxonomy evaluation (e.g., MJ-Video, CineTechBench, both cited but unused for evaluation) is absent. - Baselines are zero-shot with post-hoc dimension remapping (Table 12), so the comparison conflates architecture differences with protocol differences; a fine-tuned baseline under the same 480-pair budget with per-dimension heads would sharpen the rubric-attribution claim (the V2-Training rubric-free control partially covers this but only for one configuration). - The downstream RL claim of "less prone to reward hacking" rests on a single run against a single alternative reward (VideoReward) on one model and one dimension — weak evidence for a headline robustness claim. - Rubric-generation latency is measured per query, but the reward-model call pattern during online RL (many candidate videos per prompt) is exactly the amortizing case; the paper does not report end-to-end RL throughput or rubric quality degradation under reuse. - The r_align reward ties generated themes to seed-theme embeddings via cosine similarity, which could anchor Stage 2 toward the Gemini-authored seed distribution rather than encouraging genuinely novel criteria — no ablation removes this term. Bottom Line: A practitioner building video reward models or RL pipelines for video generators should read this: the scalar-drift diagnosis and the rubric-plus-soft-logits protocol are immediately reusable and the data efficiency is real, but the headline gains await independent replication on author-independent taxonomies and larger backbones before being treated as settled.

Spatial-Interactor: Learning Spatial Reasoning through Interaction with the Observable Physical World (41 ▲ )

Kaixiang Yao, Xu Wang, Miao Pan, Hu Xiyue, Weishi Wang, Daniel Dahlmeier, Jintao Chen, Yongliang Shen, Xuhong Zhang, Wenqi Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Spatial-Interactor, a post-training framework that teaches vision-language models to reason about physical-world state transitions using a three-level interaction curriculum (passive world changes, ego-motion changes, long-horizon trajectory integration), a 108K-pair dataset (LSI-108K), and a two-stage SFT + on-policy distillation recipe. - Why it's important: VLMs fail badly at dynamic spatial reasoning — e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B scores 8.6% on VSTI-Bench camera displacement and is nearly insensitive to frame order — which blocks deployment in navigation and embodied tasks where spatial state must be tracked over time. - How it does it: Interaction trajectories (O_t, a_t, O_{t+1}) from simulators and pose-annotated real videos supply direct supervision for local state transitions, while a privileged on-policy distillation (OPD) stage gives a teacher access to segment-level transition traces during training only, so the student learns to integrate consecutive transitions over long videos. - The good: Gains are consistent and large across four backbones (16.4–25.0 points overall on VSI-Bench/MindCube/VSTI-Bench/SPBench-MV, with the 8B model reaching 65.9 overall) and transfer to four held-out benchmarks (+4.3 to +10.6 points), supported by a carefully controlled GRPO-vs-OPD ablation that isolates the process-supervision signal. - The missing: The main comparisons include benchmarks (VSTI-Bench, MindCube) whose data appears in the SFT mixture — only the smaller cross-benchmark gains are clean — and no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on VLM spatial/embodied post-training and on-policy distillation, particularly for the privileged-trace OPD design; practitioners seeking proven closed-loop embodied agents can skip it, since closed-loop results remain weak (14% on WalkerBench).
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) and Non-Obviousness (75) are strong — the privileged-trace OPD design and the frame-shuffling diagnostic are real contributions with a cleanly controlled GRPO-vs-OPD ablation — but Rigor (62) is reduced by training on benchmark families used for headline evaluation (the honest cross-benchmark gains are an order of magnitude smaller), no seeds or variance reporting, and thin closed-loop evidence. Completeness (60) and Resilience (60) are likewise capped by the contamination issue being minimized rather than confronted. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*65 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: VLMs deployed in physical environments must track how spatial states evolve from object motion and viewpoint changes, and integrate these changes over long trajectories. The authors diagnose two failures with original experiments: (1) a frame-shuffling diagnostic on VSTI-Bench shows Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B accuracies drop by only 0.9/0.8 points when 32 video frames are randomly reordered, indicating reliance on order-invariant cues rather than modeling transitions; (2) a local-to-long-horizon comparison shows performance collapsing from 54.7 (local SAT-Real) to 8.6 (long-horizon VSTI-Bench camera displacement) for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and from 88.7 to 23.9 for GPT-5.5. Existing spatial training focuses on static QA about attributes and relations, giving no direct supervision for state transitions. The gap: how to obtain supervision that teaches models both local transitions and their composition over time. Key Idea: Interaction trajectories directly expose transition structure — each record (O_t, a_t, O_{t+1}) pairs consecutive observations with the physical change connecting them, and this can be verified from simulator or pose metadata. The core trick in the L3 stage is privileged on-policy distillation: a frozen pre-update teacher snapshot sees a question-independent, segment-ordered transition trace z (generated by a frozen annotator VLM) while evaluating the student's own sampled reasoning prefixes; the forward-KL on reasoning tokens isolates how privileged transition evidence changes the next reasoning step, with answer correctness still governed by verifiable rewards. Methodology: Three components. (1) Dataset construction (LSI-108K, 107,518 QA pairs): simulated agents execute camera motions/object operations in ProcTHOR, AI2-THOR, HSSD, Replica (51.5% of data); real camera trajectories from ScanNet++, ARKitScenes, RoomTour3D, etc. (39.2%) and robot trajectories from BridgeData V2 (9.3%) are converted via camera-center displacement math into signed motion targets; deterministic templates render QA pairs (no LLM generation), a frozen VLM verifier can reject but never generate ground truth. Curriculum: L1 passive world-state transitions (14.1%), L2 active self-state/ego-motion transitions (64.6%), L3 long-horizon integration (21.3%). (2) SFT on 82,596 L1–L2 examples plus 80K public spatial QA (VSI-590K, MindCube, VSTI-Bench data). (3) OPD within GRPO on 21,495 L3 examples: objective L_OPD = L_answer + βL_KL-ref + λt L_process, with β = 0.01, λ decaying from 0.05 to 0 over 1,200 steps; process loss is forward KL on the teacher's top-100 non-special-token support, masked to reasoning positions only; the teacher is a stop-gradient pre-update snapshot (not EMA) evaluating the same student-generated prefixes. Visual encoder frozen; LM and projector trained (8×B200, LLaMA-Factory + EasyR1/verl). Critical design decisions: privileged trace is question-independent (reduces gaming risk, justified), same-prefix evaluation (well-motivated — isolates the effect of z), and process-weight decay (plausible but the ablation for decay scheduling is thin). Backbones: Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B and Qwen3-VL-4B/8B. Key Results: On the main suite (VSI-Bench, MindCube, VSTI-Bench, SPBench-MV), Spatial-Interactor improves Overall by 16.4–25.0 points over base models; the 8B variant reaches 65.9 overall (VSI 62.7, MindCube 88.4 on SPBench-MV Rel. Dist. column, VSTI 47.1), beating GPT-5.5 (53.4) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (51.1) on average. Camera Displacement gains are largest (up to +28.0 for the 7B). On four held-out benchmarks (MMSI, ViewSpatial, SAT-Real, SAT-Syn), gains are 4.3–10.6 points; ablations attribute most transfer to SFT, with OPD adding 1.0–1.4 points. The controlled ablation (Qwen2.5-VL-7B): base 35.1 → external-data SFT 56.0 → +L1/L2 interaction data 58.4 → +GRPO 59.2 → +OPD 60.1; OPD beats matched GRPO by 5.1 on Route Planning and 3.1 on Camera Displacement. Post-training increases frame-order sensitivity (trained models drop 6.6–7.0 points under shuffling vs 0.8–0.9 for base). Trace diagnostics: ordered 4-segment trace lifts camera-displacement score 32.6→35.4, shuffled trace only 33.8. Closed-loop: WalkerBench overall 7.0→14.0 with mean actions cut from 17.71 to 6.52; ESI-Bench (240 matched questions) 32.9→41.2. Important caveat: the headline 25-point jump from base conflates the 80K external SFT mixture (~21 points) with the paper's own contributions (~2.4 points from interaction SFT, ~1.7 from OPD over GRPO on the ablation model). Baselines include recent spatial systems (SpatialLadder, SpaceR, Spatial-MLLM), though SpatialLadder-3B remains strongest on SPBench-MV (70.9 vs their 67.6). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (LSI-108K, a verifiable interaction-transition curriculum) + NEW METHOD (privileged-trace on-policy distillation for long-horizon spatial integration) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the frame-shuffling insensitivity of VLMs on spatial video is a memorable diagnostic). The genuinely novel piece is using privileged, question-independent transition traces available only to the teacher during on-policy distillation as process supervision for temporal integration. The ingredients — GRPO, on-policy distillation, curricula, synthetic QA from simulators — are standard; the authors appropriately position OPD as an application of existing on-policy distillation work (they cite Uni-OPD, self-distillation, and multimodal OPD preprints) to a new supervision source. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: the GRPO-vs-OPD comparison matches initialization, data, prompts, rollout groups, rewards, and schedule, so the process signal is cleanly isolated; the L1/L2/L1→L2 curriculum ablation and trace-order/frame-budget analyses add mechanistic evidence. Training and evaluation records are disjoint at scene/video level, and cross-benchmark evaluation uses four benchmarks absent from training. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests anywhere; the headline table evaluates on VSTI-Bench and MindCube while the SFT mixture includes 80K samples from those benchmark families (the paper argues gains over base, but Goodhart risk on the main suite is real — the honest signal is the smaller cross-benchmark delta); ESI-Bench uses only 30 questions per category; the frozen annotator VLM used for traces is not named; the 4B/8B gains over base partly reflect Qwen3-VL's stronger starting point rather than the method. A project page is listed (zju-omniai.github.io/Spatial-Interactor) and the appendix states released code includes training entrypoints, rewards, masks, and configs; no explicit link to released model weights or the LSI-108K download is given in the text provided. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL):** - Practical: Yes — post-training of 3B–8B open-weight VLMs on a single 8×B200 node with standard frameworks (LLaMA-Factory, verl, vLLM). - Efficient: Frozen visual encoder and modest data (108K SFT pairs, ~21.5K RL prompts) keep cost moderate relative to pretraining-scale efforts, though 8×B200 is still substantial. - Effective: Strong evidence on open-loop benchmarks including held-out transfer, but closed-loop absolute success remains low (14% WalkerBench), so the stated goal of acting in dynamic environments is only partially met. - Scalable: Untested beyond 8B parameters and 32-frame videos; the paper claims, but does not show, behavior at larger scale or longer horizons. Delivers: dataset (LSI-108K, per project page), released training code, and trained checkpoints implied but not explicitly confirmed — a concrete software artifact beyond the paper. Strengths: - The frame-shuffling diagnostic is a genuinely insightful, cheap experiment that cleanly demonstrates order-invariant shortcut behavior in VLMs, and the paper closes the loop by showing trained models become order-sensitive. - The privileged-trace OPD design is a well-engineered contribution: question-independent trace generation (verifier cannot see answers, annotator cannot see questions), same-prefix teacher/student evaluation, and process-loss decay together minimize reward-hacking and gaming vectors. - Controlled comparison discipline: the GRPO baseline shares everything with OPD except privileged conditioning, making the 0.9-point overall and 5.1-point Route Planning deltas attributable to the process signal. - Multi-source data pipeline with deterministic (non-LLM) ground-truth templates and a reject-only verifier produces verifiable targets at 108K scale with detailed composition reporting. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion notes future work on adaptive trajectory segmentation and more diverse real interactions, implicitly acknowledging fixed 4-segment traces and reliance on indoor/room-scale data. The paper concedes SpatialLadder beats it on SPBench-MV and that compared systems differ in architecture/data, framing base-model deltas as the primary comparison. It does not deeply confront the train/eval benchmark overlap on the main suite; this is minimized rather than directly discussed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Benchmark-contaminated SFT mixture: training data drawn from VSI-590K, MindCube, and VSTI-Bench families, then evaluated on VSI-Bench, MindCube, and VSTI-Bench — scene/video-level disjointness does not remove distributional proximity; the clean generalization numbers (4.3–10.6 points) are roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the headline (16.4–25.0). - The annotator VLM and the "frozen strong VLM" verifier are unnamed, complicating reproduction of data quality and OPD. - No seeds/variance reporting for any number, including the 0.9-point OPD-over-GRPO margin that motivates the method's core claim. - Closed-loop evaluation is thin: WalkerBench at n=100 with 14% absolute success, ESI-Bench on 240 matched questions; two categories regress (Connectivity 53.3→40.0, Long-Term Navigation 20.0→6.7 in the expanded table) without discussion. - Scalability of the privileged-trace approach is unexamined beyond 32 frames/four segments; whether trace granularity must grow with horizon length is unknown (the 8-segment result suggests insensitivity, but only in one diagnostic setting). - All evaluation is indoor room-scale navigation-style spatial reasoning; no outdoor, object manipulation, or 3D-scene-graph-dependent tasks. Bottom Line: A technically careful post-training paper whose privileged-trace OPD and interaction curriculum deliver credible (if smaller than headline) generalization gains for VLM spatial reasoning — practitioners in multimodal/embodied post-training should read it for the OPD recipe and diagnostics, but should treat the main-table numbers as partly in-distribution and look to the cross-benchmark table for the true effect size.

#31 — Innovative (66)

HappyWorld-Bench (39 ▲ )

Zhiqi Bai, Junai Cai, Yixin Chen, Jingrun Du, Tao Feng, Wei Gong, Siyuan Huang, Xiao Lin, Jiaheng Liu, Jun Luo, Yongzhe Lyu, Liya Ma, Zenan Meng, Lin Qu, Wenbo Su, Jiaming Wang, Qinghe Wang, Shaofei Wang, Yanghai Wang, Zequn Wang, Ziming Wang, Hu Wei, Jiangtao Wu, Ruiqi Wu, Jiaxin Xie, Yuchi Xu, Ze Xu, Chengting Yu, Liangyu Yuan, Gang Zeng, Yawen Zeng, Xingyao Zhang, Zizheng Zhang, Bo Zheng, Jiancheng Zhu, Song-Chun Zhu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HappyWorld-Bench, a benchmark of 1,692 test cases (1,138 video prompts, 300 spatial scenes, 254 embodied cases) that evaluates whether world models remain consistent and responsive under interaction, revisitation, and intervention, organized by a six-level capability hierarchy (W1–W6) and instantiated across video, spatial, and embodied tracks with automated metrics plus a human A/B arena (HappyWorld-Arena) producing Elo ratings. - Why it's important: World-model evaluation is fragmented across three disjoint communities (video generation, 3D scene generation, embodied prediction), so a visually impressive model can ship while failing at state persistence or action-conditioned physics — failures that matter for any downstream use of world models in planning or control. - How it does it: The unifying move is a shared W1–W6 capability taxonomy (Perceptual → Interactive → Persistent → Programmable → Scalable → Universal) operationalized differently per track, combined with matched-pair intervention tests (same initial state, edited action condition or physical rule) and VLM-assertion-based automated metrics alongside human Elo. - The good: The cross-track empirical study of 31 systems is the first of its kind and yields concrete, quantified failure modes — e.g., the best video model scores only 66.7/100 on rule programmability (W4), the best spatial system reaches 70.14% placement accuracy, and edited physical rules in the embodied track leave "no identifiable trace" in generated dynamics. - The missing: The paper reports no validation that its VLM-based automated metrics (Gemini checklists, Qwen3-VL judgments) correlate with human judgment, no confidence intervals or seeds for any score, and the strongest video-track model (HappyOyster) comes from the lead affiliation (Alibaba Token Hub), an unaddressed conflict of interest. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate world models in any of the three modalities and need the field's first unified capability map and baseline numbers; skip it if you want metric-validity evidence or a new modeling method — it provides neither.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Novelty (75) is the driver: the W1–W6 cross-modality taxonomy and matched-pair counterfactual protocol constitute a genuine new formulation uniting three disjoint evaluation communities, and the dissociation finding (perceptual quality ≠ world reliability) is non-obvious (65). Impact (75) reflects a benchmark plus live arena covering 31 frontier systems, but Rigor (55) is held back by unvalidated VLM-as-judge metrics, no confidence intervals, the unaddressed Alibaba conflict of interest on the winning video model, and preprint status; Completeness (60) suffers from the same silences even though interface-level limitations are candidly confronted. Weighted composite: 0.15*75 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*55 + 0.30*75 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: Developers of world models — and consumers of them for agent planning, robotics, and interactive content — currently cannot compare systems across modalities or probe whether generated worlds survive interaction. Existing benchmarks are siloed: video benchmarks (VBench 2.0, WorldScore, WorldMark, iWorld-Bench, WBench, MBench, WorldRoamBench, PlayWorld) assess controllability/memory; spatial benchmarks (Eval3D, SceneEval, WorldScore) assess asset or scene quality; embodied benchmarks (EWMBench, WorldModelBench, WorldArena) assess action-conditioned video or downstream utility. The gap: no shared capability framework tests whether a world stays geometrically consistent under camera motion, physically plausible under contact, temporally persistent across revisits, and correctly responsive to edits — across all three model families under one protocol. Key Idea: Treat "world reliability" as a hierarchical capability ladder (W1 perceptual coherence, W2 action-conditioned transition, W3 persistence over long horizons/revisits, W4 causal propagation of rule edits while preserving unaffected content, W5 multi-agent shared worlds, W6 unification) and require every model family to be scored against the same ladder, with the decisive measurement trick being matched-pair counterfactual testing: hold the initial frame fixed, vary only the edited action condition or physical rule, and score whether the two generated rollouts differ exactly where the intervention specifies. Methodology: Three tracks share the taxonomy. (1) Video track: each case is a first-frame image plus text plus time-indexed control sequences (WASD/arrow-key movements, natural-language actions, rule edits); cases (218/294/342/180/104 at W1–W5) are human-reviewed for feasibility and assessable targets; evaluation uses 74 fine-grained facets across four dimensions — perception (MUSIQ, HPSv3, dynamic degree via RAFT flow), consistency (masked CLIP background similarity, DA3 geometric reprojection, DINOv2/CLIP-on-SAM2.1 subject consistency), causality (Gemini-based checklists for physical/content causality), and controllability (DA3 camera-trajectory accuracy, action execution, intervention validity/state fidelity). (2) Spatial track: 266 snapshot scenes + 34 expansion scenes with task-specific annotations (424 orbit-evaluated objects, 72 support surfaces, 30 edit pairs); geometry is tested by navigation-mesh coverage and simulator-based plate placement; editing combines Qwen3-VL instruction satisfaction with preservation metrics (background RGB/LPIPS/DINOv2 retention, depth agreement); expansion scores area growth, junction coverage, and old-region/path preservation. (3) Embodied track: 254 cases (62 W2 single actions, 100 W3 ordered multi-step, 92 W4 matched-pair groups = 40 action-condition + 52 physical-rule pairs), each an image-to-video problem Y₁:T = Gθ(I₀, p) with 17 metrics (assertion-based VLM judgments plus automatic frame metrics), weighted 20/20/30/30 across Perception/Consistency/Causality/Controllability. HappyWorld-Arena aggregates blind human A/B votes into per-track Elo. Critical design decisions: no-simulator, purely generative embodied interface (justified as maximizing eligible models — but this restricts the evaluated set to general video generators); global rather than temporally aligned event conditioning for several video models (an acknowledged fidelity limit); static-scene-only spatial track (justified because no method does spatiotemporal world modeling yet). Key Results: Video track (14 interactive models + 5 generation baselines): HappyOyster tops Arena Elo at 1263 (Genie 3 at 1206; Open-Oasis last at 324); Genie 3 leads W1 at 82.8, HappyOyster leads W2 (78.0) and W3 (76.8); only HappyOyster (66.7) and LingBot-World-v2 (59.3) were evaluable at W4. Even top systems degrade from W1→W4, with texture consistency and state fidelity dropping sharply (e.g., HappyOyster W4 state fidelity 38.61). Spatial track (9 systems): Marble leads adjusted Elo (1308) but GPT-6-Astra leads W3–W5; best placement rate is 70.14% (HYWorld-2.0) and best edit success 73.33% (HYWorld-2.0), while FlashWorld and Lyra variants score 0.00–1.36 on physical usability — renderable scenes with essentially unusable geometry. Embodied track (8 video models, 62,592 blind votes): MiniMax-H3 ranks first on both Elo (1060) and W2/W3/W4 (93.60/91.42/88.62); Sora 2 trails at 872 and 60.91–64.12. A recurring counter-intuitive finding across tracks: perceptual quality does not predict consistency, persistence, or edit responsiveness (e.g., Cosmos 3 has the best W2 imaging stability at 89.91 but causality scores of 33.18). Scale is standard-benchmark scale, not stress-scale; the editing set (30 pairs) and expansion set (34 scenes) are small. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW FORMULATION (the W1–W6 cross-modality capability taxonomy plus matched-pair intervention protocol). The component metrics are standard tools (MUSIQ, HPSv3, CLIP, DINOv2, SAM, DA3, navigation meshes, simulator placement) competently composed; the genuinely novel elements are the shared taxonomy spanning three previously disjoint evaluation communities and the shared-initial-state counterfactual design for scoring rule edits, which no prior benchmark in the related-work section implements. Rigor & Reproducibility: Case-level quality control (human review filtering ambiguous/infeasible tasks), frozen assertions, a documented arena with 62,592 blind votes, and detailed per-model inference configurations in an appendix are credibility positives. Ablations of the metric suite itself are absent, no seeds/error bars/significance tests are reported anywhere, and the automated metrics' correlation with human judgment is not validated in the text provided. The spatial-track Elo requires a "capability adjustment" described only in Appendix B.8. Dataset/code release URL is not stated in the provided text (only the arena link, https://skyeval.com/sla/arena/happyworld). Methodological concerns: heavy reliance on VLM-as-judge (Gemini, Qwen3-VL) creates Goodhart risk and unquantified judge bias; several video models were evaluated through adapted interfaces that cannot express W4 interventions at all (so W4 has n=2); HappyOyster — the video-track winner — is affiliated with the lead author institution (Alibaba Token Hub), and GPT-6-Astra's provenance is unclear, so vendor-adjacent self-evaluation cannot be excluded. This is an arXiv preprint (2609.24308); results are not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a benchmark plus a live arena platform, with an empirical evaluation campaign). Practical: Yes — all evaluation runs via hosted interfaces, browser automation, or released checkpoints; no exotic hardware needed by the evaluator. Efficient: Not stated — the cost of generating 60-second rollouts and running VLM-assertion judging across 1,692 cases is not quantified. Effective: The evidence shows it diagnoses real failure modes (persistent-state, edit-propagation breakdowns) that visual-quality metrics miss, which is exactly the stated problem; it does not yet show the benchmark predicts downstream task utility. Scalable: The arena is designed for open-ended community continuation, but 10×–100× growth of test cases, human raters, and VLM-judging throughput is claimed by design, not tested. Deliverable: a benchmark suite, evaluation protocol, and live arena platform; no trained model or library is contributed by the authors themselves. Strengths: - The W1–W6 taxonomy is a real conceptual contribution: it gives video, spatial, and embodied communities a common vocabulary and exposes, with data, that perceptual quality and world reliability are dissociated capabilities (e.g., Lyra 2.0 leads texture/subject consistency at W1 yet scores 0.00 placement at spatial W2). - The matched-pair W4 protocol (shared initial frame, single edited condition, branch-difference scoring) is a clean, reusable experimental design for measuring counterfactual responsiveness, and the embodied failure taxonomy (contact never established; misdirected interaction; uncaused scene changes; state not transferred; rule edit with no observable consequence) is genuinely diagnostic. - Coverage is strong: 31 systems including frontier closed models (Genie 3, Sora 2, Cosmos 3, Marble, Kling 3, Grok Imagine) evaluated under one protocol, with per-model inference adaptations documented in detail. - Honest reporting of awkward results, e.g., that W2/W3 pools differ so score differences are not pure duration effects, and that several models simply cannot run W4. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that W2 and W3 use different case pools (so persistence effects are confounded), that the W4 video comparison is restricted to two models, that W1/W5/W6 are not operationalized in the embodied track, that the spatial track covers static scenes only, that several video models receive event instructions as global rather than temporally aligned conditioning, and that the Cosmos 3 camera-pose interface was bypassed in favor of an autonomous-driving action domain. They confront interface-level constraints directly, which is a credibility positive; they are more circumspect about metric validity and conflicts of interest, which they do not mention. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No human-validation of the automated metrics: with Gemini and Qwen3-VL doing causal/consistency/edit judging, judge bias, prompt sensitivity, and gaming surface are unquantified — the Arena Elo only weakly corroborates level scores. (2) The conflict-of-interest problem: the paper originates largely from Alibaba Token Hub, and HappyOyster (Alibaba's model) tops the video track while being one of only two models evaluable at W4; no independence safeguards are described. (3) The embodied track evaluates generic text-to-video generators (Sora 2, Kling, Seedance) rather than purpose-built embodied world models (DreamGen-style, V-JEPA-2-style, or simulator-based systems surveyed in its own related work), so the headline "embodied models struggle" partially reflects the chosen interface, not the field. (4) No confidence intervals on Elo from 62,592 votes despite local-ordering claims. (5) The editing set (30 pairs) and expansion set (34 scenes) are too small to support fine-grained conclusions per edit category. (6) No release URL for the benchmark data or evaluation code appears in the provided text, leaving reproducibility of the automated pipeline unverifiable. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or selecting world models should read this — it is the first credible cross-modality capability map with quantified baselines and a genuinely useful intervention protocol — but should treat the automated metric scores as unvalidated proxies and the Alibaba-affiliated video-track ranking with appropriate skepticism, since no independent reproduction or metric-human correlation evidence exists yet.

What Transfers, and Why: A Behavioral Account of Cross-Benchmark Generalization in Long - Horizon Agents

S Mehta · openreview.net · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper post-trains an open-weight MoE model (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B) on 363 long-horizon, MCP-based professional-workflow tasks (LHMTA) and shows the resulting checkpoint improves on five external benchmarks — Toolathlon (+9.6 pp), τ2-Bench (+5.3 pp), BFCL-V4 (+3.5 pp), SWE-Bench Pro (+5.8 pp), Terminal-Bench 2 (+2.8 pp) — including two software-engineering benchmarks with zero SWE training tasks. - Why it's important: Agents trained on a curated environment can win by exploiting environment-specific regularities (tool schemas, grader quirks) rather than learning reusable skill, so practitioners need to know whether agentic post-training environments teach transferable ways of working; environment/data design is expensive, and this addresses what makes that investment generalize. - How it does it: A two-stage SFT (3,000 rejection-sampled Kimi K2.6 trajectories) then GSPO RL recipe over LoRA adapters, using a dense per-criterion grader reward with a capped effort floor for low-scoring trajectories, evaluated under an 'external firewall' — no external-benchmark task, grader, or score influenced reward, hyperparameters, checkpoint selection, or stopping. - The good: The paired base-vs-trained trajectory analysis grounds the transfer claim in behavior: over 731 matched SWE-Bench Pro pairs, runs containing a formal test rise from 37.5% to 73.3%, mean added lines drop from 415.5 to 111.7, and repeated retrieved information falls from 22.5% to 14.3%, alongside four recurring qualitative behavioral differences. - The missing: Everything rests on a single post-training run with no error bars, no cross-benchmark significance testing, no no-effort-floor ablation, and no general-capability (forgetting) benchmarks — and the training environment was Toolathlon-inspired, with the base family and SFT teacher selected partly on Toolathlon leaderboard performance. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone designing RL environments or studying agentic generalization — the behavioral-transfer framing and honest provenance disclosure are genuinely useful — but skip it if you want statistically robust transfer claims or a reproducible artifact, since neither is provided.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (78) is the standout — the external-evaluation firewall plus exhaustive disclosure of every contamination channel (Toolathlon-inspired design, leaderboard-informed model selection, single-run caveats) is a model of honest reporting — and Non-Obviousness (72) benefits from the behavioral trajectory analysis that converts score deltas into falsifiable, recomputable metrics. Novelty (70) is a genuine cross-benchmark transfer finding with an identified failure boundary, but Impact (50) is low given no checkpoint, data, or library release and industrial-only compute requirements. Problem & Motivation Teams building RL environments for agents face a measurement problem: task-success rate on the training environment (or an in-distribution holdout) cannot distinguish a policy that acquired transferable skill from one that exploited environment-specific regularities — tool-surface idiosyncrasies, grader parsing behavior, task templates. The natural internal control (a held-out split of the same environment) shares those degrees of freedom and therefore cannot rule out exploitation. The paper argues the discriminating question is behavioral (how the agent acts, not just what it achieves) and that cross-benchmark transfer, with results firewalled from training decisions, is the right evidence. The audience is environment designers and anyone training agentic post-training pipelines on curated, self-built tasks. Key Idea Treat a training environment's value as the task pressures it exerts (forcing careful goal formation, state-building, goal stability, verification) rather than its surface domains, and test whether those pressures transferred by (a) evaluating on external benchmarks whose tasks and graders were firewalled from all training decisions, and (b) reading the score changes through paired-trajectory behavioral analysis. Methodology The pipeline has four stages. (1) Environment: LHMTA, 363 training tasks across 27 professional-workflow categories exposed as MCP servers, each with a deterministic Python grader scoring per-criterion completion from final environment state; successful trajectories run 30–40 tool turns and 80K–100K tokens. From 430 candidate pairs, 27 with rate-limited APIs or non-determinism were excluded, leaving 403 (363 train / 40 in-distribution holdout). (2) SFT: Kimi K2.6 generated trajectories on the 363 training tasks; 3,000 trajectories scoring >0.9 were retained (max length 131,072; AdamW, LR 1e-5 cosine, 1 epoch). (3) RL: GSPO sequence-level estimator (8 samples per prompt, temperature 1.0, LR 5e-5, LoRA rank 32 on all attention/MLP projections) on the same 363 tasks, on 64 H200 GPUs built on slime/Megatron-LM/SGLang. The reward is r = max(r_g, e) where r_g is the fraction of grader criteria satisfied and e is an effort floor (≤0.40) for trajectories with r_g < 0.5, rewarding tool use, normal completion, and tool diversity; a per-prefix reward variant was abandoned after the policy gamed rewarded prefixes. (4) Evaluation: greedy pass@1 under native benchmark scoring. Critical design decisions: the effort floor (boosts usable signal from 16.8% to 82.7% of tasks, but directly confounds 'capability vs propensity' — well-motivated, only partially justified by the absence of an ablation); LoRA instead of full fine-tuning (motivated by less-forgetting evidence); the external-evaluation firewall (well-justified and clearly documented, though Toolathlon-inspired task design and base/teacher selection by Toolathlon leaderboard weaken it). Key Results Greedy pass@1 base→trained: LHMTA holdout 10.0→27.5 (+17.5 pp); Toolathlon 22.2→31.8 (+9.6); τ2-Bench 54.8→60.1 (+5.3, retained from the earlier reviewed-version snapshot); BFCL-V4 55.7→59.2 (+3.5); SWE-Bench Pro 20.5→26.3 (+5.8); Terminal-Bench 2 44.9→47.7 (+2.8). Toolathlon category gains are uneven (Office 0.0→16.5 from a zero baseline; Finance +10.1, Shopping +11.5, Tech +9.9 from non-trivial baselines). BFCL slices regress slightly on Non-Live (−1.7 pp) and Hallucination (−0.7 pp). Behavioral metrics over 731 matched SWE-Bench Pro pairs: formal-test runs 37.5%→73.3%, mean added lines 415.5→111.7, reference-patch file overlap 2.69→3.08, repeated retrieved information 22.5%→14.3%, retrieval calls roughly unchanged (25.6→23.9). Baselines are the untrained base model, not competing post-training methods; the claim is directional change from the same base, not state of the art. Appendix B reports task saturation: epochs 2–3 of RL on the same 363 tasks regressed (entropy ≈0.9→≈0.6). Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a methodological stance (firewalled cross-benchmark evaluation with behavioral trajectory analysis); the training recipe itself (SFT-then-RL with GRPO/GSPO-family estimators, dense criterion rewards, effort shaping) is a standard combination of known techniques applied to a new environment. The genuinely novel element is connecting cross-benchmark score deltas to a recurring behavioral taxonomy across office workflows and code, and characterizing where transfer fails (preserving implicit contracts in mature codebases). Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are partial: there is no no-effort-floor ablation (acknowledged), no SFT-only/RL-only attribution (acknowledged), and no general-capability forgetting benchmarks (acknowledged). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests — the authors explicitly report descriptive point estimates, retain four-sample diagnostics separately from greedy results with clear provenance labeling, and refuse formal hypothesis testing given correlated benchmarks and a single run. Provenance discipline is unusually good: contamination (Toolathlon-inspired design, reused MCP server implementations, leaderboard-informed base/teacher choice, unauditable pretraining corpus) is disclosed up front. No code, data, or checkpoint release is mentioned. Concerns: single-run evidence, evaluation infrastructure differences between base and trained are not fully ruled out, and the behavioral analysis uses Claude Opus 4.8 for root-cause tracing with author verification — interpretive, not blinded or systematic. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a post-training experiment with evaluation and analysis; a small systems component in the training stack). - Practical: Requires 8 nodes × 8 H200 GPUs for RL plus an MoE-122B inference stack — outside typical academic budgets but commercially plausible for industrial labs; evaluation runs BF16 on single H200s. - Efficient: LoRA rank 32 and MoE with ~10B active parameters keep it comparatively cheap, but 80K-token trajectories with context-parallel sharding make RL runs compute-intensive, as the authors note. - Effective: The evidence shows directional improvement on external proxies of the stated problem (transferable behavior); the behavioral analysis is consistent with, but does not prove, a transfer mechanism, and the effort floor could explain part of the gain. - Scalable: Untested — Appendix B shows the recipe saturates on 363 tasks by epoch 2–3, so scaling behavior depends entirely on task diversity, which the paper only hypothesizes about. Deliverable is paper form only; no library, dataset, or trained checkpoint is stated as released. Strengths - The external-evaluation firewall with explicit disclosure of every potential contamination channel (Toolathlon-inspired design, leaderboard-informed model selection, retained snapshot results) is a model of honest reporting, and the separation of greedy vs. four-sample diagnostics by provenance is careful. - The strongest cross-domain result — +5.8 pp on SWE-Bench Pro and +2.8 pp on Terminal-Bench 2 from a training set containing zero software-engineering tasks — is a concrete, non-trivial transfer finding. - The paired-trajectory analysis converts a score delta into falsifiable behavioral descriptions (e.g., base reimports formula strings as missing data; trained reuses the repo's central validator), with deterministic correlates (test-runner usage 37.5%→73.3%, 73% smaller edit footprint) that a skeptic can recompute. - Identifying the failure boundary (implicit contracts in mature, interdependent codebases) and generating a testable next hypothesis is more useful than a uniform success claim. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and thoroughly: the effort floor may explain capability-vs-propensity changes and no ablation was run; the trajectory analysis is exploratory and interpretive, not causal; a single post-training run precludes run-variance estimates and formal tests; τ2-Bench and category/slice breakdowns come from an earlier snapshot that does not decompose the updated greedy numbers; no general-capability benchmarks were run so broader forgetting cannot be ruled out; base-model pretraining contamination cannot be audited; and the Office category gain starts from a 0.0 baseline inflated by effort-floor-encouraged task initiation. This level of self-criticism is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No comparison against any alternative post-training approach or data recipe: the reader cannot tell whether LHMTA's task pressures matter or whether any 363-task long-horizon RL set would produce similar deltas; the entire 'pressures vs. surface diversity' thesis is asserted, not tested against a surface-matched control. - The behavioral taxonomy was developed iteratively by the authors on the same trajectories they then illustrate it with — there is no held-out validation of the four categories, no inter-annotator agreement, and the LLM-assisted root-cause agent creates annotation-feedback risk. - Base and trained models may differ in scaffolding or evaluation-harness handling in ways the matched-protocol claim does not fully exclude, and the two SWE benchmarks' graders differ from LHMTA's deterministic graders in kind. - The 731 'matched pairs' include fail-to-pass and pass-to-fail pairs, but the per-pair selection criteria and how behavioral metrics weight failures vs. successes are not fully specified. - The SFT teacher (Kimi K2.6) is itself a strong agent model; SFT-only evaluation is missing, so the transfer attributable to RL versus distillation is unknown — a gap the authors flag but do not resolve. Bottom Line A practitioner designing RL environments gains real, actionable insight — behavioral transfer is measurable, has a describable boundary, and environment diversity should be chosen by task pressure — but the single-run, no-baseline, no-artifact nature of the evidence means this should be read as a well-documented case study, not settled science, and the concurrent transfer literature (Hu et al. 2026; Xi et al. 2026) covers adjacent ground with stronger experimental controls.

Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Agentic Graphic Design (22 ▲ )

Hongyang Du, Lan Yan, Christian Flores, Asim Kadav · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a continual adaptation framework that grows and refines an external library of natural-language design skills (76→139 SKILL.md playbooks) around a frozen frontier LLM operating professional design software through 230+ tools, raising GenEval2 execution success on Claude-Sonnet-4 from 72.7% to 99.3% and winning 58.5%–67.6% of pairwise comparisons against a no-skill agent. - Why it's important: Professional graphic design is a long-horizon agentic task with no programmatic success oracle, so outcome-based learning (RL, fine-tuning) is impractical when the foundation model is hosted and cannot be updated — this offers a deployment-safe route to continual adaptation with zero weight updates and zero human reward labels. - How it does it: A four-role offline loop (Prompter, Solver, Grader, Reflector) evolves the skill bank along two axes — widening (minting skills for recurring uncovered subtasks) and deepening (rewriting failure-prone skills by contrasting failed vs. successful executions) — with every candidate change admitted only through a matched replay gate that requires a win on at least one replayed prompt and zero detected regressions under randomized pairwise judging. - The good: The ablation cleanly shows neither mechanism works alone (49.4% / 48.6% win rates, cold start actually loses to BASE at 46.4%) while their combination reaches 58.5% (p=0.025) with a superadditive +3.85 completeness gain, isolating a genuinely non-obvious coupling effect. - The missing: All headline gains are judged by automated VLM/LLM graders (Graphic-Eval for internal metrics, GPT-5.4 for design benchmarks), with no human evaluation yet (the authors state a user study is only planned), and the internal held-out benchmark's prompts are withheld, so independent verification of the headline numbers is impossible. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building deployed LLM agents that must improve from production traffic without touching model weights — the replay-gate design and the coupled widening/deepening dynamics are directly transferable; skip it if you need validated human-preference evidence or a released artifact you can reuse.
Why this rank

Rigor (58) is the main drag: every headline number comes from LLM/VLM judges with the same judge driving both reward and reporting on the internal benchmark, no human evaluation exists yet, no external system baseline is compared, and win rates are single-run. Novelty (68) and Non-Obviousness (70) are genuine — the safe-policy-improvement-derived replay gate and the superadditive widening/deepening coupling (each mechanism alone within noise) are non-obvious and cleanly ablated. Completeness (68) is helped by unusually candid limitations; Resilience (62) is capped by the judge-identity and un-calibrated-gate objections. Problem & Motivation: Professional graphic design via an LLM agent is a sequential decision problem with dozens of interdependent tool operations (asset retrieval, masking, typography, compositing), where outcomes mix checkable requirements with subjective criteria like hierarchy and composition, so there is no reliable programmatic oracle. Practitioners running hosted frontier models (which cannot be fine-tuned) have no cheap way to learn from user traffic: supervised learning needs costly demonstrations, and outcome-based optimization faces long-horizon credit assignment plus imperfect proxy rewards. Creative software historically packaged workflows as macros/actions, but those are fixed sequences; the gap is a procedure representation that is specific enough to guide execution yet general enough to transfer, and an update mechanism that cannot regress a deployed product when judge feedback is noisy. Key Idea: Treat the natural-language skill library — not the model — as the learning object, and separate proposal from admission: widening and deepening propose skill edits from experience, while a matched replay gate admits a change only if it wins a majority of contexts on at least one replayed prompt with no regression on any other, using pairwise (never absolute) judging under randomized order to cancel VLM judge drift and upstream-state confounds. This conservative-gate idea is adapted from safe policy improvement (Thomas et al. 2015; Laroche et al. 2019) to prompt-level skill artifacts. Methodology: The system has a frozen agent (Claude-Opus-4.6, Claude-Sonnet-4 via Bedrock; Qwen3.6-27B via vLLM on 8×A100) controlling Photoshop/Illustrator/InDesign equivalents through 230+ tools with deterministic offline rendering and a Graphic-Eval grader (completeness 0.7 + aesthetics 0.3, threshold τ=0.6). The evolution loop runs four roles: (1) Widening — a frozen LLM extracts subtasks from trajectories; subtasks with no retrieved skill accumulate in a coverage pool keyed by canonical label; once a label recurs kmin=3 times, an LLM distills a candidate skill, gated against the no-skill agent. (2) Deepening — every skill retrieved in ≥m=2 failed trajectories is prioritized for rewrite; the Reflector receives the brief, per-requirement why-bad rationales, the current SKILL.md, and a contrastive set of the same skill's successful calls, and emits a targeted edit (escalating to a full rewrite after repeated gate failures). (3) Replay gate — prompts are replayed in a frozen batch across both arms with distinct upstream contexts; outputs are judged pairwise with order randomization and a tie band δ; acceptance requires ∄prompt lost ∧ ∃prompt won. Critical design decisions: token-overlap retrieval (deliberately not embeddings, so cold-start seeding and runtime retrieval share a tokenizer — well-justified); progressive disclosure via a load_skill tool rather than injecting skill bodies (cost-efficient, justified by token accounting); using the same judge for reward and reporting (deliberate but a self-consistency risk, partially mitigated by the pairwise gate and dual-family grader backends). Key Results: Five evolution rounds over 1,406 briefs produced 1,869 graded trajectories; the gate rejected 100/231 rewrite proposals and 67/136 mint candidates, growing the bank 76→139. On Claude-Sonnet-4, GenEval2 quality rose from 34.26 to 46.25 (Soft-TIFA) and execution success from 72.7% to 99.3%; DPG-Bench success hit 100% (from 82.7%). Average quality across four T2I benchmarks improved +3.83 (Opus-4.6), +7.70 (Sonnet-4), +9.67 (Qwen3.6-27B), though individual benchmarks regress (e.g., Qwen drops −15.3 success points on DPG-Bench). On four design benchmarks (OpenCOLE, GraphicBench, CreatiDesign, BannerRequest400; 300 prompts each), EVOLVE-vs-BASE win rates judged by GPT-5.4 reach 67.6% (Opus) and 61.8% (Sonnet) overall. On 200 held-out human-authored briefs, the combination reaches 58.5% win rate (p=0.025) and 74.04 completeness vs. 69.08 for BASE. Latency overhead is 3.4–6.2%. Notable non-monotonic dynamics: round 4 dips below baseline at low completeness thresholds (90% vs. 94% at τ≥0.3) because freshly minted unrewritten skills misfire, and round 5 (rewrite-heavy) is strongest everywhere. Ablations show the documentation-derived cold-start bank does not beat BASE (46.4% win rate, 68.62 vs. 69.08 completeness). Baselines are the authors' own no-skill agent on current frontier models; no external method (e.g., fine-tuned or RL-trained agent) is compared. Qwen results are explicitly confounded by local deployment instability (timeouts, connection drops). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the regression-gated, matched-replay admission rule for skill-bank changes under noisy unverifiable feedback in a deployed product, and (b) the empirical demonstration that acquisition and revision are individually near-useless (≤49.4% win rates) but superadditive together (+3.85 completeness, 58.5% win). The components — Voyager-style skill libraries, Reflexion/Self-Refine-style reflection, ACE-style context evolution, SkillAudit-style paired trajectory contrast — are known; the combination applied to a 230-tool professional design stack with a safe-improvement gate is the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations isolate widening and deepening with intermediate banks (+rewrite, +new skills), with statistical significance reported only for the headline combination (p=0.025); no error bars or multi-seed variance are given for benchmark scores, and win-rate margins are single-run GPT-5.4 judgments (300 prompts per benchmark). Retrieval-distinctiveness of minted skills is statistically validated (median NN distance 0.215 vs. 0.158, Mann–Whitney p<10⁻⁸, Cliff's δ=0.58) — a nice touch. Methodological concerns: (1) the same Graphic-Eval judge drives both evolution and the internal metric, an acknowledged Goodhart risk partially mitigated by the pairwise gate; (2) the internal held-out benchmark is human-authored but its prompts are withheld and no code, data, or skill bank is released anywhere in the paper; (3) design-benchmark win rates rest on one judge model (GPT-5.4) with order randomization but no inter-judge agreement check; (4) there is no external system baseline, only the authors' own agent with/without skills. Preprint (arXiv 2609.22086), not yet peer-reviewed; corporate-affiliated with proprietary user traffic, so independent replication is currently impossible. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built production-grade agent with an evolution harness, evaluated on real user traffic and public benchmarks). - Practical: Runs on commercially available hosted APIs (Bedrock Claude) or a single 8×A100 node for the open-model variant; the harness itself is software-only. - Efficient: Adds only 3.4–6.2% latency and, at k=3 retrieval, actually uses fewer tokens than cold start (436.6k/5167 vs. 445.2k/5298), despite ~28% prompt-token overhead for skill retrieval. - Effective: Evidence shows large gains on automated judges and plausible mechanism-level explanations (qualitative masking/composition cases), but effectiveness on human judgment is unmeasured — only a planned user study is mentioned. - Scalable: Only 5 rounds / 1,406 briefs are tested; behavior as the bank grows beyond ~139 skills or over many more rounds (retrieval saturation, skill interference) is claimed to be manageable but not demonstrated, and the authors concede the gate's guarantee is local to replayed cases. Delivers a production system and methodology at paper form only: no code, skill bank, benchmark prompts, or trajectories are released. Strengths: - The replay gate is a substantive, well-motivated mechanism: it explicitly names two confounds (VLM judge drift on absolute scores, differing upstream state between arms) and removes both by construction — frozen matched contexts, fresh same-batch replay, pairwise order-randomized judging, and a conservative no-loss-with-a-win acceptance rule. This is the paper's most transferable idea. - The ablation produces a genuinely non-obvious finding with clean evidence: cold start alone loses to no-skill (46.4% win), each mechanism alone is within noise, and the combination is superadditive (+3.85 completeness) with a credible explanation (minted skills need refined retrieval descriptions; rewrites route unfixable failures back to the gap store). - Honest reporting of non-monotonic evolution dynamics (R4 regressing at low thresholds due to unrevised v1 skills) and of a mostly negative personalization result (Appendix I's Droste-effect perception/verification gap) — unusually candid for an industrial paper. - The four-phase documentation cold-start pipeline (Appendix G) is a reusable recipe that guarantees seed skills are retrievable by sharing the runtime tokenizer. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) natural-language skills may not override a model's strong default strategy (retrieval alone is insufficient — needs preference-conditioned retrieval and tool scoping); (2) fine geometric operations are limited by model perception and automated verification, leaving human-in-the-loop for precision-critical detail; (3) long multi-step procedures lose fidelity at every stage — annotation, distillation, and execution — with compounding losses (shown on the full tessellation task); (4) the replay gate is local to evaluated cases and does not guarantee monotonic improvement over the full traffic distribution. They confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive), and explicitly position procedural memory as one mechanism for continual adaptation, not a replacement for model learning. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human evaluation at all in the main results; every headline number comes from an LLM/VLM judge, and the authors' own related-work section (G-Zero) argues proxy-judge dependence is a documented failure mode in open-ended domains — yet the human study is only "planned." - Reward-metric identity: the same judge scores the reward and reports the metric on the internal benchmark, so judge-specific preferences are baked into both evolution and evaluation simultaneously; the dual-backend option is described but no cross-judge agreement numbers are reported. - No external system baseline: comparisons are only EVOLVE vs. the identical agent without skills; nothing anchors performance against fine-tuning, DSPy-style prompt optimization, or prior design agents (GraphicTown, BannerAgency) on the shared benchmarks. - No released artifact: with internal benchmark prompts withheld and no code or skill bank published, none of the quantitative claims are independently checkable, and win-rate confidence intervals across the 300-prompt benchmark samples are absent. - Gate-vs-global tension is understated: the gate requires only one win and zero observed losses on a small replay set (2 good + 2 bad contexts for rewrites), which with judge noise should stall most honest improvements — the 44% rejection rate is consistent with either healthy conservatism or the gate being too tight; no calibration of δ or replay-set size against downstream accuracy is provided. - Qwen3.6-27B results are admitted to be deployment-confounded but are still tabulated in headline tables, inviting over-reading (e.g., the −15.3 DPG success drop). Bottom Line: For anyone deploying LLM agents on long-horizon, oracle-free tasks, this is one of the most practically instructive self-evolution papers available — the replay-gate discipline and the widening/deepening coupling result are worth adopting — but with judge-only evaluation, no released artifacts, and no human study, treat the exact numbers as an Adobe internal case study rather than a reproducible result.

PackLab: A Comprehensive Framework for Developing, Training, and Evaluating MLLMs in Robotic Bin Packing (10 ▲ )

Donghao Zhou, Jia-Hui Pan, Fan Zhang, Xingyuan Bu, Shilong Li, Xiaojie Gao, Yun-Hui Liu, Chi-Wing Fu, Pheng-Ann Heng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PackLab, an integrated framework consisting of a physics-based simulation and data-generation platform (PackLab-Suite), a packing-specialized multimodal LLM (PackLab-VLM, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-9B), and a standardized benchmark (PackLab-Bench), that enables an MLLM to jointly select objects and predict placements in closed-loop robotic bin packing. - Why it's important: Existing packing methods are either hand-crafted heuristics with local objectives or RL policies that fail to generalize across heterogeneous object sets and containers, and prior MLLM approaches only infer object properties for downstream planners rather than deciding actions directly — so there is no unified, physics-grounded policy for this long-horizon logistics task. - How it does it: A layout-first inverse data-generation engine partitions container space into terminal layouts, reconstructs packing trajectories by reversing object removal, validates them under physics simulation to yield 20K supervised trajectories, then fine-tunes an MLLM on multi-turn multimodal contexts (heightmaps, object attributes, action history) to autoregressively emit structured placement actions. - The good: The controlled RL retraining comparison is the most credible evidence: when TAP-Net and IR-BPP are retrained on the same task distribution with equivalent trial-and-error budget, they score 0.405 and 0.345 average Overall Score versus PackLab-VLM's 0.660, isolating the advantage of the MLLM formulation rather than the training data volume. - The missing: On hard cases (10-object buffer, 19–32 objects), PackLab-VLM (Overall 0.394) actually loses to the SDF-Pack heuristic (0.469), so the headline claim of superiority rests on easy/medium performance, and the entire quantitative evaluation is on the authors' own benchmark with no external validation set. - Read it or not: Worth reading for robotics and MLLM-post-training researchers interested in closed-loop multimodal decision-making and synthetic trajectory generation; practitioners seeking the strongest packer for large or densely constrained containers should stick with SDF-Pack per the paper's own numbers.
