Problem & Motivation: Robotic bin packing requires long-horizon sequential decision-making: each placement changes the container state and the feasibility of all subsequent placements, with applications in logistics, warehousing, and robotic manipulation. Heuristic methods (DBLF, MTA, HM, SDF-Pack) score individual placements with local geometric objectives and cannot reason about downstream feasibility; RL methods (TAP-Net, IR-BPP) learn sequential policies but only over predefined object/container distributions and generalize poorly to heterogeneous settings. Existing MLLM-based approaches (OPA-Pack, iPack, LLM-Pack) delegate action selection to conventional planners, using the MLLM only to infer object properties or constraints. The gap the paper targets is whether an MLLM can directly perform closed-loop object selection and placement across diverse configurations — and, more broadly, the absence of an integrated simulation, data-generation, training, and evaluation stack for this question. Key Idea: The core trick is the layout-first inverse data-generation engine: instead of exhaustively forward-sampling object–placement combinations, sample a scenario, partition the container into stacked layers and non-overlapping regions forming a terminal layout, recover a forward trajectory by iteratively removing geometrically accessible objects and reversing the removal order, then physics-validate each replayed trajectory and discard invalid ones. This converts the expensive generative problem of producing physically valid packing demonstrations into a constructive one, yielding 20K closed-loop supervised trajectories (PackData-20K) for fine-tuning a multimodal policy that consumes heightmaps, object attributes, and full observation–action history and emits (object, orientation, x, y) actions. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) PackLab-Suite: a physics simulator (gravity at −9.8 m/s², box collision geometries, stability feedback based on linear/angular velocity thresholds) whose data-generation engine runs scenario sampling → layout partition → replay validation → trajectory curation, producing PackData-20K spanning three difficulty levels. (2) PackLab-VLM: the scene state St = (Ht, Bt) — a top-down heightmap plus a candidate buffer — is serialized into a temporally ordered multimodal context with a system prompt, prior heightmaps (encoded by a visual encoder and projected via a vision-language merger into placeholder positions), object buffers, and action history; the model (Qwen3.5-9B backbone) autoregressively decodes a structured action text parsed into at = (bt, ot, xt, yt). Training is step-level supervised fine-tuning minimizing target-token negative log-likelihood (Eq. 10), 5 epochs, AdamW, lr 1e-5, 8-GPU FSDP with bf16 and gradient checkpointing. Orientation is discretized to {0°, 90°}, placement coordinates to a 2.5 cm grid; z is determined by gravity settling. (3) PackLab-Bench: 60 held-out test cases (905 packing steps) across easy/medium/hard levels, disjoint from training data, scored by Success Ratio (packed volume fraction), Compactness (packed volume over packing-envelope volume), and their product as Overall Score. Critical design decisions: full-history conditioning (justified by ablation: dropping history costs 0.071–0.127 Overall), mixed-difficulty data recipe (justified: 0.660 vs 0.587 easy-only), and 2D-heightmap state abstraction — which is asserted rather than justified, since it discards object shape detail beyond dimensions. Key Results: On PackLab-Bench (60 cases, 3 seeds averaged), PackLab-VLM achieves average Success Ratio 0.882, Compactness 0.718, Overall 0.660, versus the strongest heuristic SDF-Pack at 0.602 Overall, DBLF 0.554, HM 0.534, MTA 0.439, FFP 0.333; official RL checkpoints score TAP-Net 0.474 and IR-BPP 0.442. Under the controlled retraining comparison, TAP-Net and IR-BPP drop to 0.405 and 0.345. Fine-tuning lifts the zero-shot backbone from 0.209 to 0.660 Overall (Easy 0.246→0.922, Medium 0.220→0.665, Hard 0.162→0.394). Ablations: distractor heightmap 0.494, current-observation-only 0.533, no action history 0.589 vs full 0.660; data scale 25%/50%/100% gives 0.578/0.630/0.660; model size 2B/4B/9B gives 0.617/0.645/0.660. On hard cases SDF-Pack (0.469) and DBLF (0.469) beat PackLab-VLM (0.394) — the authors state this openly. Real-world validation is a single qualitative eight-object case on an AUBO arm with suction cup, RealSense + Photoneo cameras, SAM3 segmentation, achieving Success Ratio 1.00 and Compactness 0.72 versus a baseline packing 3 of 8 objects; no aggregate real-world statistics are reported. Baselines are representative and mostly current (SDF-Pack is 2023; RL checkpoints are 2020–2021 with a same-distribution retraining), though no contemporaneous MLLM packing system (e.g., PackingGPT) is quantitatively compared. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, with a NEW METHOD component in the layout-first inverse trajectory generation. The genuinely novel element is the full integration — physics-validated inverse data generation feeding an MLLM that directly emits closed-loop packing actions rather than property annotations for a planner. The policy itself is standard supervised fine-tuning of an existing backbone on synthetic demonstrations, and the heightmap state encoding, autoregressive action decoding, and evaluation metrics are competent combinations of known ideas applied to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover input context (visual, history), data scale, data recipe, and model size, and results are averaged over three seeds; however, no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any comparison. Code, model, dataset, and benchmark are stated to be publicly available at https://github.com/Correr-Zhou/PackLab. Methodological concerns: (a) evaluation is entirely on the authors' own PackLab-Bench, which is also the basis of the difficulty recipe used in training — the easy/medium/hard taxonomy links training and evaluation design, though the paper asserts test cases are independently sampled and disjoint; (b) the controlled RL retraining is a strong methodological point, but the official-checkpoint rows in Table II reflect checkpoints trained on other distributions, making those rows weak baselines; (c) the real-robot evidence is one qualitative case, so sim-to-real claims rest on an n=1 demonstration; (d) the "general-purpose MLLM baseline" named in the abstract appears to be the zero-shot Qwen3.5-9B backbone rather than a distinct competing MLLM system. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built framework evaluated in simulation plus a physical robot demonstration). - Practical: Yes — fine-tuning a 9B MLLM on an 8-GPU cluster and inference on a real AUBO arm with commodity cameras are within reach of an academic lab, with 2B/4B variants for tighter budgets. - Efficient: Not quantified; the paper reports no inference latency, tokens per decision, or wall-clock packing time, which matters since long-history multimodal contexts grow with packing horizon. - Effective: In simulation, it solves the stated problem better than all baselines on easy/medium but not hard cases; in the real world, evidence is a single successful case, so effectiveness is demonstrated on a proxy (simulation benchmark) more than the deployment setting. - Scalable: Tested up to 32 objects and 4 layers; behavior beyond this (longer contexts, taller stacks, irregular non-box objects, arbitrary orientations beyond 0°/90°) is untested and acknowledged as future work. The work delivers a substantial software artifact (simulator, data engine, 20K-trajectory dataset, trained 2B/4B/9B checkpoints, benchmark) plus a reusable inverse data-generation technique, not merely a paper. Strengths: (1) The layout-first inverse data-generation engine is a real algorithmic contribution — it sidesteps forward sampling and produces physics-validated closed-loop demonstrations at 20K-trajectory scale. (2) The controlled RL retraining (same task distribution, equivalent iteration budget) is the right experiment for the paper's actual claim and is rarely done in this literature. (3) The open reporting that SDF-Pack and DBLF beat the learned policy on hard cases is an honest counter-finding that delineates where MLLM-based packing currently does and does not win. (4) The ablation set (visual, history, data scale, recipe, model size) maps the contribution to specific design decisions rather than the framework as a whole. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that hard cases remain challenging due to tighter space constraints and complex residual layouts, with heuristics retaining an advantage in densely constrained settings; that the 9B model was the largest tested due to computational resource constraints; and that future work must extend to broader object geometries and physical settings and user-defined objectives. They confront the hard-case result directly rather than burying it, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (a) The action space is severely restricted — orientations limited to 0°/90° and coordinates to a 2.5 cm grid — yet the paper claims applicability to packing generally; all training objects are effectively box-like, so the claim about "diverse object sets" means diverse dimensions, not shapes. (b) The Compactness metric (packed volume over an envelope defined by the terminal max height) can be gamed by low-volume final states and has no comparison to standard packing-quality measures in the literature. (c) No error bars or significance tests despite three-seed averaging, and the margin over SDF-Pack (0.660 vs 0.602) is within plausible seed variance for a 60-case benchmark. (d) The sim-to-real gap is examined on exactly one case with one baseline; perception noise, grasp-induced displacement, and replanning frequency are not quantified. (e) No comparison against a non-MLLM supervised-learning baseline (e.g., a supervised behavior-cloned small policy on the same PackData-20K), so it is impossible to tell whether the MLLM backbone is necessary or a smaller sequence model trained on the same data would match it — this is the most important missing ablation for the paper's central claim. (f) No inference-cost accounting against the millisecond-scale heuristics it outperforms. Bottom Line: A practitioner in robot packing or MLLM decision-making gains concrete value from the data-generation engine, dataset, and benchmark, but should read the hard-case rows carefully before believing MLLMs are the right tool for dense packing — for tightly constrained containers, SDF-Pack remains the stronger choice per the paper's own evidence.

IntBMoE: Integrating Block-Level Conditioning into Expert Composition for Full-Participation Mixture-of-Experts (33 ▲ )

Ran Cheng, Longfei Xu, Zheng Liu, Kaikui Liu, Xiangxiang Chu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces IntBMoE, a block-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts architecture that uses a hypernetwork to pre-compose a finite codebook of expert-pool-spanning blocks, then sparsely routes tokens to Top-k of them, decoupling expert participation from execution and memory costs. - Why it's important: Existing MoE designs force a trade-off between every expert contributing to a token (dense compute) and cheap sparse execution (few experts contribute); breaking that coupling could yield better accuracy per unit of serving cost, which matters for latency-constrained production systems. - How it does it: A learned codebook of K embeddings conditions a shared hypernetwork that merges all E expert bases per layer into K reusable multi-layer blocks (via Dual-Path Residual Gating), which are precomputed and cached at inference so tokens only pay for executing k of them. - The good: On ImageNet-1K with a parameter-matched 24M budget, IntBMoE reaches 73.76% Top-1, beating the strongest of 12 baselines (SMEAR, 71.78%) by 1.98 points, with thorough ablations, 3-seed means, and a real deployment showing 19 ms average latency and +2.4% relative UVCTR at ~5,000 QPS. - The missing: IntBMoE activates 23.1M of its 24.3M parameters and costs 4.06 GFLOPs/image — more compute than every sparse baseline tested (e.g., V-MoE at 1.92, SMEAR at 1.49) — so the accuracy gain may largely reflect spending more activated compute than the baselines, and this confound is not resolved by a compute-matched comparison. - Read it or not: Worth reading for MoE architecture researchers and anyone building parameter-merged or hypernetwork-based experts, since the participation/execution/materialization framing and cached-block composition are genuinely useful; skip it if you need large-scale LLM evidence, which is absent.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Impact (80) is the standout — released code plus a real production deployment at ~5,000 QPS — and Novelty (72) reflects the genuinely new participation/execution/materialization decoupling with cacheable full-pool composition. Rigor (65) shows disciplined evaluation (13 baselines, 3 seeds, component ablations) but is undermined by the unresolved compute-matching confound: IntBMoE spends ~2.7× the FLOPs of its strongest baselines. Completeness (55) and Resilience (50) drop because the paper minimizes that confound, the A/B control lacked any MoE, and language-modeling evidence is a single-epoch MiniPile run — the headline attribution claim would likely collapse under reviewer scrutiny. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*80 = 65.
empirical Novelty 72 Rigor 65 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 55 Resilience 50 Impact 80
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Standard sparse MoEs couple three quantities the authors argue should be independent: participation (how many experts contribute knowledge to a token's output), execution (how many are computed), and materialization (how many expert-sized parameter sets must be built/stored). Sparse routing (Switch, GShard, DeepSeek-V3 MoE) keeps execution cheap but limits each token to a few experts; dense output mixing (MMoE, PLE, Soft MoE, µMoE) gives full participation but computes every expert; parameter merging (SMEAR, Lory, DSFNet) achieves full participation in one execution but must materialize a merged parameter set per routing unit, which scales poorly. The target users are anyone training or serving MoE models — the paper's own production stake is AMap's generative recommendation system serving hundreds of millions of users under a 60 ms latency budget. The gap closed is the first architecture claimed to satisfy full participation, sparse execution, and bounded materialization simultaneously. Key Idea: Decouple expert composition from execution by pre-composing a bounded set of K reusable blocks — each a hypernetwork-generated linear combination (over the full span, not the convex hull, with 1/√E variance-preserving scaling) of all E expert bases at each internal layer — conditioned on input-independent codebook embeddings rather than tokens. Because conditioning is finite and input-independent, blocks are token-independent and cacheable; a token router then selects Top-k blocks, so every token's composition draws on the whole pool (full participation) while only k blocks are executed and only K parameter sets ever exist. Methodology: IntBMoE replaces FFN sublayers in a Transformer backbone. (1) Block-level synthesis: K learned codebook embeddings c_b pass through a shared linear-LayerNorm-ReLU hypernetwork with two linear heads producing unconstrained value and gate coefficient vectors α_v, α_g ∈ R^E; these coefficients linearly combine each internal layer's expert pool into composed value/gate weights for K blocks of depth L. (2) DPRG: each internal layer computes a value path and an RMSNorm'd gate path whose product is v ⊙ (1 + λ·SiLU(g)) with a learnable residual scale λ — nonlinear in the expert bases despite linear composition, at constant factor overhead. (3) Token-level routing: a two-layer MLP router selects Top-k blocks per token; a shared, block-conditioned sigmoid feature filter produces block-specific token views; outputs are routing-weight averaged and added to an always-active shared SwiGLU expert. Complexity is O(KED + TkD) uncached, reduced to O(TkD) at request time with cached blocks, independent of E. Critical design decisions: (a) unconstrained, variance-scaled rather than softmax-normalized coefficients (ablated: softmax normalization costs 1.1 Top-1 points — justified); (b) two-layer blocks instead of single-layer with a bigger pool (ablated: 1-layer costs ~5 points — justified); (c) the gate path (largest ablation impact, ~5.7 points on ImageNet) — justified. Training uses standard cross-entropy losses with no auxiliary routing/load-balancing loss described. Key Results: On ImageNet-1K (DeiT-Tiny-style 8-layer backbone, 24M total params, 3 seeds), IntBMoE achieves 73.76% Top-1 / 91.48% Top-5 at 4.063 GFLOPs (3.457 cached), versus the best baselines SMEAR (71.78/90.33, 1.493 GFLOPs), Expert Choice (71.70, 1.958), V-MoE (71.67, 1.920), Soft MoE (71.22, 1.656), and the dense backbone (66.40). On MiniPile (18-layer Llama-style, 1 epoch), IntBMoE gets 14.5878 PPL vs 15.0306 for the best baseline µMoE (CP). On IntTravel sequential recommendation (162.8M users), it gets HR@1 0.6852 / NDCG@5 0.7850, best but with margins of ~0.001–0.002 over several baselines. Baselines are recent and current (including 2025–2026 methods: ReMoE, DynMoE, MASS, µMoE), and are parameter-matched to ~24M. Notably, IntBMoE's activated-parameter count (23.1M) and FLOPs (4.06G) exceed nearly all baselines — V-MoE activates 5.1M at 1.92 GFLOPs — so comparisons are parameter-matched, not compute-matched. A well-designed expert-removal study (64 settings, no retraining, with scale compensation) shows every expert basis contributes (minimum drop 0.26 points), and class-conditioned routing/recipe-diversity analyses support that blocks learn distinct compositions. Production deployment: 19 ms average / 38 ms P99 latency on Alibaba PPUs, +2.4% relative UVCTR in a one-week A/B test at ~5,000 QPS. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (cached composition). The participation/execution/materialization decoupling framing and the input-independent, codebook-conditioned, pool-spanning block composition are genuinely new as a package. Individually, the ingredients are known: hypernetwork parameter generation (Ha et al.; HyperMoE), routing-weighted expert merging (SMEAR, Lory), sparse Top-k routing over blocks, and input-conditioned precomputed parameters (DSFNet) — IntBMoE's contribution is the specific decomposition that makes full-pool merging cacheable, plus DPRG, which is a modest residual-gating variant. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and cover every component (gate path, block depth, shared expert, feature filter, learnable λ, coefficient parameterization) on all three tasks. Three random seeds with mean reporting are used on all benchmarks; no error bars, variance, or significance tests are reported. Hyperparameter sensitivity (K, E, k, L) is systematically explored. The expert-removal analysis with 1/√(E−1) scale compensation is a thoughtful control. Code is released at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/DreamX-Rec/. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation is parameter-matched but not compute- or activation-matched — IntBMoE activates ~23M params vs 4–10M for sparse baselines, and a compute-matched dense or sparse control is missing; (2) the MiniPile and IntTravel results are small models/short training (1 epoch, d=768) and thin IntTravel margins (~0.0015 NDCG over µMoE) without significance testing; (3) the A/B test's control is the existing production model without any MoE, not a compute-matched alternative, and the UVCTR gain is a vendor self-report on the authors' own dataset (IntTravel is also from the same group). Not evaluated at anything beyond toy/small scale for language modeling. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS deployment component). Practical: Yes — runs on 8 Alibaba PPUs with 96 GB each, and is deployed in production under 60 ms latency. Efficient: Cached inference costs 3.457 GFLOPs and fixed 104 MB peak memory regardless of E, but this exceeds several sparse baselines (SMEAR 1.493, V-MoE 1.920 GFLOPs), so it is not compute-efficient relative to the field; cached mode uses more memory than uncached for pools below ~16 experts. Effective: It beats all tested baselines on its benchmarks, and the production UVCTR gain evidences real-world effect, but the causal attribution is weak (control lacked any MoE). Scalable: Only claimed and partially measured — FLOPs/memory-vs-E curves go to E=128 on the ImageNet config, but model scale is stuck at 24M (vision) and 18-layer/1-epoch (LM); behavior at modern MoE scales (billions of params, E in the hundreds, distributed expert sharding) is untested, and caching K full blocks could become a memory bottleneck at large d. Delivers a software artifact: released code (DreamX-Rec repository) plus a fully deployed production model. Strengths: - The participation/execution/materialization taxonomy is a clean, reusable lens that crisply explains why sparse routing, dense mixing, and parameter merging each fail, and the architecture is derived directly from it rather than bolted on. - The input-independent codebook conditioning is the key non-obvious move: it converts hypernetwork-generated merged experts (normally per-token, uncacheable) into a finite, precomputable set — directly fixing the materialization blow-up that limits SMEAR-style methods. - Evaluation discipline above typical industry papers: 13 parameter-matched baselines including very recent work, component ablations on every task, 3-seed means, hyperparameter sweeps, and a compensating-scale expert-removal experiment that actually tests the "full participation" claim rather than assuming it. - Cached inference genuinely decouples request-time cost from expert-pool size (measured flat at 104 MB / 3.457 GFLOPs from E=16 to 128), which is the property that made production deployment under 60 ms feasible. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper does not include a dedicated limitations section. Implicitly acknowledged scope boundaries: primary quantitative claims rest on an 8-layer 24M-param vision model (larger-scale results are deferred to the deployment anecdote), the IntBMoE composition term is linear in E before caching, and the A/B control is the non-MoE production baseline. The authors do not confront the activated-parameter/FLOPs disadvantage relative to sparse baselines; the paper reports these numbers in Table 1 but never discusses the compute-matching confound, which reads as minimizing it. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No compute-matched baseline: IntBMoE uses 2.7× the FLOPs of SMEAR and ~2× that of V-MoE/Expert Choice while activating 4–5× more parameters; a strong dense backbone or sparse MoE given the same 4 GFLOPs budget is absent, so the +2-point gain over SMEAR cannot be attributed to the architecture alone. - The "full participation" claim is architectural, not functional: because blocks are input-independent, IntBMoE with K=8, k=2 is functionally close to a standard sparse MoE with 8 fixed experts (plus a shared expert); the paper's own recipe-similarity analysis (cosine similarity 0.796 across blocks at layer 0) suggests early-layer blocks are nearly identical. A direct comparison against a plain Top-2 sparse MoE with 8 large experts is not reported. - Language-modeling evidence is minimal (1 epoch on MiniPile at d=768); no downstream-task, scaling-law, or expert-count-at-scale results, so the central decoupling claim is untested where MoEs are actually used (multi-billion-parameter LLMs, distributed expert parallelism). - The cacheability advantage degrades when composition must be token- or request-conditioned (the regime where merged experts are most attractive); the paper does not explore input-conditioned variants that retain caching. - IntTravel is a dataset from the same author group, and the headline deployment metric (+2.4% UVCTR) is a self-reported A/B against a weaker control — both warrant discounted confidence. Bottom Line: This is a genuinely interesting and well-executed MoE architecture paper whose participation/execution/materialization framing and cacheable full-pool composition are worth any MoE researcher's time, but the headline accuracy gains are confounded by higher activated compute than its baselines and are only demonstrated at small scale, so practitioners should treat it as a promising design direction rather than a validated replacement for sparse MoE at production LLM scale.

Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing (29 ▲ )

Ji Xie, Dewei Zhou, Xinyu Huang, Zhennan Chen, Xun Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Paint-Anything, a finetuning recipe and dataset (Paint-500K) that teaches a rectified-flow image model to follow explicit 24-bit hex color specifications per object for both text-to-image generation and image editing through a single prompt-native interface. - Why it's important: Professional design workflows (brand logos, product imagery) require exact color values, not words like "blue"; current T2I models degrade sharply when color words are replaced by raw hex strings (FLUX.2-4B's CompColor average drops from 0.72 to 0.38). - How it does it: It wraps hex codes in explicit <color></color> tokens in the prompt, supervises object-level hex grounding via MeanShift clustering in CIELAB on real images, and adds solid-color "pure-color anchor" samples restricted to high-noise timesteps (t ∈ [0.8, 1]) to give a clean hex-to-RGB mapping without corrupting low-noise semantics. - The good: On the same 8B backbone, finetuning lifts ACBench-T2I from 37.02 to 68.58 and ACBench-Edit from 58.90 to 75.57, allowing the 8B model to beat the 56B FLUX.2-dev (51.70 / 68.87), with an ablation table isolating each recipe component. - The missing: Paint-500K is built from an internal, non-public image collection, so the core data contribution cannot be rebuilt or independently verified; the authors also do not test whether the recipe harms general (non-color) image quality beyond a small 200-judgment preference check. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on controllable T2I generation, color fidelity, or data-centric finetuning of flow models; skippable for practitioners who only need named-color control, where existing models are already stronger.
Why this rank

Rigor (65) is above average for the strong ablations and independent-benchmark transfer, but dragged down by single-seed evaluation, a non-public training set, and a self-authored headline benchmark. empirical Novelty 72 Rigor 65 Non-Obv 75 Completeness 55 Resilience 60 Impact 55
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Designers, brand teams, and e-commerce pipelines need to specify object colors as exact 24-bit hex values, but current text-to-image models treat color as fuzzy language: swapping a color word for its hex code collapses FLUX.2-4B's compositional color-binding score from 0.72 to 0.38. Prior color-control work splits into task-specific learned representations (learnable color tokens, numeric-color encoders), training-free inference-time guidance, and specialized editing/colorization systems — each difficult to transfer across architectures, costly at inference, or limited to a single task. The gap is a single, prompt-native capability where any hex value can be bound to any object across both generation and editing without extra modules or inference-time optimization. Key Idea: Hex strings are already text-legible to the frozen text encoder, so color control can be learned as pure prompt-following via object-level hex supervision — with the critical trick that noisy real-image color labels are repaired by "pure-color anchors" (solid-color images paired with their exact hex) trained only at high-noise timesteps t ∈ [t_gate, 1], where the model's color statistics stabilize early in the generation trajectory (empirically near t ≈ 0.8), leaving low-noise training to natural images so anchor supervision helps generation without degrading editing fidelity. Methodology: The base is a rectified-flow T2I model (flow-matching objective L_FM = E‖v_θ − (ε − z₀)‖²) with frozen text encoder and VAE; editing samples concatenate a clean source-image latent z_c to the noisy target latent, so generation and editing share one denoising objective. Training minimizes L = λ_t2i·L_t2i + λ_edit·L_edit + λ_rgb·L_rgb (all λ = 1) over three streams: (1) Paint-500K T2I data — VLM (Seed1.8) grounds caption-relevant objects, SAM3 produces masks, MeanShift in normalized CIELAB (bandwidth 0.05) extracts dominant colors with coverage filters (≥15% cluster, ≥90% joint coverage), and a VLM rewrites captions inserting <color>#HEX</color> spans; 400K samples (100K single-object crops, 300K multi-object); (2) 100K editing pairs — a pretrained editing model (Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Lightning) recolors a real image to create the source, with the original photograph as target; (3) 10K solid-color anchors at 512×512, sampled only for t ∈ [0.8, 1]. Full finetuning (not LoRA) of the denoising transformer for 4,000 steps on 4 GPUs, batch 72 (30 T2I / 30 edit / 12 anchors), lr 2×10⁻⁵. Critical design decisions: tag wrapping (well-justified by ablation: +13.1 T2I points over bare-hex finetuning), MeanShift over fixed-K k-means (motivated qualitatively, Figure 5, but not ablated quantitatively), and the timestep gate (well-justified: t_gate = 0.8 beats ungated by 4.75 T2I / 5.18 Edit points, with low sensitivity across 0.7–1.0). Key Results: On ACBench (authors' new benchmark; 1000 T2I + 500 edit prompts), FLUX.2-4B + Paint-Anything scores 68.58 T2I overall (Single 72.67 / Two 64.49) and 75.57 Edit, versus the base model's 37.02 and 58.90 — the stated 85.3% and 28.3% improvements. It beats the strongest specialized baselines by 22.04 points over ColorWave on T2I and 15.19 points over ColorBind/Edit on Edit, and exceeds the 56B FLUX.2-dev by 16.88 (T2I) and 6.70 (Edit) points. The recipe transfers to Z-Image Base (53.77 T2I). On independent benchmarks: hex-prompt CompColor average rises from 0.38 to 0.79 (also beating the base's named-color 0.72), and GenColorBench NCU improves from 34.00 to 57.89, above the quoted FLUX + NumColor result (51.90). A user study (15 participants, 80 prompts) gives an 80.9% non-tie win rate on color preference but a near-tie 52.4% on image quality. Notably, Paint-Anything had the highest SAM3 localization-failure rate (5.50% vs 0.17–4.17% for baselines); excluding failures raises its T2I score to 70.93. Editing quality is strongest for large color shifts (Q4 quartile 88.9 vs base 56.3; near-complementary 86.9 vs 50.8). Baselines include current strong systems (Qwen-Image/Edit 27B, FLUX.2 family, Z-Image), though NumColor was not rerun (published scores used) and ColorWave was the authors' own reproduction. Testing is at standard academic scale (4B–10B backbones, 4,000 training steps). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (timestep-gated pure-color anchors for hex grounding) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (Paint-500K pipeline and ACBench) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (prompt-native hex control as a unified generation/editing capability). The genuinely novel elements are the high-noise gating of exact-color anchors — a non-obvious schedule insight — and the demonstration that an 8B finetuned model can surpass a 56B model on color fidelity. The remaining machinery (flow matching, VLM grounding, SAM segmentation, CIELAB clustering, instruction-editing data synthesis) is a competent combination of known techniques; MeanShift over k-means and <color> tag wrapping are incremental refinements. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: Table 2 isolates full finetuning vs rank-256 LoRA (68.58 vs 48.45 T2I), wrapping, anchors, and gating; Table 3 sweeps the gate threshold; Appendix I sweeps anchor resolution; Appendix H stress-tests the evaluation across five region-color estimators, a 36-setting SAM3 threshold/coverage grid (gap stability +0.248 to +0.331), and a localization-failure audit. However: no error bars or multi-seed runs are reported (one image per T2I prompt, one seed); a 96/100 manual spot check is the only label-quality audit; Paint-500K's source images and ACBench-Edit source images come from internal, non-public collections, and no code, data, or checkpoint release is stated in the paper. Methodological concerns: ACBench is the authors' own benchmark, and the MAE-to-score mapping (full credit at MAE ≤ 16) is a design choice that favors flat-colored objects, though transfer to CompColor and the official GenColorBench NCU protocol mitigates Goodhart risk; NumColor is compared only via quoted published numbers; the editing training data's sources are generated by a third-party editing model, which could leak that model's editing priors into the evaluated editing task. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a released-method character, though no artifact release is stated). - Practical: Yes — finetuning runs on 4 GPUs for 4,000 steps, and inference is a standard flow-model forward pass with no extra controller. - Efficient: Training cost is modest (4 GPUs, 4,000 steps, batch 72); inference adds zero overhead over the base model since color control lives entirely in the text prompt. - Effective: Evidence covers exact-color generation, two-object binding, and real-image recoloring across three benchmarks plus a human study, so the core claim is supported beyond a proxy — though the near-tie image-quality preference (52.4%) means general fidelity is unproven. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 4B–10B backbones and 500K samples; claims of transfer across backbones are shown for two models only, and behavior on palette-level or many-object prompts (beyond a 3-object CompColor extension) is unexplored. The paper stops at paper form in the provided text — no public code, dataset, or model release is mentioned. Strengths: - The timestep-gated pure-color anchor is a real, non-obvious insight: it resolves the tension between exact color supervision and noisy natural-image labels, and the paper grounds it mechanistically (early color stabilization in pure-color trajectories, Appendix E) rather than presenting it as a tuned hack. - The head-to-head result that an 8B finetuned model beats the 56B base model by 16.88 points on hex fidelity is a striking, capability-over-scale finding with practical weight. - Evaluation hygiene is above average for a system paper: independent-benchmark transfer (CompColor hex protocol, official GenColorBench NCU), a five-estimator robustness sweep, a 36-setting mask-threshold sweep, a localization-failure audit that counts against the authors' own model, and an explicit train/eval string-overlap check (Appendix L). - The editing-data construction (generated source, real target) is a clean design that keeps target images free of generative artifacts. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section is thin — the authors state only that training data lack palette-specific supervision and that future work could extend the interface to broader color-control tasks. They do not directly confront data non-disclosure, the self-authored benchmark, single-seed evaluation, or the image-quality near-tie in the user study (though Appendix K honestly qualifies the study as descriptive and warns about dependence in the judgments — a credibility positive). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Reproducibility: Paint-500K's source image collection is internal and not released; without it, the data pipeline — the paper's second contribution — cannot be reproduced or independently validated. - The ACBench metric rewards region-mean color matching, which a model could satisfy by rendering unnaturally flat, texture-free objects; no texture/material-fidelity metric or image-quality benchmark (e.g., FID/HPS on general prompts) is reported to rule out a capability-for-quality trade, and the 52.4% image-quality win rate hints at one. - Single seed and single sample per prompt mean no variance estimate; several headline margins (e.g., vs FLUX.2-dev) are large enough to survive this, but finer comparisons may not be. - The editing stream trains on sources produced by Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, so ACBench-Edit gains may partly reflect distillation of that editing model rather than pure hex grounding; no control experiment isolates this. - MeanShift-vs-k-means is argued from one qualitative figure; no quantitative ablation of the clustering choice on label accuracy or downstream scores. - General-prompt regression (does heavy hex finetuning hurt normal T2I quality, prompt diversity, or other attributes?) is unmeasured beyond CompColor named-color scores. Bottom Line: For researchers building controllable or instruction-following image generators, this is worth reading for the timestep-gated anchor trick and the unusually careful evaluation-transfer checks; practitioners needing exact-color control today will find the demonstrated gains compelling, but the undisclosed training data and unreleased artifacts mean most readers will consume the recipe, not the system.

OmniEcho: Spatial Audio Understanding for Embodied Agents (20 ▲ )

Ruixun Liu, Yuxuan Wang, Jiacheng Xie, Yuhuan You, Donghua Cai, Junming Lin, Xiong-Hui Chen, Zhifang Guo, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Yiwu Zhong · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OmniEchoBench, a real-world benchmark of 2,972 spatial audio-visual QA pairs and 900 sound-guided navigation episodes over 30 real scanned indoor scenes with first-order ambisonics (FOA) audio, plus OmniEcho, a Qwen3-Omni-30B-based model with a dedicated FOA spatial encoder for these tasks. - Why it's important: Embodied agents currently cannot localize sound sources outside the camera's field of view the way humans can, and no existing benchmark evaluates spatial audio understanding in real-world embodied settings — this blocks progress on agents that find occluded or out-of-view targets by sound. - How it does it: A frozen ~12M-parameter FOA encoder (trained in two stages for CLIP-aligned semantics and query-conditioned azimuth/elevation/distance regression) injects spatial tokens via a trainable projector into a Qwen3-Omni backbone alongside its frozen mono semantic audio pathway, trained on ~363k examples synthesized with a trajectory-consistent FOA rendering pipeline. - The good: The benchmark is built from real human-performed recordings with 2 Hz panoramic-video-annotated source trajectories and deterministic ground-truth answers, and the model beats all evaluated omni baselines on it (28.5% vs. 18.5% for Qwen3-Omni-30B and 11.4% for Spatial-Omni-7B overall in the audio-visual setting), with a credible sim-to-real experiment showing +6.4 points from only 1,000 real samples. - The missing: Absolute performance is low (28.5% QA accuracy, 16.2% navigation success rate with 36.7% of episodes entering the 1 m goal region but failing to stop), the headline comparisons are on the authors' own benchmark against only four omni baselines, and the VLN-CE R2R result (22.2% SR) trails strong text-guided baselines by 28 points. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on audio-visual embodied AI or spatial audio understanding — the real-FOA benchmark and failure-mode analysis are genuinely useful reference points; skip it if you want a validated navigation method, since the navigation evidence is weaker than text-guided VLN alternatives.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is the driver: the first real-recorded FOA spatial-audio benchmark with deterministic trajectory-grounded answers plus a credible dual-pathway integration finding (un-pretrained or unfrozen spatial encoders add nothing or hurt). Completeness (75) is high due to unusually candid failure analysis — oracle success 52.89% vs. 16.22% SR honestly dissected — while Rigor (58) is limited by self-referential training/eval on the same 197-scene distribution, generous scoring tolerances with no human ceiling, and an unconfirmed ('will be available') release. Impact (62) reflects a valuable reference benchmark but preliminary, non-deployable model performance (16.2% navigation SR, trailing text-guided VLN by ~28 points). Composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*62 = 65.

Problem & Motivation: Embodied agents that navigate and reason in homes and workplaces cannot exploit spatial hearing: existing omni-modal models process audio as mono semantic content, existing VLN systems are vision-text driven, and existing audio-visual navigation work (SoundSpaces, AVLEN, RILA) evaluates only on simulated acoustics. Collecting real spatial audio is expensive because the received signal depends jointly on source/listener pose, scene geometry, reflections, and reverberation, and prior benchmarks therefore rely on rendered acoustics with a sim-to-real gap. The gap the paper closes is the absence of (a) a real-recorded FOA benchmark covering off-screen and dynamic sound sources and (b) a training recipe for injecting spatial audio into pretrained omni-modal LLMs without destroying their semantic audio ability. Key Idea: The core trick is a dual-pathway audio design: keep the pretrained semantic audio tower untouched on the down-mixed mono W channel, and add a parallel frozen FOA encoder whose spatial tokens (from a 5-channel map of W log-mel, DirAC active-intensity ix/iy/iz, and diffuseness) are projected into reserved placeholder embedding slots inserted after the semantic audio tokens. Because the FOA encoder is separately pretrained for semantics (SigLIP alignment to frozen CLIP text embeddings, class-balanced for ~0.3% positive rate over 644 labels) and then for query-conditioned localization, the expensive spatial capability is acquired before instruction tuning, and freezing it during stage 3 avoids interference — the ablation confirms that unfreezing it degrades every subtask and that a naive FOA encoder without the two pretraining stages brings no gain. Methodology: The pipeline has three parts. (1) Benchmark construction: 197 real scripted recordings (first-person video + 360° panorama + 4-channel FOA at 48 kHz) with annotators labeling source positions at 2 Hz from the panorama; QA ground truths are computed deterministically from trajectories across eight subtypes (direction, 3D localization, source motion, camera rotation, cognitive map). OmniEchoBench-Nav densely samples FOA receiver grids (12–17 receivers/scene on ~1 m grid) in 30 real scanned scenes, with 900 navigation episodes evaluated closed-loop in Habitat using nearest-receiver audio rotated into the agent's egocentric frame. (2) Data synthesis: an LLM "director" produces JSON scene specifications (source trajectories, LUFS loudness, visibility windows), Seedance generates video, monocular depth and open-vocabulary segmentation recover the actual source geometry from pixels, off-screen sources and camera yaw are appended, and everything is rendered to FOA via real spherical harmonics with optional image-source reflections; VLN corpora (R2R, RxR, ScaleVLN, VLN-PE) are converted to sound-guided supervision by placing TTS/Seedance sounds at episode endpoints with 1/r attenuation and CoT annotation. (3) Model: the three-stage FOA encoder training described above, then stage 3 trains only the projector and LLM of Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B on 363,193 examples (32×A100, ~4 days). Design decisions — feature-based (feat5) rather than raw-waveform FOA input, (sin, cos) angular encoding to avoid wrap-around, and encoder freezing — are each justified by ablations (17.9° vs. 30.5° azimuth error; overall 28.5% frozen vs. 26.2% unfrozen). Key Results: On OmniEchoBench-QA (audio-visual), OmniEcho reaches 28.5% overall accuracy vs. 18.5% for its own backbone Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, 12.6% for Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, and 11.4% for Spatial-Omni (SO-7B); the Cognitive Map subtask shows the largest gain (47.5% vs. 20.0–22.8%), while absolute 3D Localization accuracy is only 14.2%. On OmniEchoBench-Nav, OmniEcho achieves 16.2% SR / 11.5% SPL, below InternVLA-N1 with text instructions (17.8% / 16.7%) but above Seq2Seq (11.3%) and CMA (9.8%); SoundSpaces with converted binaural audio collapses to 5.4% SR. On VLN-CE R2R val-unseen, OmniEcho gets 22.2% SR / 16.3% SPL — above Seq2Seq and CMA but far behind VLN-R1 (30.2%), NAViLA-SAGE (38.0%), and InternVLA-N1 (50.6% SR). The failure analysis is the most diagnostic result: oracle success is 52.89% but SR is 16.22% (36.67% of episodes enter the 1 m goal region and still fail to stop), distance MAE is 2.20 m with Pearson r = 0.27, and ground-truth direction guidance raises SR only to 23.7% while SPL doubles to 22.1%. Baselines on the QA benchmark are current omni models but few in number; navigation baselines are a mix of outdated (Seq2Seq, CMA from 2020) and recent (InternVLA-N1) systems, and no FOA-capable navigation baseline exists by construction. Tested scale: 30 real scenes, ~10 minutes of recordings, single physical robot demonstration. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first real-world FOA benchmark unifying spatial audio-visual QA and sound-guided navigation) + NEW METHOD (the dual-pathway semantic/spatial audio integration and three-stage FOA encoder recipe) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the trajectory-consistent FOA rendering and VLN-augmentation pipeline) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (existing omni models fail at real spatial audio; audio guidance approaches early text-VLN performance). The FOA encoder itself is a standard conv-Transformer with SigLIP alignment, and spherical-harmonic ambisonics rendering is textbook — the genuine novelty is the real-recorded benchmark with deterministic trajectory-grounded ground truth and the empirical demonstration that spatial tokens and semantic tokens are complementary, not the individual components. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: native vs. FOA encoder, frozen vs. tuned encoder, feat5 vs. raw4 input, with/without Stage-1 pretraining, and a sim-to-real split (1,000 real training samples raise overall accuracy from 28.5% to 34.9%, +10.9 on Source Motion). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere. Scoring combines LLM-based answer normalization (qwen3.7-flash) with deterministic rules — reproducible in principle, but the ±45° angular tolerance and ±2 m distance tolerance are generous, and no human-agreement ceiling on those tolerances is given. Code and data are promised at a GitHub URL (PKU-VaLuE-Lab/OmniEcho) but the text says "will be available" — not confirmed released. Methodological concerns: the model is trained on synthetic data aligned in distribution to its own benchmark and the sim-to-real fine-tuning splits the benchmark itself (train/test on the same 197 scenes' distribution), so headline numbers are partly self-referential; the QA baseline pool is small (four models, all from the Qwen/GLM families); navigation metrics use a 1 m success radius on their own benchmark versus 3 m on VLN-CE, which inflates cross-benchmark comparisons; and the sim-to-real gain from benchmark-derived data partially measures distribution matching rather than general spatial ability. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (benchmark + trained model, evaluated in simulation and one robot demo). - Practical: Inference runs on a Qwen3-Omni-30B MoE (~3B active parameters), feasible on a single data-center GPU; training required a 32×A100 cluster, out of reach for most academic labs. - Efficient: The FOA encoder adds only ~12M parameters and 384-d tokens at a 7 Hz resampled grid, so overhead over the backbone is modest; however, the 4-day × 32-GPU training and dense real-world acoustic-field collection (12,900 recordings) are the dominant costs. - Effective: Perception evidence is real but the ceiling is low (28.5% QA accuracy, 14.2% on 3D localization, distance Pearson r = 0.27), and navigation solves the stated problem only partially — 47% of episodes never reach the goal region. - Scalable: Not tested; the authors claim the synthesis pipeline scales supervision, but scaling behavior beyond the current 363k examples and 30 scenes is unexamined, and the physical-robot deployment is a single qualitative episode. The work delivers (or promises) a concrete artifact: benchmark, rendering pipeline, model weights, and code at the stated GitHub repo, contingent on the "will be available" release actually happening. Strengths: - The benchmark's ground truth is deterministic and trajectory-derived rather than LLM-judged, with panoramic-video annotation at 2 Hz, per-category answer-bucket balancing, and explicit scoring tolerances — a more auditable construction than most MLLM benchmarks. - The dual-pathway design with a frozen spatial encoder is empirically justified: the ablation showing that an un-pretrained FOA encoder adds nothing and that unfreezing during stage 3 hurts every subtask is a real, transferable finding about how to inject a new modality into a pretrained omni LLM. - The failure-mode analysis (52.89% oracle success vs. 16.22% SR; OS–SR gap partially attributable to the action-execution protocol, which the authors honestly flag rather than over-attribute to stopping) is unusually candid and actionable. - The distributional-alignment reporting for synthetic data (JSD = 0.14 bits on source types, KS = 0.20 on distances, matched medians of 2.8 m) quantifies a sim-to-real concern most synthetic-data papers leave unstated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge (1) that synthetic training data introduces bias, mitigated only by distribution alignment and demonstrated partially correctable with small amounts of real data; (2) that fine-grained spatial localization and distance estimation remain open challenges, illustrated with failure cases (135° predicted vs. 47° actual camera rotation); (3) that reliable stopping and efficient navigation are unresolved, with the caveat that the OS–SR gap cannot be attributed solely to stopping errors; (4) that baseline task formulations cannot be fully aligned in the navigation comparison; and (5) that spatial-audio guidance still trails strong text-guided VLN systems, especially in path efficiency. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The "state-of-the-art" claim applies only to the authors' own benchmark with four baselines, none of which is a dedicated spatial-audio-language system other than SO-7B (which the authors argue suffers a sim-to-real gap without testing that explanation); established spatial-audio MLLMs like BAT are cited but not compared. - The sim-to-real experiment trains and tests on disjoint subsets of the same 197-scene benchmark, so the 34.9% number partially reflects distribution matching on the evaluation set rather than real-world generalization. - QA scoring tolerances (±45°, ±2 m) are generous but no inter-annotator or human-performance ceiling is reported, so it is unknown how far models are from human performance on the same protocol. - Only 20 of 197 scenes are outdoor and the LLM extractor (qwen3.7-flash) itself is a potential noise source; extractor accuracy against gold-normalized answers is not reported. - The nearest-receiver audio delivery approximates a continuous acoustic field with hard switches between fixed microphones as the agent moves; the perceptual artifacts of this switching on the model are unanalyzed. - Multi-source scenes, dynamic sources during navigation, and reverberation-heavy multi-room acoustics are trained with simplifications (direct-path propagation for ScaleVLN/VLN-PE), so the model's robustness to richer acoustic scenes than the training distribution is untested. Bottom Line: This is the most credible real-world FOA benchmark and data pipeline currently available for spatially aware embodied agents, and the failure analysis alone justifies a read by anyone building audio-visual agents — but the model results are preliminary, absolute performance is far from deployable, and the strongest claims are self-referential, so treat it primarily as a benchmark-and-findings paper rather than a validated navigation solution.

GameHorizon Suite: Multi-Horizon Data and Evaluation in Gameplay (111 ▲ )

Yiran Wang, Xingyilang Yin, Junfu Pu, Guangzhi Wang, Kaifeng Li, Mingyu Ouyang, Huiqiang Sun, Lingen Li, Cheng Cheng, Wangbo Yu, Honghao Chen, Xiaodong Cun, Chi-Man Pun, Zhiguo Cao, Ying Shan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 22 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GameHorizon Suite, a three-part artifact — an automated annotation pipeline, a 5,000-hour AAA-gameplay dataset with aligned video/actions/multi-horizon instructions, and a hybrid offline/online benchmark — for evaluating gameplay capabilities across temporal horizons and model families. - Why it's important: Existing game datasets cover single titles (mostly Minecraft), lack language-instruction annotations, and rely on low-sample online rollouts (e.g., 3 trials per scene), so reported comparisons across game agents and general-purpose VLMs are neither reproducible nor diagnostically useful. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a bottom-up annotation pyramid: action-aware segmentation of human-recorded keyboard-mouse traces into short clips, progressive VLM-driven merging into medium- and long-horizon clips, and per-level instruction synthesis, which then feeds both a 5,000-question MCQ offline benchmark and a stepwise online track with game-reset-based failure localization. - The good: The evaluation scale is unusually large and credible — 47 models, over one million model invocations, a 35.6-point accuracy spread (44.6% to 80.2%), and an offline–online rank correlation validated on 12 models that shows the cheap offline track is a usable proxy for actual gameplay. - The missing: The online track — the part that validates the whole offline proxy claim — runs entirely in Minecraft, not in the AAA games the dataset and offline benchmark cover, so the offline-to-AAA-gameplay association is never directly tested. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate game agents, VLA models, or interactive VLM benchmarks and need a large annotated gameplay corpus or a standardized scoreboard; skip it if you want new modeling techniques — the paper trains no models and contributes data, annotation tooling, and evaluation only.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) and Impact (70) are solid — a genuinely new AAA-scale gameplay corpus with a sharp bottom-up/top-down design argument and a promised artifact suite — but Rigor (60) is dragged down by unvalidated VLM annotation, no error bars, and the online proxy validation confined to 12 models and 20 Minecraft tasks, which also caps Resilience (55) since the central offline-to-AAA-gameplay claim is extrapolated rather than measured. Completeness (62) benefits from direct limitation acknowledgment but is reduced by the absent annotation audit and missing training experiments. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*70 = 64.

Problem & Motivation: Game-playing AI splits into two disconnected communities: dedicated game agents (Open-P2P, JARVIS-VLA, NitroGen) optimized for high-frequency action control but weak at planning, and general-purpose VLMs/agents (Gemini, GPT, Claude) strong at planning but never systematically measured on action execution, with only bespoke, incomparable demos like Gemini/Claude playing Pokémon. Practitioners lack a dataset with (a) diverse AAA titles rather than Minecraft or mini-games, (b) human-recorded actions rather than IDM-inferred pseudo-labels, (c) dense language instructions for instruction following and goal decomposition, and (d) a reproducible evaluation that does not collapse distinct failure modes into a single online success rate. Prior corpora are single-game (MineDojo, VPT, WildWorld), instruction-free (NitroGen, D2E, gaming-500-hours), small (300–500 hours for D2E and gaming-500-hours), or manually annotated and unreleased (Game-TARS). Key Idea: The core insight is that multi-horizon instruction structure can be produced bottom-up rather than top-down: because VLMs cannot reliably interpret hour-long gameplay, first segment video using the recorded keyboard-mouse action stream itself (key action transitions define clip boundaries, with VLM disambiguation of input semantics), then recursively merge clips upward — L1 operations (1–5 s) → L2 goals (1–2 min) → L3 strategies (5–8 min) — having the VLM synthesize each level's instruction from frames, actions, and the constituent lower-level instructions. The paper's second, evaluation-side insight is the deliberate asymmetry that bottom-up abstraction (L1→L2) is nearly determined and hence good for annotation, while top-down decomposition (L2→L1) is underdetermined and hence good as a hard benchmark task — an argument the paper supports empirically (98.4% vs. 69.5% accuracy). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Data collection: 100 trained human players record 5,000 hours across 21 games at 2K/60 fps with timestamped keyboard-mouse events (20 Hz mouse, 2.84 keyboard events/s), followed by automated and VLM-based quality filtering that retains 86.8% of footage for annotation. (2) GameHorizon-Annotator: action-aware segmentation (keybind-based semantic mapping → primitive-action classification → rule-based coarse segmentation → VLM refinement), bottom-up temporal merging with a dynamic-programming constraint enforcing level-specific duration ranges (Bellman-style DP over clip boundaries), and per-level VLM annotation with prompts differing in inputs (actions included at L1/L2, excluded at L3) and granularity. (3) GameHorizon-Bench: an offline track of 5,000 four-option MCQs (T1 single-horizon action, T2 multi-horizon decomposition, T3 cross-horizon consistency, 1,000 each; ten diagnostic variants at 200 each) and an online track of 20 long-horizon Minecraft tasks (10 causal, 10 thematic; 62 subtasks) with environment resets on subtask failure and a 400-call budget per subtask. Game agents that cannot answer MCQs are scored on T1 via Needleman–Wunsch sequence alignment against options. Key design decisions: direct human action recording instead of IDM inference (well-justified — pseudo-label deviation is a known failure mode), bottom-up annotation justified by the top-down/bottom-up variant experiment, and Minecraft for the online track (justified only by AAA games lacking accessible game-state APIs — a pragmatic but consequential choice). No objective function is involved; this is a data/annotation/evaluation system, not a learning method. Key Results: Offline (44 QA-capable models): mean accuracy 64.7% over T1–T3, range 44.6% (InternVL-U-4B) to 80.2% (GPT-6-Astra), against a 25% random baseline; difficulty hierarchy T1 = 57.3% < T2 = 65.1% < T3 = 71.6%. Proprietary models take 10 of 11 Tier-1 slots; Kimi-K3 is the only open-weight model in Tier 1 (74.5%). Dedicated game agents score 22.0–28.1% on unseen AAA games — near or below random — while JARVIS-VLA reaches 54.2% in-domain on VPT/Minecraft, demonstrating severe domain dependence. Diagnostic variants (4 models): short-horizon instructions lift current-action perception by 14.1 points (44.5% → 58.6%) and multi-horizon instructions lift future-action planning by 7.0 points (34.8% → 41.8%); bottom-up abstraction saturates at 98.4% while top-down decomposition sits at 69.5% (28.9-point gap); action-decoding adds only 0.6 points of error to cross-horizon consistency, localizing the bottleneck in goal decomposition rather than action decoding. Thinking mode helps strong models (Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro +9.3 points) and hurts weak ones (UI-TARS-1.5-7B −8.2 points). Online (12 models): success rates align with offline tiers (Tier-1 models occupy online ranks 1–3; Tier-4 models ranks 10–12); best long-horizon success is GPT-6-Astra at 45.0%, with 10 of 12 models at ≤10%. Scale: standard-plus for a benchmark (5,000 MCQs, 21 games), but the online track is small (20 tasks). Baselines compared are current frontier models, which strengthens the results' currency. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the offline–online rank association and the perception-vs-planning gap). The genuinely novel elements are the combination of AAA-game scale (5,000 hours, 21 titles) with direct human-recorded actions and a dense three-level instruction pyramid — no prior corpus provides all three — plus the stepwise online protocol with reset-based failure localization. The annotation pipeline itself is a competent assembly of known techniques (keybind mapping, VLM captioning, DP-constrained segmentation merging) applied to a new setting, and the offline MCQ format is a standard benchmark design. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the T1–T3 variants isolate the effect of instruction horizons, decomposition direction, and action decoding, and the thinking-mode analysis adds a useful negative result. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and MCQ accuracy on 1,000 questions is the only uncertainty signal. The annotation pipeline relies on a single VLM (Gemini) whose instruction quality is never quantitatively validated against human labels — no inter-annotator agreement, no manual audit sample, no instruction-quality metrics are reported. The online track uses only 12 models and 20 tasks sampled for cost. Code, dataset, and benchmark are promised for release (project page and GitHub given: gamehorizon-suite.github.io, github.com/TencentARC/GameHorizon), but the paper text says "will release," so public availability is not yet verified. Methodological concerns: (a) the benchmark is built from the same VLM-annotated data it evaluates on, so models could exploit annotator-style artifacts; (b) MCQ distractor construction is described only at a high level, leaving distractor-leakage risk unexamined; (c) scoring game agents via sequence alignment against MCQ options is a nonstandard hack whose threshold choices are not ablated. Vendor-API model results (GPT, Gemini, Claude, Doubao) are self-reported-by-proxy through API access, though the MCQ protocol is standardized. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (built data pipeline and benchmark, evaluated by running it). - Practical: Yes for the offline track — standard API calls or single-GPU local serving of open models; the online track requires a Minecraft harness, which is freely available. - Efficient: Offline evaluation costs 5,000 MCQs per model (with 200-question sampling for variants), modest by current standards; the online track is expensive (up to 400 model calls per subtask, which is why only 12 models were tested). - Effective: The evidence shows the offline track solves its proxy-validation goal for the 12 tested models in Minecraft, but the demonstrated effectiveness is for ranking and diagnosis, not for replacing online evaluation on AAA titles. - Scalable: Not tested — the paper does not run 10× more games, longer horizons, or more models; the annotator's per-frame VLM calls over 4,341 hours imply significant annotation compute, but no cost figures are given. The work delivers a concrete artifact suite (dataset, annotator, benchmark) intended for public release, plus reusable prompts and keybind tables. Strengths: (1) Scale and provenance of the data asset: 5,000 hours of directly recorded human keyboard-mouse actions across 21 AAA titles avoids the IDM-pseudo-label noise that plagues VPT/D2E-style corpora, and 6.18M instructions at one distinct L1 instruction per 2.63 seconds is an order of magnitude denser than Open-P2P. (2) The bottom-up-annotation/top-down-evaluation asymmetry is a genuinely sharp design argument, backed by the 98.4%-vs-69.5% variant experiment rather than asserted. (3) The offline–online validation, while limited in scope, is a step almost no competing gameplay benchmark takes — most report online rollouts only or offline proxies only, and never test the link. (4) The bottleneck-localization findings (perception 9.9–23.8 points above planning; action decoding only 0.6 points of added error) give model builders actionable diagnosis, and the thinking-mode trade-off is a useful, non-obvious negative result. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the online track is implemented in Minecraft because underlying game states are inaccessible in most AAA titles, that the online track was limited to 12 models and 20 tasks due to evaluation cost, and that variant tasks were sampled at 200 questions for cost reasons. They also note that bottom-up abstraction saturates (98.4%), limiting its discriminability. They confront these limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which is credible, but they do not discuss annotation-quality validation or the offline/AAA-generalization gap. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The central validation claim — offline scores predict real gameplay — is tested only in Minecraft with 12 models and 20 tasks, yet the dataset and offline benchmark are AAA games; the offline-to-AAA-gameplay association, which is what the benchmark is actually for, is extrapolated, not measured. (2) No human verification of the VLM-generated instructions: a systematic annotator bias (e.g., Gemini's descriptive style or hallucinated action semantics) would propagate into both the dataset and the benchmark's ground truth, and the paper reports no audit. (3) No training experiments: the paper never fine-tunes any model on GameHorizon-Data, so the dataset's value as a training corpus — its headline scale claim — is untested; the 7.2-point planning gain is from prompting alone. (4) Game agents score below random via a sequence-alignment scoring path with unstated threshold sensitivity, making the headline "game agents fail on AAA games" claim weaker than it appears. (5) MCQ distractor construction is under-specified, leaving open the possibility that distractors are distinguishable by superficial statistics rather than gameplay understanding. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating game-playing agents or interactive VLM benchmarks, this is currently the most complete gameplay data-and-evaluation suite available and worth reading closely; for the broader modeling community, the absence of training experiments and the Minecraft-only online validation mean the dataset's headline value remains a promise rather than a demonstrated result.

All-in-One Multilingual Scene Text Recognition with Script-aware Mixture-of-Experts (35 ▲ )

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ScriptMoE, a script-aware Mixture-of-Experts recognizer that reads scene text in 10 scripts (229 languages) from a single 45.85M-parameter model, backed by a 10M-sample synthetic training set (TextMuSS-10M) and a 10,899-image real benchmark (TextMuSS-Bench). - Why it's important: Deployed multilingual OCR today either cascades per-language recognizers with a brittle language-identification step or relies on billion-scale VLMs that are slow and inaccurate on low-resource scripts like Arabic, Thai, and Tibetan; a lightweight single model directly cuts deployment cost and eliminates routing error accumulation. - How it does it: It replaces the dense FFN of an autoregressive STR decoder with an image-level-routed Top-2 MoE whose 4 experts are pre-assigned to script families (Latin/Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic, Others), plus an always-on shared expert and a light 4-way script-classification auxiliary loss. - The good: The end-to-end result is convincing: swapping only the recognizer in PP-OCRv5 lifts F1 on the CC-OCR multilingual task from 65.71% to 80.89%, slightly beating the best zero-shot VLM (Qwen3.5-9B, 80.73%) at roughly 1/100th the parameters. - The missing: The headline TextMuSS-Bench margin (+1.31% over the strongest baseline) is reported from single-seed runs without significance tests, and one of three evaluation scripts (plus part of the benchmark itself) is the authors' own collection, so the margin's robustness is unverified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for OCR/multilingual-vision practitioners deciding between per-language models, VLMs, and a unified recognizer — the data recipe and per-component ablations are directly reusable — but MoE researchers will find the architecture standard.
