Problem & Motivation: Scene text recognition is near-saturated for English and Chinese but weak for most other scripts, because real training data exists almost exclusively for those two languages. Practitioners building multilingual OCR systems currently choose between (a) expert pipelines like PP-OCRv5 MLT that maintain ~ten per-script recognizers plus a language classifier (costly to train, deploy, and maintain, and a misrouted crop is unrecoverable), or (b) general/OCR-specialized VLMs that cover many languages but are expensive at inference and collapse on several scripts (e.g., InternVL3.5-8B scores 0.00% word accuracy on Arabic, Bangla, and Tibetan on the new benchmark). The paper targets the gap of a single recognizer that is simpler than expert cascades, lighter than VLMs, and more accurate than both, noting that grouping languages by script (10 scripts cover 229 languages) makes the unified problem tractable. Key Idea: The single-image-few-script prior: a cropped scene-text instance almost always contains exactly one script, so the recognition decoder does not need dense multi-script fluency — it needs to switch to the right specialist. This makes a Mixture-of-Experts a natural fit, with routing decided once per image (mean-pooled visual features) rather than per token, and experts pre-assigned to script families rather than discovered freely. Methodology: The pipeline has two parts. (1) Data: extending the UnionST synthesis engine, the authors build TextMuSS-10M — 1M word-level synthetic samples per script (10 total), using a four-source corpus mix (40% real lexicon words, 20% shuffled-character strings, 20% rare-character expansion strings, 20% News Crawl sentences), 8k SynthText backgrounds, layout templates (horizontal/vertical/curved/rotated/perspective), script-specific adjustments (20% vertical text for CJK, right-to-left logical-order rendering for Arabic), and a merged 19,684-character vocabulary. (2) Model: an SVTRv2 hierarchical visual encoder feeds a 2-block autoregressive Transformer decoder where each FFN is replaced by MoE(h) = α·FFN_share(h) + (1−α)·Σ g_i·FFN_i(h); the router is a softmax over mean-pooled visual tokens with multiplicative Gaussian jitter (σ=0.05), Top-2 of 4 experts selected and renormalized, and a learnable per-token sigmoid gate α balancing the shared expert. A 4-way script-group classification head sharing the router input (but not weights) adds cross-entropy loss weighted λ=0.1 against the dominant autoregressive CE loss (label smoothing 0.1). Critical design decisions: (a) image-level vs token-level routing — justified by ablation showing token routing is a wash on accuracy while costing more; (b) 4 grouped experts vs 10 per-script experts — ablated, 4 wins (10-expert version drops to 81.32% from 82.06% because each expert sees too few samples); (c) the auxiliary script loss — ablated in both directions (removing it costs 0.43%, over-weighting to 0.5 costs 0.71%), a well-executed sweep. Key Results: On TextMuSS-Bench (10,899 images; MLT2019 test split plus newly collected Russian, Thai, Tibetan), ScriptMoE reaches 82.06% average word accuracy vs 80.75% for the strongest re-trained baseline SVTRv2-AR (+1.31%), with the largest gains on Arabic (+2.98%), Thai (+2.40%), and Tibetan (+1.96%). Generalist VLMs trail by 18–70 points on average (Qwen3.5-9B best at 63.77%). On CC-OCR end-to-end multilingual OCR (PP-OCRv5 detector held fixed, recognizer swapped), ScriptMoE lifts F1 from 65.71% to 80.89%, edging Qwen3.5-9B (80.73%), Gemini-3.5-Flash (80.52%), and GoogleOCR (71.78%). The model stores 45.85M parameters and activates 41.13M (89.69%) per image — one to two orders of magnitude fewer than VLMs. Baselines include 15 STR models (2016–2026) re-trained on identical data and 9 zero-shot VLM/OCR systems; this is a fair, current baseline set for the STR comparison. Counter-intuitive findings: synthetic-only training beats real-only training on the MLT2019 average (79.61% vs 77.12%) and enables scripts with zero real data (Tibetan 87.08% synthetic-only); Latin accuracy drops when synthetic data is added while Russian drops when real data is added, traced to Latin–Cyrillic homoglyph confusion. The model is nonetheless slower than its own dense baseline (541.07 ms vs 395.92 ms per batch of 256 on a V100). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK + NEW METHOD with an EMPIRICAL contribution. The genuinely novel elements are TextMuSS-10M (a balanced 10-script, 229-language synthetic STR corpus; SynthMLT, the only prior multilingual synthetic set, is shown to be inadequate) and the image-level script-aligned routing scheme with a shared expert under the single-image-few-script prior. The architecture itself is a standard combination of known techniques — SVTRv2 backbone, conventional Top-K MoE (Switch/Sparse-MoE style) placed in the decoder FFN, auxiliary classification loss — applied to a new problem setting; the closest prior (MRN's router for incremental multilingual recognition) differs mainly in parameter growth, not in the core routing idea. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough and component-resolved: expert count (2/4/10), Top-K (1/2/4), routing granularity (image vs token), script-classification loss on/off, shared expert on/off, plus appendix sweeps over λ_scls, shared-expert width ratio, and router jitter — each tied to specific per-script deltas. All 15 STR baselines are re-trained under an identical data/schedule/hardware protocol rather than quoted from prior papers, a credibility positive. Routing behavior is validated qualitatively (router softmax plots) and the Latin–Cyrillic confusion analysis includes homoglyph visualizations. However: everything runs with a single fixed seed, no error bars or significance tests are reported, and margins as small as 0.3–0.5% (the size of some ablation effects the authors interpret) may sit within noise. TextMuSS-Bench's Russian/Thai/Tibetan portions (2,160 of 10,899 images) are the authors' own collection, each annotated by a single non-verified-in-domain expert with a non-specialist reviewer. Code is released (https://github.com/YesianRohn/ScriptMoE and https://github.com/Topdu/OpenOCR); the dataset release is implied by code links but no separate dataset URL is stated. Mild Goodhart risk: the benchmark was assembled by the same team in the same project as the method, though the MLT2019 core is external. This is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.24058), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent integration test). - Practical: Yes — trained and evaluated on 8× V100 (32GB); inference fits in ~2.1GB and needs a single GPU. - Efficient: Mixed — 45.85M stored / 41.13M activated parameters is 100× smaller than VLMs, but latency (541.07 ms/batch-256) exceeds its own dense baseline SVTRv2-AR (395.92 ms) and all AR baselines except MAERec; training cost is 92.7 GPU-hours. - Effective: Yes for the stated problem — the CC-OCR swap experiment isolates recognition and shows real pipeline gains (65.71%→80.89% F1), though end-to-end scores remain capped by the fixed PP-OCRv5 detector, and monolingual sanity checks on BCTR (86.85%) and Union14M (88.95%) confirm no regression on high-resource scripts. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 10 scripts; the authors claim extensibility via a grouping heuristic for unseen scripts (fold into one of 4 expert families) but provide no experiment adding an 11th script, and the 10-expert ablation suggests per-script expert scaling does not work. The work delivers a software artifact (code, configuration, and presumably dataset via the linked repos) and an integration recipe, not just a paper. Strengths: - The data contribution is the real lever: demonstrating that synthetic-only training beats real-only training on the MLT2017 scripts (79.61% vs 77.12%) while covering three scripts with zero real data is an actionable finding for anyone building long-tail OCR, independent of the architecture. - The CC-OCR evaluation is well-designed: holding the detector fixed and swapping only the recognizer cleanly attributes the 15.18-point F1 gain to recognition, and comparing against 12+ external systems under a shared protocol avoids vendor-style self-reporting for the headline claim. - The ablation suite is unusually complete, including two-sided sweeps (e.g., showing that both removing and over-weighting the script loss hurt) that turn design choices into evidence rather than assertions. - The honest per-script analysis of the Latin–Cyrillic homoglyph failure, with a mechanistic explanation and a synthetic-data experiment that partially mitigates it, is a genuinely useful diagnostic for the community. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) a residual domain gap between synthetic training data and real imagery; (2) Latin–Cyrillic homoglyph confusion is reduced but not eliminated (with a visualization); (3) end-to-end performance is bounded by the upstream PP-OCRv5 detector's multilingual detection quality. They also note in the main text a cross-script trade-off (aggregate accuracy vs per-script peaks) and that Latin's real-data advantage keeps the Russian gap hard to close. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical rigor: single fixed seed, no variance estimates; several interpreted effects (0.28–0.43% on the reference benchmarks, 0.43% from the script loss) are exactly the size of differences that seed noise could produce. The 1.31% headline margin over SVTRv2-AR is not significance-tested. - Benchmark composition: Latin script contributes 5,885 of 10,899 images (54%) in TextMuSS-Bench, so the average is dominated by the script where the method's advantage is smallest; the low-resource scripts driving the gains carry 356–750 images each. - Newly collected benchmark portions (Russian, Thai, Tibetan) come from the same team that built the method, with one annotator per language and a non-specialist quality reviewer; annotation error rates are not reported. - VLM zero-shot evaluation uses a single generic prompt for general VLMs; whether prompting or output-format mismatch (e.g., the shown "。" suffix errors) inflates some VLM failures is not probed, though per-model prompts are used for OCR-specialized VLMs. - The "Others" expert group lumps Hindi, Bangla, Tibetan, and Thai — scripts with distinct topologies — into one expert; the paper never explains why this grouping outperforms finer splits beyond the 10-expert under-training argument, and no intermediate grouping (e.g., 5–6 experts) is tried. - Scalability of the recipe to the 11th script is asserted via a heuristic, not demonstrated; the failed 10-expert ablation suggests adding scripts may require re-tuning the grouping entirely. - No comparison against a simple dense model trained with the same MoE-sized decoder parameter budget that does not use routing (the ablation's "0 experts" row matches SVTRv2-AR depth, so the MoE gain partly conflates added parameters with specialization). Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying multilingual OCR should read this paper — the synthetic-data recipe and the detector-swap evidence that a 46M recognizer beats billion-scale VLMs on multilingual F1 are immediately actionable — while researchers seeking architectural novelty in MoE design will find the mechanism conventional and the statistical support thin.

Rufus-Air: An Open LLM Post-Training Recipe (6 ▲ )

Chia-Yuan Chang, Renyuan Cheng, Rui Feng, Xiaotian Han, Yuan He, Hongye Jin, Linwei Li, Shiyang Li, Fenglin Liu, Xin Liu, Priyanka Nigam, Haoyang Wen, Zhenghao Xu, Zhuocheng Xu, Bing Yin, Qingyu Yin, Chao Zhang, Rongzhi Zhang, Zhihan Zhang, Zixuan Zhang, Zixuan Zhang, Tuo Zhao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper documents Rufus-Air, an open, reproducible eight-stage post-training recipe (SFT → Reasoning RL → Coding RL → IF RL → General Agent → Coding Agent → Search Agent → RLHF) applied to the public GLM-4.5-Air-Base MoE checkpoint (106B total / 12B active), with per-stage data, rewards, infrastructure, and stagewise metrics released. - Why it's important: Most post-training pipelines are reported as thin system cards, so teams outside frontier labs cannot reproduce how a competitive model was actually built; this report fills that gap at a compute footprint (8–64 8×H200 nodes) accessible to non-frontier teams. - How it does it: The pipeline orders stages from hard, verifiable rewards to soft judge/model-based rewards to minimize exposure to reward hacking, applies difficulty filtering to keep RL prompts in a productive learnability band, and treats infrastructure (token-in/token-out rollouts, consistent chat templates, Firecracker sandboxes, Rollout Routing Replay) as part of the recipe. - The good: Stagewise attribution is unusually honest and detailed — e.g., IF RL raises Multi-challenge by +24.7, General Agent raises Tau2-Retail by +9.8 and MCP-Atlas by +7.8, Coding RL raises LiveCodeBench v6 by +7.3 — with contamination screening, simulator-sensitivity analysis (Tau2-Bench moves up to 23.7 points with the user simulator), and a full Table 2 tracing which stage moved which benchmark. - The missing: The claimed general principles (stage ordering by reward reliability, difficulty filtering) are supported by one successful run plus partial ablations rather than controlled comparisons — the authors admit the order is "one that worked, not one shown to be optimal," and the Coding Agent stage is undertrained, with its SWE-bench gain not surviving to the shipped checkpoint. - Read it or not: Yes, if you are a practitioner building or planning an LLM post-training pipeline — the per-stage data/reward/infra detail is the substance the field usually omits; skip it if you want novel algorithms, since every component is a competent assembly of existing published techniques.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (80) is the paper's standout dimension — rare, direct confrontation of limitations including negative RLHF results, a non-converged stage, and unattributed deltas — and Resilience (75) is strong because claims are explicitly bounded as 'one that worked, not shown optimal.' Rigor (65) reflects unusually thorough contamination screening, stage-attributed measurement, and selected ablations, undercut by single-run headline numbers, developer-reported baselines, and eval-harness alignment with training. Novelty (45) is deliberately low — every component is a published technique — and Impact (75) is high because the documented recipe plus pinned infrastructure is genuinely actionable for non-frontier teams. Weighted composite: 0.20*45 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*75 + 0.10*75 = 64.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Open-weight base checkpoints have made post-training research broadly accessible, but the recipes themselves remain thinly reported — post-training sections "read more like a system card than like a reproducible recipe." Teams who want to post-train a competitive model from a public base (e.g., for products, research, or study) lack stage-level detail on data mixtures, reward design, stage ordering, and the infrastructure decisions that determine whether RL stages work at all. The work targets anyone post-training LLMs without in-house frontier-lab resources, and positions itself alongside Tülu 3 as one of the few fully documented open recipes. Rufus-Air is the model behind Amazon's Rufus shopping assistant post-training, repackaged here as an open, reproducible artifact. Key Idea: The core insight is that reward reliability — how easily a reward can be gamed — provides a practical principle for ordering post-training stages: run hard-verifiable-reward RL first and soft judge/model-based rewards last, so a gameable reward spends minimal time under optimization pressure. Combined with the claim that strong, diverse SFT establishes a capability floor that RL refines rather than builds (SFT checkpoint 3799 already beats the vendor post-trained GLM-4.5-Air release on IFEval +5.3, IFBench +24.2, AIME25 +6.6, AIME26 +3.5, before any RL), this yields a serial pipeline where each stage's reward exposure is managed by position. Difficulty filtering (dropping prompts solved >80% or never solved, DAPO-style dynamic sampling) forms an automatic curriculum throughout the RL stages. Methodology: Eight serial stages on GLM-4.5-Air-Base, each consuming the previous stage's checkpoint. (1) SFT: 9.01M samples / 27B supervised tokens from 17 public datasets (zero Rufus-side regeneration), 3 epochs on 512 H200 GPUs, assistant-token loss only, 128K context packing; note held-out scores flatten within one epoch, so an intermediate checkpoint (3799) is carried forward. (2) Reasoning RL: 121K verifiable prompts (math/science/puzzles), binary rewards via Math-Verify/Python checkers/fuzzy match, GSPO with tight clipping (ε=1e-3), online learnability filtering (keep groups with mean reward in (0, 0.8]), relative length penalty. (3) Coding RL: 29.4K problems from EvolveCoder/Nemotron/Dolci/ADR, sandboxed execution rewards, GSPO, mid-run response-budget extension from 64K to 128K after truncation masking was diagnosed. (4) IF RL: 14K synthesized multi-constraint prompts with Python-checkable rubrics plus 13K adversarial multi-turn conversations with rubric-judge rewards, GRPO; deliberately excludes "optional" rubrics to avoid length bias. (5–7) Agent stages: General Agent on ~2K filtered AgentWorldModel MCP tasks with binary state-verification rewards; Coding Agent on ~4K Harbor-format tasks with a single execute_command tool and Firecracker sandbox rewards; Search Agent on ~2.2K MiroVerse questions with a noisy Qwen3-32B LLM-judge reward, using Dr. GRPO-style mean-only advantages (dropping std normalization, justified analytically because normalization erases reward-gap magnitude and amplifies judge noise — supported by a paired ablation). (8) RLHF: on-policy GRPO against the public Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-8B reward model on HH-RLHF prompts, after negative findings on HelpSteer3 and unfiltered HH-RLHF. Infrastructure: Rufus-Slime (Slime/Megatron/SGLang) and Rufus-Gym (Strands Agents) with token-in/token-out rollouts to prevent retokenization drift, Rollout Routing Replay for MoE train/rollout routing mismatch, and FP8-rollout/BF16-training with truncated importance sampling. Key Results: Rufus-Air leads the official GLM-4.5-Air release on every one of 16 reported benchmarks except Arena-Hard v2 Creative Writing (53.0 vs 60.3), including IFBench 76.9 vs 33.6, Multi-challenge 65.8 vs 36.0, Tau2-Telecom 93.0 vs 32.7, BrowseComp 37.1 vs 22.7, SWE-bench Verified 65.6 vs 50.6, and AIME25 88.3 vs 84.2. Against Nemotron-3-Super (different base, strongest measured baseline) it leads on instruction following, search, and most agentic rows, and trails on Creative Writing and Tau2-Airline by ~2 points. Against INTELLECT-3 (same base), it leads on all rows except Creative Writing. Largest single-stage moves: Multi-challenge +24.7 (IF RL), Arena-Hard v2 CW +14.4 (RLHF), Tau2-Retail +9.8 (General Agent), LiveCodeBench v6 +7.3 (Coding RL); the compute-limited Coding Agent stage moves least (+1.4 Terminal-Bench, +2.2 SWE-bench), and the SWE-bench gain does not survive to the shipped checkpoint. A notable negative finding: the sandbox service costs ~$10K/month to maintain, and one BrowseComp evaluation pass costs a few hundred dollars in search API fees. Six of ten comparison columns are developer-reported numbers, not measured under a common harness. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and, arguably, a NEW BENCHMARK-adjacent contribution in reproducibility reporting; it is fundamentally a documented SYSTEM/TOOL (recipe + infrastructure). There is no new algorithm: GSPO/GRPO, DAPO dynamic sampling, Dr. GRPO mean-only advantages, Rollout Routing Replay, difficulty filtering, and RLHF are all existing published techniques, and the novelty lies in (a) the empirically grounded principle of ordering stages by reward hackability, (b) the stage-attributed measurement protocol (Table 2), and (c) the unusual completeness of the infrastructure disclosure. This is explicitly positioned as sitting "between a research paper and an engineering experience report." Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a technical report. Ablations exist in places — the mean-only vs. std-normalized advantage comparison in Search Agent (55.8–64.8 vs 49.7–58.7 on held-out), the negative RLHF data findings across three preference datasets, the optional-rubric length-bias observation, and the scratchpad context-management ablation (−10.7 BrowseComp when disabled) — but several headline principles are admitted to come from "training experience rather than full ablations." No error bars or multi-seed runs on the main results; the authors do disclose same-condition AIME re-runs differing by 4.6 points to contextualize small deltas. Contamination control is unusually thorough (8-gram + exhaustive n-gram + dense retrieval, 4,187 samples removed, per-stage re-screening). Code, stack pins (commit hashes), per-stage hyperparameters (Table 16), and data licenses are documented; no explicit code/model-release URL is stated in the text. Methodological concerns: agentic benchmarks are evaluated "with the harness the corresponding stage trains in" (reward and eval can share structure, risking alignment of eval to training); the reward-hackability ordering principle is validated on a single successful run; some ablations (e.g., the paired advantage-estimator run) are single-comparison without seeds. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model plus measured benchmark outcomes, with a SYSTEMS component in the infrastructure). Practical: Yes — 8×H200 nodes, a scale many non-frontier teams can access, with the caveat that the agent-stage sandbox tier (~10K concurrent Firecracker microVMs, ~$10K/month) is a nontrivial operational commitment. Efficient: SFT alone costs ~832 node-days (~13 days on 64 nodes), the largest single expense; RL stages run on 8–32 nodes; the report argues this is small enough for non-frontier labs. Effective: Evidence covers proxy benchmarks convincingly and stage-attributed, though the Coding Agent stage is explicitly not converged and the Search Agent trains on a cheaper internal search backend than evaluation uses. Scalability: Not tested beyond the reported scale; the authors do not claim scaling, and the reward-hackability ordering is unvalidated at other scales or base models. Delivers a documented recipe plus two in-house infrastructure components (Rufus-Slime, Rufus-Gym) built on open-source software; the final artifact is a model checkpoint, with reproducibility hinging on the pinned open-source stack and public data. Strengths: - Stagewise attribution discipline: Table 2 plus per-stage tables tie each metric movement to the stage that produced it, with explicit warnings about incomparable protocols and unattributed final-row deltas — rare transparency that lets readers audit the recipe's actual causal structure. - Genuine negative results reported: three RLHF dataset failures, the optional-rubric length-bias reversal, the format-bonus reward hack in Search Agent, the SWE-bench gain that did not survive to the shipped checkpoint, and the flat held-out scores after epoch one of SFT despite falling loss. - The analytical justification for mean-only advantages in noisy-judge RL (normalization erases reward-gap magnitude, giving a lone success at a 0.1 gap a +3.75 advantage) is a concrete, reusable design insight backed by a paired ablation. - Contamination screening and evaluation-protocol honesty are above the norm: detailed n-gram + retrieval screening, an entire appendix on how each of six developer-reported baseline columns was sourced, and a demonstration that the Tau2-Bench user simulator alone moves scores by up to 23.7 points. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly state that the stage order "is one that worked, not one shown to be optimal"; that some conclusions come from training experience rather than full ablations (§6); that the Coding Agent stage was trained on available compute, not to convergence; that no single benchmark suite was tracked across every stage, so some stage-to-final differences are unattributed; that Creative Writing lags because no style-tuned reward model was tried; and that n-gram/embedding filters cannot rule out all contamination. They also flag the domain-expert-merging alternative (multi-teacher on-policy distillation) as unexplored. This is a credibility positive — limitations are confronted rather than minimized, and the discussion section consolidates them explicitly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Agentic benchmarks (Tau2, MCP-Atlas, Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench) are evaluated with "the harness the corresponding stage trains in," so training and evaluation share an environment scaffold the public baselines did not train against — a structural advantage the same-base comparison partly controls for but does not eliminate. - The four headline findings (strong SFT floor, difficulty filtering, reward-reliability ordering, infrastructure-as-recipe) are extracted from one pipeline; there is no controlled test of the ordering principle (e.g., RLHF before the verifiable stages) on this or any base model, and no second base model to support generality. - The strongest comparison (Nemotron-3-Super) has a different base, so "the recipe moves most where it spends the most training signal" is best supported only against INTELLECT-3 and GLM-4.5-Air, whose own post-training data and compute are not disclosed — the same-base comparison cannot isolate recipe quality from post-training compute. - No confidence intervals or seed replication on the headline Table 1 numbers; several claimed stage effects (e.g., Coding Agent's +1.4/+2.2) are within plausible run-to-run variance by the paper's own AIME variance estimate. - The IF RL judge (teacher LLM, unspecified scoring protocol at eval time for Multi-challenge/AdvancedIF relative to the training judge) introduces a soft-reward channel the "reward reliability" principle classifies as safe based on observed absence of hacking — an argument from one run's behavior, not a measurement of judge exploitability. Bottom Line: For any team about to post-train an open-weight MoE model, this is one of the few documents that tells you what actually happens stage by stage — including the failures — and it is worth reading for that alone; as an algorithmic contribution it is deliberately derivative, and the reader seeking new RL methods should look elsewhere.

OmniVChat: Synthesizing, Benchmarking, and Training for Native Audio-Visual Dialogue (30 ▲ )

Haolin He, Yunfei Chu, Qi Chen, Wen Huang, Yuan Feng, Muzhi Zhu, Zheqi Dai, Haoning Xu, Dongchao Yang, Chunyat Wu, Zining Liang, Zhengxi Liu, Xiquan Li, Xie Chen, Xize Cheng, Qize Yang, Jin Xu, Qiuqiang Kong · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OmniVChat, a full stack for native audio-visual dialogue — a multi-agent data engine (OmniVChat-Studio) that synthesizes audio-visual dialogues with tiered rubrics, a 2,800-instance benchmark (OmniVChat-Bench) plus a 360-clip human-recorded probe, and an RL reward design (OmniVChat-RL) that fine-tunes Qwen3-Omni-Instruct on the synthetic data. - Why it's important: Real recordings of people talking to omni models through their own devices are scarce, and keyword matching cannot grade open-ended replies grounded in the user's scene, emotion, and gestures — so progress on this task has been blocked by both data and evaluation. - How it does it: A Director/Renderer/Reviewer/Validator multi-agent pipeline renders synchronized audio-visual clips from text corpora, and the same tiered rubric used for grading doubles as the RL correctness reward, supplemented by group-normalized brevity (efficiency) and LLM-judged style terms, trained via GSPO with rank-64 LoRA. - The good: Gains transfer from synthetic to human-recorded data without any training on it: Subcategory Mean rises 0.465→0.652 on the synthetic benchmark and 0.402→0.632 on the recorded probe, with reply efficiency improving from 5.75 to 18.38 rubric-points per 1,000 words. - The missing: The ablations undercut the headline — removing the efficiency reward yields higher correctness (Mean 0.697, Human 0.691) than the full model (0.652, 0.632), and the recorded probe is only 360 Chinese single-turn clips graded by a judge from the same lab as the base model. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building omni-model evaluation or RL-on-rubrics pipelines, since the data engine and judge-agreement audit are detailed and reusable; skip it if you only want a stronger audio-visual dialogue model, since Gemini-3.5-Flash still leads the synthetic benchmark.

Problem & Motivation: Native audio-visual dialogue — a model receiving raw microphone and camera input with the query embedded in both, no ASR cascade or text prompt — is the target interaction mode for GPT-4o-style omni assistants, but research is stuck on two bottlenecks. First, there is almost no open data of people using their own devices: camera motion, device posture, and acoustic noise create a long tail of conditions that staged recordings miss. Second, good replies must account for the user's surroundings, facial expression, and nearby objects, and can be phrased countless ways, so rule-based or keyword evaluation is unreliable. Existing benchmarks (OmniBench, WorldSense, AV-Odyssey, OmniInteract, Full-Duplex-Bench, etc.) test perception, streaming understanding, or turn-taking, but few target this native dialogue setting, which pushes practitioners back to ASR cascades that drop prosody and add latency. Key Idea: The core move is generation-for-comprehension applied end-to-end: because modern joint audio-visual generators can render controllable, realistic clips, the same synthesis pipeline can produce (a) training dialogues, (b) benchmark instances, and (c) instance-specific tiered rubrics — and the rubric scoring function then serves double duty as the evaluation metric and the RL reward. The tier-gated rubric (Tier 0 language gate zeroing the score; later tiers earn credit only if all earlier tiers pass) is the connective tissue between evaluation and training. This is an identifiable, reconstructable key idea rather than an ad-hoc combination. Methodology: Three pipelines. (1) OmniVChat-Studio: an Attribute & Corpus Sampling module draws a configuration over 22 scenario domains, camera setups, interference levels, and languages (Gumbel-top-k/exponential-race sampling over a joint attribute space, Eq. 7); a Director agent writes scripts and plans, a Renderer produces 1080p clips with 44.1 kHz stereo audio, a Reviewer captions and quality-checks the rendered evidence (with focused Q-A probes), and a deterministic Validator enforces config rules; bounded repair loops (re-seed, rewrite, plan update) discard unrecoverable runs. Reply Plan deliberately grounds replies only in what the rendered clip actually shows, discarding unsupported script details. The multi-turn subsystem adds a joint plan, per-turn prompts with media-ID placeholders for earlier clips, and cross-turn reference validation. (2) OmniVChat-Bench: 2,550 single-turn + 250 multi-turn instances across 5 ability categories (Dialogue-State & Link Perception, Multimodal Entity Alignment, Model Self-Awareness, Anti-Hallucination, Emotion Recognition) and 17 subcategories, scored by the gated rubric function r(y) (Eq. 1) judged by qwen3.7-max, aggregated by Subcategory Mean (Eq. 2). (3) OmniVChat-RL: GSPO objective (Eq. 3) with group-mean advantage, total reward R = r(y) + 0.5·format + 0.1·group-normalized efficiency (rubric credit per counted word, Eq. 5–6) + 0.5·style (all-seven-pass LLM check); LoRA rank-64 on attention and MoE projections of Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct (vision/audio towers frozen), 1,000 iterations, 32 prompts × 4 completions per step, no KL penalty. Critical design decisions: grounding replies in rendered evidence rather than scripts (well justified, prevents rubric-label drift), rubric-as-reward reuse (justified by matching eval/train metrics), and using a same-family judge (qwen3.7-max) for both reward and evaluation (acknowledged but a residual Goodhart risk). Key Results: On OmniVChat-Bench, OmniVChat-RL raises Subcategory Mean from 0.465 (base Qwen3-Omni-Instruct) to 0.652 at step 940; on the 360-clip human-recorded Chinese probe, 0.402→0.632. Reply efficiency (RE) rises 5.75→18.38 rubric-points/1,000 words; Style rises 0.710→0.992; mean reply length falls from 91.5 to 36.6 words during training. Against 12 released systems, Gemini-3.5-Flash leads synthetic Mean at 0.667 and Gemini-3.7-Flash leads Human at 0.575 and RE at 16.96 — so the trained open model beats all other open baselines (best open baseline JoyAI-VL-Interaction at 0.431 Mean) and is competitive with but not above the leading closed models, with the paper noting synthetic and recorded leaderboards disagree. Ablations show the trade-off explicitly: dropping the efficiency term yields Mean 0.697 and Human 0.691 (above the full model) but RE collapses to 7.12 at 99-word replies; dropping style yields Mean 0.661 and Style 0.788. Judge audit across six GPT-5.6/Qwen3 judges: pooled score spread 0.034 (5.2× the bootstrap SD of 0.0066), pairwise Cohen's κ 0.532–0.845, criterion agreement 87.8–96.5%. Multi-turn results are thin: 50 instances per subcategory, gaps resolved only to about ±0.05, and post-training Spearman correlation between paired single-/multi-turn gaps drops to 0.10. Scale is standard (2,800 synthetic + 360 recorded instances; 5,600 training dialogues), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW TASK DEFINITION (native audio-visual dialogue with no text query), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (OmniVChat-Bench and its human-recorded probe), NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (OmniVChat-Studio data engine), and a NEW METHOD only in the specific sense of rubric-as-reward applied to this setting. The genuinely novel part is closing the loop: one synthesis engine, one rubric format, and one scoring function shared by benchmarking and RL training, with a recorded probe testing distribution transfer. The components are standard — multi-agent video generation pipelines, LLM-judged rubrics, and GSPO/GRPO-style group-relative RL are all established (Rubrics-as-Rewards, GSPO cited directly) — so novelty lies in the integration and the transfer claim, not in any single algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above-average rigor for a benchmark-plus-training paper. Ablations isolate the efficiency and style reward terms and expose the correctness/brevity trade-off; checkpoint selection is on a 560-dialogue development split separate from the 2,800-instance benchmark (no training-video overlap claimed); judge agreement is audited with six judges, bootstrap SDs, variance decomposition (95.7% subcategory difficulty, 1.1% judge severity, 3.3% judge-by-subcategory), and honest notes that differences near 0.01 are within noise. A deterministic audio tail-artifact repair procedure is specified to the sample index. Concerns: (1) no error bars or seeds for the headline Table 1 comparisons; (2) rubrics, reference replies, and reward are all produced by the same Director/qwen3.7-max LLM family that grades the outputs, and the base model shares a vendor with the judge — a structural circularity only partially mitigated by the cross-judge audit (which itself was run on one fixed Gemini reply set, not on remeasuring the RL gain); (3) the human probe covers only Chinese, single-turn dialogues, so the transfer claim generalizes beyond that cell only by assumption; (4) the paper is an "Under Review" preprint, and code/data are promised ("will be publicly released") but no URL or weights are given yet. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the data engine). Practical: The trained artifact is a rank-64 LoRA on a released 30B-A3B open model (3B active params), so inference runs on commodity multi-GPU hardware; the synthesis pipeline depends on unspecified third-party audio-visual generators. Efficient: Training is modest (1,000 iterations, 128 completions/step, adapters only), but the per-clip video-generation cost of building the corpus is never reported, which matters since 5,600 dialogues plus renders and re-renders were produced. Effective: Evidence shows improved rubric-scored dialogue on synthetic data and transfer to 360 recorded clips — but the metric is an LLM-judged proxy, and the ablation table shows the full-reward model sacrifices ~0.045 Mean correctness relative to its own no-efficiency variant, so the deployed configuration optimizes brevity+style, not peak correctness. Scalable: Not tested — no experiments at 10× data or longer training, and multi-turn performance rests on 250 instances; the paper claims but does not demonstrate scale. Deliverable: benchmark, data engine, and training code promised for release; model weights not stated; currently paper-form until artifacts land. Strengths: - The unified rubric-as-metric-and-reward design is a real, transferable contribution: the same tiered gating function (Eq. 1) is the benchmark score and the RL correctness reward, making training gains directly interpretable as benchmark gains by construction. - Evidence-grounded reply synthesis — the Reply Plan stage discards scripted details unsupported by the rendered clip, and focused Video Q-A resolves ambiguity before acceptance — addresses the classic synthetic-data failure of rubrics describing things the media never shows. - The measurement self-audit is unusually honest for this genre: judge-severity spread quantified against bootstrap noise, variance decomposition, explicit warnings that checkpoint-level change correlations are consistent with chance, and an appendix deriving why adjacent-checkpoint noise can mask true gains. - The 360-clip human-recorded probe, built by improvising actors rather than following scripts, gives the synthetic-to-real transfer claim a genuine (if small and Chinese-only) out-of-distribution test rather than a purely self-referential one. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the recorded probe covers only single-turn dialogues, excludes live interruption and real-time latency, and is Chinese-only; that synthetic and recorded benchmark scores are "not directly comparable"; that matched gains only "indirectly suggest" distribution alignment; that the single-/multi-turn comparisons use independently sampled dialogues and "do not isolate the effect of more turns"; that judge differences imply scores near 0.01 need care; that non-significant paired tests "do not show equivalence"; and that annotation-caption agreement "does not make the tasks independent or guarantee that grader bias cancels." They confront limitations directly and with unusual granularity — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The full-reward model is dominated on correctness by its own no-efficiency ablation (Mean 0.697 vs 0.652; Human 0.691 vs 0.632), yet the headline narrative frames the full reward as the contribution; the paper reports the trade-off but does not defend why brevity is worth ~0.045 correctness, nor test whether a smaller efficiency weight dominates both. - Vendor circularity: the reward judge (qwen3.7-max) and base model are both Alibaba/Qwen artifacts, so the trained policy is optimized against a same-family grader; the six-judge audit is run on a fixed Gemini reply set and never remeasures the reported 0.465→0.652 gain under alternative judges. - Rubric quality itself is never independently validated against human judgment on a sample — we know judges agree with each other, not that rubric criteria capture what humans consider a good reply. - Video-generation cost and failure rates of OmniVChat-Studio (renders discarded for malformed hands/arms, re-seed budgets) are narrated qualitatively but never quantified, so the engine's throughput economics are unknown. - Training/eval instances come from the same subcategory configurations and the same engine, so the benchmark's absolute numbers may overstate general dialogue ability relative to naturally occurring usage; no external benchmark (e.g., OmniInteract, WorldSense) is used to cross-check. - Only one base model is trained; the claim that the reward design (rather than this particular model) works rests on a single run, and no seeds/variance for the RL run are given. Bottom Line: A practitioner building omni-model evaluation or rubric-based RL should read this for its unusually well-audited synthesis-to-training-to-transfer pipeline and honest measurement analysis, but should treat the leaderboard numbers as vendor-adjacent and note that the paper's own ablations suggest a simpler correctness-only reward variant may be the stronger model.

Lean Pool: An AI-Maintained Archive of Formalized Mathematics (11 ▲ )

Vasily Ilin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 23 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Lean Pool, a repository of 211 completed Lean formalizations of named mathematical results (3.23M lines of source) that is discovered, imported, upgraded, reviewed, optimized, and documented largely by AI agents, and reports measurements of that operation. - Why it's important: As AI-generated proofs outpace human review, Mathlib's human-gated growth cannot absorb research-level formalizations, leaving verified results unmaintained and unreusable; this work proposes the maintained, formal counterpart to arXiv. - How it does it: The core move is decoupling admission from curation — the Lean kernel guarantees proof correctness, cheap mechanical gates (axioms, license, project cards, no `sorry`) plus an LLM mathematical review handle admission, and scheduled agent workflows handle the recurring maintenance (dependency bumps, proof golfing, compilation optimization) that a human community cannot afford. - The good: The paper's strongest evidence is the operational record: six real Lean/Mathlib version upgrades were survived (e.g., 191 projects probed, 97 compiler failures, 95/97 automated repair jobs succeeded before human-assisted integration), and a third-party LeanEval audit found Lean Pool is the most-reused external repository in research-level solutions (20 matching solutions). - The missing: The mathematical review service — the sole gate on statement faithfulness — was manually disabled before the observation date, its verdict accuracy was never independently labeled, and the same-PR verdict agreement was only 37/69. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on formalized mathematics infrastructure, AI-for-math agents, or repository maintenance automation; skip it if you want rigorous evaluation of agent capabilities, since this is a system report with descriptive statistics, not a controlled study.

Problem & Motivation: AI systems now produce mathematical arguments faster than mathematicians can read them, and Lean formalizations (e.g., OpenAI's Ten Advances and Navier–Stokes blowup releases) make such arguments mechanically checkable before human absorption. But a formalization that is dropped into a stale repository becomes unusable as Lean and Mathlib evolve: Mathlib itself grows only linearly under strict human review and cannot absorb research-level projects, while static registries (e.g., Palomar-style archiving) do not keep content compatible. The unstated beneficiaries are researchers who want to import a verified result of, say, the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture or Gödel incompleteness into new formal work without repairing it first. The gap addressed is that no existing venue — Mathlib (curated shared API), AFP (human-reviewed), Palomar (frozen verified versions), Tau Ceti (AI-authored on human roadmaps) — maintains independently developed, attributed formalizations as a living collection. Key Idea: The key insight is that kernel-checked correctness plus cheap mechanical linting lowers the marginal cost of keeping a formalization alive enough that AI agents — not scarce human reviewers — can perform the recurring maintenance (version bumping, proof shortening, compilation profiling), so a repository can scale super-linearly where Mathlib's human review cannot. This is a workflow/infrastructure insight rather than an algorithmic one; the paper has no new algorithm, and the technical machinery (Lean kernel, Mathlib linters, agentic repair, LLM review) is assembled from existing components applied to a new target: independently authored, attributed projects maintained together. Methodology: The system is an operational archive plus automation repository. (1) Admission: daily discovery jobs find completed Apache-2.0/MIT-licensed formalizations (human, AI, or mixed provenance, identified by project cards); admission requires no `sorry`/`admit`, only the standard three Lean axioms, no `set_option` bypasses, size limits, and passing CI (full combined-library build, Mathlib environment/style linters, archive-specific quality gates) plus an LLM mathematical review of statement faithfulness, novelty, and significance. (2) Maintenance: a scheduled dependency workflow detects new Lean/Mathlib releases, probes the unchanged archive, assigns compiler failures to repair agents, and assembles patches for a combined build and human merge. (3) Optimization: agents and contributors golf proofs and reduce elaboration cost; accepted changes are measured with paired clean full-library builds (fixed dependencies, same Azure VM, elapsed time and sampled peak proportional-set memory). (4) Discovery: an Exposition site exposes per-project dependency graphs (1,389,967 intra-project links over 173,362 declarations across 203 documented projects) linked to informal statements on project cards. Critical design decisions: kernel-trusted correctness (well-justified — Lean's kernel cannot be gamed by `sorry`-free axiom discipline); LLM review as the faithfulness gate (weakly justified — its accuracy is unvalidated, see gaps); advisory rather than blocking performance profiling (contrast with Tau Ceti's required performance gate — the paper documents this tradeoff but does not justify Pool's choice). Key Results: All numbers are self-reported descriptive measurements of the authors' own system at a single-maintainer scale. Scale: 211 completed projects, 7,043 files, 3,228,485 physical lines, 193,862 declarations, 837 registered main results, provenance 70 human / 102 AI / 39 mixed, 18 commit contributors, 63 community PRs, over roughly four months (June–September 2026). Maintenance: six upgrades from Lean 4.30.0-rc2 to 4.34.0; the hardest (4.34.0-rc1→4.34.0) broke 97 of 191 projects; 95/97 automated repair jobs succeeded, with 2 failures requiring follow-up integration (639 files, 5,951 lines changed). Optimization: library-wide compression removed 45,217 lines for a 3.3% build-time gain (16.11→15.59 min); elaboration-cost reduction removed 54,965 lines for 5.8% (28.46→26.82 min); contributor golfing removed 12,515 lines but slowed builds 5.4% (21.83→23.01 min) — an honest counter-intuitive result that proof shortening does not uniformly speed compilation. Clean-build comparison: Lean Pool (3.23 MLOC) builds in 60.28 min / 20.03 GiB peak RAM vs matching Mathlib (2.33 MLOC) at 37.44 min / 7.35 GiB on the same VM. Review service: 296 retained reports (188 approve, 71 changes requested, 37 discussion), recorded costs $308.52 (285 API reports, median $0.20) and $752.38 (6 Codex-equivalent reports, median $89.03). Reuse: per the external LeanEval audit, Lean Pool leads all external repositories with 20 solutions containing matching declarations. There are no baselines in the experimental sense; comparisons with Mathlib/Tau Ceti/Palomar/AFP are policy-level (Table 9) and resource-level (one clean build each). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (quantified agent-performed maintenance of a multi-million-line formal library across real dependency upgrades, and the finding that proof golfing can regress build time). What is genuinely new is the operating model — an archive that maintains independently attributed projects via agent labor rather than curating a shared API — not the components: the kernel, linters, agentic repair, LLM review, and exposition tooling are all existing techniques recombined. AFP and Mathlib pioneered maintained formal archives; Tau Ceti already applies AI workers to library maintenance; the differentiator is attribution-preserving admission of third-party research-level projects at minimal human cost. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations as such are absent, but the paired before/after clean-build protocol for each optimization PR (Appendix E, Table 20) is a reasonable controlled measurement, and the paper commendably reports negative results (golfing slowing builds; the Navier–Stokes API refactor increasing project build time from 879.67 to 887.78 s). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported — appropriate for build measurements but noted for the single-run comparisons; some project-level timings are single builds or medians with differing machines and cache states, and the paper says so. The archive, CI rules, workflow definitions, exposition site, and per-PR records are public (GitHub: Vilin97/lean-pool, revision bc6f18b2; exposition at vilin97.github.io/lean-pool), and appendices pin exact source revisions and observation timestamps. Methodological concerns: everything is measured on the authors' own system (vendor-style self-report); review accuracy was "not independently labeled" (the paper's own words); the observation window is ~4 months of a young system; the review service was disabled before observation; and the paper honestly concedes GitHub accounts do not measure human-vs-agent division of labor. The manuscript is a preprint (arXiv:2609.25199), substantially AI-drafted per the AI use statement, which the author owns explicitly. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS — a built archive with automation infrastructure, evaluated by operational deployment records. Practical: Yes — everything runs on commodity hardware; the reported builds used a single 16-core, 125.8 GiB Azure VM, and admission is open to any Apache-2.0/MIT Lean project. Efficient: Maintenance cost is favorable to human review (median $0.20 per historical LLM review) but the recent Codex-equivalent review cost jumped to a median of $89.03 per report, and the full library costs 60.28 CPU-heavy minutes and 20 GiB RAM to build — 1.7× Mathlib's time and 2.7× its memory for 1.4× the code. Effective: Partially — the evidence shows compatibility is restored and code is reused, but the faithfulness gate (does the statement match the advertised mathematics?) rests on an unvalidated, currently-disabled review service; correctness of statements-to-intent is a proxy at best. Scalable: Unproven — 211 projects and 2 maintainers over 4 months shows a working regime, but the growth curves in Figure 2 span one summer, the 4.34.0 upgrade already needed human-assisted follow-up beyond agent repairs, and no evidence addresses 10× project count or upgrade cadence. The artifact is real and public: the archive repository, automation repository, exposition site, and Zulip channel all ship. Strengths: (1) The first operational demonstration that agent labor can keep a multi-million-line, multi-project formal archive compatible across six real Lean/Mathlib releases, with repair-job success recorded honestly (95/97) rather than inflated. (2) The negative and awkward results are reported, not hidden: proof golfing regressing build time by 5.4%, review-verdict agreement at only 37/69, the service's cost escalation, and its manual shutdown are all in the paper. (3) The related-work positioning (Table 9) against Mathlib, Tau Ceti, Palomar, and AFP is precise and policy-level rather than dismissive, clearly isolating what Lean Pool does differently. (4) The reuse evidence is outsourced to an independent audit (LeanEval) rather than self-defined, with complementary source-level reuse cases (Kurosh, Feige, Poincaré) documented separately. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: review outcomes "are merge and closure decisions; review accuracy was not independently labeled"; the structured review service was manually disabled before observation, so recent imports lack it; recorded review prices are "not invoices" and exclude unrecorded/overwritten executions; the stable-version migration "does not establish equivalence of every declaration type before and after the upgrade"; GitHub accounts "do not measure the division of labor" between humans and their agents; job definitions "do not establish which model performed each historical contribution"; and source churn is a proxy for maintenance effort, with monetary charges and human labor not logged. This is unusually direct confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The central unvalidated claim is faithfulness: a kernel-checked proof of a wrong or weakened statement passes admission, and the only defense is an LLM review whose accuracy was never measured and which is now off — the paper never reports a single case of the review catching a real statement mismatch, only verdict counts. (2) Same-PR review agreement of 37/69 (54%) suggests the review is noisy, yet its verdicts are treated as part of the admission pipeline without calibration. (3) No human-time accounting: the claim that agents replace scarce human review is never tested against a measured human-hours baseline, and the maintainer's own merge labor is invisible. (4) Survivorship in the reuse evidence: the LeanEval audit and the documented reuse cases (several in maintainer-controlled projects) plausibly overstate organic adoption by the paper's author's own ecosystem — references [7, 15, 108, 109, 119, 126, 216, 222] share the author. (5) The build-resource comparison (Table 12) acknowledges background tasks on the shared VM; single runs without repetition leave those numbers unconfirmed. (6) There is no analysis of statement duplication or fragmentation across 211 independently developed projects (e.g., how many define entropy or spanning trees from scratch), which is the main cost of the attributed-archive model versus Mathlib's shared API. (7) Publication integrity of pooled content is taken on trust: projects citing AI-authored manuscripts (e.g., refs [84], [85]) are admitted based on upstream documents the archive does not verify mathematically beyond kernel checking. Bottom Line: For anyone building AI-for-math infrastructure this is a genuinely useful and unusually honest operations report on a real, public, agent-maintained formal archive — but it is a system description with self-measured, single-observer statistics and an unvalidated review gate, not rigorous evidence that the model scales, so read it as an early prototype announcement with credible telemetry rather than a validated result.

IterSynth: Rethinking Deep Search Agents via Role-Decoupled Iterative Synthesis (8 ▲ )

Xingyu Wu, Yuchen Yan, Zhengxi Lu, Siqi Chen, Xin ZHANG, Aiting Liu, Chao Deng, Jie Liu, Jin Ma, Jian Shao, Jun Xiao, Yongliang Shen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces IterSynth, a deep-search agent paradigm in which a single shared LLM policy alternates between a Planner (issues queries or answers from a compact summary) and a Synthesizer (rewrites the summary from retrieved evidence), plus RDPO, an RL recipe that normalizes GRPO advantages separately per role over composite outcome-plus-rubric rewards. - Why it's important: ReAct-style search agents fail on long horizons because one context must handle planning, evidence use, and synthesis — the authors measure 59–65% of ReAct trajectories on BrowseComp exhausting a 64K context without answering — so workflow-level fixes matter for anyone training small search agents. - How it does it: The evolving summary replaces the raw trajectory as the MDP state (workspace reconstruction), and credit assignment is decoupled by normalizing advantages within role-specific reward pools rather than across mixed Planner/Synthesizer turns. - The good: The ablation evidence is unusually thorough and internally consistent: RDPO lifts the SFT model from 44.1% to 50.7% average, the same composite reward without role decoupling drops to 47.2% (below outcome-only GRPO's 48.9%), and role-swap tests (replacing either role with the base model costs −17.4 and −41.1 points) show both roles were genuinely optimized. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere, the headline average is carried disproportionately by BrowseComp-ZH (+15.2 over the best ≤8B baseline) while GAIA (55.3) is actually beaten by the 4B baseline AgentCPM-Explore (63.9), and the headline numbers appear to include a test-time resampling trick (Table 15 shows +5.2 to +9.0 from a single resample) whose contribution is not separated in Table 1. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or train search agents and want a well-ablated template for workflow-RL co-design at 8B scale; empirical Novelty 65 Rigor 66 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 62 Resilience 58 Impact 62

Problem & Motivation: Deep-search agents must decompose complex queries, search the web, and synthesize grounded answers over long horizons. Open-source agents following the ReAct recipe (SFT on trajectories, then outcome-driven RL) put planning, evidence filtering, and synthesis in one undifferentiated policy over an ever-growing context. The authors empirically show (Appendix H) that with DeepSeek-V3.1 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 at a 64K budget, non-completion due to context exhaustion reaches 27–30% on xBench-2510, 31–34% on BrowseComp-ZH-100, and 59–65% on BrowseComp-100 — a paradigm-level failure, not a backbone-level one. Prior remedies address half the problem: multi-agent decompositions (e.g., InfoFlow) decouple capabilities but multiply parameters and coordination cost, while summary-based methods (IterResearch, AgentFold, ReSum) bound context but still couple planning with evidence use and treat summarization as an unlearned external module. The gap is a single-policy method that is simultaneously role-decoupled and context-bounded, with summary updates learned. Key Idea: Make the summary the MDP state and the two roles two prompt-conditioned views of one policy: the Planner sees only (question, summary) and outputs search/answer; the Synthesizer sees the Planner's decision plus retrieved documents and outputs a rewritten summary, with the context truncated after each round. The complementary training trick is RDPO: broadcast the terminal 0/1 outcome reward to every turn, add a turn-level rubric score from an LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite over rubrics auto-distilled from 20 contrastive trajectory pairs, capped at five criteria per role), then normalize advantages separately within the Planner pool and the Synthesizer pool so that dense Synthesizer signals and sparse Planner signals do not contaminate each other's baselines. Methodology: Two-stage recipe on Qwen3-8B. (1) Cold-start SFT: ~10K Planner–Synthesizer trajectories synthesized by rolling out Qwen3.5-397B-A17B in a live search environment, filtered for format validity and verifiably correct answers, unrolled into ~87.4K role-conditioned per-turn samples; full-parameter SFT (loss on role responses only, tool outputs masked) on 32×H20 for ~24h. (2) RDPO on verl: ~1,000 queries chosen so the SFT policy solves exactly 1–2 of 5 rollouts (moderate difficulty), G=8 group rollouts, reward r = r_acc + α·r_rubric with α=0.5, per-role group normalization (Eq. 7), 64×H20 for ~90h; training uses cached retrieval, evaluation uses live tools; T_max=30 rounds in training, 50 at evaluation. Three design decisions stand out: (a) role specialization via prompts and action constraints rather than separate parameters — justified by an ablation showing shared parameters beat two independently fine-tuned 8B models by +3.5 average (Appendix F.1); (b) rubrics induced from contrastive pairs rather than hand-written — reasonable, and judge-swap robustness is checked (±1.0 point across four judges); (c) moderate-difficulty query selection for RL — standard practice but reduces coverage of hard queries. The formal contribution is an augmented MDP ⟨S, D, E, T, R⟩ with role-conditioned sub-steps; the objective is otherwise vanilla GRPO, which the authors correctly present as a strength (no new optimizer). Key Results: IterSynth-8B averages 50.7% across BrowseComp (30.9), BrowseComp-ZH (55.4), GAIA text-only (55.3), xBench-DS-2505 (66.0), and xBench-DS-2510 (46.0), beating the strongest prior ≤8B agent (MiroThinker-v1.0-8B, 46.5 avg) by +4.2, with the largest margin on BrowseComp-ZH (+15.2) and xBench-2510 (+5.4). It surpasses several 30B agents (ReSum-30B 33.3, AgentFold-30B 50.2, OpenSeeker-30B 50.6) but trails Tongyi-DR-30B (58.2), MiroThinker-v1.5-30B (67.0), and MiroThinker-v1.7-mini (69.4); wall-clock comparison shows it is 1.5–1.6× faster than Tongyi-DR-30B at ~87% of its accuracy. As a training-free prompting workflow it beats ReAct by +5.5 avg on Claude-4.5-Opus (66.1 vs 60.6) and +4.5 on DeepSeek-V3.1 (47.9 vs 43.4), and beats IterResearch on most benchmarks. A controlled comparison (Appendix E) trains a ReAct baseline on identical questions, teacher, and pipeline: IterSynth-SFT beats ReAct-SFT by +11.5 and IterSynth-RDPO beats ReAct-RL by +12.6, disentangling architecture from trajectory quality. Baselines are current (2025–2026 systems), and scale is standard research scale (benchmarks of 100–1,266 questions), not stress-scale. Counter-intuitive details: adding rubric rewards without role-decoupled normalization (47.2) is worse than outcome-only GRPO, and the α coefficient shows an inverted-U (46.6 at 0.3, 50.7 at 0.5, 49.0 at 0.7). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (IterSynth workflow + RDPO) with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the context-exhaustion measurements in Appendix H). The genuinely new piece is per-role group advantage normalization under composite outcome-plus-turn-rubric rewards — a small but real algorithmic delta on GRPO — plus making summary rewriting a first-class, RL-optimized action constrained to its own role. Workspace reconstruction exists in IterResearch, researcher/refiner decoupling exists in InfoFlow, and rubric-shaped rewards exist in prior agentic-RL work; the contribution is their joint instantiation in a single policy, which the authors honestly frame via a feature table (Table 7) rather than overclaiming component novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a clear strength: training-recipe ablation (Table 3), role-swap ablation (Table 4), controlled ReAct-trajectory comparison (Table 8), shared-vs-independent parameters (Table 9), α sensitivity (Table 13), judge-model robustness (Table 14), plus training-dynamics curves (entropy, rubric scores on correct trajectories, validation accuracy tracking training accuracy — evidence against reward hacking). However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported on any benchmark; several test sets are tiny (GAIA 103 questions, xBench splits 100 each), where 1–2 questions shift the average materially. Code and artifacts are promised at https://github.com/Tencent/IterSynth with a permissive-license release statement for the checkpoint, SFT corpus, and RDPO pipeline. Methodological concerns: (1) the LLM judge is also a Gemini model while evaluation includes frontier proprietary models — self-referential reward provenance is partially mitigated by the judge-swap check; (2) training uses cached retrieval while evaluation uses live tools, a reasonable but distribution-shifting choice; (3) the reference list contains at least one evidently wrong citation — "DeepForge (Petrik & Bambach, 2024)" is a Journal of Manufacturing Processes paper on metal-forming control yet is cited as a deep-search QA dataset — which undermines confidence in data-provenance documentation; (4) headline Table 1 numbers appear to correspond to the resampling-enhanced configuration in Table 15 (e.g., xBench-2510: 37.0 base → 46.0 resampled), so the contribution of the test-time trick is not disentangled in the main table. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained 8B agent with experiments actually run). Practical: Yes — an 8B backbone on 96GB H20s (32 GPUs for SFT, 64 for RL), runnable on comparable commercial hardware, plus a zero-prompting variant for anyone with API access to Claude-4.5-Opus or DeepSeek-V3.1. Efficient: Favorable — 13–15% less inference wall-clock than a dual-model deployment of the same total hardware, 1.5–1.6× faster than Tongyi-DR-30B, and the rubric judge adds only ~$192 (~1,120–1,440 calls/step, ~128K calls over 100 steps) to the RL stage. Effective: Strong evidence on the target failure mode — context-exhaustion rate drops from 59–65% (ReAct) to <5% with 7–8 average rounds — though GAIA performance (55.3) lags a 4B baseline, so effectiveness on general assistant-style tasks is only partial. Scalable: Untested beyond 8B and 50 rounds; the claim that the paradigm scales with size is inference from the prompting results on much larger backbones, not a trained scaling experiment. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (checkpoint, ~10K-trajectory SFT corpus, verl-based RDPO pipeline, GitHub repo), not just a paper. Strengths: - The disentangling experiments are the paper's best asset: the controlled ReAct-vs-IterSynth comparison under identical questions, teacher, and RL reward (Table 8) directly answers the obvious confound that gains come from better teacher trajectories, and the shared-vs-independent parameter ablation (Table 9, +3.5) pre-empts the capacity-competition objection. - RDPO's core insight — that dense Synthesizer rewards and sparse Planner rewards corrupt each other under shared advantage normalization, proven by the w/o-RD ablation dropping to 47.2 (below outcome-only GRPO) — is a genuinely non-obvious empirical finding about credit assignment in multi-role agentic RL. - Appendix H's measurement that ReAct context exhaustion is backbone-independent (59–65% non-completion on BrowseComp-100 for both DeepSeek-V3.1 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 at 64K) is a useful, quotable empirical result in its own right, and the main gains concentrate exactly on the benchmarks with the highest exhaustion rates. - The qualitative failure analysis (relation-dropping summaries on GAIA; confirmation-bias consolidation of wrong sources on BrowseComp) names specific, actionable failure modes rather than hand-waving. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations more directly than most. Appendix F.4 identifies two failure modes: summary information loss (the Synthesizer omits relational links between retrieved facts, causing wrong answers despite correct retrieval) and incorrect evidence consolidation (a wrong but authoritative source entering the summary biases later rounds, resembling confirmation bias). They propose structured summary representations and explicit contradiction detection as future work. They also implicitly acknowledge that RDPO's gains depend on judge quality (addressed via the judge-swap robustness check) and that the shared-parameter design could cause role interference (addressed via Table 9). Not stated: any acknowledgment of missing statistical significance testing, the small GAIA/xBench test sets, or the contribution of the test-time resampling trick to headline numbers. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical rigor: all comparisons (including the +4.2 headline margin over MiroThinker-8B) rest on single runs with no seeds, CIs, or significance tests, on benchmarks where GAIA has 103 questions and xBench 100 per split — the margin on GAIA-class noise-prone sets cannot be trusted at the reported precision. - The headline Table 1 numbers seem to embed the not-attempted resampling strategy (Table 15: xBench-2510 37.0→46.0, BrowseComp 25.7→30.9, BC-ZH 49.1→55.4), yet Table 1 never states this; without it, IterSynth-8B's average would be roughly 44.9, below MiroThinker-v1.0-8B's 46.5. This is the single most serious reporting issue. - Benchmark profile: the average is inflated by BrowseComp-ZH and xBench-2510; on GAIA the model underperforms AgentCPM-Explore-4B (55.3 vs 63.9) and on BrowseComp it ties MiroThinker-8B (30.9 vs 31.1), so "strong frontier among small agents" holds mainly for exploration-heavy Chinese and newest-split tasks. - Reward-model circularity risk: rubric rewards are generated by an LLM judge and rubrics distilled by Claude-4.6-Sonnet; only coarse judge-swap correlation (±1.0 point) and a small (200-sample) human-agreement spot-check back the reward signal, and no reward-hacking red-teaming beyond training-curve inspection is provided. - The reference "DeepForge (Petrik & Bambach, 2024)" is a metal-forming manufacturing paper cited as a deep-search training dataset — a data-provenance documentation error that a careful reviewer cannot ignore. - Efficiency comparison against 30B agents omits MiroThinker-v1.7-mini, the actual accuracy leader; only Tongyi-DR-30B (58.2 avg) is benchmarked on wall-clock. Bottom Line: A practitioner training small search agents should read this paper for its unusually well-controlled ablations and the role-decoupled advantage-normalization trick, which is cheap to adopt and credibly worth ~2 points over outcome-only GRPO — but treat the headline ranking with caution until the resampling contribution is separated from the main results, and note that at frontier scale MiroThinker-v1.7-mini still leads by nearly 19 points.

From Pretraining to Proficiency: Real-World Subtask RL for Long - Horizon Manipulation with Minimal Human Intervention

S Su, B Yang, Z Deng, B Liang, YF Yeung, Z Wang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PARTS, a real-world RL framework that adapts a pretrained VLA policy to long-horizon manipulation by training lightweight residual policies only at human-identified bottleneck subtasks, improving full-task success from 32% to 61% on bimanual YAM earbud insertion and from 50% to 95% on single-arm Franka cable insertion using 17–29 minutes of real-robot rollouts per task. - Why it's important: Real-world RL on full long-horizon tasks wastes scarce robot time re-executing subtasks the base policy already solves, and sparse terminal rewards starve the learner of signal; concentrating practice at the few failing subtasks directly attacks the data-cost bottleneck that limits deploying foundation policies on precise industrial-style manipulation. - How it does it: Keep the VLA frozen, confine TD3+BC residual actors to a few masked action dimensions during bottleneck windows, and use coding-agent-authored programs (policy selector, success verifier, auto-reset) plus periodic success-reweighted retraining so every local attempt yields a usable reward without human corrections or switching decisions. - The good: Under an exactly matched robot-rollout budget, PARTS beats three recent real-world RL fine-tuning baselines (DSRL, EXPO-FT, RLT) by more than 25 percentage points in full-task success, with per-stage success gains of 20–35 points on the hard insertion subtasks. - The missing: Evaluations use only 20 episodes per task with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, and the success-reweighted retraining ablation is run on a single task, so the headline gaps may not be statistically robust. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on real-world RL fine-tuning of VLA policies or autonomous data-collection systems, since the failure-localized training recipe and human-involvement accounting are directly reusable; skip it if you only care about simulated benchmarks or scaling laws for foundation models.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is the top contributor — failure-localized subtask RL for frozen VLA adaptation is a genuine new formulation, and the restaging-overfitting insight plus the finding that full-task RL baselines actively degrade reliable subskills push Non-Obviousness to 72. Rigor (55) is the primary drag: 20 evaluation episodes with no error bars or seeds cannot substantiate the headline margins, only one component is ablated, the matched-budget accounting excludes reset overhead, and no code or model artifact is released (Impact 55), limiting real-world usefulness beyond the three tasks. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*55 = 64.
