Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying pretrained robot foundation policies (VLAs) on long-horizon manipulation tasks face a specific failure pattern: the policy completes most subtasks but repeatedly fails at a few consequential ones — millimeter-precision insertions, or preparatory actions whose terminal state degrades later stages. Supervised fine-tuning requires humans to re-demonstrate behaviors that already work, and full-task RL with sparse terminal reward (which factorizes as the product of per-subtask outcomes, Eq. 1) provides almost no learning signal when base success is low, since most rollouts return zero and repeated early failures prevent the learner from ever practicing later subtasks. The problem is how to concentrate limited real-robot interaction time at the bottlenecks while keeping training rollouts autonomous. Key Idea: Failure-localized policy repair: freeze the pretrained policy everywhere it is reliable, and for each bottleneck train a small bounded residual actor-critic rewarded by that subtask's own binary outcome, so every 3–15 s attempt (instead of every 20–120 s episode) produces a learnable signal, with the local reward replacing the unobservable full-task factorization. The secondary insight is that online-only updates overfit to restaged local reset distributions, which is fixed by periodic retraining of fresh networks on a success-reweighted replay (all successes plus a fraction ρ of failures) followed by redeployment. Methodology: The pipeline has two phases. (1) Setup: humans identify bottlenecks K from base-policy failures and write contracts (entry set, correctable action dimensions and bounds, outcome criterion, motion budget) with a few subtask demonstrations; coding agents (Claude Fable 5, GPT-6 Astra) author three executable programs — policy selector, success verifier (SAM3 segmentation + Gemini VLM queries for geometric predicates), and reset policy — which humans review on labeled episodes but which run as ordinary code thereafter. The base policy is π0.5 after SFT on a small offline demonstration set. (2) Training: at each bottleneck the frozen VLA supplies nominal action chunks Āt; a residual actor fθ(z, p, Ā) outputs a normalized residual chunk in [−1,1]^(C×d_k), masked to bottleneck-relevant action coordinates and clipped to physical bounds (Eq. 2), trained with chunk-level TD3+BC (twin critics, C-step TD targets per Eq. 3) with an actor loss (Eq. 4) balancing critic value, cloning of successful residuals, and anchoring failed attempts toward zero residual, plus reference dropout of Ā to prevent the actor from merely copying. Each bottleneck keeps its own replay buffer. Periodically, fresh actor/critic networks are retrained on the curated success-weighted buffer and redeployed to collect more data. Three well-justified design decisions: the coordinate mask restricting RL to relevant dimensions (prevents disruption of reliable behavior); restage-vs-retry reset logic (reduces human resets); and success-reweighted retraining (ablated, discussed under Results). Less justified: the choice of ρ and loss weights λ is not ablated, and verifier reliability for the earbud task still requires human label checking. Key Results: Three real tasks, two platforms, 20 evaluation episodes per method: earbud insertion (bimanual YAM, 4-stage dependent chain, ~mm precision) full-task success 32% (SFT) → 61%; cable unplug-and-plug (Franka FR3) 50% → 95% after 29 min of RL rollouts, with insertion stage success roughly doubling (50% → 95%); LEGO sorting (ten bricks in 150 s, out-of-distribution small bricks) progress score 54 → 82 with 17 min of rollouts. Under a matched robot-rollout budget, baselines score: earbuds — DSRL 48.3% progress/15% binary, EXPO-FT 40%/0%, RLT 41.7%/0%, vs PARTS 66.7%/40%; cable — DSRL 82.5%/65%, EXPO-FT 37.5%/20%, RLT 85%/70%, vs PARTS 97.5%/95%. Notably, EXPO-FT (which updates the backbone) degraded previously reliable behaviors such as cable unplugging, and per-stage data show DSRL halved unplug success (100% → 55%), supporting the claim that full-task RL with sparse rewards damages non-bottleneck behaviors. Baselines are recent (2025–2026) and current, run with official code where available (RLT reproduced from paper). Scale is standard for real-robot RL — tens of minutes of rollouts, not stress-scale — and the paper claims (but does not test) broader applicability. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW FORMULATION component (failure-localized subtask RL for adapting a frozen pretrained policy, evaluated on full-task success). The genuinely novel element is the full integration: executable agent-authored contracts (selector/verifier/reset) that make local outcome rewards and resets autonomous, combined with success-reweighted retraining and redeployment so the data-collection policy co-evolves with learning. The individual pieces are known — residual RL (Ankile et al., Johannink et al.), TD3+BC, chunk-level action RL, offline retraining for online RL (Mark et al.), phase-restricted learning (RLT, MORI, BORA) — applied and coordinated in a new setting; the retraining mechanism is adapted from prior work rather than invented here. Rigor & Reproducibility: A single ablation (PARTS without success-reweighted retraining on earbuds) shows the retraining mechanism matters (binary success 40% → 25% with the hatched-bar ablation), but no other component ablations exist — the contribution of the coding-agent-authored verifiers, reference dropout, or the λ− anchoring term is not isolated. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; 20 episodes per task gives binomial confidence intervals of roughly ±10–20 points at these success rates, so some baseline gaps (e.g., RLT 85% vs PARTS 97.5% progress on cable) are tighter than they appear. Matched rollout budgets are counted as elapsed robot time excluding resets, which favors PARTS since its wall-clock overhead from resets/updates is excluded — a defensible but favorable accounting choice. DSRL and EXPO-FT use official code on Franka but were reimplemented for YAM; RLT has no official code and was reproduced from the paper. No code or model release is stated; a project page (destiny000621.github.io/PARTS) exists. All evaluation is on the authors' own three tasks; no external benchmark. This is an arXiv preprint, apparently under review (formatting suggests a robotics conference submission), so results are not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a real-robot system actually run on hardware). Practical: Runs on commodity research arms (YAM, Franka FR3) with consumer-grade perception models (SAM3, Gemini) and coding agents for setup — deployable by any lab with a VLA inference stack, though π0.5 access and agent-authored program review require ML expertise. Efficient: 17–29 min of robot rollouts per task is very cheap by real-world RL standards, and freezing the VLA avoids backbone-gradient costs, but human setup (bottleneck identification, contract writing, program review, earbud label checking, occasional resets) is non-trivial and not quantified in hours. Effective: The evidence shows it improves full-task success on the authors' three tasks, which is the stated metric — but generalization to new tasks or to bottlenecks where the verifier is hard to specify is untested, and the earbud task already required a human in the reward loop. Scalable: Not tested beyond three tasks and two platforms; the paper claims reduced human involvement improves scalability, but the number of tasks, the reliance on humans for bottleneck identification, and per-task contract engineering all suggest setup cost grows roughly linearly with task count. Deliverable: paper plus project page; no stated code, dataset, or trained-model artifact. Strengths: (1) The failure-localization formulation is a genuine conceptual contribution to real-world VLA adaptation: it reframes the problem from global policy improvement to repairing a few subtasks, and the per-stage measurements directly support the bottleneck analysis (e.g., second-earbud insertion improving 30% → 50% while case preparation stays at 80–90%). (2) The human-involvement accounting in Table I is unusually honest and specific — the paper states plainly that earbud verification and some resets remain human tasks rather than claiming full autonomy. (3) The restaging-overfitting observation — that local resets narrow the state distribution and cause online-updated residuals to fail under nominal execution at evaluation — is a non-obvious empirical insight about subtask RL that most phase-restricted methods (RLT) do not address, and the retraining ablation ties it to a measurable outcome. (4) The finding that full-task RL baselines actively degrade reliable subskills (DSRL dropping unplug success from 100% to 55%; EXPO-FT to 0% binary success) is a useful negative result for the field. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that humans identify bottlenecks, write contracts, review agent-generated programs, check earbud verifier labels, and perform resets the robot cannot (e.g., extracting a seated earbud, retrieving dropped objects) — confronted directly, with Table I enumerating exactly which supervision types remain per method. The future-work section acknowledges the lack of autonomous bottleneck identification, dense reward generation, and recovery-behavior practice after failures. They do not, however, discuss the small evaluation sample sizes or the single-task scope of the retraining ablation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical rigor: 20 episodes with no variance estimates cannot support the claimed >25-point margins at these success rates; multiple seeds per RL run are also absent, and real-world RL is notoriously high-variance. (2) The matched-budget metric excludes reset and update time; since PARTS performs many more local attempts with restaging, its total wall-clock and human cost per experiment may be understated. (3) The coding-agent scaffolding is never ablated against simpler hand-coded selectors/verifiers, so the paper cannot show the agentic component is necessary rather than a convenience. (4) All three tasks are precise-insertion-style or grasp-repeat manipulation with visually verifiable outcomes; the framework's dependence on specifiable success criteria means tasks with ambiguous or continuous-quality outcomes are unaddressed, and the earbud task already pushed the verifier past its limit (requiring human labels). (5) The generalization of a retrained residual to states produced by the preceding base policy is asserted to be fixed by retraining, but the paper does not measure the entry-state distribution shift directly. (6) Baselines were run by the authors with modifications (reimplementation on YAM, disabled human-intervention features in EXPO-FT's released regime), so baseline numbers may not reflect those methods' best configuration. Bottom Line: For anyone doing real-robot RL on top of pretrained VLA policies, this is worth reading as one of the more complete demonstrations of failure-localized fine-tuning with concrete human-cost accounting, but the missing statistical rigor, three-task evaluation, and una­blated agentic scaffolding mean its headline numbers should be treated as promising rather than established — RLT-style phase refinement plus better reset handling covers much of the same ground.

GeoPair: Geometry-Preserving Cross-Layer Factorization for Training-Free Transformer Compression (11 ▲ )

Baher Mohammad, Ammar Ali, Stamatios Lefkimmiatis · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GeoPair, a training-free post-training compression framework that optimally pairs cross-layer weight matrices and learns shared dictionaries under layer-specific whitening transforms, using a closed-form generalized Sylvester equation solver plus HTP-based sparse coefficient updates. - Why it's important: Transformer memory and compute footprints block deployment in resource-constrained settings, and existing data-aware factorization pipelines either optimize layers in isolation or force cross-layer sharing through covariance averaging that distorts each layer's activation geometry, degrading fidelity at high compression. - How it does it: It casts layer grouping as a global maximum-weight matching problem (solved exactly with Edmonds' Blossom algorithm over a whitened-space Frobenius submatrix distance) and solves the coupled two-layer dictionary update exactly via simultaneous diagonalization of the two matrix pencils, avoiding iterative solvers and step-size tuning. - The good: The ablations are genuinely component-isolating — on Llama-3 8B at CR=0.2 the full pipeline reaches 68.17 average zero-shot accuracy vs. a 70.36 uncompressed baseline (~97% recovery) and 9.43 Wiki perplexity, while Basis Sharing drops to 53.47 and 41.26 — and a 5-seed appendix study reports 45.85% ± 0.19%, showing low variance. - The missing: The claimed motivation of sublinear storage scaling through cross-layer sharing is never demonstrated beyond pairs (the closed-form solver fundamentally cannot handle m > 2 layers), and no inference latency/throughput numbers are reported — only parameter-count compression ratios. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM compression or structured factorization and want the current strongest training-free recipe with real math behind the grouping step; skip it if you need multi-layer (m > 2) sharing or runtime speedup evidence, which it explicitly does not provide.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (68) reflects real mathematical contributions — the closed-form generalized Sylvester solver and exactly-solved Blossom matching replace genuine heuristics — supported by Rigor (65) with unusually thorough component-isolating ablations and convergence proofs, though main tables lack error bars and three baselines are the authors' own preprints. Completeness (65) and Resilience (60) are dragged down by the oversold 'sublinear storage scaling' motivation (never demonstrated beyond pairs and arguably impossible with the closed-form solver) and the complete absence of inference latency or throughput numbers, which undercuts any compression-for-deployment claim. Impact (40) is the weakest dimension: code only in supplementary materials with no public repository URL, no released compressed checkpoints, and parameter-count ratios standing in for measured speedups. Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying large transformers in memory- or compute-constrained environments need post-training compression that avoids costly recovery fine-tuning. Data-aware matrix factorization (SVD-LLM, ASVD, DRONE) approximates each layer independently and ignores the cross-layer redundancy that deep stacks naturally exhibit. The one prior attempt at principled cross-layer sharing, Basis Sharing (ICLR 2025), pairs fixed adjacent layers and averages layer covariances into a global whitening transform; the authors argue this distorts layer-specific activation geometry, restricts sharing to adjacent pairs, and requires model-specific manual constraints. The open problem is how to share a dictionary across layers whose calibration-induced whitening spaces differ, without degrading either layer. Key Idea: The core trick is that the joint two-layer shared-dictionary objective — minimizing Σᵢ ‖LᵢWᵢ − LᵢDCᵢ‖²F with distinct Cholesky whitening transforms Lᵢ — has a dictionary-update optimality condition that is a two-term generalized Sylvester equation, which can be solved in closed form by simultaneous diagonalization (GEVD of the two matrix pencils), since both Gram matrices are SPD after Tikhonov regularization. This eliminates the covariance-averaging heuristic entirely: each layer keeps its own whitening geometry while sharing one dictionary. The second half of the idea is replacing heuristic adjacent pairing with a globally optimal assignment: a scale-invariant whitened submatrix distance δ(Wᵢ, Wⱼ) converted to edge weights and solved as maximum-weight matching via Blossom, with the matching unrestricted across projection types. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Distance computation: for every candidate weight pair sharing input dimension d, compute the normalized Frobenius submatrix distance in each layer's whitened space, efficiently evaluated as a sliding-window 1D cross-correlation with prefix sums. (2) Optimal matching: build a complete graph over all projections, set edge weights to C − δ(Wᵢ, Wⱼ), and solve maximum-weight matching exactly (NetworkX Blossom, <2 s for N=560 weights). (3) Shared-dictionary learning per pair: alternating minimization on the bi-convex objective of Eq. (2); the coefficient update is a closed-form regularized weighted least-squares solve (or an ℓ0-constrained version via Hard Thresholding Pursuit with a batched conjugate-gradient restricted projection, T_HTP=2, 10 CG iterations); the dictionary update solves the generalized Sylvester equation via two constant GEVD decompositions and element-wise division. Initialization is truncated SVD of the concatenated original-space weights. Convergence to a block-stationary point is argued under BSUM and Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz theory with the four required conditions verified in Appendix A.2. Critical design decisions: (a) pairwise-only sharing — well-justified mathematically (simultaneous diagonalization works for two pencils only) but it caps the storage-saving potential; (b) Tikhonov-regularized whitening — standard and justified; (c) unrestricted cross-projection-type pairing (attention and FFN weights may be paired) — asserted to help but only implicitly tested. The objective is strictly activation-reconstruction error over 256 FineWeb calibration samples; no distillation or output-logit matching. Key Results: On Llama-3 8B at CR=0.2, the full pipeline achieves 68.17 average zero-shot accuracy vs. 70.36 uncompressed, against Basis Sharing at 53.47; at CR=0.4 on Llama-3.2 1B it reaches 45.6 vs. 57.6 baseline. Against dictionary-learning baselines (SVD-LLM, CoSpaDi, ROCKET, COMPOT) on Llama-3 8B across CR 0.2–0.7, GeoPair is consistently highest in both average accuracy and Wiki perplexity. Against pruning methods on Llama-2 7B at 20%, GeoPair (training-free) scores 63.58 average vs. 62.22 for LoRAShear (which uses recovery fine-tuning) and 57.23 for WANDA. Cross-architecture results (Qwen3 8B/32B, Gemma 3 12B, Phi-4 14B at 1B–32B scale) show GeoPair dominating Basis Sharing on both accuracy and perplexity at every ratio, with a denoising effect at low CR (e.g., Qwen3 32B perplexity 3.26 vs. 3.74 uncompressed at CR=0.2). Cross-modal: Wan2.2 5B video model loses only 1×10⁻⁴ X-CLIP score at 20% compression (0.2164 vs. 0.2165, 50 prompts); VibeVoice 1.5B audio goes from WER 6.6/UTMOS 4.17 to 14.5/3.98 at 20%, while Basis Sharing fails outright (WER >100%). Compression runtime: 850 s (1B), 3,010 s (8B), 19,906 s (32B) on 4×A100-40GB. Baselines are current within the factorization paradigm (2024–2026 work, including the authors' own prior systems), though the pruning baselines (WANDA, ShortGPT, LLM-Pruner) are older. Testing is at standard, not stress, scale — 32B is the largest model; no 70B+ experiments. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with a secondary NEW FORMULATION element). The genuinely novel pieces are the closed-form generalized Sylvester solver for shared-dictionary updates under distinct per-layer whitening transforms, and the casting of cross-layer grouping as an exactly-solved maximum-weight matching problem. The ingredients themselves — Sylvester equations, Blossom matching, HTP sparse coding, calibration-weighted factorization — are all established; the contribution is their composition into the first optimization-driven cross-layer pairing + sharing pipeline, replacing the heuristics of Basis Sharing and Matrix PCA (the latter a self-citation from the same group). Rigorous & Reproducibility (Rigor & Reproducibility): Ablations are unusually thorough: grouping metric (Frobenius vs. cosine vs. greedy adjacency), KS sparsity ratio, HTP vs. IHT (HTP with 2 iterations matches IHT-10 in quality at ~4× less time), initialization strategy, calibration dataset (FineWeb) and count (256), and HTP/CG iteration budget. Statistical significance is reported for one configuration (Llama-1B, CR=0.4, 5 seeds: 45.85% ± 0.19%), but main-table results carry no error bars. Code is stated to be in the supplementary materials; no public repository URL is given. Methodological concerns: (i) several baselines (CoSpaDi, ROCKET, COMPOT, Matrix PCA) are the authors' own preprints, so baseline selection is partly self-referential; (ii) Table 2 switches to a different benchmark suite "to follow the experiments of the corresponding pruning papers," so accuracy numbers are not comparable across tables; (iii) all evaluation is zero-shot benchmark accuracy/perplexity — standard but a proxy for downstream utility; (iv) ROCKET and COMPOT citations are 2026 preprints, unverifiable at review time. This is a preprint (NeurIPS-formatted with checklist), not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method the authors run end-to-end, with energy/CO₂ reporting). Practical: Yes — runs on 4×A100-40GB GPUs with a CPU-only matching step; no exotic hardware. Efficient: Compression is cheap relative to fine-tuning-based recovery (0.147 kWh for a 1B model, ≤1.4 kg CO₂eq at 32B, runtime scaling roughly linearly with parameters), though ~5.5 hours for a 32B model is non-trivial. Effective: Evidence supports the stated goal of preserving function without fine-tuning at moderate compression (CR ≤ 0.3), but at CR=0.4 on small models degradation is severe (45.6 vs. 57.6 accuracy on 1B), so the claim holds in a regime, not universally. Scalable: Tested to 32B with near-linear compression-cost scaling, but the pairwise-sharing structure means storage scales as ~2× dictionary + coefficients per pair — the sublinear-storage motivation is claimed, not measured, and no inference-latency or throughput numbers appear anywhere. Deliverable: code in supplementary materials; no released compressed checkpoints or public repo URL stated. Strengths: (1) The generalized Sylvester formulation is a real contribution — it converts a heuristic (covariance averaging) into an exact, well-conditioned closed-form solve with a clear feasibility proof (denominator 1 + λⱼσₖ ≥ 1), and the appendix verification of BSUM/KL convergence conditions is more careful than typical compression papers. (2) Replacing greedy adjacent pairing with an exact global matching over a shape-agnostic distance is a clean, optimal-by-construction alternative, and the ablation shows grouping matters (greedy adjacency: 43.35 avg accuracy vs. 45.61 for Frobenius matching at CR=0.4). (3) The component-wise ablation cleanly attributes gains — e.g., on Llama-3 8B, Sylvester alone gives 56.4, +grouping 57.46, +HTP 68.17 — showing sparsification, not just sharing, drives most of the recovery. (4) Honest limitation section and operational details (energy, seeds, convergence-iteration ablations) exceed field norms. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict the framework to pairwise grouping and state that extension to m > 2 layers is non-trivial because the exact closed-form solver relies on simultaneous diagonalization of two matrix pencils, which does not analytically generalize; they name multi-group sharing as the primary future direction. They also acknowledge in the appendix that the ℓ0 subproblem is NP-hard (convergence is only to a local stationary point, mitigated by SVD initialization and restarts) and that premature HTP truncation can stall the loop. This is a direct, credible confrontation of the main scope boundary — a positive signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The introduction's promise of "sublinear storage scaling" is never tested — with only pairwise sharing, storage scales linearly with layers minus one dictionary per pair; the framing oversells what was built. (2) No inference-time latency, memory, or throughput measurements: a compression ratio defined purely in parameters does not establish deployability, and per-column top-k sparsity in coefficients may not map to speedups without custom kernels. (3) Heavy authorial overlap with three of the four dictionary-learning baselines (CoSpaDi, ROCKET, COMPOT) raises baseline-selection fairness questions that the paper does not address. (4) Main results lack error bars or significance tests (only one configuration gets 5 seeds); (5) the cross-modal evaluations are thin — X-CLIP on 50 prompts for video and 100 held-out samples for audio are proof-of-concept, not evidence of generalization, and X-CLIP is a weak proxy for video fidelity. (6) The "training-free" advantage over fine-tuned pruning baselines is not controlled for compute: GeoPair's calibration cost is reported, but the fine-tuning budget of the fine-tuned baselines is not, so the comparison's fairness is unverifiable. Bottom Line: For anyone building training-free LLM compression, this is worth reading — it replaces the two weakest heuristics in cross-layer factorization (adjacency grouping and covariance averaging) with principled, exactly-solved alternatives and backs them with unusually thorough ablations — but the sublinear-storage promise remains unproven until the m > 2 extension exists, and the absence of any latency numbers means deployment claims should be treated as parameter-count proxies only.

A Framework to Quantify the Probability of Future Cyber Loss Events

S Peters, M Eian · arxiv.org · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LEFSA, a probabilistic framework that reformulates FAIR-style Loss Event Frequency estimation as calibrated machine-level Cyber Loss Event prediction from endpoint telemetry, with hierarchical aggregation to services, business processes, and organization-level risk distributions. - Why it's important: Quantitative cyber-risk frameworks like FAIR have always struggled to estimate loss-event likelihood from data rather than expert guesswork, leaving cyber risk quantification largely qualitative despite rising attack frequency and insurance claims. - How it does it: A supervised model (XGBoost) outputs calibrated per-machine probabilities of being in a security incident next week, and these marginals are combined into aggregate predictive distributions — Poisson-binomial/normal under independence, or Monte Carlo over a joint (copula-based) distribution when machines are dependent. - The good: The strongest evidence is a real deployed evaluation on 110,924 machines across 23 organizations using Mnemonic's MDR telemetry, where XGBoost achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.90 and mean Expected Calibration Error of 0.094% under rolling-window validation. - The missing: The framework's headline contribution — dependence-aware hierarchical aggregation — is never empirically evaluated; the paper itself measures that aggregates are heavily overdispersed (dispersion statistic 37.23, p < 0.001 under the independence assumption) yet the copula machinery needed to fix this is left as future work. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on quantitative cyber-risk management, FAIR operationalization, or security-telemetry-based prediction; skip it if you want a complete, validated end-to-end system, since the aggregation layer is propositional only.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations practicing quantitative cyber-risk management (typically via FAIR) cannot estimate Loss Event Frequency credibly: scenario-specific incident data is scarce, and contact-frequency/susceptibility inputs are hard to operationalize. Existing frameworks (ISO/IEC 27005, NIST SP 800-30, OCTAVE, CORAS) prescribe processes but no data-driven estimation procedure. Prior quantitative work either operates at the organization level on external data (offering no machine-level attribution) or predicts only malware infection at the machine level (offering no path to organization-wide risk aggregation). Security teams and MSSPs/MDR providers need likelihood estimates that are simultaneously data-driven, machine-attributable, and aggregable to the asset levels that carry business risk. Key Idea: Reformulate the FAIR LEF quantity as a supervised, calibrated per-machine classification problem — "will machine m experience a CLE next period?" — and then treat infrastructure-level risk as the distribution of a sum of these Bernoulli outcomes, so the entire risk stack inherits from calibrated marginals plus an explicit dependence model. The aggregation mathematics (Poisson-binomial, CLT-based normal approximation, Monte Carlo over a joint distribution for VaR/Expected Shortfall) is standard; the reframing of FAIR's LEF as machine-level prediction is the genuinely new move. Methodology: LEFSA has two stages. (1) Machine-level LEF: define CLE as a measurable outcome (here, machine reported in a SOC security incident), construct an information set F_t of features in four groups (exposure, vulnerabilities, security controls, threats) built from hourly machine profiles aggregated weekly, plus the one-period lagged outcome, and fit a model mapping F_t to [0,1], with post-hoc calibration (Platt/isotonic) available if needed. (2) Infrastructure-level LEF: for a group of machines M_{t,g}, the aggregate Y_t+1 is the count of machines with a CLE. Under conditional independence, Y is Poisson-binomial with mean Σp̂ and variance Σp̂(1−p̂), approximated by normal or Poisson. Under dependence, the paper specifies a joint conditional distribution estimated via copulas (including dynamic copula parameters θ_t+1 = h(θ_t, Z_t, ε_t+1)) with Monte Carlo simulation to produce aggregate predictive distributions and tail metrics (P(Y>k), VaR, ES). Critical design decisions: (a) calibrated probabilities as the interface between layers — justified by the explicit calibration requirement and verified empirically; (b) joint cross-organizational training rather than per-organization models — justified by results (joint training outperformed organization-specific models); (c) the copula-based dependence layer — specified in detail but never fitted or evaluated. Hyperparameter tuning used Optuna over the first two rolling windows; evaluation used rolling-window training on weeks 1..t and testing on week t+1 across 11 consecutive weekly windows. Key Results: On proprietary MDR data (110,924 machines, 23 organizations, 12 weeks, 952,770 machine-period instances, 0.134% positive rate), XGBoost beat Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Histogram Gradient Boosting in model selection. Across the evaluation windows: mean ROC-AUC 0.90 (range 0.82–0.95), mean PR-AUC 0.23 (baseline positive rate 0.06–0.27% per week, so roughly 45–500× a random classifier by the authors' ratio), accuracy above 99.8%, mean ECE 0.094%, calibration slope ~1.00. SHAP analysis showed the lagged outcome was the most influential predictor in every period. A key negative result: despite well-calibrated marginals, aggregate CLE counts showed substantial overdispersion (37.23, p < 0.001), demonstrating that machine-level CLEs are not conditionally independent given F_t and that the independence-based aggregation would understate tail risk. One evaluation window showed markedly degraded performance and calibration, attributed to distribution shift. Computational cost is modest: per 1,000 machines, ~6.3% of one core for streaming and 15% for weekly training, under 600 MB peak RAM. Scale is standard (tens of organizations, 12 weeks) — not stress-scale, and the time horizon is short for rare-event risk. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD (partial). The genuinely novel element is the reformulation of FAIR's LEF as calibrated machine-level probabilistic prediction plus a formally specified hierarchical aggregation scheme spanning machines to organization. The machine-level classifier itself (XGBoost on endpoint telemetry) is a competent application of known techniques, extending prior malware-infection predictors (e.g., RiskTeller) to a generalized CLE target; the copula aggregation layer is assembled from established financial-econometrics machinery (Patton dynamic copulas, vine copulas) and is not validated here. The empirical finding that calibrated marginals still leave strong aggregate overdispersion is a genuinely useful NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Rigor & Reproducibility: Reasonable for the machine-level layer, absent for the aggregation layer. Ablations exist in the form of model comparison (4 model families) and evaluation of class-weighting/calibration variants (neither helped). Rolling-window validation is appropriate for temporal data, and calibration is measured (ECE, slope) rather than just discrimination. However: no multiple seeds or confidence intervals are reported; PR-AUC of 0.23, while far above the positive-rate baseline, is modest in absolute terms and is reported without precision@k or cost-sensitive metrics that would matter operationally; labels derive from SOC incident reports and may include non-compromises and missed detections; the dataset is proprietary and cannot be released, so nothing is reproducible; no code is published; no baseline from the prior machine-level malware-prediction literature is run for comparison. The overdispersion analysis is a credibility positive — the authors report evidence against their own independence assumption rather than hiding it. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — the framework was deployed as a live service across the 23 organizations). - Practical: Yes — it runs on a single 48-core Intel Xeon Gold 5118 server with 251 GB RAM and already operates as a production service in the authors' MDR offering. - Efficient: Very — sub-10^2 MB storage and well under one core per 1,000 machines per week for both streaming and training; cost is dominated by telemetry infrastructure, not modeling. - Effective: For machine-level prediction, yes — ROC-AUC 0.90 with verified calibration on rolling out-of-time windows; for infrastructure-level risk quantification, not demonstrated — the dependence-aware aggregation that would deliver VaR/ES at service and organization level was never run, and measured overdispersion shows the implemented independence path is biased for tail risk. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested beyond 23 organizations and 12 weeks; the authors flag that dependence amplification at group level worsens with more machines, so scaling may aggravate the miscalibration of aggregate risk rather than resolve it. The work delivers a production-internal framework and trained models within the authors' company but no public artifact — no library, dataset, or weights. Strengths: - The reformulation of FAIR's LEF as a measurable, supervised, machine-level prediction task is a real conceptual contribution that closes a well-identified gap between qualitative risk frameworks and operational telemetry. - Rare empirical access to multi-organization MDR telemetry (110,924 machines, 23 organizations) with a live deployment, which almost no academic work has; the cross-organizational joint-training result is a practically relevant finding for MSSP-scale learning. - The paper measures calibration, not just discrimination, and reports an honest overdispersion analysis (dispersion 37.23, p < 0.001) that refutes its own independence assumption — this is the most scientifically valuable number in the paper. - The probabilistic aggregation specification (Poisson-binomial → dynamic copula → Monte Carlo → VaR/ES) is worked out at enough mathematical detail that others could implement and test it, even though the authors did not. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct: the proprietary dataset prevents reproducibility; the 12-week horizon limits evaluation of temporal dynamics and rare large-scale incidents; CLE labels derive from incident cases that may not be confirmed compromises, with possible systematic label bias from missed detections; unmonitored machines are excluded, biasing aggregate risk downward; machine churn and inconsistent identifiers complicate tracking; the dependence-aware aggregation layer is explicitly left as an open problem; and cross-organizational training requires contractual and privacy governance. They also note the one degraded evaluation window (distribution shift) and the need for continuous retraining. This candor is a significant credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central mismatch: the paper's stated primary contribution is the aggregation framework, yet zero infrastructure-level results are shown — no service-, process-, or organization-level predictive distribution, no VaR/ES validation, no comparison of Poisson-binomial vs. simulated joint outcomes. The copula layer is pure specification, unimplemented and untested, and copula identification for discrete marginals is known to be problematic (the authors cite Genest & Nešlehová on this but do not resolve it). - PR-AUC of 0.23 is weak in absolute terms; the "45–500× random" framing is a flattering ratio on a 0.134% base rate. No precision@k, alert-budget analysis, or operational utility evaluation is provided — a SOC acting on these predictions is not characterized. - The lagged outcome being the dominant feature suggests the model may largely learn incident recurrence/persistence; a temporal-persistence baseline (predict positive iff incident last week) is not reported, so how much the 40+ feature groups add is unclear. - Evaluation uses the same 23 organizations and telemetry stack for tuning and testing within a 12-week window; no external validation on a different data source, and only ~11 test weeks, so the distribution-shift degradation seen in one window is unquantified in frequency or severity. - Label noise direction (missed detections) could inflate apparent predictability if SOC incident tagging correlates with the same telemetry signals used as features — a potential leakage channel not discussed. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile read for cyber-risk quantification practitioners because it convincingly demonstrates that operational endpoint telemetry supports calibrated machine-level loss-event prediction and honestly exposes the dependence problem that blocks the aggregation layer — but as a complete risk-quantification framework it is only half-built, and the copula-based aggregation it promises remains to be demonstrated by anyone.

Problem & Motivation: Open-ended text-to-SVG generation maps one instruction to many valid renderings, so there is no absolute visual ground truth. This hurts two audiences: practitioners evaluating SVG generators (CLIPScore, Aesthetic classifiers, and HPS, calibrated on photorealistic images, sometimes rank broken SVGs above faithful ones on stylized vector content) and practitioners training them (SFT degenerates into template cloning, and RL with the same unreliable scalar rewards drives the policy toward whichever signal is easiest to inflate — a documented reward-overoptimization pathology). Prior reward paradigms each fail at least one desideratum: pixel metrics need references, rule-based signals ignore the rendering, CLIPScore is coarse and gameable, and existing universal rubrics ignore instruction-specific correctness. Key Idea: Replace a single opaque reward scalar with a query-conditioned checklist: for each instruction, a frontier model writes six instance-aware, deliberately non-reconstructive criteria (design intentions, not pixel specs) grouped into semantic fidelity, visual quality, and rendering style; a VLM judges each rendered rollout against these criteria independently, and the weighted average satisfaction becomes a dense GRPO reward. The trick that makes it work is deriving the rubric from text alone at the level of intentions, which keeps the one-to-many solution space open while still making quality explicitly verifiable per prompt. Methodology: The task is formalized as a token-level MDP where the deterministic reward is computed post-rendering. Pipeline: (1) rubric generation — Claude-Opus-4.6 receives only the instruction, internally drafts one 'ideal SVG' as a quality anchor (never used as a scoring reference), and emits six items with fixed weights (5,5,5,4,5,5) and continuous scoring guides; rubrics whose ideal SVG scores below 0.9 under the judge are filtered out, yielding 30,737 prompt–rubric pairs; (2) RL — Qwen3-8B samples G=8 rollouts per prompt, each rendered with CairoSVG at 512×512 and scored item-by-item by a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B judge; reward is the normalized weighted average of satisfactions (Eq. 2); advantages are group-normalized (Eq. 3) and optimized with the clipped PPO surrogate (GRPO), no KL regularization. Critical design decisions: (a) rubric items are intentions, not reconstruction constraints — justified by the open-endedness argument and qualitatively; (b) a fixed six-item structure with fixed weights shared across prompts — pragmatic but the weight choice is not ablated; (c) rubric-quality filtering via the ideal SVG — sensible, though it anchors rubrics to the generator's own visual priors. Key Results: On MMSVG-Illustration/MMSVG-Icon, RULER (Qwen3-8B backbone) lifts the Rubric score from 0.432/0.395 (zero-shot) to 0.693/0.683, exceeding DeepSeek-V3 (0.686/0.673) at ~1/6 the parameter count and beating SVG specialists IconShop (0.262/0.586), OmniSVG-8B (0.288/0.565), and JanusCoder-8B (0.390/0.384). Blinded human preference on 150 MMSVG-Bench prompts gives non-tie win rates of 53.3% (VectorFusion) to 96.5% (JanusCoder). The reward-design ablation shows Universal Rubric RL (query-agnostic checklist) reaches only 0.660/0.591, while C+A+H scalar RL hacks (Aesthetic 6.697, sequence length 6.3k tokens vs 0.3k baseline, Rubric 0.262 on Icon — below zero-shot). Axis ablations: removing visual quality costs most (−16.32%/−9.35%), rendering second (−13.53%/−7.66%), semantic least (−10.14%/−4.64%); the stricter Rubric-S variant drops to 0.536 and induces text-hint hacking. Gains replicate on Qwen3-4B (0.372→0.561 Illustration) and with GPT-5.5 as rubric generator (0.646 vs 0.662 on Icon), with mean±std over five seeds. Baselines are current (2025-era specialists, frontier LLMs); testing scale is standard (30K training prompts, 2×150 eval prompts, 8×H800 node), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (instance-aware, ground-truth-free rubric rewards for open-ended visual code via a VLM judge) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (systematic quantification that scalar metrics mis-rank stylized SVGs: ρ=0.7929 vs 0.6051/0.5518). The genuinely new element is conditioning the rubric on the instruction and grounding scoring in the rendered image; the machinery (LLM rubrics as rewards, GRPO, VLM judging) is a competent transfer of existing text-domain techniques (RaR, RGR-GRPO, LLM-Rubric) to a new modality, and the universal-rubric baseline is the paper's own control for what instance-awareness adds. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-targeted: axis removals, rubric-prompt sensitivity (Rubric-S), reward-paradigm comparison holding model and optimizer fixed, policy-scale (4B/8B), and rubric-generator swaps, with mean±std over five inference runs. Main-table results are single-run, though Appendix E.1 shows five-run stability. A genuine strength is that the human-alignment evaluator (GPT-5-mini, universal rubric) differs from the training reward model (Qwen3-VL-8B, instance rubrics), partially mitigating self-evaluation circularity. Methodological concerns: (1) training prompts come from MMSVG-Icon/Illustration training splits and evaluation from the same benchmark distribution — the authors acknowledge this is not OOD; (2) render-success-rate differences across methods affect aggregate metrics, though rates are disclosed (RULER: 99.3%/100%); (3) the primary metric is a VLM judge of the same rubric paradigm as the reward; (4) rubric weights (5,5,5,4,5,5) are fixed by fiat and un-ablated. Code, training data, and rubrics are promised for release; a project page exists but no repository URL is confirmed in the text. This is an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained RL systems with benchmark and human evaluation). - Practical: Training needs a full 8×H800 80GB node plus API access to a frontier rubric generator ($2,013 one-time, $0.0655/prompt) and a served 8B judge VLM — accessible to well-resourced labs, not hobbyists. - Efficient: Inference is a single 0.7–2.0k-token autoregressive pass versus 72.1 minutes per sample and 31.4k tokens for VectorFusion, but RL training is expensive: every step renders rollouts and queries a VLM judge, admitted by the authors to be substantially costlier than scalar rewards. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on-distribution (human win rates >50% against all five baselines), but effectiveness is bounded by the benchmark distribution and by judge quality on out-of-distribution prompts. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B policies and ~31k prompts; the authors explicitly flag that judge-in-the-loop cost may limit scaling to larger models and longer rollouts, and no 10× experiment exists. Deliverable: a method plus promised release of code, rubrics, and processed training data; no trained model weights confirmed. Strengths: - The reward-paradigm comparison is a clean controlled experiment: same 8B backbone, same GRPO, only the reward varies, and it isolates both the reward-hacking failure of scalar rewards and the specific contribution of instance-awareness (+0.033/+0.092 Rubric over a universal rubric). - The Rubric-S failure case is an unusually honest and informative negative result: a stricter, structurally focused rubric reopens a text-hint hacking channel even with a −2-weighted penalty, showing rubric design is fragile in a way no single-axis ablation reveals. - The dual-use framing — the same rubric primitive validated for evaluation (900-sample human study, ρ=0.7929, γ=0.7574) and then repurposed as reward — connects the metric-reliability problem to the training-signal problem coherently. - The rubric-generation pipeline is engineered to be reference-free and open-ended (ideal SVG used only for filtering, never for scoring), which is the right design for a one-to-many generation task. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) dependence on two external models (frontier rubric generator, VLM judge) whose biases and blind spots the reward inherits, especially off-distribution; (2) substantially higher RL compute cost from rendering plus per-rollout VLM judging, which may limit scaling; (3) the fixed semantic/visual/stylistic decomposition may not capture all artistic intents or domain-specific preferences. They confront these directly and concretely — a credibility positive — though they do not quantify how often the judge errs or how bias propagates. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Circularity remains at the paradigm level: the headline metric and the training reward are both rubric-based VLM judgments; conventional metrics and the human study mitigate this, but a reviewer should weight the human-preference study (53.3% vs VectorFusion is a near-tie) more than the Rubric-score margins. - No comparison against the two closest prior rubric-reward methods (RaR, RGR-GRPO) as empirical baselines — only a related-work contrast; the universal-rubric baseline partially covers this but is the authors' own construction. - Judge scale is unexplored: Qwen3-VL-8B as the frozen judge is small relative to the judgments being asked of it, and no experiment tests how judge capability bounds final policy quality. - Rubric weights are fixed and un-ablated, and only one alternative rubric specification (Rubric-S) is tested, so sensitivity to the six-item structure is under-sampled relative to the paper's own claim that 'rubric design is the active lever.' - Evaluation is confined to two MMSVG splits plus 150 MMSVG-Bench prompts for the human study; no genuinely out-of-distribution prompt set (e.g., user-submitted or adversarial instructions) tests the rubric generator's coverage. - Data contamination between MMSVG training splits and MMSVG-Bench evaluation prompts is not audited. Bottom Line: For anyone training generative models against subjective visual quality, this is one of the more credible demonstrations that instance-aware rubric rewards beat scalar rewards in both stability and human preference, and the documented hacking case studies alone justify reading it — but the headline numbers should be discounted modestly because the evaluation metric shares the method's own paradigm and everything is tested inside one benchmark family.

Problem & Motivation: Robot foundation models inherit their priors from pretrained backbones: VLAs from vision-language models and world-action models from video generators. Neither pretraining objective forces the representation to expose the precise metric 3D location and extent of task-relevant objects, so the action learner must infer this mapping from robot demonstrations alone — and when demonstrations cover narrow layouts, the policy latches onto visual correlations that fail under object relocation, background changes, or a different designated target. This hurts anyone deploying manipulation policies under scene variation. The gap the authors target is choosing a pretraining foundation whose objective itself requires explicit, metric, promptable grounding of the objects the task is about. Key Idea: Make a pretrained, promptable 3D grounding model (not a language or video model) the frozen foundation of the policy, and condition the action head exclusively on what the grounding model selects: image tokens restricted to task objects plus the robot arm, and detection tokens carrying each object's point cloud, metric 3D box (center, extents, 6D rotation), and Fourier-encoded position. Because the observation is defined by the grounding rather than by the raw scene, relocating a target or designating a new one simply changes the grounded input — no memorized trajectory is invalidated. A side benefit is a unified task-specification interface (language, 2D points, 2D boxes) through which a VLM planner can drive the same low-level policy. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Prompt-to-detection: a span-tagging head over a frozen Flan-T5 encoder parses object phrases from language (or accepts points/boxes directly); the frozen WildDet3D backbone returns per-object 2D boxes, oriented metric 3D boxes, a dense metric depth map, and dense visual features. For sim, the backbone is first fine-tuned once on 2D/3D boxes and depth exported from simulator state, then frozen. (2) Detection-to-observation: image tokens are a 16×16 pooled DINO-feature grid with cells kept only if they overlap task-object boxes (≥30%) or the URDF-projected robot silhouette (>10%); detection tokens encode 512-point object clouds via a shared-MLP encoder with max-, mean-, and octant-pooling, concatenated with the 2D box, Fourier center features, extents, and 6D rotation; a state-history token carries current and previous joint states. (3) Observation-to-action: a 12-block MM-DiT with per-stream parameters and adaptive layer-norm conditioning on language and flow timestep predicts an H-step chunk of absolute joint-position targets via flow matching (L2 velocity loss, Eq. 3), integrated with K Euler steps; only the action head trains. Critical design decisions: (a) freezing the grounding backbone — justified by the ablation showing gains come from output selection, not backbone strength; (b) dual image+detection streams — well-justified by ablations (either alone: 16.0% / 20.3% vs. 46.8% combined); (c) masking unselected scene content — the largest ablation driver (removing both filters: 46.8% → 10.3%). Key Results: On RoboTwin 2.0 (50 bimanual tasks, 100 rollouts/task, single-task training), GAM averages 55.3% (Easy 63.0%, Hard 47.6%) vs. 52.0% for Spatial Forcing and 45.0% for π0.5 trained under the same protocol; on Hard, the margin over the next best entry (Abot-M0, 30.4%) is 17.2 points, while co-trained FastWAM collapses to 1.9% and DP3 to 5.0%. On LIBERO-PRO (single policy, 16 perturbation settings), GAM averages 0.61 vs. 0.53 for π0.5, with the largest gains on Pos and Task perturbations (e.g., Spatial-Task 0.88 vs. ≤0.11 for all baselines) but trailing baselines on Obj perturbations (e.g., LIBERO-Goal 0.69, LIBERO-10 0.50). On a bimanual YAM (20 trials), both GAM and π0.5 score 19/20 in-distribution; under visual shift GAM retains 17/20 (89%) vs. π0.5's 4/20 (21%). On a Franka with a Molmo2 planner over four long-horizon/memory-dependent tasks, GAM reaches 64.7% ID and 49.8% OOD step completion (77% retention) vs. 24.0% (π0.5) and 17.1% (MolmoAct2) OOD. Baselines are current (π0.5, Spatial Forcing, X-VLA, Flex-π) and mostly leaderboard-sourced; the scale is standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale. The surprising finding is that explicit metric geometry plus object filtering, not 3D input per se, drives robustness — full-scene 3D (DP3) fails under randomization. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD — the genuinely novel move is proposing promptable 3D grounding as the pretraining foundation for action learning (a paradigm-level claim), instantiated via a concrete tokenization of grounded objects into image/detection/state streams; the components (flow matching, MM-DiT, point-cloud encoders, point tracking with CoTracker3, VLM planners) are standard, and prior work has separately used 3D representations, selective vision, and spatial interfaces — the unification under one frozen grounding backbone is the new element. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are targeted at the paper's core claim (observation construction), isolating image masking, point cropping, and each stream on 10 RoboTwin tasks × 20 rollouts; however, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and real-robot evaluations rest on 10–20 trials per condition. No code, data, or model release is mentioned beyond a project page URL. Methodological concerns: (1) the grounding backbone is fine-tuned on oracle 3D boxes and depth exported from simulator state — a supervision signal unavailable outside simulation, and the real-robot experiments do not clarify what supervision WildDet3D had there; (2) RoboTwin comparisons mix GAM's single-task training with co-trained baselines (the authors flag this via † but the leaderboard protocol averages them regardless); (3) most RoboTwin baseline numbers come from the benchmark team, introducing protocol-consistency risk; (4) the LIBERO-PRO training/evaluation uses the same benchmark whose perturbations define the claim (mitigated because GAM trains on unperturbed LIBERO data). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component via the planner composition). Practical: Yes — the architecture is a small transformer policy plus off-the-shelf perception, demonstrated on standard Franka and YAM arms with commodity cameras. Efficient: Not stated in absolute terms; the frozen backbone removes pretraining cost, but per-frame 3D grounding, monocular depth, and point tracking add inference overhead relative to a plain VLA — unquantified. Effective: The evidence shows robustness to the tested perturbations (randomization, relocation, visual shift) rather than a proxy, but success is confined to tabletop pick-place-style tasks with 25–50 demonstrations per task. Scalable: Not tested — no evidence at 10× the task count, longer horizons beyond 4 steps, or cluttered real scenes; the planner composition is a plausible but unproven scaling path. Deliverable: a paper plus project page; no software artifact or weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The core insight — that the choice of pretraining objective determines whether metric grounding must be learned implicitly from demonstrations — is articulated and then tested directly, and the DP3 comparison (full-scene 3D fails, grounded 3D succeeds) cleanly separates "having 3D" from "grounding to task objects." - Ablations are decision-relevant: they show the robustness gain comes from observation construction with the same frozen backbone (46.8% → 10.3% without filtering), and that appearance and geometry streams are complementary rather than redundant. - Evaluation breadth across four settings (two sim benchmarks, two real embodiments, two task-specification modes) with consistent direction of effect strengthens the central hypothesis beyond a single benchmark. - The point-prompt interface enabling a VLM planner to drive the same frozen policy for memory-dependent tasks is a genuinely useful systems-level contribution, evidenced by 77% OOD retention on the Franka. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that grounding errors propagate to actions without recovery, that object-centric filtering can omit relevant context such as unselected obstacles, that GAM depends on the quality and diversity of 3D grounding datasets, and that 3D boxes may be inferior to dense 3D instance segmentation. They confront these directly in a dedicated Limitations section — a credibility positive — though they do not quantify how often grounding failure causes policy failure. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The sim experiments rely on oracle depth and 3D boxes from the simulator for backbone adaptation; the paper does not report grounding accuracy on real-robot data or how WildDet3D was supervised there, leaving open whether the real-robot gains depend on a backbone fine-tuned in ways not reproducible in the wild. - No comparison against a VLA baseline given the same point/box prompts (π0.5 uses language only on the YAM), so part of the gap may be attributable to the richer specification interface rather than the grounding foundation itself. - Statistical rigor: 10–20 trials per real-robot condition with no variance estimates; the 17/20 vs. 4/20 contrast is likely real, but 64.7% vs. 42.4% step completion is within plausible noise at these sample sizes. - RoboTwin averages mix single-task and co-trained methods under one ranking; GAM's clean-scene performance (63.0%) is actually below the best co-trained baselines (77.2–77.8%), so the headline "best average" rests on the Hard split where co-trained methods are handicapped by protocol. - No failure analysis of when grounding itself fails (occlusion, transparent/deformable objects), and no test on cluttered scenes where masking relevant context (acknowledged) would bite. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on robust manipulation policies should read this: the grounding-as-foundation hypothesis is clearly framed, unusually well tested across four settings, and the object-filtering ablations alone justify the read — but the oracle-sim supervision for the backbone and thin real-robot statistics mean the paradigm claim is promising rather than proven.

Beyond Isomorphism: Mining Frequent Subgraphs up to Graph Class Membership

D Bikmetov, M Prihodko, U Abdullaeva, I Savitskii… · preprints.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces two theoretical frameworks that generalize frequent subgraph mining in a single graph beyond exact isomorphism — one mining subgraphs up to weighted homeomorphism of arc-weighted directed graphs, and one mining frequent memberships in a library of chain-hereditary graph classes via a new class-level frequency measure (cMIS). - Why it's important: In routing, communication, and metabolic networks, a single arc of weight W and a chain of arcs totaling W are semantically identical, so isomorphism-based mining fragments recurring structure by segmentation granularity — a real modeling pain point the paper claims to fix. - How it does it: The core move is type-based abstraction with provable pruning: enumerate only canonical representatives (base graphs / class members) via purpose-built construction operations, and prove operation-level anti-monotonicity so that standard frequent-pattern search-tree pruning survives the relaxed matching notion. - The good: The correctness machinery is complete and self-contained — Theorem 1 shows the attachment/joining operations generate exactly all connected base graphs, and Theorems 2–3 prove anti-monotonicity for the new MISh, MNIh, and cMIS measures with clean, verifiable proofs. - The missing: There is no empirical evaluation whatsoever — no implementation is reported, no runtime or output comparison against GraMi/gApprox on any real or synthetic dataset, only a hand-worked toy example on one small graph; every scalability and practicality claim is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for algorithm designers in graph mining who care about the theory of frequency measures and relaxed matching; practitioners wanting a usable frequent-subgraph tool should skip it until an implementation and benchmarks exist.
Why this rank

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Frequent subgraph mining in a single graph (find all connected subgraphs whose frequency, e.g., MIS or MNI, exceeds a threshold) almost universally relies on exact subgraph isomorphism. The authors argue this is too rigid in two settings: (1) weighted networks (transport, communication, metabolic pathways) where a chain of pass-through 1-1 vertices is interchangeable with one aggregated arc of equal total weight — isomorphic mining cannot recognize the same route "shape" recorded at different granularities; and (2) domain analysis where the user cares about membership in a structural family (stars, Cayley-tree segments, dual-homed graphs) rather than one exact subgraph, and no existing framework mines such classes with frequency guarantees. Prior relaxed-matching work (Calders et al. [7]) handles homeomorphic embeddings but enumerates all isomorphism-distinct candidates and only applies equivalence post hoc, so equivalent classes appear many times in the search; gApprox's proximity matching is non-transitive and admits no anti-monotonicity, hence no pruning. Key Idea: Replace isomorphism with an equivalence relation (or class membership), enumerate only one canonical representative per class, and restore search-tree pruning by designing a custom operation set on canonical graphs for which anti-monotonicity can be re-proved at the operation level (Lemma 1: any graph equivalent to S' contains a subgraph equivalent to S). For the class framework, the analogous trick is restricting to chain-hereditary classes described by programs generating minimum BFS codes, which makes membership testing fast and enables chain-based pruning of the embedding search. Methodology: The paper is a theory paper with two algorithm designs and no implemented pipeline. Framework 1 (weighted homeomorphism, digraphs with positive real arc weights): graphs are reduced to unique "base graphs" (no 1-1 vertices except loop cases); two graphs are homeomorphic iff their base graphs are isomorphic. The authors define 2 attachment and 7 joining operations on base graphs (Theorem 1: these generate exactly all connected base graphs from an isolated vertex, proved by case analysis on arc deletion), define MISh (max number of pairwise arc-disjoint homeomorphic embeddings) and MNIh (min over pattern vertices of attainable image counts), and prove both anti-monotonic under the operations (Theorem 2). The mining algorithm is GraMi-like DFS over base graphs, but candidates are patterns (S, C) — base graphs with some unweighted arcs plus weight-sum constraints of form (e1,e2,w) or (e1,e2,e3,w), at most 5 unweighted arcs and 2 constraints per generated pattern — whose homeomorphic embeddings (an NP-hard problem, per Fortune–Hopcroft–Wyllie) are enumerated; discovered base graphs are deduplicated via minimum DFS codes. Framework 2 (class mining, simple undirected graphs): classes are chain-hereditary and described by generating programs emitting minimum BFS codes (11 hand-written programs: paths, stars, cliques, complete bipartite, dual/triple-homed, open wheels, triangle-with-path, Cayley-tree segments, symmetric trees). The new cMIS(C,G) measure is the max number of pairwise vertex-disjoint maximal embeddings of class C; Theorem 3 proves cMIS anti-monotonic under class inclusion for hereditary sequences sharing a minimum vertex count; Lemmas 3–4 give an anytime upper bound pack_C(G,U) for an incremental maximal-embedding search that grows vertex sets one at a time, pruning via chain-heredity. The top-level mining procedure filters the class library using small frequent subgraphs (MNI mining with threshold τ0, size cap k≈4–5), then computes cMIS per surviving class. Critical design decisions: operation-level (rather than equivalence-class-level) anti-monotonicity — well justified by explicit proof; the pattern/constraint device to avoid enumerating real-valued weights — reasonable but caps pattern expressiveness; requiring chain-heredity for the class framework — necessary for pruning but a substantive restriction the authors acknowledge. Key Results: The results are theorems, not benchmarks: Theorem 1 (completeness of the 9 operations), Lemma 1 (operation monotonicity condition), Theorem 2 (anti-monotonicity of MISh and MNIh), Theorem 3 (anti-monotonicity of cMIS under class inclusion), Lemmas 2–4 (upper bounds for anytime cMIS computation). The only quantitative content is a toy illustrative example on one small hand-drawn graph (Figure 6), reporting e.g. MNI(P4,G)=22, MNI(S4,G)=9, MNI(J4,G)=13, MNI(K4,G)=16 for four-vertex induced subgraphs, and cMIS≥4 values of 5 (paths), 4 (stars), 5 (triangle-with-path), 3 (cliques), 4 (dual-homed). No datasets, no baselines, no runtimes, no implementation. Baseline comparison is limited to a qualitative table (Table 1) contrasting match notion, candidate enumeration, and anti-monotonicity guarantees against GraMi, ScaleMine/SSiGraM, Calders et al., gApprox, VoG/ConDeNSe, and GraphMDL. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD (partially), plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in the weak sense of new measures: the representative-only enumeration with operation-level anti-monotonicity is genuinely new relative to Calders et al., who enumerate all isomorphism-distinct candidates and use equivalence only post hoc; the cMIS measure and the program-described chain-hereditary class library are new constructs. The underlying engine is a competent adaptation of known machinery — GraMi-style DFS, minimum DFS/BFS canonical codes, MIS-style packing on overlap structures — so the novelty is in the formulation and proofs, not in algorithmic components. Rigor & Reproducibility: The proofs (Theorems 1–3, Lemmas 1–4) are stated carefully and appear correct at the level of detail given; Theorem 1's exhaustive case analysis is the most substantive. However, there are no ablations, no experiments, no error bars, no seeds, and no implementation, so nothing about practical behavior is verifiable; no code or data is released (Data Availability statement says none apply). Methodological concerns: the entire practicality story rests on NP-hard homeomorphic embedding checks and NP-hard maximal-embedding search, with only qualitative mitigation arguments; no Goodhart-style benchmark reuse occurs (there is no benchmark), but the toy example is authored by the same people who designed the measures, so it demonstrates definitional behavior, not usefulness. The comparison in Table 1 is self-assessed. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL (proofs and algorithm designs with no primary experimental claim; the sole "experiment" is a toy figure). - Sound: Assumptions are explicit (connected graphs, positive real weights, chain-hereditary classes, hereditary sequences with shared minimum vertex count) and proofs are complete as presented, though Theorem 3's anti-monotonicity holds only within that restricted family, not for arbitrary class libraries as the framing might suggest. - General: The homeomorphism framework is specialized to arc-weighted directed graphs (extension to undirected is listed as future work), and the class framework is restricted to chain-hereditary classes with linear-time BFS-code generators — realistic for the 11 showcased families, restrictive beyond them. - Tight: Not a bounds paper in the approximation sense; the cMIS upper bound (Lemma 3) is tight in the algorithmic sense that it is exact at convergence, but no worst-case quality guarantee for early stopping is given. - Implementable: The algorithms are concrete enough to implement (the class framework more so than the pattern-based homeomorphism search), but nothing has been operationalized; the proposed library extension via (LLM-assisted) program synthesis is explicitly deferred to future work. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form, with one worked micro-example. Strengths: - The operation-level anti-monotonicity formulation is the paper's real intellectual contribution: it cleanly identifies why prior relaxed-matching schemes lose pruning (non-transitive proximity, post-hoc equivalence) and repairs it by co-designing the enumeration operations with the frequency measure. - Theorem 1's case analysis is genuinely careful — covering all ways arc deletion can create 1-1 vertices, including the subtle two-vertex cycle/loop cases — and the completeness claim it supports is what makes representative-only enumeration sound. - The cMIS measure with anytime upper bounds (Lemmas 3–4) is a practical-for-theory design: the incremental algorithm degrades gracefully to a valid upper bound when stopped early, an anytime property most exact miners lack. - Honest positioning: the authors repeatedly and explicitly state the approaches are complementary tools for specific application regimes, not replacements for isomorphism-based mining. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually candid: the homeomorphism approach has high computational complexity (homeomorphic embedding search is NP-hard even for a single check; embedding counts grow exponentially with the number of simple directed paths), it is difficult to generalize to other equivalences (each requires new operations and new anti-monotonicity proofs), approximate frequency estimation is hampered because even membership tests like ScaleMine's phase-1 rely on NP-hard homeomorphic tests; the class framework is limited to chain-hereditary classes, lacks anti-monotonic pruning for arbitrary libraries (so cMIS must be computed per class, mitigated only by pre-filtering on small frequent subgraphs), and cMIS favors classes with many small and no large occurrences — which may or may not be desired. They also state the program-synthesis extension is unsystematized future work. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Complete absence of any empirical validation — no implementation, no runtime measurements, no comparison of mined output vs. GraMi/gApprox even on synthetic graphs — despite the abstract claiming the approaches "enable more flexible and scalable mining"; scalability is claimed, not tested. - No analysis of pattern-space blowup in Framework 1: the pattern mechanism (≤5 unweighted arcs, ≤2 constraints) is asserted to bound per-call complexity growth, but the authors give no bound on the number of patterns generated or the search-tree size relative to standard MNI mining, so the net benefit of representative-only enumeration over Calders-style post-hoc equivalence is unquantified. - Theorem 3's anti-monotonicity requires all classes to be hereditary sequences with the same minimum vertex count k, which quietly undercuts the advertised generality of "a library of graph classes not necessarily related to each other"; the mining procedure's pruning story for heterogeneous libraries reduces to heuristic pre-filtering. - The toy example computes cMIS values by hand with "upper bounds from analytical considerations" — no demonstration that the incremental algorithm recovers these values efficiently, even at toy scale. - The 11 class-library programs are presented without a correctness argument that each program's BFS codes indeed characterize the intended class (e.g., the incomplete Cayley-tree/symmetric-tree definitions admit ambiguity). - LLM-based program synthesis for library extension is mentioned as a headline capability but receives zero technical development. Bottom Line: As a theory contribution — new frequency measures (MISh, MNIh, cMIS) with correct anti-monotonicity proofs for relaxed matching notions — this preprint is worth a careful read by graph-mining theorists, but with no implementation, no benchmarks, and no comparison data it offers a practitioner nothing usable today, and the burden of demonstrating that representative-only enumeration beats naive enumeration with post-hoc equivalence remains entirely unmet.

Circuit Hypernetworks for Quantum-Augmented Diffusion Language Models (24 ▲ )

Xiaoqiang Wang, Mengyang Xiong, Jun Dai, Bang Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 23 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HyperQ, a trainable quantum residual branch attached to every transformer block of a frozen 1.1B-parameter masked-diffusion language model (LLaDA-1.1B), in which a low-rank hypernetwork emits a token-specific IQP circuit per token and injects the measured expectation values back into the QKV tensors. - Why it's important: It is the first systematic test of whether increasing quantum circuit width improves language-model quality — prior quantum-LLM integrations evaluate a fixed circuit size and cannot answer the scaling question — and it does so within a feasible compute budget. - How it does it: The core move is restricting emitted circuits to a degree-4 (ring+chord) two-body IQP family, whose ⟨Zq⟩ readout has an exact closed form costing Θ(n) instead of 2^n, and whose coordinate-gradient variance is 1/48 independent of qubit count, avoiding both simulation blow-up and barren plateaus. - The good: The width sweep is clean and internally controlled: the six-benchmark average rises monotonically from 47.65 (16q) to 52.80 (32q) to 54.30 (64q), beating the frozen backbone (49.59) and same-backbone LoRA (50.63) by 4.71 and 3.67 points while using 10× less fine-tuning data, and the emitted route beats fixed ansätze and discrete motif search at every width with a widening margin (1.78 → 3.68 points). - The missing: There is no classical nonlinear control — the LoRA baseline is linear/low-rank, so the comparison cannot separate the benefit of the quantum circuit from that of any token-conditioned nonlinear feature map of similar parameter count, and the hardware validation covers only 256 items per benchmark. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on hybrid quantum-classical ML or parameter-efficient LLM adaptation — it is the most credible width-scaling study in the quantum-LLM space to date — skip it if you want evidence of quantum computational advantage, which the authors explicitly do not claim.
