Problem & Motivation: Prior quantum-augmented transformer work (variational circuits in a 150M transformer, quantum self-attention, Cayley unitary adapters, quantum-tensor/low-rank adapters) evaluates a quantum component at a fixed resource level, so the field has no answer to whether adding qubits helps language modelling. Two obstacles block such a study: (1) trainability — generic variational circuits hit barren plateaus where gradient variance vanishes exponentially in qubit count n; (2) practicality — exact simulation of a generic n-qubit circuit costs 2^n amplitudes, prohibitive for per-token evaluation inside a billion-parameter model. A width study needs a circuit family that is simultaneously trainable and cheaply simulable. The affected audience is quantum machine learning researchers and anyone exploring non-transformer-class computations inside LLMs. Key Idea: Replace task-level circuit selection with continuous, token-conditioned circuit emission on a fixed degree-4 IQP skeleton: because the commuting two-body generators give a product-of-cosines closed form for each ⟨Zq⟩ (cost Θ(n)) and the derivative variance depends on qubit degree (fixed at 4) rather than on n, a hypernetwork can emit and train 16–64-qubit circuits per token inside a frozen 1.1B model without ever building a statevector. Methodology: A LLaDA-style masked-diffusion denoiser (22 blocks, 1.1B params) is kept frozen; only per-block quantum branches are trained under the masked cross-entropy diffusion bound (Eq. 1). Each branch: (i) down-projects the token hidden state h through a rank-16 adapter; (ii) emits coordinates (α ∈ R^n, ω_E ∈ R^2n, ψ ∈ (S2)^n) — single-qubit rotation angles, coupling angles on a fixed ring+chord edge set E (degree 4, |E| = 2n), and readout axes; (iii) evaluates the closed-form readout zq = (ψq,z cos αq − ψq,y sin αq)·∏k cos ωqk (Eq. 5) via XLA-compiled, vmapped code on 8×A100 GPUs; (iv) projects readouts into the 2560-wide fused QKV residual. The authors derive an analytic gradient-variance result Var = 1/48 at all widths under uniform reference initialisation (Eq. 6), verified against statevector at n = 4–8, and contrast it with 4×10^-20 for an all-to-all skeleton at 64q. Critical design decisions: strict two-body IQP restriction (justified — higher-weight generators break the closed form), fixed degree-4 skeleton (justified by the variance result and readout cost), and per-token compilation with routing fixed once per width (justified by the budgeted synthesis/transpilation pipeline). The variance result applies only at initialisation, which the authors state plainly. Key Results: On a six-benchmark suite (ARC-e, HellaSwag, PIQA, BoolQ, RACE, GSM8K), HyperQ averages 47.65 / 52.80 / 54.30 at 16 / 32 / 64 qubits versus 49.59 for the frozen LLaDA-1.1B backbone, 50.63 for LoRA on the same backbone, 48.73 for TinyLlama-1.1B, and 53.79 / 53.37 for Qwen3-8B / LLaDA-8B — the 64-qubit model beats 8B classical models with 10× less fine-tuning data (20k vs 200k pairs), though Qwen3-8B still wins WikiText perplexity (10.61 vs 10.95). Emission beats the best fixed ansatz by 1.78/2.74/3.68 points and the 6-motif discrete search at every width; fixed ansätze saturate after 32 qubits while emission keeps gaining (+1.50 from 32→64). Analysis of emitted circuits shows token-dependent support selection (only 6.4% of tokens retain all edges at 16q, 0.1% at 64q; Identity class concentrated on punctuation at 30.2%, rare subwords get 3.73 active couplings/qubit). Hardware runs on ibm_quebec (156-qubit IBM processor, 10,000 shots, 256 items/benchmark) lose 0.34/0.68/1.12 average points at the three widths versus analytic readout. At 16 qubits HyperQ is below the backbone — the gain only appears as width grows. Baselines are current (Llama-3, Qwen3, LLaDA-8B); numbers for earlier quantum-augmented methods on this suite were produced by the authors since no shared benchmark existed. Means are over three runs (Fig. 5). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the token-conditioned circuit-emission formulation combined with a degree-fixed IQP family whose readout cost and gradient variance are both width-bounded — this specific combination is what makes a per-token quantum width study in an LLM feasible, and it is the first quantum-LLM result where quality demonstrably increases with qubit count. The components (IQP circuits, hypernetworks, LoRA, masked diffusion) are all standard; the novelty lies in the structural restriction and the scaling evidence, not in any single piece. Explicitly NOT claimed: quantum computational advantage. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: the paper isolates emission vs search vs fixed circuits at each width, ensembling controls (diversity beats circuit count: 3-circuit ensemble 52.24 < single emitted circuit 52.80), and the LoRA baseline controls for added adapter capacity. The closed-form readout is cross-validated against dense statevector (deviation 1.1×10^-5, complex64) and exact tensor-network contraction (3.2×10^-7) at 16q before use at larger widths; analytic variance results are verified by brute force at n = 4–8. Full training hyperparameters are given (8×A100, AdamW, peak LR 2×10^-4, rank 16, seed 3407, three epochs). Means over three runs are shown with individual runs, but no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. No code release URL is stated. Methodological concerns: the derivation is at initialisation only; the hardware validation covers 2.5–19.4% of each benchmark's full split; no data-matched classical baseline (all classical baselines get 200k pairs while HyperQ gets 20k — this flatters HyperQ's efficiency claim unless the classical baselines also hold at 20k, which is not shown). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a bounded SYSTEMS component via hardware execution). - Practical: Training ran on 8×A100 80GB — commercially available hardware; simulation-only inference needs no QPU. - Efficient: Readout is Θ(n) per token and per-call branch latency is flat (24.0–24.2 ms/call) with activation memory growing linearly in n; the frozen backbone cuts per-token FLOPs from ~6N to ~4N, but per-token circuit evaluation at every block of every step is a real overhead relative to plain LoRA. - Effective: Strong zero-shot benchmark evidence at 32–64 qubits with data-efficiency controls, but no proof the quantum branch beats a classical nonlinear token-conditioned feature map — effectiveness against the right control is unestablished. - Scalable: Tested only at 16–64 qubits and 1.1B parameters; the paper explicitly disclaims a scaling law beyond three widths, and the Θ(n) readout itself relies on the degree-4 restriction that caps expressivity, so 10× scaling is untested. The work delivers a trained model configuration and a detailed compilation/transpilation pipeline but no publicly released artifact (no repo or weights URL is mentioned). Strengths: - The central trade-off is identified and engineered honestly: the same degree-4 restriction that prevents barren plateaus also makes the readout classically simulable, and the paper states this connection to known Lie-algebraic theory rather than overselling. - The width sweep with three circuit-construction routes (fixed/searched/emitted) at matched widths is the first controlled experiment of its kind in the quantum-LLM literature, and the widening margin (1.78→3.68 over fixed ansätze) is a genuine empirical finding. - Quantitative characterisation of what the emitted circuits actually do — token-category-dependent entanglement allocation, support rank-frequency long tails, off-Pauli-axis readouts — moves beyond aggregate scores to mechanistic evidence. - The simulation-to-hardware protocol is properly paired (identical weights, identical 256-item subsets, analytic-vs-device differences isolated per benchmark). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state explicitly: no quantum advantage is claimed (the readout is classically efficient at every tested width); the variance result characterises only initialisation, not the optimisation trajectory or the backbone; no scaling law is established beyond three widths; the 16-qubit model underperforms the backbone; hardware evaluation is bounded (256 items/benchmark, inference-only, no on-device training); the WikiText perplexity gap to Qwen3-8B is not closed. This is an unusually candid limitations posture — a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The decisive missing control: a classical token-conditioned nonlinear branch (e.g., a small MLP or a random-feature map through the same rank-16 bottleneck) of matched parameter count. LoRA is linear, so the +3.67-point margin could in principle come from added nonlinearity/per-token adaptivity rather than anything quantum. - No data-matched comparison: HyperQ's 10× data-efficiency headline compares against baselines given 200k pairs; a LoRA baseline trained on 20k pairs is absent, so the efficiency claim is confounded. - Benchmark numbers for HyQuT, QTHA, Cayley adapters, and Quantum-PEFT in Table 1 were presumably re-run by the authors on their own suite under unstated tuning, and no uncertainty is attached to any comparison. - The per-token hidden-state analysis (Fig. 3b-c) is done at 16 qubits, the only width where the model is below the backbone, raising questions about whether the reported angle statistics generalise to the widths that matter. - Hyperparameters for the discrete-search and fixed-ansatz baselines (capacity, tuning effort) are not shown to be as carefully optimised as the emitted route, risking an asymmetric comparison. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous width-scaling study of quantum-augmented language models published so far and a clear methodological template for the field, but with the classical-nonlinear control and data-matched comparison missing, its gains should be read as evidence for adaptive token-conditioned circuits rather than for quantum mechanics per se — essential reading for quantum-ML researchers, optional for mainstream LLM practitioners.

RBS-Attention: Radius-Bounded Sparse Prefill for Long-Context Large Language Models

C Song, J Wei, Z Peng · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces RBS-Attention, a training-free sparse-prefill method that adds a radius-adaptive "rescue" branch on top of centroid-based block scoring to prevent pruning key blocks that contain a few highly relevant tokens ("mean dilution"), integrated with block-sparse FlashAttention. - Why it's important: Prefill attention is quadratic in prompt length and dominates time-to-first-token for 64K–128K-context serving, where discarding one block containing a critical evidence span can silently break retrieval and multi-hop tasks. - How it does it: Each key block stores a centroid and max radius; a prompt-, layer-, and head-dependent coefficient β (from radius quantiles) scales the radius uplift into a second score, and independently thresholded base/rescue masks are unioned with forced sink/local-window blocks before sparse execution. - The good: The H100 measurements are strong and honest about density: 20.65× standalone prefill-attention and 5.97× end-to-end TTFT speedup at 128K on Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8, with 88.65 vs 89.52 RULER overall on dense Qwen3-32B at ~6% density at 128K, and matched-density recalibration of baselines rather than nominal-budget-only comparison. - The missing: The core ablation justifying the design (RBS 76.67 vs centroid-only 73.63 vs Quest-style 73.71 on 130 examples) has paired-bootstrap differences whose intervals include zero, so the headline mechanism is not statistically distinguished from simpler selectors. - Read it or not: Worth reading for systems engineers building long-context sparse-prefill pipelines and for researchers in block-sparse attention; if you only need the geometric idea (Cauchy–Schwarz radius bound as a risk signal), Appendix E suffices.

But Rigor (62) is capped by the core selector ablation resting on 130 examples with bootstrap intervals including zero, Qwen-only coverage, no code release, and preprint status — the headline mechanism is not statistically distinguished from simpler selectors. empirical Novelty 58 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 68 Completeness 72 Resilience 60 Impact 45
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Long-context LLM serving (repo-level code, multi-document QA, RAG, video understanding) is bottlenecked by prefill, where dense self-attention over 64K–256K-token prompts is quadratic. Sparse-prefill systems score key blocks cheaply, typically with the key-block centroid, but a centroid hides individual relevant tokens: one aligned key among many unaligned ones contributes little to the mean, so the block is pruned and its tokens removed from attention entirely. The authors name this failure mode "mean dilution" and measure it: mean-only rank underestimation grows with block radius, and the highest-radius quintile contains 39.5% of top-5% attention blocks (vs 20% uniform). Existing systems (FlashPrefill, FlexPrefill, MInference, XAttn) use pattern inference or mean-style block scores and are weakest exactly where long-context benchmarks are hardest — retrieving a small buried span. Key Idea: Use the block radius r_b = max_k ||k − c_b||₂ as a dispersion-based risk signal: an attenuated Cauchy–Schwarz upper bound q·c_b + ||q||₂·r_b·β_b, with β_b clamped from the per-(prompt, layer, KV head) radius distribution between the median and 90th percentile, forms a second "rescue" score. The rescue branch is thresholded independently of the centroid branch and the masks are unioned, so radius uplift can admit dispersed blocks without letting a loose bound displace genuinely relevant blocks (which a single full-L2 ranking would allow). Methodology: Pipeline: (1) partition Q/K/V into B=128 blocks; (2) compute per-key-block centroid c_b and radius r_b — O(Nd); (3) per layer/KV head compute radius quantiles r_low (median), r_high (P90) and β_b = clamp((r_b − r_low)/(r_high − r_low), 0, 1); (4) per query block, aggregate exponentiated token logits (with shared max-shift, Eq. 10–11) into base scores S_base = f(q·c_b) and rescue scores S_rescue = f(q·c_b + ||q||₂·r_b·β_b); (5) apply two relative thresholds (α_base = 0.22, α_rescue = 0.18, offline-calibrated) and union with forced sink/local-window/recent blocks; (6) run block-sparse FlashAttention on retained pairs. Selector costs O(N²d/B) scoring plus O(M²) thresholding; sparse attention is O(M·K_avg·B²·d). Critical design decisions: (a) attenuating the radius via quantile-normalized β rather than using the full L2 bound — justified empirically (full-L2 scores 72.41 vs RBS 76.67 at matched density), since the unattenuated bound over-protects dispersed-but-irrelevant blocks; (b) dual thresholds + union rather than a single rescue ranking — motivated by the observation that rescue-only thresholds can evict base-selected blocks; (c) relative thresholds (following FlashPrefill) instead of fixed Top-K, which makes actual density content-dependent — the paper reports measured density throughout, which is handled correctly but complicates cross-method comparison. Key Results: On H100 with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8 at 128K: 20.65× standalone prefill-attention speedup (vs 11.98× FlashPrefill, 4.78× FlexPrefill, 2.25× MInference, 2.97× XAttn), 11.92× vLLM prefill-attention, 5.97× end-to-end TTFT; measurements span 16K–256K. RULER-128K budget sweep (MoE model): 80.28% at 5.34% actual density and 88.36% at 11.03% (dense 89.69%); after strict recalibration to RBS's density anchors, RBS 80.28 vs MInference 76.87, FlashPrefill 74.73, XAttn 66.77, FlexPrefill 58.56. On dense Qwen3-32B: RULER overall 88.65 (dense 89.52, MInference 88.63 at 83.75% density vs RBS 31.11%); LongBench-v2 total 0.376 (dense 0.394) at 9.72% estimated density; InfiniteBench macro 0.362 (dense 0.372, FlashPrefill 0.338, XAttn 0.352); Video-MME 65.98 (dense 66.16) on Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B. Baselines are recent (2024–2026) and reasonably current. The counter-intuitive finding: the fully conservative full-L2 bound (72.41) underperforms centroid-only (73.63) at matched density — more geometric conservatism is not better selection. A100 sweeps show 4.47× TTFT at the 5% target and 4.47×/3.85× prompt throughput at 128K batch 1/4. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (radius-adaptive dual-branch selector with quantile-normalized rescue) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (mean dilution: centroid underestimation correlates with block radius, and 39.5% of top-5% blocks sit in the highest-radius quintile). The relative-threshold selection, block-sparse FlashAttention execution, and forced sink/window blocks are standard prior practice (explicitly credited to FlashPrefill and streaming-attention work); the genuinely new element is the attenuated, distribution-adaptive radius term combined with an independently thresholded base branch — a modest but real delta over Quest's box bound and SpargeAttention's self-similarity gating, both of which the paper compares against carefully rather than strawmanning. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and unusually transparent: matched-density selector comparison (centroid-only, full-L2, Quest-style, RBS at ~5.3% density), block-size sweep (B ∈ {64,128,256}), threshold transfer across models, calibration cost (0.885 GPU-hours, max density error 0.0078 pp), selector time (694.81 ms vs 349.89 ms FlashPrefill), workspace (1,155.6 MiB vs 515.5 MiB centroid-only), and full-model peak memory (60.5 vs 61.6 GiB at 128K). Per-selector bootstrap CIs are reported but between-method significance is not established. Concerns: the selector ablation uses only 130 examples (10 per RULER-128K task) and its CIs include zero — the paper admits this; density figures in the main quality tables are estimated from 20–60 sampled examples, not the full benchmark; all models are Qwen-family; the Quest comparison is a reimplementation in the authors' prefill backend, not the official system; no code or weights release is mentioned. The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.20971), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built method integrated into vLLM/FlashAttention and run on real hardware). - Practical: Yes — H100 (primary) and A100 (supplementary) with standard vLLM 0.10.0 + FlashAttention 2.8.3 stacks; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: Selector overhead is nontrivial (694.81 ms vs 349.89 ms for FlashPrefill at 128K) and temporary workspace more than doubles vs centroid-only (1,155.6 vs 515.5 MiB), though persistent metadata is negligible (+0.031 MiB/layer); end-to-end it wins at 128K (5.97× TTFT) but some methods approach or fall below dense at short contexts. - Effective: Strong on retrieval-heavy RULER (80.57 vs 80.70 dense at 128K with 6.03% density); on LongBench-v2 it matches the best sparse score but with a 0.018 gap to dense, so it approximates rather than preserves dense quality. - Scalable: Tested to 256K; behavior beyond that, and the growth of the O(M²) thresholding/workspace path, is extrapolated rather than measured. Delivers no released software artifact in the text (no repo URL stated); the artifact exists as described implementations on top of vLLM/FlashAttention. Strengths: - The mean-dilution diagnosis is a concrete, quantified failure mode of centroid-based selectors with a clean geometric motivation (Cauchy–Schwarz radius bound) and a measured correlation (39.5% of top-5% blocks in Q5), giving the method a reason to exist beyond kernel tuning. - The dual-threshold/union design is validated against the obvious alternatives (centroid-only, full-L2, Quest-style) at strictly matched density in a shared backend, and the full-L2 result showing that maximum conservatism hurts is a genuinely useful negative finding. - Reporting discipline: measured actual density accompanies every quality number, density estimates' sampling protocols are disclosed, and speedups are normalized per model/hardware/context — avoiding the nominal-budget traps common in this subfield. - Quality evaluation spans dense, MoE, and multimodal models and four benchmarks, with multimodal speedup claims explicitly disclaimed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper states that benefits shrink at short contexts; that a large radius signals risk, not relevance, and thresholds drive variable content-dependent density; that block-size/threshold settings may not transfer beyond tested operating points; that the 130-example selector comparison is underpowered (bootstrap intervals include zero); that H100 speedups must not be read onto the dense or multimodal models; that LongBench-v2/RULER densities are sampled estimates; and that the Quest-style experiment is a policy isolation, not the official Quest system. The authors confront these directly and with appropriate hedging — a credibility positive; the memory discussion (workspace vs persistent statistics vs model peak) is notably careful. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical significance testing for the headline RULER/LongBench-v2 comparisons; single-run accuracies on 503-sample LongBench-v2 leave the dense-vs-RBS gap (0.018) within plausible noise. - The block-size sensitivity sweep shows RBS below centroid-only at B=64 and B=256 (71.86/70.73 vs 74.17/72.15), suggesting the union mechanism's benefit is fragile to the chosen B=128 — the authors note it but do not explain it. - Model coverage is limited to the Qwen3 family; generalization to other architectures (Llama, attention-pattern-divergent models) is untested. - No task category where RBS might lose to dense-sparse hybrids at its own density is surfaced beyond aggregate scores; per-task LongBench-v2 breakdowns show RBS weakest on Short tasks relative to XAttn (0.411 vs 0.439 on the dense model). - No public code release is stated, which materially limits reproducibility of the exact vLLM integration and workspace accounting. - The mean-dilution diagnostic (Figure 1) is measured on the authors' own selection outputs and RULER-derived data; an independent confirmation of the phenomenon across models/tasks is absent. Bottom Line: A practitioner building long-context serving on Qwen-class models with vLLM should read this — the measured-density methodology and the full-L2-beats-centroid negative result are worth the time — but the core selector's advantage over simpler alternatives rests on a 130-example ablation without significance, so treat RBS-Attention as a promising, carefully evaluated engineering contribution rather than a settled advance.

OmniVBench: A Benchmark and Large-Scale Dataset for Omni Reference-to-Video Generation (19 ▲ )

Wenxue Li, Peiyan Guan, Haoyang Jiang, Junxian Cai, Hualuo Liu, Chunjie Zhang, Chong Guan, Kai Huang, Songlian Li, Taiyi Wu, Yongjian Yu, Xiaotong Zhao, Alan Zhao, Eric Liu, Xi Chen, Yu Liu, Lei Zhu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OmniVBench, an 813-case benchmark covering 7 task families and 18 sub-tasks of reference-to-video (R2V) generation with a factor-grounded checklist evaluation protocol of 12,172 case-specific items, plus the Omni-R2V Dataset of ~340K processed R2V training samples. - Why it's important: Current R2V benchmarks evaluate mostly content/subject references with holistic similarity metrics, while real creative workflows require motion, style, structure, narrative, and multi-reference control — so model progress on these capabilities cannot currently be measured or trained for at scale. - How it does it: The core move is factor-grounded evaluation: each test case is decomposed into manually verified, case-specific checklist questions that separately score Reference Fidelity (is the intended reference factor preserved?), Instruction Realization (is the factor disentangled and routed to the right target?), and Video Quality, with a VLM judge applying fixed rubrics. - The good: The protocol is validated against humans on 965 model outputs: Spearman correlation reaches 0.77 (RF), 0.74 (IR), and 0.82 (VQ), and the checklist method beats holistic VLM scoring by 0.10 (RF) and 0.05 (IR) Spearman — evidence the fine-grained decomposition measures something real. - The missing: The dataset is never validated by actually training a model — there is no experiment showing that training on Omni-R2V improves R2V performance, so its central value proposition rests on scale and human-audited sample quality (95.5% pass rate), not on demonstrated training utility. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or evaluating R2V/multi-reference video generation models who needs a finer-grained evaluation target than OpenS2V-Eval or VACE-Bench; skippable for readers outside controllable video generation.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is the strength: factor-grounded checklist evaluation with the IRDR/IRTC routing decomposition is a genuine new formulation of R2V evaluation, validated against humans (0.74–0.86 Spearman) and ablated against holistic scoring. Rigor (60) and Resilience (55) are dragged down by the judge-circularity problem (Gemini as both evaluation judge and dataset/benchmark constructor, no judge-choice ablation), unquantified judge variance on 1–2 point leaderboard gaps, and a vendor-preprocessing asymmetry favoring MiniMax H3. Problem & Motivation: Reference-to-video generation is expanding from subject/content conditioning toward heterogeneous controls — motion, camera trajectory, style, structure (line art/greybox/storyboards), narrative (story continuation, preceding-shot), and multi-reference compositions. Three groups have the problem: model developers who cannot diagnose which reference factor their model mishandles (existing benchmarks like OpenS2V-Eval, VACE-Bench, UniVBench cover only subsets per Table 1), practitioners who lack compositional R2V training data (existing datasets like Phantom-Data and OpenS2V-5M are content-reference-centric per Table 2, and some ship raw videos rather than processed reference–target pairs), and the field at large, which lacks an evaluation that distinguishes whether a reference factor is preserved, correctly disentangled from its carrier, and bound to the intended target rather than just whether the output looks globally consistent with the reference. Key Idea: The key idea is factor-grounded checklist evaluation: instead of one holistic VLM judgment of "reference consistency," each benchmark case is pre-decomposed into atomic, manually verified questions targeting the specific reference factors the case involves — e.g., "Is the pattern from Reference Image 2 applied to the subject's vest, rather than the umbrella?" — so that preserve-vs-change partitions, factor–carrier separation, and condition–slot binding are scored independently. This is paired with the observation that R2V errors split into orthogonal failure types (wrong factor extracted vs. right factor routed to wrong target vs. poor video quality), which holistic metrics collapse into a single number. Methodology: The work has two artifacts. (1) OmniVBench: 813 evaluation cases organized as 5 single-reference families (content: object/character/scene; motion: action/camera-motion; style; structure: greybox/line-art/rough-storyboard; narrative: multi-panel storyboard/story/preceding-shot) plus 2 multi-reference families (multi-content, cross-aspect, e.g., 335 cross-aspect cases). Cases come from a rights-cleared internal Tencent video corpus; instructions are rewritten from target captions to avoid textual leakage of reference-borne information; all cases pass three-annotator verification. Scoring: a VLM-based criterion activator selects applicable criteria per case, criteria are instantiated as checklist questions (RF on a 1–5 scale, IR on 1–3), and scores are hierarchically aggregated with equal weight per active L2 sub-dimension; VQ uses off-the-shelf DOVER++ (technical), Aesthetic Predictor V2.5, and UnifiedReward 2.0 (physics). (2) Omni-R2V Dataset: 339,570 samples built via source-video segmentation, task-specific pair construction using two strategies — cross-pair matching (retrieve semantically related clips/frames) and inverse construction (extract line maps via Canny/HED/PiDiNet/TEED, synthesize greybox with Wan2.2-VACE, animate action references with Wan-Animate) — followed by VLM filtering and instruction generation (Gemini-3.1-Pro captions; DeepSeek-V4-Pro writes instructions). Critical design decisions: fixed checklists across models for the same case (prevents per-model rubric drift), separate RF/IR judge calls, and task-differentiated evidence presentation (matched temporal frame pairs for temporally aligned references). The criterion-activation rules and rubrics are fully specified in the appendix, a strong reproducibility practice; the reliance on proprietary judges (Gemini-3.1-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) is stated but not ablated by judge choice. Key Results: Eleven models are evaluated: closed-source Kling 3.0 Omni, Seedance 2.0/2.5, Gemini Omni, Happy Horse 1.0, Vidu-Q2-Pro, and open-source UniVideo, OmniWeaving, LoomVideo, Bernini, MiniMax H3. Overall scores: Seedance 2.5 72.68, MiniMax H3 72.41 (open-source, best on 5 of 7 IRDR sub-dimensions, e.g., 98.21 IRDR on content), Kling 3.0 Omni 68.59, with the weakest open-source models at ~48.8–51.3. Surprising finding: the open–closed gap has largely closed (MiniMax H3 statistically at the top), and no model dominates all families — content-reference scores (up to ~79) far exceed motion, style, narrative, and multi-reference scores for most models. The IR decomposition is the most diagnostic result: several models score high on target compliance but much lower on disentanglement/routing (e.g., Vidu-Q2-Pro IRTC 77.77 vs. IRDR 86.77 on cross-aspect; LoomVideo narrative IRTC 37.48 vs. IRDR 58.88), meaning models copy reference content they should suppress or bind factors to the wrong target. Protocol validation: 100 cases × 11 models = 965 outputs rated by 3 annotators; automatic–human Pearson 0.81 (RF), 0.78 (IR), 0.86 (VQ); checklist beats holistic evaluation (Spearman 0.77 vs. 0.67 RF, 0.74 vs. 0.69 IR). Dataset quality audit: ~100 samples per family rated by 2 annotators, 95.5% average pass rate (lowest: motion at 89.7% instruction correctness). Baselines are current (2025–2026 commercial and research models), so the leaderboard is informative, though it self-heals quickly in this fast-moving area. Test scale is modest — 813 cases, with per-sub-task counts as low as 19 (greybox). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and, arguably, a NEW FORMULATION of R2V evaluation (factor-grounded, routing-aware checklists) — the taxonomy extension to motion/style/structure/narrative/multi-reference in one benchmark is genuinely broader than prior R2V benchmarks, and the IRDR vs. IRTC split surfaces failure modes no holistic metric exposes. The data pipelines themselves (cross-pair matching, edge extraction, VACE-based inverse construction, LLM instruction writing) are competent compositions of existing tools applied at new breadth, not new methods; the benchmark's main novelty is coverage plus the evaluation protocol, not algorithmic technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for the evaluation protocol (checklist vs. holistic, Table 6) and human-correlation validation is above average for a benchmark paper. Human verification of benchmark cases (3 annotators) and dataset samples (2 annotators, pass rates reported per family) is documented. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported — for LLM-judge scoring with 813 cases, per-case judge variance is not quantified. The project page URL is given (https://wxliii.github.io/OmniVBench/); the paper claims the benchmark and dataset will be "constructed and released," but the text does not confirm public availability of code, data, or evaluation scripts at publication. Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluation judge (Gemini-3.1-Pro) is also used in dataset construction (captioning, storyboard verification), creating a shared-model bias loop; (2) no judge-choice ablation is reported; (3) source videos come from an internal Tencent corpus — the benchmark's scenario distribution reflects that corpus, and independence of evaluation data from any vendor's training distribution cannot be verified; (4) MiniMax H3 receives a special preprocessing workflow (H3-Context-IR) that other models do not, an asymmetry in the comparison. This is an arXiv preprint (2609.22069, Sep 2026), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (benchmark + dataset artifact, evaluated by running 11 models through the protocol). - Practical: Evaluation runs on API-accessible VLM judges plus commodity-GPU quality metrics, so any lab can replicate the harness; training on Omni-R2V requires video-generation-scale compute, as with any comparable dataset. - Efficient: Evaluation cost is 2+ VLM calls per case per model plus standard VQ metrics — modest relative to video generation itself; the 340K-sample dataset with provided processed pairs avoids per-lab reconstruction cost, which is its main efficiency claim over OpenS2V-5M/Phantom-Data for these task types. - Effective: Evidence shows the benchmark discriminates models and diagnoses routing failures, and correlates with human judgment (0.74–0.86); whether the dataset solves the training-resource problem is untested (no training experiment). - Scalable: Not tested and not claimed in either direction — 813 cases cannot shrink via amortization, but the checklist construction is manual/verified, so scaling to new task families requires human effort; dataset pipeline scalability is evidenced only by the 340K already produced. Deliverables: a benchmark, a released dataset (claimed), detailed rubrics/prompts in the appendix; no trained model or evaluation library is described. Strengths: - The IRDR/IRTC decomposition produces the paper's most valuable finding: models can satisfy instructions while failing to suppress or correctly route reference factors (e.g., LoomVideo's 58.88 vs. 37.48 on narrative IRDR vs. IRTC), a failure mode holistic benchmarks structurally cannot see. - The evaluation protocol is validated, not just asserted: 965-output human study with per-dimension correlations (0.74–0.86 Spearman) and a direct ablation showing the checklist beats holistic scoring. - The dataset construction appendix is unusually complete — per-task pipelines with specific tools (Wan-Animate for action references, 12 line-extractor variants with controlled sampling, TransNetV2 shot detection with VLM coherence filtering for preceding shots), making the recipe genuinely reusable. - Coverage is real, not incremental: cross-aspect compositions alone (335 cases testing content×motion/style/structure/narrative binding) have no counterpart in the four prior benchmarks in Table 1. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that current models show "clear performance gaps across task families" and that "progress on one reference condition does not necessarily transfer to others." They acknowledge reliance on internal video collections for the corpus (with stated rights clearance) and note that some prior resources lack processed data, which their pipeline addresses. They do not include a dedicated limitations section; limitations are surfaced through results discussion rather than confronted head-on. They do not acknowledge the VLM-judge dependency, benchmark–judge shared model bias, or the absence of training validation for the dataset. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No training experiment: the paper's second headline contribution (a 340K training dataset) is never used to train or fine-tune any model, so the claimed value for "advancing omni R2V" is a plausibility argument, not a measurement. - Judge circularity: Gemini-3.1-Pro is the evaluation judge and also generates captions, verifies storyboards, and constructs benchmark references — systematic bias toward VLM-legible outputs or shared failure modes is possible and unmeasured; no alternative judge (open-weight VLM) is cross-checked. - Single-judge, no-variance reporting: with 813 cases and one judge per call, score differences of 1–2 points between top models (72.68 vs. 72.41) are not shown to be significant. - Benchmark scale per sub-task is thin (greybox n=19, preceding-shot n=25), so per-sub-task rankings rest on very few cases. - Provenance asymmetry: MiniMax H3 is the only model given task-specific input preprocessing; its tie with Seedance 2.5 at the top could partially reflect this. - The dataset's composition is dominated by narrative references (167,881 of 340K samples); cross-aspect is only 28,498, so the rarest-capability data is also the scarcest — a mismatch with where the benchmark shows models are weakest. Bottom Line: For teams building or selecting R2V models, this is currently the most diagnostic evaluation suite available for multi-factor reference control and is worth adopting despite the unvalidated training dataset and VLM-judge risks; for the dataset alone, wait for evidence that training on it helps.

GraphSkillEvo: Evolutionary Optimization of Graph-Structured Agent Skills (9 ▲ )

Rui Sun, Zhi Zheng, Zhenkun Wang, Zhichao Lu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GraphSkillEvo, a framework that represents LLM agent skills as graph-structured natural-language artifacts (global guidance plus reusable step nodes plus condition-keyed workflow paths) and optimizes them with a population-based evolutionary loop of structure-aware mutation and crossover operators. - Why it's important: Prompt-level "skills" are the cheapest way to give LLM agents task-specific procedural competence that survives model replacement, but existing optimizers refine one unstructured text blob at a time, yielding redundant, hard-to-follow instructions — especially for small, cheap models. - How it does it: It reformulates each skill as a directed graph whose nodes are execution steps with self-contained guidance and whose edges come from per-task-type workflow paths, then evolves a population of N=4 skills for T=5 generations using four LLM-driven operators (global-guidance mutation, graph-structure mutation, and the matching crossovers) selected round-robin, with validation-set gating. - The good: The ablations are decisive — removing the graph structure drops average test success on three benchmarks from 71.52 to 64.08, removing crossover to 66.59, and removing mutation to 54.50 — so the paper shows which components actually matter, and it beats its main baseline SkillOpt in 13 of 14 model–harness–benchmark settings while consuming ~24–27% fewer optimization tokens. - The missing: The optimization scale is very small (population of 4, five generations, validation sets as tiny as 18 instances for LiveMath), and only one competing skill optimizer (SkillOpt) is compared, so the claimed superiority of evolution over other search strategies rests on a single baseline at toy evolutionary scale. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building skill/memory layers on LLM agents or applying LLM-driven evolutionary search to prompt artifacts, since the structured-representation argument and token-cost analysis are directly reusable; skip it if you already work on skill-graph retrieval (GraSP, HiSkill, SkillDAG) and only need the optimization angle.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying LLM agents want reusable natural-language "skills" — procedural guidance attached to a task — because skills transfer across model versions without retraining. Two failure modes plague current skill-optimization methods (SkillOpt, EvoSkill, Trace2Skill, SkillX): (1) optimized skills are long unstructured checklists that weaker models (the paper's GPT-5.4-nano) cannot reliably follow because there is no explicit notion of "which guidance applies now"; and (2) the unconstrained natural-language space is redundant, so an optimizer wastes capacity exploring textual variants that encode the same workflow. The paper targets the practitioners who run automated skill optimization loops over training trajectories and validation gates. Key Idea: The core insight is that a skill is structurally a flow diagram, so representing it as one — a global-guidance section plus a node library of reusable execution steps plus a set of condition-keyed ordered paths over those nodes — simultaneously (a) gives the executing agent explicit, stage-relevant workflow guidance and (b) shrinks the search space enough that population-based evolutionary operators (mutation/crossover over guidance and structure separately) become meaningful, rather than pure single-skill LLM self-reflection. Methodology: A graph-structured skill is a tuple ⟨global guidance h_s, directed graph g_s⟩ where the edge set is induced by M workflows, each an applicability condition c_m plus an ordered node sequence p_m. GraphSkillEvo runs a standard generational EC loop: (Step 0) initialize N=4 skills via an LLM prompt plus one seed, score all on the validation set; (Step 1) per generation, execute each skill on a batch of B=15 training instances and retain up to K=5 failed trajectories as reflection material; (Step 2) generate N offspring via one of four operators in round-robin order — global-guidance mutation (revise h_s from failures), graph-structure mutation (revise nodes/paths from failures), global-guidance crossover (merge guidance from two parents, keep one parent's graph), graph-structure crossover (merge nodes/paths, keep one parent's guidance) — with rank-based parent sampling p ∝ 1/(r+N); (Step 3) select the top-N of parents+offspring by validation fitness. A schema validator regenerates any offspring that violates graph consistency (referenced nodes exist, every node is used, exact name matching). The objective is average task reward J_D(s) on the validation split; the LLM and harness are frozen throughout. Critical design decisions: (i) representing "edges" implicitly via ordered workflow lists rather than an explicit adjacency structure — pragmatic, keeps skills LLM-readable, but means the "graph" is a family of linear paths sharing nodes, not a branching DAG; (ii) round-robin operator selection rather than adaptive operator selection — simple but unjustified, and the ablation showing mutation ≫ crossover suggests the mix may matter; (iii) hard enforcement of graph schema via validator — well-justified given LLMs drift on structural constraints. Key Results: Across five benchmarks (SearchQA, SpreadsheetBench, DocVQA, LiveMath, ALFWorld), two models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-nano), and two harnesses (none, Codex), GraphSkillEvo wins 13 of 14 settings. Against the SkillOpt baseline it gains +1.76% average success (GPT-5.4 no-harness), +4.01% (GPT-5.4-nano no-harness), and +1.33% (GPT-5.4 Codex); the largest single-setting gain is SpreadsheetBench with nano: 60.71 vs 50.11 (+10.60). Benefits concentrate on procedural tasks (Spreadsheet, ALFWorld) and weaker models; the sole loss is LiveMath with nano (−0.80 vs SkillOpt). Total optimization tokens are lower than SkillOpt: 61.94M vs 81.08M (GPT-5.4) and 75.94M vs 103.54M (nano). Removing explicit workflow organization (keeping content) costs 0.75–4.52 points per benchmark. Cross-model transfer: skills optimized on nano and executed on GPT-5.4 score 71.78 on Spreadsheet — above the skill optimized directly on GPT-5.4 (69.40). Significance (one-sided Welch's t-tests, 5 runs, nano): p<0.05 on Spreadsheet (0.016) and ALFWorld (0.038), but only 0.069 on SearchQA and 0.089 on DocVQA. SkillOpt is a strong, recent baseline; the no-skill/human/LLM one-shot baselines are sanity checks. Test scale is standard-benchmark (e.g., Spreadsheet 280 test tasks, DocVQA 374), but the optimization loop itself is toy-scale (population 4, 5 generations, validation sets of 18–200 instances). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD. The genuinely new elements are (1) representing each individual skill (as opposed to a skill library) as a guidance/node/workflow graph, and (2) structure-aware mutation and crossover operators over that representation inside an EC loop — prior graph-based skill work (GraSP, HiSkill, SkillDAG, Graph-of-Skills) uses graphs for retrieval/composition over libraries, not for evolving a single skill. The EC scaffolding itself (population, rank-based selection, round-robin operators, validation gating) is a standard combination of existing EC and LLM-self-reflection ideas applied to the new representation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the paper isolates graph structure (vs. unstructured content-preserving counterpart), mutation, and crossover on three benchmarks, and each contributes measurably, with mutation the dominant component. Three repeated optimization runs back the main table; five runs with mean/std and Welch's t-tests appear in the appendix. Two of the four headline benchmarks fail conventional significance thresholds (p≈0.069 and 0.089), which the authors report honestly. Code is released at https://github.com/ruisun7/GraphSkillEvo, with prompts (Appendix E) and dataset splits (seed 42) documented. Methodological concerns: (a) candidate skills are selected by validation fitness on val sets as small as 18–53 instances, creating a real Goodhart risk that the population overfits D_val, and no experiment measures this; (b) only one skill-optimization baseline is compared head-to-head despite the related-work section naming at least four (EvoSkill, Trace2Skill, SkillX, AutoRefine); (c) main results report three-run averages without error bars or per-run variance; (d) the LiveMath ablation and significance table omit one benchmark (LiveMath) from Table 7 and ALFWorld from Table 4 without explanation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent released codebase). Practical: Yes — it needs only API access to a single LLM and a validator script; no GPUs or training. Efficient: It is cheaper than the SkillOpt baseline in total optimization tokens (61.94M vs 81.08M for GPT-5.4; ~1.3× reduction), though the improvement is partly because SkillOpt's own token use is dominated by a few benchmarks. Effective: The evidence shows improved test-set success on five heterogeneous benchmarks with cross-model transfer, which is the stated goal; but the ceiling effect of tiny validation sets means deployed skills may be validation-lucky rather than genuinely better. Scalable: Not tested — the framework is claimed to explore more comprehensively, but at population 4 and 5 generations there is no evidence about behavior at larger populations, longer horizons, or bigger training sets. The work delivers a released software artifact (framework code, operator prompts, optimized skill examples) rather than only a paper. Strengths: - The representation contribution is validated by the right experiment: the unstructured counterpart in Table 3 preserves all content and removes only the workflow organization, cleanly attributing 0.75–4.52 points to explicit structure rather than to content or prompt length. - The cross-model transfer result (nano-optimized skill reaching 71.78 on GPT-5.4 Spreadsheet, beating the direct 69.40) is the most interesting and least anticipated finding, and directly supports the paper's portability motivation. - Honest statistics: reporting p-values of 0.069 and 0.089 for benchmarks where the win is not significant, and the single negative LiveMath result, is more transparent than typical for this subfield. - Token-cost accounting (Table 2) is a dimension most skill-optimization papers omit, and it shows the population method is not merely buying gains with more compute. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge only one negative result (LiveMath with GPT-5.4-nano, −0.80 vs SkillOpt) and, in the conclusion, point to future work on combining with parametric optimization, richer graph composition, and cross-domain skill merging — implicitly conceding that the current graph model is limited to within-task workflows. They do not otherwise confront limitations directly; there is no dedicated limitations section, and the fragility of validation-based selection on tiny val sets is never raised. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The graph is not really a graph: edges only arise as consecutive steps in linear workflow lists with condition-keyed path selection; there is no branching, looping, or learned routing, so claims of "graph-structured" search may overstate the representational difference from a well-organized markdown document with a task-type table of contents. - Missing baselines: the related-work survey names EvoSkill, Trace2Skill, SkillX, and AutoRefine, but none is empirically compared — the evolutionary-search claim ("broader exploration than self-refinement") is tested only against one self-refinement method (SkillOpt). - Validation-set overfitting is unexamined: with 18–53 validation instances on LiveMath/DocVQA/ALFWorld, selecting the best of 40+ candidates per run invites Goodhart effects; no generalization-gap or held-out-val analysis is offered. - The round-robin operator schedule and the population size N=4, T=5 are never tuned or justified; it is unknown whether the gains survive (or improve) at population 16–64, or whether the mutation dominance in the ablation means crossover is only helping via a lucky initial population. - The transfer experiment covers one direction (nano→GPT-5.4) on three benchmarks; transfer to a non-GPT family or to a weaker-than-optimizer model is untested despite portability being the headline motivation. - ALFWorld is missing entirely from the Codex-harness setting and LiveMath from the significance table, so "14 settings" quietly becomes fewer in each analysis. Bottom Line: A practitioner building self-improving agent skill pipelines gains concrete, reproducible techniques here — the structured skill format, the schema validator, and the four-operator design are immediately reusable, and the token analysis makes a credible efficiency case — but the narrow baseline comparison and toy evolutionary scale mean this is a promising formulation whose superiority over simpler alternatives beyond SkillOpt remains unproven.

MOSAIC-SR: Transformer-Guided Symbolic Regression for Scientific Equation Recovery

P Zheng, Y Kang, H De Sterck, G Tran · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MOSAIC-SR, a hybrid symbolic regression framework in which a pretrained Transformer proposes multiple structural equation sketches that seed MCTS-based variable assignment and parallel local-search repair, and shows it achieves the highest symbolic solution rate on every one of eight benchmarks tested (e.g., 84.7% vs. PySR's 60.0% on SRSD-Feynman Easy). - Why it's important: Symbolic regression for scientific discovery requires recovering the actual generating equation, not just a good numerical fit — high R² predictions with wrong algebraic structure are scientifically useless, and existing methods trade off structural flexibility against inference cost. - How it does it: The core trick is decoupling structure from instantiation: pretraining learns operator skeletons with variable/constant placeholders (deliberately excluding affine transforms that would corrupt symbolic matching), then a pretrained Transformer proposes diverse sketches, MCTS assigns observed variables, and local tree edits alternate with scale-aware constant refitting (Levenberg-Marquardt from log-spaced initializations). - The good: Component ablations credibly isolate the contribution — decoder-only reaches 30.0–43.3% symbolic recovery on SRSD-Feynman Easy, adding MCTS gives 30.0–66.7%, and the full pipeline reaches 83.3–90.0%, showing the learned prior and the repair search each matter and neither suffices alone. - The missing: There is no stated code or data release, the pretraining operator vocabulary plausibly overlaps the Feynman benchmark equations (a contamination channel the paper does not discuss), and no significance testing accompanies the five-seed means. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in symbolic regression or neural-guided combinatorial search who need the current best symbolic-recovery numbers and a clean demonstration that neural proposals plus explicit search outperform either alone; practitioners outside this niche can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: Symbolic regression seeks closed-form expressions from data, and its consumers are scientists who need interpretable equations, not black-box predictors. The field faces a tension: search-based methods (PySR, Operon, GP-GOMEA) can edit both structure and constants after seeing data but solve each problem from random initialization in a vast combinatorial space, while pretrained neural generators (NeSymReS, E2E-SR, SNIP-SR) propose expressions almost instantly but frequently produce symbolically wrong formulas that still fit numerically. The paper targets the gap between predictive accuracy and exact algebraic recovery — a high-test-R² polynomial can hide a wrong exponential law on a narrow domain. This distinction matters because SRBench-style evaluation treats symbolic solution rate as a separate, harder metric than R². Key Idea: Use the pretrained Transformer only as a structural prior — decoding sketches that preserve the operator tree while deferring variable assignment and constant estimation to inference-time search — so that neural proposal quality concentrates local search in promising regions while explicit tree repair retains the flexibility to fix residual symbolic errors. Two supporting pretraining decisions operationalize this: normalizing expressions with SymPy to collapse algebraic duplicates, and omitting affine transformations (scales/offsets) from skeletons so learned sketches match the ground-truth algebraic structure rather than a rescaled variant that fits well but fails symbolic verification. Methodology: Three phases. (1) Pretraining: synthetic expressions (1–10 variables; binary operators {+,−,×,÷}; unary operators including sin, cos, exp, log, sqrt, tan, tanh, arctan) are sampled in prefix notation, SymPy-normalized, and evaluated on 200 points under randomized input distributions. A Set Transformer numeric encoder with signed-log transform φ(a)=sign(a)log(1+|a|) and attention pooling is aligned to a Transformer symbolic encoder via bidirectional CLIP-style InfoNCE (temperature-scaled cosine similarity); then an autoregressive decoder is trained with cross-entropy on sketch sequences (variable/constant leaves replaced by special tokens) plus auxiliary structural heads (root arity, root operator class), loss L = L_CE + λ_aux·L_aux. (2) Inference initialization: 48 diverse sketches via nucleus sampling, MCTS maps decoded variable tokens to observed inputs, top-24 expressions by training NMSE seed 24 parallel search paths. (3) Local recovery: each path performs 300 mutation attempts (operator/variable/subtree replacement), refitting constants by minimizing squared error with Levenberg-Marquardt from 16 log-spaced initializations; a shared Hall of Fame pools candidates, final selection uses validation NMSE with a 10⁻¹⁵ near-exact threshold preferring fewest operators, then constants near zero are zeroed and near-physical-constant values snapped symbolically (retained only if validation error tolerance holds). Critical design decisions: deferring variable/constant assignment to inference (justified ablatively — decoder-only collapses without it), excluding affine transforms from pretraining (argued but not ablated directly), and log-spaced constant initializations for scientific constants spanning orders of magnitude (motivated, not isolated in an ablation). The framework is essentially a hybrid of neural sequence decoding, MCTS planning, and hill-climbing tree search — the architecture is a 17.4M-parameter Transformer. Key Results: On SRSD-Feynman (120 equations; Easy/Medium/Hard = 30/40/50; 8,000 train samples per problem), MOSAIC-SR achieves symbolic solution rates of 84.7%/55.0%/34.8% and accuracy (R²>0.999) of 96.7%/90.0%/53.2%, versus the best hybrid baseline SR4MDL at 63.3%/43.0%/21.2% symbolic. Under the dummy-variable variant, MOSAIC-SR retains 74.0%/54.5%/31.2% symbolic recovery — exceeding the strongest baseline by 34.0/18.5/14.0 percentage points while degrading only 10.7/0.5/3.6 points from the clean setting; PySR falls from 60.0% to 20.0% on Easy. On six standard benchmarks (Nguyen-12, Korns-15, Keijzer-15, Vladislavleva-8, Strogatz-14, Livermore-22) at a 3,600 s/problem budget with test NMSE<10⁻⁶ as accuracy, MOSAIC-SR posts the highest symbolic rate on all six (e.g., 75.0% vs. PySR's 8.3% on Nguyen; 53.3% vs. PySR's 26.7% on Keijzer), 1.3–2.2× faster than PySR and 6.8–24.3× faster than SR4MDL per equation. Direct neural baselines (E2E-SR, SNIP-SR, GenSR) reach at most 6.7% symbolic recovery on these benchmarks. Baselines are current and strong (PySR, TPSR, SR4MDL from ICLR 2025, GP-GOMEA, RSRM), though some SRSD-Feynman rows are cited from the original paper rather than re-run under identical conditions. Testing is at standard symbolic-regression scale (≤10 input variables, ≤8,000 training rows), not stress scale. Appendix E adds a Taylor-truncation robustness study showing MOSAIC-SR recovers log(x₀+1) from order-7 and order-10 polynomial data while PySR/Operon/TPSR return polynomials or worse. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (hybrid neural-guided recovery) with a NEW FORMULATION element (recovery-oriented pretraining that withholds variable/constant assignment and affine transforms to keep sketches symbolically matchable) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (decoded sketch operator count predicts local-search convergence better than ground-truth operator count — an inference-time-observable difficulty signal). The individual components are standard: Set Transformer encoders, CLIP-style InfoNCE, autoregressive sketch decoding (NeSymReS), MCTS planning (TPSR), and mutation-based local search with constant refitting (classical GP practice). The genuinely novel part is the assembly discipline — sketches as search initialization rather than predictions, with pretraining engineered specifically for symbolic recoverability — and the demonstration that this closes the accuracy-to-recovery gap that defeats pure neural generators. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: a component ablation (decoder / decoder+MCTS / full) on three seeds and a search budget sweep (1–48 paths × 100/300/500 steps) showing diminishing returns beyond 24 paths (48 paths adds only +2.2 points symbolic over 24 at 500 steps). Results are means over five seeds with error-bar plots and rank comparisons in Appendix A, but no significance tests are reported. The SRBench symbolic verifier is a fixed, community-recognized protocol, and test sets are used only for final scoring with returned expressions re-evaluated externally — good hygiene. However, no code, data, or model weights release is mentioned anywhere in the paper, which limits reproducibility given the many hyperparameters (nucleus sampling passes, MCTS trigger at validation NMSE 10⁻⁴ with 1,500 expansions, 16 constant-fitting starts, snapping tolerances). Methodological concerns: (a) pretraining samples from a vocabulary that likely covers most SRSD-Feynman equations, so the learned prior may partially memorize the benchmark distribution — unaddressed; (b) some SRSD-Feynman baselines are cited from Matsubara et al. rather than re-run, mixing evaluation conditions in one table; (c) the paper does not report variance in the main tables, only in appendix figures. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method with experiments actually run by the authors). Practical: Training ran on single 80 GB H100/A100 GPUs and the 17.4M-parameter model is small, so the method fits commodity accelerated hardware, though the paper reports cluster use. Efficient: Per-equation inference costs 75.6–288.1 s across the six benchmarks — faster than PySR (99.6–619.6 s) and SR4MDL (873.5–2,218.6 s) but 10–60× slower than Operon or GP-GOMEA, which recover far less often. Effective: The evidence directly supports symbolic recovery (verified externally against ground truth via the SRBench protocol), which is the stated goal, not just a proxy — though recovery is measured on benchmarks whose equations live inside the pretraining vocabulary. Scalable: Not tested beyond 10-variable problems; the authors themselves state recovery degrades for high-dimensional equations as the search space grows, so 10–100× scale behavior is claimed-limitation, not measured. The work delivers no stated software artifact — it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The clearest empirical demonstration to date that neural sketch proposals plus explicit repair search dominate either alone on symbolic recovery: identical numerical accuracy to PySR on Nguyen and Strogatz but symbolic rates of 75.0% vs. 8.3% and 64.3% vs. 42.9% respectively, isolating the fit-versus-recovery distinction. - The dummy-variable evaluation is a genuinely informative robustness test that most SR papers skip, and MOSAIC-SR's 10.7/0.5/3.6-point degradation against multi-tens-of-points drops for PySR and DGSR substantiates the multi-sketch design rather than merely asserting robustness. - The recovery-oriented pretraining decisions (SymPy normalization of duplicates, no affine transforms in sketches) are a concrete, transferable insight: they directly target the symbolic verifier rather than numeric fit, and Appendix E's Taylor-order study shows the resulting robustness to polynomial-approximation decoys. - The Appendix B finding that decoded sketch operator count — observable at inference — separates local-search outcomes more strongly than ground-truth operator count suggests an actionable adaptive-budget mechanism. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states that recovery becomes harder for high-dimensional equations because the search space grows rapidly, and that targets far outside the pretraining distribution may require a larger search budget. Future-work directions (broader pretraining distributions, recovery from sparse observations reflecting real-world data availability) implicitly acknowledge that current evaluation uses dense, in-distribution synthetic and benchmark data. The authors confront these boundaries directly rather than minimizing them, which is credible, but they do not address the pretraining-benchmark vocabulary overlap or absence of code release. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Possible benchmark contamination: pretraining samples expressions from a vocabulary (add/sub/mul/div, squares/cubes, sin, cos, exp, log, sqrt, tan, tanh, arctan) that almost certainly covers the bulk of SRSD-Feynman's 120 physics equations; a leave-equations-out or disjoint-vocabulary experiment is absent, so the symbolic-recovery headline could partly reflect memorization of the operator grammar rather than generalizable priors. - No code or weights release is stated, yet the method has a long hyperparameter chain (sketch sampling passes, MCTS expansions, 10⁻¹⁵ selection threshold, constant-snapping tolerances) that materially affects results and cannot be independently verified from the paper. - Mixed provenance in Table 1/2: cited SRSD-Feynman numbers (uDSR, PySR, DSR, AI Feynman, E2E, AFP) come from the original benchmark paper under potentially different budgets, while the lower block was re-run by the authors — the two blocks are visually comparable but not procedurally identical. - The affine-transform exclusion is argued as central but never ablated (no comparison against a pretraining variant that includes affine terms), so its causal contribution to symbolic recovery is unquantified. - Statistical significance is never tested; several baseline gaps (e.g., SR4MDL vs. MOSAIC-SR on Medium accuracy) may be within seed noise, and only appendix bar-plots, not confidence intervals, support the ordering. - Cross-benchmark evaluation omits uDSR and DSR, hybrid/RL baselines that appear in the SRSD-Feynman tables, leaving the strongest recent competitors unevaluated on half the evidence. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing symbolic regression should read this: MOSAIC-SR sets the best published symbolic-recovery numbers on every benchmark it touches with honest ablations isolating why, but the missing code release, plausible pretraining-benchmark vocabulary overlap, and untested high-dimensional scaling mean the headline numbers deserve verification before being treated as a general-purpose solution over alternatives like PySR for truly out-of-distribution science.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a structured evidence map of 120 verified studies (2015–2025) on smart TV / IPTV / OTT content recommendation, cross-classifying eight technical paradigms against six mutually exclusive functional goals and profiling evidence quality across five reporting domains. - Why it's important: Smart TV recommendation differs from web/mobile recommendation (shared household accounts, passive lean-back viewing, sparse feedback, live schedules, constrained hardware), yet existing surveys' conclusions do not transfer, and the field lacks public benchmarks and deployment-grade evidence. - How it does it: A PRISMA 2020/PRISMA-S-aligned evidence-mapping protocol: 216 database-native searches across six sources, deduplication and title/abstract screening (2,526 → 112 records), full-text eligibility screening yielding 25 new studies combined with a 95-study initial corpus, plus an independent dual-reviewer eligibility audit of 126 records (97.6% agreement, Cohen's κ = 0.788). - The good: The methodological hygiene is unusually high for a mapping review — frozen query strings, Crossref/OpenAlex verification, a documented database-priority attribution sequence, a pre-registered contingency table for the audit, and explicit refusal to pool incomparable performance numbers. - The missing: The headline synthesis rests heavily on proprietary industrial logs (DeepTV, COSMO, Globoplay) that cannot be independently reproduced, and the inter-rater κ covers only the 126-record audit cohort, not the taxonomy coding that actually drives the map. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate recommenders for TV-like platforms or want a defensible literature map of household-aware recommendation; skip it if you want quantitative meta-analysis, effect sizes, or a new method — it delivers none.

Problem & Motivation: Smart TV platforms (IPTV, OTT, VOD, live TV) must recommend under conditions that break standard recommender assumptions: one account serves multiple viewers with conflicting tastes, explicit ratings are rare because remote controls and lean-back viewing discourage interaction, live schedules constrain the candidate set, programmes are long and semantically rich, and set-top hardware limits on-device computation. Platform teams, academic researchers, and public-service broadcasters all lack a structured account of which techniques have credible evidence in this setting versus which are extrapolated from mobile/web results. Prior surveys cover recommender methods, cold start, graphs, privacy, and multimodality generically, but none maps evidence specifically against TV constraints. Key Idea: The core move is a two-tier evidence design: each study is classified as either TV-specific (direct smart TV/IPTV/OTT evidence) or enabling/contextual (transferable only via a prespecified TV challenge such as shared accounts, long-form representation, or on-device inference), and then each study is cross-classified by one primary technical category and one of six mutually exclusive primary functional goals — with secondary labels capturing hybrid methods. This lets the authors distinguish established findings from weakly validated directions (e.g., LLM-based recommendation) without pretending a single quality score can span algorithm papers, industrial case studies, and reviews. Methodology: The review follows PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S. Search construction crossed six television-domain phrases with six challenge blocks into 36 frozen conceptual variants, executed as 216 database-native strings across Google Scholar, ACM DL, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Engineering Village (2,526 total hits; per-source yields reported). An integrated deduplication (DOI, then normalized-title) plus title/abstract screen removed 2,414 records; 112 full texts were assessed, 87 excluded, 25 retained and merged with a pre-existing 95-study corpus to form the 120-study evidence map (71 TV-specific, 49 enabling; 68 journal articles, 39 proceedings, 7 book chapters, 6 preprints). A separate randomized 20-record calibration exercise preceded a 126-record dual-reviewer eligibility audit (all 120 included + 6 boundary exclusions), yielding 123/126 agreement (97.6%, κ = 0.788) with three discordant records adjudicated as Include. Evidence quality was profiled as separate reporting domains (data transparency, reproducibility, evaluation design, external validation, deployment validation) rather than a composite score. Critical design decisions: (1) the two-tier scope with explicit transfer rationales — justified, and honestly flagged as a heterogeneity risk; (2) refusing meta-analysis of incomparable metrics — well justified given dataset/metric heterogeneity; (3) reserving the κ statistic for the audit cohort only, with consensus coding for taxonomy — transparent, but it leaves category-level reliability unmeasured. Key Results: As a mapping review, the outputs are distributional, not performance numbers. Headline findings: no universally dominant paradigm across 120 studies; traditional/hybrid methods form the largest primary category (40/120), deep/sequential/multi-task 19, content understanding and foundation models 14, shared-account/group modeling 10, interaction and deployment systems 11, graph methods only 4, and evaluation/trust/responsible recommendation only 3. Dedicated shared-account studies remain uncommon despite household coupling being central; the two strongest household models (COSMO, session-aware co-attention with device weak supervision; PSJNet, cross-domain role separation) lack a shared benchmark. Only 2 of 90 available abstracts named a public dataset while 16 cited proprietary logs; only 16/90 abstracts named any evaluation metric. Representative deployed evidence is thin: PLE reported +2.23% views and +1.84% watch time online at Tencent; COSMO reports offline plus online A/B tests; a time-aware quadratic programming method reported 5–50% improvement over baselines on a standalone TV. LLM evidence is restricted to MovieLens-100K-scale movie experiments with no smart-TV online validation. These are the authors' characterizations of the included studies, not measurements made by this paper itself. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the verified 120-study corpus and reproducible search protocol, though no artifact dataset is released as a benchmark in the benchmark sense) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the first structured cross-classification of TV-recommendation evidence against TV-specific functional goals, surfacing the scarcity of shared-account, evaluation, and deployment studies). The component techniques — PRISMA screening, evidence tiers, dual-reviewer audit — are standard review methodology competently combined; the novelty is the domain-scoped synthesis and the honest separation of TV-specific from merely transferable evidence. Rigor & Reproducibility: The protocol is above the norm for mapping reviews: all 216 search strings, dates, and yields are documented in supplementary material; the eligibility contingency table is published; deduplication rules are stated; each extracted field is linked to the depth of source examined. The dual-reviewer audit with κ = 0.788 is genuinely independent. Ablation-equivalents (which evidence tiers and boundary records were included and why) are explicit. However: the κ covers only the 126-record audit, not title/abstract screening or taxonomy coding (authors acknowledge this); the 95-study "initial corpus" predates the formal search and its provenance is thinner than the 25 newly screened studies; the accompanying workbook is promised but no public URL for code/data is given in the text, and full-text evidence notes are explicitly "restricted internal records." No quantitative pooling was attempted, which the authors correctly justify but which means the review offers no effect-size synthesis at all. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a protocol-driven observational study of the literature, no system built). - Practical: Yes — the method is a manual/semi-automated review workflow executable by any research team; no special hardware or compute required. - Efficient: The protocol is labor-intensive (dual full-text review of 126 records, 216 search executions) but cheap in compute; the search framework is reusable for future evidence updates. - Effective: It credibly answers its mapping questions (RQ1–RQ4) at the distribution level, but cannot and does not establish which method is best — it explicitly refuses to rank. - Scalable: Not tested; corpus refreshes would require repeating the labor-intensive pipeline, and the reliance on an un-audited pre-existing 95-study corpus suggests scaling the protocol outward may be uneven. The deliverable is a paper plus a described supplementary workbook (bibliographic corpus, search strings, codebook, audit table); no public code repository, dataset release, or URL is stated in the provided text. Strengths: - The two-tier TV-specific vs. enabling classification, with per-study transfer rationales, is a genuinely useful methodological contribution that most domain reviews lack — it prevents generic recommender results from being silently imported as TV evidence. - Unusually transparent accounting: published contingency table, frozen queries, per-database attribution priority, and an explicit statement that κ applies only to the audit cohort — this is how review reliability should be reported. - The evidence-reporting domain profiling (transparency, reproducibility, external validation, deployment) surfaces a real, quantified gap: 2/90 abstracts with public data and only 3/120 studies on evaluation/trust, which is the paper's most actionable empirical finding. - The research roadmap (household identity as uncertainty, a public TV benchmark with exposure/schedule/remote-event fields, modular grounded foundation models, Pareto-exposed multi-objective trade-offs, deployment evidence as scientific evidence) is specific and falsifiable, with minimum-evidence criteria per priority. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors list five: (1) heterogeneity from combining TV-specific and enabling studies in one map; (2) possible retrieval misses for studies using only general recommender terminology; (3) inter-rater reliability measured only on the 126-record audit cohort, not the full screening pool or taxonomy coding; (4) no quantitative meta-analysis due to task/data/metric incompatibility; (5) weak boundary evidence retained for six included studies that are not treated as validation. They also disclose generative AI use for grammar and figure plotting, and that full-text evidence notes remain internal. They confront limitations directly and with appropriate specificity — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 95-study "initial corpus" is not subjected to the same audited screening as the 25 new studies; its selection provenance is opaque relative to the rest of the protocol, yet it constitutes 79% of the evidence map. - No public release URL is given for the promised workbook, so reproducibility claims rest on descriptions rather than an artifact a reader can inspect. - Taxonomy coding (the actual map) has no reported inter-rater reliability — the published κ measures only include/exclude eligibility, the least consequential judgment in the pipeline. - Six of six databases are commercial/English-centric; no non-English literature is considered despite the TV/IPTV domain having substantial Chinese and Korean industrial research, and both search dates postdate the 2015–2025 window by months, creating a coverage cut-off risk the authors do not discuss. - The paper criticizes the field for lacking public benchmarks but does not itself release even a de-identified household-simulation protocol, despite naming this as roadmap priority 2 — an inconsistency a reviewer could flag. - Industrial evidence (COSMO, Tencent PLE, DeepTV) is treated as the strongest deployment signal but consists of vendor self-reports that cannot be independently checked; the review profiles this but does not down-weight conclusions drawn from it. Bottom Line: This is the most methodologically careful map of smart TV recommendation research available and is worth reading in full for anyone building household-aware or TV-platform recommenders, but readers seeking quantitative evidence of which method wins — or a reusable public artifact — will find a well-documented gap analysis rather than an answer.

StableVQ: Practical Guidelines for Stable Vector-Quantized Tokenizer Training (20 ▲ )

Bao Tang, Jiahao Guo, Haoxiang Cao, Wenyu Liu, Changqian Yu, Kun Gai, Xinggang Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 23 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StableVQ, a set of three parameter-free training interventions (Dynamic STE, Region VQ Loss, Decoupled Schedule) that stabilize vector-quantized tokenizer training and achieve rFID 1.22/1.05 on ImageNet 256×256 with 16K/262K codebooks using only a single linear shared projector. - Why it's important: VQ tokenizer training is notoriously fragile — codebook collapse, NaN divergence, and utilization crashes mid-training waste compute and cap the quality of autoregressive and masked image generators built on these tokens. - How it does it: The core move is a separation-of-concerns diagnosis: weight STE gradients by within-batch relative quantization error (Dynamic STE), propagate token targets from active codes to persistently inactive codes so every code gets supervised (Region VQ), and give the codebook a separate constant high learning rate while the encoder–decoder gets warmup-plus-annealing. - The good: The strongest evidence is the robustness metric (UR-AUC): StableVQ scores 60.59±1.52 versus 8.08±0.24 for FVQ and 2.17±0.32 for SimVQ under adversarial codebook–token distribution mismatches, and ablations isolate each component's contribution under codebook expansion and shrinkage stress tests. - The missing: All experiments are on ImageNet 256×256 reconstruction and a single downstream AR generation setup, with SimVQ and FVQ baselines re-implemented by the authors rather than taken from published numbers, and no code release is mentioned. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone training or scaling VQ tokenizers — the failure-mode taxonomy and parameter-free fixes are directly actionable — but skippable if you work outside discrete visual tokenization.
