Problem & Motivation: Teams training discrete visual tokenizers for autoregressive (LlamaGen, VAR), masked (MaskGIT), and multimodal generation models face training instability even after shared-projection codebooks (VQ-STE++, SimVQ, FVQ) largely solved codebook collapse: convergence is sensitive to initialization, utilization can stagnate at low levels, and abrupt utilization collapse can occur mid-training, occasionally escalating to NaN gradients. The authors argue these failure modes stem from entangled optimization — the encoder–decoder and codebook can only succeed when they happen to cooperate, which masks latent dysfunction in each module. The paper targets the gap that prior shared-projection methods guarantee neither that inactive codes receive directed learning signal (it is diffuse and decays once a few codes suffice) nor that the encoder's STE gradients remain reliable when assignments are poor. Key Idea: The key insight is a modular responsibility analysis: characterize VQ training failure modes (code scale ≪ token scale → prolonged low utilization; code scale ≫ token scale → permanent dead codes; transient scale divergence → positive-feedback utilization collapse), then give each module a self-sufficient objective. The enabling trick for the codebook is shifting from point-wise to region-wise alignment — active codes propagate their token-mean targets to their nearest persistently-inactive neighbors with quotas proportional to selection counts, so every code receives a directed target without waiting for encoder drift. The enabling trick for the encoder is per-token STE gradient weighting by relative quantization error, which attenuates (never amplifies) unreliable gradients and self-deactivates (w→1) when training is healthy. Methodology: The pipeline builds on a VQGAN-style tokenizer (f=16, 256 tokens/image) with a shared-projection codebook, keeping the standard three-term loss (reconstruction + commitment + VQ loss) and modifying three parts. (1) Dynamic STE: each token's STE gradient is weighted w_ij = sg[d_k / ||z_ij − fθ(e_k)||²] ∈ (0,1], where d_k is the minimum token-to-code distance in the batch; this is implemented via the standard straight-through reparameterization ẑ = w·z + sg[ẑ − w·z], so the intervention requires no threshold hyperparameter. (2) Region VQ Loss: a FIFO window of length W defines window-active and persistently-inactive sets; each currently active code k propagates its mean token target to q_k ∝ n_k nearest inactive codes; the unified loss is L_code = (1/|M_t|) Σ_k ||fθ(e_k) − sg[t_k]||² over codes with effective targets. (3) Decoupled Schedule: encoder–decoder uses warmup-plus-annealing (10% warmup, anneal 1×→0.01× over 63% of training); codebook uses constant LR 1e−3 with no warmup. Each component is supported by a controlled pilot study (frozen codebook for Dynamic STE; frozen encoder for Region VQ; 2×2 schedule ablation for Decoupled Schedule). Design decisions are generally well-justified empirically, though the FIFO window length W and quota mechanics introduce new hyperparameters the paper does not deeply ablate. Key Results: On ImageNet 256×256 (ImageNet val for metrics), StableVQ with a single linear projector reaches rFID 1.22 / LPIPS 0.2235 at 16,384×256 codebook (40 epochs) and rFID 1.05 / LPIPS 0.1947 at 262,144×256, versus re-implemented FVQ at 1.70/1.29 (which needs a 2-layer ViT-block projector) and SimVQ at 2.89/3.16; at 120 epochs StableVQ reaches rFID 0.92 and 22.81 PSNR (262K). All methods report 100% utilization under their standard settings, so the discriminating evidence is stress tests: UR-AUC of 60.59±1.52 (StableVQ) vs 8.08±0.24 (FVQ) vs 2.17±0.32 (SimVQ) across initialization-induced mismatches (3 seeds); under codebook-expansion stress, the full combination yields 100% utilization and rFID 1.70 while single components fail (Region VQ alone → NaN; Dynamic STE alone → 1.27% utilization); under shrinkage stress, FVQ drops to 18.75–62.5% utilization while Region VQ holds 100%. Against prior STE corrections (15-epoch controlled test), Dynamic STE gives rFID 2.794 vs 3.644 for the Rotation Trick, with VQ-STE++ collapsing; against explicit distribution alignment, Region VQ holds 99.4% utilization at ζ=4 on the non-Gaussian mixture benchmark where Wasserstein VQ falls to 34.8%, at ~1.24× Wasserstein VQ's per-step time and 34.2× faster than MMD VQ. Training overhead is small: Region VQ adds ≤2.16% step time and ≤1.24% memory at 262K codes; Dynamic STE is within noise; inference is unchanged. Downstream, class-conditional AR transformers on StableVQ tokens achieve FID 2.35 (342M) and 2.18 (649M) vs IBQ's 2.88 and 2.45. Baselines are recent (2023–2025) and reasonably current, but all shared-projection baselines were re-implemented by the authors under an on-the-fly evaluation pipeline. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are Region VQ Loss (target propagation from active to inactive codes with FIFO-based inactivity tracking — distinct from prior distribution-matching losses like Wasserstein/MMD VQ), the UR-AUC robustness protocol, and the failure-mode taxonomy; Dynamic STE is a lightweight variant of prior STE-correction ideas (VQ-STE++'s alternating optimization, Rotation Trick), and Decoupled Schedule is a straightforward but well-motivated engineering fix. The separation-of-concerns framing is a useful synthesis rather than a formal result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: each component is validated in isolation via frozen-module pilot studies, a 2×2 schedule ablation, component-combination ablations under expansion and shrinkage stress, projector-capacity and initialization-scale sweeps, STE-correction comparisons, and distribution-alignment comparisons on a third-party benchmark. Error bars (mean ± std over 3 seeds) are reported for UR-AUC; most other tables are single-run. Methods and hyperparameters are documented in detail (Appendix G, Algorithm 1). However: no public code, data, or model release is mentioned; baselines SimVQ and FVQ are author re-implementations rather than published numbers (though measured under a fairer on-the-fly evaluation); the headline UR-AUC metric is proposed by the authors and evaluated on their own constructed mismatch settings, which invites Goodhart concerns; and evaluation is confined to ImageNet 256×256. Several references (FVQ, VQ-Transplant) are arXiv-only or concurrent, so the baseline maturity is limited. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor via the training recipe). - Practical: Yes — interventions are training-only, parameter-free, built on standard VQGAN-style architectures and Adam, and inference is unchanged. - Efficient: Low cost — measured overhead ≤2.16% training time and ≤1.24% memory (262K codebook), and StableVQ removes the need for FVQ's ViT-block projector. - Effective: Strong evidence for the stated problem (stable utilization and reconstruction) on ImageNet, including adversarial stress tests; downstream generation gains (FID 2.18–2.35) are competitive but not decisive versus FVQ (2.07 at 775M params in Appendix C). - Scalable: Not tested beyond 262K codebooks and a VQGAN-scale encoder on a single dataset; claims about scaling to video/audio/multimodal are stated as future directions, not demonstrated. Deliverable: paper form only — no code, library, or trained weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The failure-mode taxonomy (Figure 1: low-utilization stagnation, permanent dead codes, positive-feedback utilization collapse) is a genuinely useful diagnostic contribution that reframes instability as modular responsibility failure rather than an inherent quantization limitation. - Region VQ Loss is a real algorithmic idea with a clean mechanism (quota-proportional target propagation to FIFO-tracked inactive codes), validated against both STE-correction and explicit distribution-matching alternatives on a third-party benchmark at 34.2× lower cost than MMD VQ. - The robustness evaluation (UR-AUC over initialization-induced mismatches, 3 seeds) is a more honest protocol than the field's standard single-configuration utilization numbers, where all methods already hit 100%. - Removing dependence on projector engineering (single linear layer matching/exceeding FVQ's ViT-block projector) is a concrete, practical simplification backed by the sweeps in Appendix D. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: In Appendix B, the authors state that StableVQ addresses only training stability and utilization — it does not address balancing reconstruction quality, semantic structure, and generation-friendliness; that connection to unified understanding/generation tokenizers is open; and that validation is image-only with video, audio, multimodal, and compression as untested domains. This is a direct, non-minimizing statement of scope, which is a credibility positive, though the limitations section is brief and does not discuss hyperparameter sensitivity of the new components (FIFO window W, quota scaling) or evaluation breadth. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No code or model release is mentioned, which materially limits reproducibility for a paper whose central claims rest on author-run re-implementations of SimVQ and FVQ. - UR-AUC is an author-defined metric evaluated on author-constructed mismatch settings; while the stress tests are sensible, the headline robustness claim has no external benchmark corroboration beyond the small non-Gaussian mixture test. - Single dataset (ImageNet 256×256), single tokenizer architecture (VQGAN f=16), and no higher-resolution, video, or text-conditioned tokenizer results — the paper's ambition is reliable scaling, but the tested scale stops at 262K codes on one dataset. - The most decisive downstream comparison (Appendix C) shows FVQ tokens actually beat StableVQ tokens at the largest generator size (FID 2.07 with LlamaGen-XL-775M vs 2.18 with IBQ-L-649M), and generator/tokenizer configurations are not held constant, slightly muddying the claim that better tokenizer training translates to generation gains. - The FIFO window length W, the collision-handling quota adjustment used in the synthetic benchmark, and sensitivity of Dynamic STE under ℓ2-normalized vs unnormalized codebooks are not ablated. - The three components' interaction is shown only for the expansion setting; a full factorial under the shrinkage and mid-training-divergence settings is absent. Bottom Line: A practitioner training or scaling VQ tokenizers gains concrete, low-cost, well-ablated fixes and a better evaluation protocol here, and this is currently the strongest published evidence on training robustness in the shared-projection line — but without a code release, independent replication of the re-implemented baselines, and results beyond ImageNet, the headline robustness claims should be treated as promising rather than settled.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations routinely express production planning, routing, scheduling, and inventory decisions as mathematical programs, and solvers are mature; the bottleneck is the expensive, expert-scarce translation between a messy business situation and a correct formulation, and back into an actionable argument. LLM agents that parse, formulate, generate solver code, execute, and self-repair have reached competitive benchmark accuracy within roughly three years (OptiMUS, Chain-of-Experts, OR-LLM-Agent), but the evidence base is fragmented across ML, OR, software engineering, and supply chain venues with incompatible vocabularies and evidentiary standards. Prior reviews cover supply chain LLM applications (Song et al., 2026), LLM supply chains (Wang et al., 2025), or LLM architectures generally (Raiaan et al., 2024), but none integrates architecture, benchmark validity, and assurance practice for this specific system class, nor positions it against the enterprise analytics infrastructure it must run on. That integration gap is what this review targets via four research questions on archetypes, task coverage, evaluation design, and assurance reporting. Key Idea: The core insight is an epistemic-independence principle: verification mechanisms that share a base model with the proposing mechanism (homogeneous reviewer agents, reflective self-repair) inherit correlated failure modes and tend to ratify rather than challenge errors, whereas verification by a mechanism external to the language model — a solver's feasibility and optimality certificates — supplies a deterministic oracle that produces the corpus's most consistent reliability gains. This reframes architectural progress as a function of verification independence rather than agent count, and motivates the five-layer reference architecture separating interaction, reasoning, formalization, execution, and assurance, with assurance spanning the stack. Whether this counts as a genuine key idea or a well-argued synthesis of what practitioners already suspect about LLM-as-judge bias is debatable; it is the review's most defensible intellectual contribution regardless. Methodology: The review follows PRISMA 2020 with a protocol fixed before screening. Five sources (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, curated arXiv categories cs.AI/cs.CL/cs.SE/math.OC) were searched on 30 June 2026 with a three-block query (language model terms × optimization/decision terms × agency terms). From 1,824 records, 596 duplicates were removed, 1,228 screened on title/abstract (1,001 excluded), 215 assessed in full text, 128 excluded with recorded reasons, yielding 87 studies; two independent reviewers screened with Cohen's kappa of 0.81 (title/abstract) and 0.88 (full text), with a third reviewer resolving 19 disagreements. A five-criterion, 0–2-point quality rubric (decision-task clarity, baseline adequacy, setup transparency, correctness criterion, artifact availability) excluded 9 studies scoring ≤4. Studies were coded on four dimensions aligned to RQ1–RQ4: architecture, decision task (mapped to SCOR processes), benchmark/evaluation design, and reliability/security/reproducibility reporting. Notable design decisions: (1) preprints included but subject to the same rubric, justified by the field's preprint-first culture; (2) assignment of hybrid systems to a single dominant archetype, acknowledged as lossy; (3) the rubric's solver-verification criterion is well-matched to the domain. The coding scheme and extraction form are stated but the data extraction itself is not shown per-study, so individual codings cannot be audited from the paper. Key Results: The corpus skews young: 79.3% (69/87) of studies appeared in 2024 or later; H1-2026 alone produced 17 studies. Archetype distribution: role-based multi-agent 23 (26.4%), modular pipeline 19 (21.8%), solver-in-the-loop 16 (18.4%), single-agent prompting 14 (16.1%), domain fine-tuned 9 (10.3%), search-augmented 6 (6.9%). Task coverage concentrates in Plan (34, 39.1%) and Deliver (21, 24.1%), with Make (9), Return (5), and cross-process (6) underrepresented; only 3 of 12 sourcing studies connect extraction to an optimization model. Evaluation weaknesses are quantified: 47.1% of studies rely on benchmarks alone; 19 studies rely wholly or partly on textual (not solver-verified) correctness comparison; 43.7% release code/prompts, 26.4% pin model versions, 21.8% report cost/latency, 16.1% report repeated runs with variance, 12.6% include human-expert baselines. Only 7 studies address adversarial security despite agents ingesting untrusted documents; only 5 discuss data confidentiality; 9 report industrial deployments; none reports an end-to-end decision audit trail. Fine-tuned open models match prompted frontier models on formulation benchmarks at lower inference cost, but only 2 studies do a like-for-like cost comparison. The key comparative finding — solver grounding beats orchestration — is a qualitative cross-study pattern, not a controlled comparison. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (first systematic integration of architecture, benchmark validity, and assurance for LLM-solver agent systems) plus a NEW FORMULATION (the verification-independence principle and five-layer reference architecture). The underlying observations — benchmark gaming on structured formulation tasks, correlated errors in same-base-model multi-agent systems, prompt injection risk — are each known from prior work (the review itself cites Nwakamma et al. on LLM-as-judge bias and Greshake et al. on indirect injection); the genuine contribution is the synthesis and the measurement-grounded research agenda (Table 6), not any individual finding. Rigor & Reproducibility: Methodologically this is a competently executed PRISMA review: fixed protocol, dual independent screening with reported kappa (0.81/0.88), recorded exclusion reasons, an adapted quality rubric applied uniformly, and an explicit threats-to-validity section covering coverage bias, currency, classification judgment, and preprint heterogeneity. No public artifact is released — the coding sheet, screening decisions, and search strings are "available from the corresponding author on reasonable request," which falls short of the reproducibility standard the paper itself demands of its corpus (43.7% artifact release). No meta-analysis or effect-size synthesis is performed (appropriate given corpus heterogeneity). Two concerns a reviewer should flag: first, the reference list is saturated with publications from obscure venues (e.g., "Gyanshauryam International Scientific Refereed Research Journal," "Shodhshauryam") that feature heavily overlapping author groups, several of which appear on this paper's own author list or are cited dozens of times as the "enterprise substrate" (Sections 3.2, 3.6); the substrate and governance claims are built substantially on this mutually-referencing cluster, which the paper does not disclose as a relatedness concern. Second, the quantitative reporting-practice statistics are the review's headline numbers, but the extraction instrument and per-study coding are not inspectable from the paper. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: this is an EMPIRICAL paper in the systematic-review genre (it runs a documented screening and coding process, not a system). - Practical: The review process itself required only database access; its recommended five-layer architecture relies on solvers, IAM, and audit infrastructure enterprises already operate, per the authors' own argument. - Efficient: Not applicable to a review; the actionable efficiency finding is that fine-tuned small models match prompted frontier models on benchmarks, but only 2 studies support like-for-like cost claims. - Effective: The evidence supports the negative-space claims (benchmark validity, reproducibility gaps) more strongly than the prescriptive architecture, which is unvalidated by any deployment in the corpus. - Scalable: The reviewed evidence covers only 9 live deployments and small routing/scheduling instances; the review explicitly warns that benchmark results do not extrapolate to large scheduling, stochastic multi-period, or reverse-logistics settings. The work delivers no software artifact or dataset; it stops at paper form, with an eight-item research agenda (A1–A8) each paired with a proposed measurement (e.g., error-detection rate of verifiers against injected formulation faults; attack success rate under a standardized injection corpus). Strengths: - The verification-independence principle is a genuine, transferable design insight: it converts scattered observations about reviewer-agent ablations, LLM-as-judge bias, and solver-in-the-loop gains into one falsifiable architectural claim, and it predicts a concrete research direction (heterogeneous verification, agenda item A3). - The gap quantification is unusually specific and actionable: reporting-practice percentages (26.4% version pinning, 16.1% repeated runs, 12.6% human baselines) and the observation that 4 of 11 reviewer-ablation studies report gains within run-to-run variance give the field measurable targets rather than exhortations. - Task-coverage analysis (Table 4) correctly identifies that the Plan/Make/Return imbalance is a capability boundary exposed by benchmark shape (compact LP/MILP vs. large constraint-indexed scheduling), not just researcher neglect — a non-obvious diagnostic. - The framing of a wrongly formulated model as a "quiet" failure that borrows authority from the solver's optimality certificate is a sharp, memorable statement of why this domain's evaluation problem differs from general agentic software. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The threats-to-validity section (3.8) is direct and credible: possible coverage bias from practitioner/proprietary venues (only 9 deployment studies likely undercount practice); currency truncation at June 2026 in a fast-moving field; forced single-archetype classification of hybrid systems, mitigated but not eliminated by inter-rater agreement; and heterogeneity from preprint inclusion. The authors also explicitly scope their strongest claims to "recurring patterns in architecture and reporting practice rather than a fixed ranking of individual models," and they confine generalization boundaries in Section 4.4 (no extrapolation from compact LP benchmarks to scheduling, reverse logistics, or stochastic planning). This is a model of candid limitation reporting. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The citation base problem the authors do not acknowledge: a large share of the "enterprise substrate," security, and governance literature cited in Sections 3.2 and 3.6 comes from low-visibility journals with overlapping and self-referential authorship (including works by this paper's own authors), yet these citations carry argumentative weight as established evidence. A sensitivity analysis excluding the interlinked cluster would test whether the substrate and governance conclusions survive. - The headline claim that solver grounding outperforms orchestration is drawn from cross-study comparison of non-comparable setups (different benchmarks, models, years); no within-study controlled comparison is cited, and the review does not mark this inference as weaker than its quantified reporting statistics. - Inter-rater kappa is reported for screening but not for the coding of the four synthesis dimensions (archetype assignment, task mapping, evaluation-design classification), where judgment is arguably hardest. - The review does not search grey literature or vendor documentation beyond arXiv, yet bases deployment-deficiency claims (no audit trails, no injection defenses in practice) on an academic corpus that structurally cannot contain such practice — a dogs-not-barking issue the authors half-acknowledge via coverage bias but do not trace to its effect on the governance conclusions. - Publication venue quality is not factored into the quality rubric: a 2023 preprint and an Operations Research paper score on the same five criteria, and the rubric weights artifact availability equally with correctness-criterion rigor. Bottom Line: A rigorously executed and unusually honest systematic review whose quantified evaluation gaps and verification-independence principle earn it a place on the reading list of anyone building or benchmarking optimization agents — but its governance and enterprise-substrate arguments are built on a citation ecosystem of dubious independence, so its prescriptive architecture should be treated as a well-reasoned hypothesis, not established practice.

Grounded Skill Synthesis from Code at Scale for Agentic Intelligence (85 ▲ )

Yongqi Tong, Pan Wang, Hang Wang, Jianshe Li, Xin Zhang, Jiang-Ming Yang, Wei Wu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Code2Skill, a fully automated pipeline that mines 19,769 curated GitHub repositories into a verified skill bank (CodeSkillBank, 1,006,822 records) of atomic-operation, composite-workflow, and recurring-pattern skill records, each grounded through source-body-blind code reconstruction. - Why it's important: Existing skill synthesis either depends on agent trajectories (coupled to one model/harness, unavailable before deployment) or on documents (no executable evidence); code offers a large, pre-existing substrate of tested procedures that agents can reuse before accumulating any experience. - How it does it: The core trick is round-trip grounding: an LLM regenerates the source unit using only the synthesized skill record (source body hidden), then a source-aware judge compares reconstruction against the original code, filtering records whose descriptions are not actually supported by the implementation. - The good: The most credible evidence is the controlled comparison in Table 2: under one shared agent loop on one model, Code2Skill beats Trace2Skill, ExpeL, and SkillRL-Bank on all seven shared benchmarks (49.5 average vs. 31.0/27.9/32.8), with mean±std over five runs. - The missing: The paper never tests for contamination between the GitHub source pool and GitHub-derived benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified instances are real GitHub issues), and the RL experiment is a single checkpoint with simulated rewards and no repeated seeds — a gap the authors partially acknowledge. - Read it or not: Read it if you build agent harnesses or skill/memory systems and want a scalable alternative to trajectory distillation; skip it if you only want the benchmark numbers, which are unusually favorable and warrant independent replication first.

Non-Obviousness (72) is the driver — source-body-blind reconstruction converts an uncheckable abstraction step into a checkable round-trip consistency problem, a real methodological idea — and Novelty (70) reflects both a new method and a large new resource. However, Rigor (52) is pulled down by the never-tested contamination question (GitHub skill pool vs. GitHub-derived benchmarks), a single-checkpoint RL experiment without seeds, and uncertain baseline fidelity, while Resilience (48) is low because contamination is the first objection an adversarial reviewer would raise and the paper does not address it. Problem & Motivation: Agent harnesses increasingly rely on retrievable skills — reusable procedural knowledge with applicability conditions — as a cheap, plug-and-play complement to model weights. Two existing synthesis routes limit scaling: trajectory-based methods (Trace2Skill, ExpeL, SkillRL) are coupled to the generating agent's competence, task distribution, and harness, and produce nothing before deployment; document-based methods (SKILL.md-style mining) lack executable evidence for grounding. The paper targets teams building agentic systems who want procedural knowledge that is grounded, transferable, and maintainable from day one. The gap closed: a synthesis substrate that requires no prior agent experience yet retains concrete, verifiable implementations — source code from actively maintained repositories. Key Idea: Source-body-blind reconstruction as a grounding filter. Once understood, the approach is reconstructible: abstract a code unit into a structured skill record (applicability, workflow, invariants, failure handling, anti-goals, evidence spans), then ask an LLM to re-implement the unit from the record alone; if the reconstruction matches the original under a source-aware judge, the record's procedural claims are supported by real implementation evidence, otherwise it is adjudicated or rejected. This converts a notoriously uncheckable abstraction step (does the skill actually capture the code?) into a checkable consistency problem. Methodology: Four pipeline stages: (1) candidate selection — parse functions, methods, CLI entry points, and file-level components from 19,769 repositories (>500 stars, scanned through April 2026), then an LLM tagger scores six rubric signals (reusable intent, procedural steps, boundary conditions, transferability, interface sufficiency, non-triviality); (2) extraction into three typed granularities (atomic/composite/pattern) with a strict JSON schema including invariants, error cases, and anti-goals, filtered at skill_value_score < 0.45; (3) verification — reconstructor generates code from the skill JSON alone (interface visible, body hidden), an equivalence judge directly accepts or routes to an adjudicator that distinguishes bad skills from failed reconstructions (Algorithm 1); (4) retrieval — feature tagging into controlled vocabularies plus deterministic purpose clustering (task family/action/target key) that selects representative records without LLM synthesis. Downstream, retrieval is formalized as a rendered context z_t injected at a chosen decision point (Eq. 1). Critical design decisions: three record granularities (justified by evidence-scope analogy to IE and faceted software reuse); human adjudication stage for reconstruction failures (justified by Appendix B showing adjudicated accepts retain 88% description accuracy); summary rendering for retrieval (empirically validated in RQ4). The framework is prompt-pipeline engineering over LLM calls; no explicit training objective except in the RL evaluation section. Key Results: Across 72 protocol-matched comparisons (9 model settings × 8 benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified, BigCodeBench, TerminalBench, LongCLI-Bench, AgentBench-OS, AIME 2026, HMMT 2025, GPQA), skills improve the macro-average from 42.90 to 47.90 (+11.7% relative, +2.26 to +7.39 points per model/mode), winning 57 of 72 and all 9 SWE-bench Verified pairs. RQ2: with DS4-Flash in a shared loop, Code2Skill averages 49.5 vs. 31.0 (Trace2Skill), 27.9 (ExpeL), 32.8 (SkillRL-Bank), exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.6–13.3 points per benchmark and an oracle-best-of-three by 9.5 points. RQ5: in coding RL on a Qwen3-32B SWE-World checkpoint (simulated test-pass rewards, step 150), post-generation review reaches 38% resolve rate vs. 24% no-skill. RQ6: skills from 25 tested AI-generated implementations achieve 93.50% vs. 93.00% from human code on a 400-task LiveCodeBench subset. Human annotation of pipeline outcomes: 92% description accuracy, 80% retention value among accepted records vs. 32%/28% for rejected. RQ4: summary rendering cuts rendered context 88.9% (6,352→707 chars at k=3) with no loss. Baselines include recent (2024–2026) trajectory methods; benchmarks are current. Notably, AgentBench-OS declines for several models (e.g., Qwen3.5-27b no-reasoning 55.56→50.69), and gains on math/reasoning benchmarks are small and sometimes negative. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Code2Skill pipeline with source-body-blind reconstruction as the verification mechanism) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (CodeSkillBank, 1,006,822 provenance-rich skill records). The genuinely novel elements are (a) formulating skill synthesis from repository code as a grounded-abstraction problem and (b) the blind-reconstruction round trip as a scalable, specification-free grounding check — the paper explicitly positions this against test-based verification. The retrieval, tagging, purpose-clustering, and agent-loop integration are competent combinations of known ideas (faceted classification, RAG-style context injection, review loops from Self-Refine/Reflexion); the headline numbers are impressive but the pipeline is assembling existing components around one new verification idea. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: RQ3 (insertion point), RQ4 (depth/rendering/indexing with context-cost accounting), and the outcome-stratified human annotation (Appendix B) that honestly distinguishes direct-accept from adjudicated-accept quality. Error bars: RQ2 reports mean±std over five runs; Table 1 comparisons appear single-run without significance tests; the authors state paired tests are used only when item-level outcomes exist. A website and dataset link appear on the title page, but no concrete repository URL is given in the text; release status of code and the bank itself is Not stated. Methodological concerns: (1) baselines in RQ2 are all built on one model (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) and evaluated only with DS4-Flash; (2) Table 1 uses a randomly sampled 10% retrieval pool — potentially favorable but uncharacterized; (3) the RL experiment is one checkpoint, simulated rewards, no seeds (authors flag this themselves); (4) RQ6 uses only 25 source pairs and 50-skill banks; (5) human annotation sample sizes are not stated in the main text. The protocol-matched design is a genuine strength — changing only skill access — but no independent replication exists. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built data-construction pipeline and resource, evaluated by downstream experiments). Practical: Yes — the pipeline uses LLM calls plus AST parsing and retrieval, all runnable on commercial API/model infrastructure; skills are plain-text context, requiring no model changes. Efficient: Constructing 1M+ records presumably required substantial LLM inference (cost not reported); consumption is cheap — 0.7K-char summaries preserve most utility, an 88.9% context reduction. Effective: Evidence shows gains on coding/SWE/terminal tasks (SWE-bench Verified +7.09 points for GPT-5.2), but math/reasoning gains are small and mixed, so effectiveness on the stated 'agentic procedural knowledge' framing is solid while the broader 'reasoning transfer' claim rests on weaker evidence. Scalable: The bank itself is at 10^6-record scale, but evaluation used a 10% retrieval sample and only ~1M of GitHub's much larger repository space; 10–100× scaling is claimed as a paradigm, not tested. Deliverable: a dataset resource (CodeSkillBank) plus pipeline; artifact availability is indicated but no verifiable URL appears in the text. Strengths: (1) The source-body-blind reconstruction check is a real methodological idea — a specification-free, repository-scale grounding filter that exploits code's round-trip verifiability, with human annotation showing accepted records separate sharply from rejected ones (92% vs. 32% description accuracy). (2) The evaluation design is unusually careful for this genre: protocol-matched pairs isolate skill access, a unified downstream interface enables fair bank-vs-bank comparison, and the outcome-stratified annotation avoids conflating stage effects. (3) The RQ2 result — beating an oracle that picks the best trajectory baseline per benchmark by 9.5 points — is the paper's strongest single piece of evidence that code-derived skills add something trajectories cannot. (4) Provenance-preserving record design (source spans, commit-level evidence, acceptance traces) makes the bank auditable and maintainable, which is what actually matters for long-lived deployment. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: RQ3 does not attribute differences to insertion point alone; purpose indexing has mixed effects and may displace locally relevant candidates; the RL experiment reports a single checkpoint without repeated seeds and 'does not establish differences in learning speed, convergence, or final policy performance'; RQ6's 0.5-point aggregate difference 'does not establish equivalence' between human- and AI-code sources; skills help less on short problems capable models already solve (BigCodeBench); macro-averages are descriptive rather than pooled success rates. They confront these directly, which strengthens credibility. They also explicitly scope reconstruction checking as not a substitute for test-based verification when specifications exist. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Contamination is never discussed: SWE-bench Verified, BigCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench derive from public GitHub repositories, and the skill pool is public GitHub repositories — retrieved skills could encode solutions or issue-specific fixes for evaluation tasks, inflating gains; no de-duplication against benchmark repos is reported. (2) No compute or cost figures for building 1M records, so the 'scalable' claim is unverifiable. (3) RQ2 baselines are built by the authors from published pipelines rather than using released original banks, so baseline fidelity is uncertain. (4) The skill records are LLM-generated natural-language artifacts — LLM-judged acceptance may correlate with LLM-extractable (vs. genuinely reusable) knowledge, and the judge's false-accept rate on adversarial or subtly wrong records is unmeasured. (5) Small per-benchmark task counts in Tables 1–2 (e.g., TerminalBench, LongCLI scores in single digits and moving in 2–15 point jumps) suggest high-variance small-N evaluations for some benchmarks. (6) Only the authors' loop (draft-review-revise) is used for the headline result; generalization to other harnesses is untested. Bottom Line: Practitioners building agent skill or memory systems should read this for the reconstruction-based grounding mechanism and the careful protocol-matched evaluation template, but should treat the benchmark margins — especially SWE-bench — as unreplicated until the contamination question and the bank's release are independently resolved.

#59 — Moderately Innovative (59)

LLaDA2. 2: Enabling Agentic Diffusion Language Models via

L Editing · openreview.net · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds LLaDA2.2, a mixture-of-experts block-diffusion language model that replaces fixed-length token substitution with flexible Levenshtein editing (keep/substitute/delete/insert), extends context to 128K tokens, adds block-level MoE routing for inference efficiency, and trains with an agentic RL algorithm (L-EBPO) that optimizes editing decisions from environmental rewards. - Why it's important: Diffusion LMs' block-parallel decoding makes them brittle in multi-turn, long-horizon agentic workflows where early decoding errors corrupt the task state and cascade; fixing this without sacrificing the ~1.6× decoding speedup over autoregressive models is the central open question for practical dLLM agents. - How it does it: The core trick is supervising the diffusion denoiser with edit labels derived from longest-common-subsequence alignment between intermediate drafts and ground truth, then extending the RL action space from vocabulary tokens to V ∪ {DELETE, INSERT} so trajectory-level policy optimization flows through structural edit decisions. - The good: A controlled ablation isolates the effect of Levenshtein editing on identical SWE trajectories and shows SWE-bench Verified improving from 35.8 to 44.4 (+8.6 points), directly supporting the central claim. - The missing: L-EBPO itself is never ablated — there is no comparison of RL-with-editing against SFT-with-editing or against standard EBPO on the agentic suite, so the contribution of the RL algorithm (the paper's second headline component) is unevaluated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building diffusion LM agents or MoE inference infrastructure; skip if you want evidence that dLLMs now match autoregressive agents — the paper shows a 1.91-point average deficit on agentic benchmarks and a 9-point deficit on general ones.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Rigor (52) is the main drag: the headline RL contribution (L-EBPO) is never ablated, block-routing and context-extension effects are unquantified, there are no error bars, and the numbers are effectively vendor self-reports from an anonymous industrial paper with no released weights or code. Novelty (60) and Non-Obviousness (58) are moderate — Levenshtein editing into block diffusion is a competent integration of known components, with the controlled +8.6 SWE-bench ablation as the one genuinely convincing causal result. Problem & Motivation: Diffusion language models decode blocks of tokens in parallel, which reduces sequential latency but creates two failure modes in agentic settings. First, structural rigidity: LLaDA2.1's token-to-token (T2T) editing fixes output length, so n-gram repetitions, malformed JSON, and merged tool-call boundaries cannot be repaired by insertion or deletion. Second, error accumulation: in multi-turn tool use, erroneous tokens from early blocks become hard context for later blocks, corrupting the task state and causing goal drift — a failure mode the authors argue is worse for block diffusion than for autoregressive models, which can self-correct via sequential conditioning. The intended audience is anyone deploying dLLMs as autonomous agents over 128K-token, multi-turn interaction histories. Key Idea: Supervise block-diffusion denoising as a Levenshtein edit prediction problem: compute the LCS between the model's current draft and the target, use matched anchors as KEEP labels, and assign SUBSTITUTE/DELETE/INSERT to gaps, so the diffusion process can change sequence length during parallel decoding while keeping block size fixed (deletions left-shift; insertions expand a position into [MASK] + token and the block is re-padded or truncated to m positions). The same LCS machinery recovers transient edit tokens during RL likelihood estimation, unifying token prediction and editing in one ELBO-based policy-gradient objective (L-EBPO). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages from the LLaDA2.1 base model. (1) Continued pre-training: progressive context extension from 8K to 64K (300B tokens) then 128K (200B tokens) with document-aware packing, and a switch from token-level to block-level MoE routing — a block-level admission score g_j = max_i s_{i,j} admits the top-C of E=256 experts (C=48), after which token-wise top-k routing operates only within the admitted pool, bounding the active expert footprint at O(C) instead of min(B·k, E). (2) SFT with Levenshtein editing using the LCS-derived labels over four operations. (3) Agentic RL (L-EBPO): a two-level control formulation (trajectory-level EBPO plus intra-block splice editing) with an extended action space, log-ratio estimated over block actions via an ELBO approximation; rewards sum tool-call execution correctness, format validity, and task completion; infrastructure uses ASystem for orchestration, SGLang for rollouts, and AKernel sandboxes, with asynchronous training. Critical design decisions: the fixed-length block constraint (justified as necessary for batching, but it forces multi-round insertions); the max-based token racing rule for expert admission (motivated by an empirical observation that expert preferences concentrate within blocks, but with no quantitative supporting figure in the paper); and one-insert-per-gap-per-round (a practical compromise, acknowledged implicitly via the asymmetry discussion). Key Results: On 7 agentic benchmarks, LLaDA2.2-flash averages 53.83 vs 55.74 for the autoregressive Ling-2.6-flash baseline (−1.91), winning on τ²-Bench (80.33 vs 76.36), PinchBench (81.66 vs 81.30), and MCP-Atlas (46.21 vs 41.12), but losing 11.92 points on SWE-bench Verified (49.28 vs 61.20 — though with a disclosed scaffold mismatch: Claude Code vs OpenHands) and 8.73 on SWE-bench Multilingual. On 10 general benchmarks it averages 56.81 vs 65.90 for Ling-2.6-flash and 59.23 for the prior LLaDA2.1-flash; it beats Ling-2.6-flash only on LongBench v2 (45.13 vs 42.94) and regresses relative to LLaDA2.1 on AIME 2026 (74.01→62.24), GPQA-Diamond (67.30→48.67), LiveCodeBench (45.37→44.77), and IFBench (37.07→30.20). Throughput across 11 workloads averages 1.64× Ling-2.6-flash in BF16 (Ling's MTP enabled with 4 draft tokens), with FP8 quantization adding 18.6%. The ablation attributing +8.6 points on SWE-bench Verified to Levenshtein editing is the cleanest causal result. The baseline (Ling-2.6-flash, same lab's contemporaneous AR model) is current rather than outdated, and testing at 128K context with repository-level tasks is genuine stress-scale evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (integrating Levenshtein editing — keep/substitute/delete/insert with LCS-derived labels — into block-diffusion denoising) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the +8.6-point SWE-bench effect of length-changing edits), plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (block routing for MoE block diffusion, and the 128K context extension). The constituent ideas are all established: Levenshtein/insertion editing dates to Stern et al. 2019 and Gu et al. 2019 (Levenshtein Transformer), EBPO is inherited from LLaDA2.1, and expert-pool restriction is a known MoE efficiency pattern. The genuine novelty is the integration into the block-diffusion denoising loop and the edit-aware extension of the RL action space; L-EBPO is an incremental modification of existing dLLM RL rather than a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: One clean ablation exists (Levenshtein editing on/off, same base model, same SWE trajectories), but it covers a single benchmark, and no ablation isolates L-EBPO, block routing (quality effect described only as "little to no degradation" with no numbers), or the context-extension schedule. SWE-bench series scores are arithmetic means of 5 runs, but no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear anywhere. No code, weights, or data release is mentioned; the paper is anonymous under TMLR review, but references to Ant Group infrastructure (ASystem, AKernel, SGLang day-0 support) mark it as an internal industrial report, so the numbers are effectively vendor self-reports. Methodological flags: the headline SWE-bench Verified comparison mixes evaluation scaffolds (disclosed, but it makes the 11.92-point gap uninterpretable); the agentic RL is trained and evaluated on overlapping tool-use-style task distributions; and the throughput comparison depends on configuration choices (MTP draft-token count for the baseline) that are stated but not swept. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL (a built model with deployment-oriented evaluation, not a proof paper). Practical: Runs on commercial infrastructure — the paper reports BF16 and FP8 inference via SGLang, implying standard serving stacks. Efficient: 1.64× average throughput advantage over the AR baseline in BF16 (e.g., 703.82 vs 331.5 TPS on BFCL-v4), and block routing bounds expert memory traffic at O(C) experts per block; however, the latency cost of multi-round edit refinement is not decomposed. Effective: The evidence supports competitive interactive tool-use performance and faster decoding, but not parity on the hardest long-horizon tasks (SWE-bench Verified 49.28 vs 61.20) — the paper solves the speed problem more convincingly than the reliability problem. Scalable: 128K context and trillion-parameter-adjacent infrastructure are tested, but the paper only claims, and does not measure, behavior at longer horizons or more turns than the benchmark suite covers. The work stops at paper form: no public weights, code, or dataset artifact is stated. Strengths: - The LCS-based label construction is a concrete, reproducible mechanism that converts an arbitrary draft into edit supervision without changing block length — a genuinely reusable recipe for masked-diffusion post-training. - The controlled SWE-trajectory ablation (+8.6 points from enabling insertions/deletions) is the kind of isolation rarely found in industrial model reports, and it directly implicates the mechanism rather than scale. - Block routing is a well-motivated systems contribution: identifying that per-token top-k routing in a block makes the expert working set the union of B token choices, then bounding it via block-level admission, is a real diagnosis of a bottleneck specific to MoE dLLMs. - The limitations section is unusually candid, naming the local-consistency problem of parallel decoding, the DELETE/INSERT learnability asymmetry, and the ELBO-vs-confidence-decoding and MoE train-inference discrepancies that the method does not solve. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that Levenshtein editing only partially repairs structural errors (parallel positions cannot condition on each other, so nested JSON, SQL, and multi-argument tool calls remain error-prone); that DELETE is easier to learn than INSERT, making missing-content repair harder than redundancy removal; that uncorrected errors still compound into goal drift; that ELBO-based likelihood estimation is a proxy with train-inference mismatch (including MoE routing discrepancy); and that data-mixing/curriculum strategy for agentic vs general corpora is unresolved. They also disclose the SWE-bench scaffold mismatch in a footnote and flag general-capability regressions explicitly in the results discussion. This is a direct, non-defensive limitations section — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation of L-EBPO against (a) SFT-only editing or (b) plain EBPO without the edit action space — the RL contribution is asserted, not demonstrated, and Figure 4 conflates the SFT editing mechanism's effect with the full pipeline. - No ablation quantifying block routing's quality or throughput contribution separately; the claimed efficiency win is entangled with the 128K extension and FP8 quantization in Table 3. - Missing baselines among other dLLM agents or edit-capable models (e.g., non-LLaDA diffusion baselines), so all comparisons are within the same lab's model family. - The throughput advantage is measured only against Ling-2.6-flash with a specific MTP configuration; no sweep over the baseline's decoding settings. - Reward hacking risk in the three-component additive reward (correctness + format + completion) is not discussed, and no reward-component ablation is provided. - Whether the claimed "reasoning-path collapse" diagnosis (Challenge I, citing Ni et al. 2026) is actually mitigated is never measured — the paper motivates the method with this failure mode but reports no metric on it. - No contamination analysis for the SWE-bench family, despite repository-level code being a stated component of the continued-pre-training mixture. Bottom Line: A credible, honestly-reported industrial systems paper that demonstrates Levenshtein editing is a real win for block-diffusion agents and delivers a measured 1.64× throughput advantage, but its RL component is under-evaluated and the model still trails its autoregressive sibling on both agentic and general quality — read it for the editing and routing machinery, not as evidence that dLLMs have closed the agentic gap.

A Matter of Perspective: Case Notion Selection for Object-Centric Performance Analysis

JN van Detten, P Schumacher, SJJ Leemans · leemans.ch · business process mining or process mining - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces a semi-automatic framework that selects a case notion for object-centric event logs by approximating the case notion that maximizes a chosen distribution property (standard deviation, skewness, or kurtosis) of a chosen performance measure (cycle time, resource usage, or cost). - Why it's important: Object-centric logs admit exponentially many possible case notions, and practitioners currently have no automated guidance on which grouping of objects/events yields performance insights — the choice drastically changes analytical results. - How it does it: It restricts case notions to a two-part specification (a starting object type plus a set of allowed directed relations between object types and activities) and greedily expands relation edges in a type-activity graph, at each step keeping the edge expansion that most increases the target distribution property, reducing an exponential search to a polynomial greedy pass. - The good: Across 10 public OCEL logs and all 9 measure/property combinations, the framework's case notion always matched or exceeded the best value achievable by brute-force selection among existing case notions (traditional flattening, connected components, advanced notions), at feasible runtime (mean 735s, range 7s–3156s). - The missing: There is no evidence that maximizing a distribution property produces case notions that are semantically meaningful or actionable — no human evaluation, no ground-truth process knowledge, and no comparison against instance-level or view-based alternatives; the 'interestingness' of the resulting insights is asserted, not measured. - Read it or not: Worth reading for object-centric process mining researchers and tool builders wrestling with case notion selection; skippable for anyone outside process mining, since the contribution is a domain-specific greedy heuristic with modest formal depth.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (65) is the standout — framing case notion selection as optimization of a performance-distribution property is a genuine new problem formulation connecting previously parallel literatures. Rigor (60) is solid within scope: an exhaustive brute-force baseline over all existing case notions and starting types across 10 public logs, deterministic algorithm, and public code, but reduced by missing adjacent baselines it cites, the unproven complexity claim deferred to a repository, and preprint status. Resilience (50) is the main drag: the entire effectiveness argument rests on the unvalidated assumption that maximizing dispersion yields actionable insights, and the paper does not report case-count/size statistics despite having observed the degenerate mega-case pathology in its own connected-components baseline. Completeness (55) benefits from candid design-trade-off acknowledgment, while Impact (50) reflects a usable public implementation for a narrow practitioner community. Problem & Motivation: In object-centric process mining, event logs capture interactions among multiple typed business objects (orders, items, deliveries, etc.), and any performance analysis (cycle time, cost, resource usage) depends on deciding which subset of objects and events constitutes one process execution — the case notion. Unlike the classical single-object case, object-centric logs allow exponentially many case notions (the number grows with object types and activity-relation combinations), and the resulting performance distributions differ drastically across choices. Prior work offers fixed case notions (flattening per type, connected components, complexity-guided advanced notions) but nothing that selects a case notion aligned with a performance-analysis goal. The authors — affiliated with RWTH Aachen and process mining vendor Celonis — target practitioners who must pick a case notion without exhaustive domain knowledge or manual trial and error. Key Idea: Formulate case notion selection as an optimization problem — maximize a chosen distribution property of a performance measure over all case notion specifications — and make it tractable by (a) restricting case notions to a compact specification space of one starting type plus type-activity-level relation sets, and (b) greedily growing the relation set from each candidate starting type, accepting only node expansions that increase the property. The core move is reifying a case notion as a set of edges in a type-activity graph, turning case notion search into a feature-subset-style greedy hill climb. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Specification: a case notion is a tuple (start, rel) with start ⊆ object types and rel ⊆ relations between object types and activities; cases are extracted by initializing from an unassigned object of the starting type and iteratively pulling in objects/events connected via allowed relation types until fixpoint (Definitions 1–3; Equations 1–3). (2) Optimization: the objective is arg max over specifications of the distribution property σ/γ₁/γ₂ of performance measure p across resulting cases (Equation 4); exact search is exponential, so a greedy approximation (Algorithm 1) starts each candidate object type with only its outgoing relations, iteratively adds the full outgoing edge set of the neighbor node yielding the largest property increase, stops when no improvement exists, and returns the best specification over all starting nodes. (3) Evaluation: runtime measurement and comparison against brute-force over existing case notions on 10 public logs. Three critical design decisions: (a) type-activity-level relation consistency (all instances treated uniformly) — justified by analogy to relational database extraction but admittedly discards instance-level nuances; (b) all-or-nothing node expansion (no per-node subset selection) — justified purely by runtime, explicitly trading optimality for polynomial complexity; (c) local-optimality-only guarantee — the authors are upfront that the greedy result is not globally optimal. The paper states (in an extended report in the accompanying repository) that the algorithm runs in polynomial time. Key Results: Evaluated on 10 public object-centric logs from the OCEL library (532 to 23,771 objects; 1,798 to 38,528 events; 3 to 12 object types). Runtime averaged 735 seconds per log across all measure/property combinations (min 7s on Github, max ~3,156s on Production) on an Intel Core i9-13980HX with 64GB RAM. Against a brute-force selection over traditional flattening [1], connected components [3], and advanced case notions [8] — testing all possible starting types for the latter two — the proposed approach achieved equal or higher values of the target distribution property in all logs, performance measures, and distribution properties; detailed plots show cycle-time standard deviation (log scale), with the other eight combinations reported as consistent and placed in the repository. Two notable empirical observations: the starting-type choice for traditional/advanced notions has large impact on results, and the connected-components notion collapses into a single case on half of the logs due to high connectivity. Baselines are the current state of the object-centric case notion literature (2022–2025 work), so the comparison set is appropriate for the subfield, though all baselines are from the same research group's line of work or direct predecessors. No significance testing or multiple-run variance is reported (the algorithm appears deterministic, making this less of a concern). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD: the genuine novelty is framing case notion selection as optimization of a distribution property of a performance measure — prior work optimized case notions for complexity, correctness, or representativeness in exploratory analysis, not for performance-distribution interestingness. The mechanism itself (greedy expansion over a typed relation graph with a monotone-ish proxy objective) is a standard combinatorial heuristic applied to a new problem; the case extraction semantics and the specification language build directly on the authors' own prior advanced case notion framework [8]. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation is honest about what it measures: runtime feasibility and property values relative to existing case notions — not that the identified case notions yield correct or useful process insights. There is no ablation isolating which components of the specification language matter, though the greedy-per-node restriction is itself an acknowledged ablation of the full search space. The deterministic algorithm and the exhaustive brute-force baseline make the 'equal or better everywhere' claim credible within its scope, but the baseline set is small (three families of prior case notions) and omits alternative optimization approaches (e.g., the view-materialization approach of Basmer et al. [6] or per-type flattening combinations from Estrada-Torres et al. [9], which the related work distinguishes but does not empirically compare against). Code and the extended report are publicly released at https://github.com/Nik314/CaseNotionPeformance (note the URL typo 'Peformance' as printed). Concern: the paper is a short-format workshop-style paper (with the 2026 version citing 2025 work), likely a preprint/early version; the polynomial-complexity claim is deferred to the repository rather than proven in the paper. A subtler concern: maximizing standard deviation, skewness, or kurtosis is a proxy that could be gamed by degenerate case notions (e.g., few huge, highly connected cases), and the paper does not check for or report case-count/size statistics of the winning notions. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor via the released implementation). Practical: Yes — it runs on a consumer laptop CPU (i9, 64GB RAM), no specialized hardware. Efficient: 7s–3,156s per log per configuration is acceptable for offline analysis but not interactive; cost grows polynomially in types/activities per the authors' claim, though the per-iteration case-extraction cost on large logs is not broken out. Effective: The evidence shows it maximizes the chosen distribution property better than existing case notions — a proxy; whether the resulting case notions solve the practitioner's actual analysis problem is untested. Scalable: Only claimed via the polynomial complexity argument; largest tested log has ~38.5K events, so 10×–100× industrial-scale logs (millions of events) are untested, and iterative re-extraction of cases at each greedy step could become the bottleneck. Deliverable: a public implementation plus extended report; no trained model or library-grade artifact. Strengths: - First formulation of case notion selection as optimization of a performance-distribution property — a well-motivated reframing that connects case notion literature to performance indicator literature, which previously developed in parallel. - Clean, formally specified case notion language (Definition 3) that makes the search space explicit and reproducible, with correctness of the extraction procedure clearly stated. - Exhaustive-baseline evaluation design: comparing against the brute-force best over all existing case notions and all starting types is a stronger and fairer test than comparing against a single default; the 'equal or better in all 90 combinations' result is a solid empirical claim within that scope. - Candid identification of the two approximation sacrifices (type-level consistency, no per-node subsets) with reasoned justification for each. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (1) only local, not global, optimality from the greedy strategy; (2) the enforced type-activity-level consistency, conceding that better case notions may exist at the instance level; (3) omission of per-node relation-subset selection for runtime feasibility; and (4) intention to quantify the optimality gap and provide domain guidance on distribution-property selection in future work. They confront these directly and frame them as deliberate design trade-offs — a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge any concern about whether maximizing distribution properties yields practically useful case notions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human or domain evaluation: the entire effectiveness argument rests on the assumption that a higher standard deviation/skewness/kurtosis equals a more 'interesting' or actionable analysis, which is never validated with a practitioner study or a case where the discovered case notion led to a real insight. - No reporting of the structural statistics (number of cases, case sizes, objects-per-case) of the winning case notions — maximizing spread could be driven by degenerate groupings (e.g., a single mega-case), and the paper does not rule this out despite observing exactly this pathology in the connected-components baseline. - Missing baselines from adjacent work it cites: the view-based optimization of [6] and the flattening-combination performance measures of [9] are discussed as alternatives but not run. - The complexity proof and eight of nine result plots live only in the external repository, so the paper itself under-evidences its central tractability claim. - Single testbed of small-to-medium public OCEL logs; no industrial-scale or proprietary-log validation despite the Celonis affiliation, and no exploration of how noisy or sparse O2O relations affect the greedy choices. - No seeds/variance discussion — likely fine given determinism, but unstated. Bottom Line: For researchers and tool builders in object-centric process mining, this is a worthwhile read as the first concrete, reproducible step toward goal-driven case notion selection — but the field still lacks evidence that optimizing distribution properties produces case notions practitioners would actually trust, so treat it as a promising formulation, not a solved problem.

CodeMidas: Scaling Agentic Coding RL Environments from Code Itself (88 ▲ )

Bowen Ye, Lei Li, Shicheng Li, Zihao Yue, Linghao Zhang, Hanglong Lv, Yuanxin Liu, Wenhan Ma, Hao Tian, Rang Li, Jinhao Dong, Yikai Zhao, Xiangwei Deng, Hailin Zhang, Liang Zhao, Qi Liu, Lingpeng Kong, Tong Yang, Fuli Luo · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CodeMidas, an agentic pipeline that converts implemented functionality in existing open-source codebases into executable reinforcement-learning environments for coding agents, using source code as its only task-specific input, and releases a 5,545-task training dataset. - Why it's important: Prior environment-construction pipelines are bottlenecked by development artifacts (issues, PRs, commits, pre-existing tests, documentation), so the supply of verifiable coding RL tasks is limited; decoupling task creation from these artifacts unlocks the entire open-source code corpus as training data. - How it does it: Agents explore a codebase to identify implemented functionality, delete the core implementation to create a development starting point, generate tests whose expected outputs are grounded in executing the original reference code, then filter tasks via leakage probes, solution-vs-verifier agreement audits, and mixed-outcome rollout filtering. - The good: The quality-vs-scale ablation is the strongest evidence: a filtered 3k-task pool beats an unfiltered 8k pool on all three reported evaluations (e.g., DeepSWE 19.05 vs 17.11), directly showing that environment reliability matters more than raw task count. - The missing: All results come from training exactly one model (MiMo-V2.5) with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests on headline benchmark numbers, and no public release of the dataset, code, or pipeline is mentioned anywhere in the paper. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building coding-RL data pipelines or test-oracle synthesis — the four-stage filtering funnel and execution-grounded test construction are directly reusable — but skippable if you only want new RL algorithms, since the training method is vanilla GRPO.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is dragged down primarily by Rigor (55) and Impact (45): headline benchmark gains have no seeds or error bars, only one author-owned model is trained, no data-source baseline (SWE-rebench, R2E-Gym) is compared head-to-head, and — critically — the 5,545-task dataset that is the paper's principal artifact is not released. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (62) are solid, as execution-grounded test oracles plus rollout-based verifier auditing is a genuinely useful advance in task-supply decoupling, and the quality-beats-scale ablation is well controlled. Completeness (55) and Resilience (55) suffer from the missing external baseline and bundled filtering ablation, leaving the central 'source code is a better substrate' claim supported only by absolute gains. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*45 = 58.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training agentic coding models with RL need large, diverse sets of tasks with reliable, executable verifiers. Existing pipelines derive tasks from development records: issues, PRs, and commits (SWE-rebench V2, SWE-Universe, R2E-Gym), fault synthesis around existing tests (SWE-smith, SWE-Flow, SWE-Hub), or documentation and docstrings (R2E, MindForge). Each of these input requirements caps task supply at the coverage of recorded changes, tests, or docs, and favors 1–11 languages. The gap CodeMidas targets: construct verifiable tasks from any implemented functionality, independent of whether the codebase has issues, tests, or documentation, across many languages. Key Idea: The core trick is execution-grounded specification: the original, working implementation serves simultaneously as (a) the latent task specification — agents observe its behavior to write a behavioral statement — and (b) the test oracle, since running the reference code on chosen inputs yields expected outputs without any human annotation. Combined with post-rollout filtering that uses agent rollouts themselves as a verifier-quality probe (leakage exploits, false-positive/false-negative audits, mixed-outcome retention), this makes the codebase itself the sole task-specific input. Methodology: Four-stage pipeline. (1) Task design: an agent inspects codebase structure, identifies functionality with public entry points and observable outcomes (CLI tools, pure functions, stateful APIs), removes the core implementation, and adapts the remainder into a coherent starting point; the task statement specifies inputs, observable behavior, and required interfaces while leaving internals free; the original code is kept as a reference solution. (2) Test construction: an agent maps behavioral requirements to test inputs and boundary cases, records reference-execution outputs as assertions, then reviews every assertion for restrictions unsupported by the statement (exact wording, incidental ordering, internal structure) and replaces them with behavioral checks; tasks whose assertions depend on private symbols without substitutes are rejected. (3) Environment preparation: containerized environments are cleaned of artifacts that could leak the solution (compiled outputs, caches, construction-agent files, original tests); execution consistency requires 2/2 starting-state runs to fail and 4/4 reference runs to pass in fresh containers. (4) Post-rollout filtering: adversarial rollouts search for exploitable leakage; four solution attempts per task are audited by a reviewing agent against the verifier (flagging verifier false positives/negatives); a frontier model's rollout outcomes are used to drop all-pass or all-fail tasks. Training is GRPO on MiMo-V2.5 with binary execution rewards, batch size 32, 32 rollouts per task, max response 516,096 tokens, max 500 turns. Critical design decisions: (i) grounding expected outputs in reference execution rather than model imagination — well-motivated by prior work on bad test oracles (EvalPlus, PatchDiff) though not ablated in isolation; (ii) mixed-outcome rollout filtering, which conflates task difficulty with defects — acknowledged but not disentangled; (iii) heavy funnel-based rejection (22,575 → 5,545 tasks, ~75% discarded) — justified by the 5k-vs-8k ablation. Key Results: The pipeline retains 5,545 tasks from 3,185 codebases (funnel: 22,575 → 5,545), spanning 23 languages (Python 21.4%, TypeScript 18.3%, Go 16.2%) and 15 domains; median reference patch is 142 lines (IQR 66–305), with 65.9% of patches touching ≥2 files. Training MiMo-V2.5 with GRPO improves all five external benchmarks: SWE-bench Pro 50.3→54.4 (+4.1 pp), DeepSWE v1.1 10.0→21.7 (+11.7 pp), ProgramBench Almost Solved 4.5→21.5 (+17.0), RepoZero C2Rust 40.5→51.8 (+11.3 pp), Terminal-Bench v2.1 63.7→72.2 (+8.5 pp). On the held-out CodeMidas Val (200 tasks, 3 attempts), pass rate rises 35.0→44.7. Scale ablation: high-quality 1k/3k/5k pools yield DeepSWE 17.57/19.05/21.70, with the 5k pool leading from checkpoint 40 onward; the unfiltered vanilla 8k pool scores 17.11 on DeepSWE, below even the 3k pool. Behavioral analysis: pre-edit read/search calls rise 27.2→40.1, drafting ratio 0.358→0.629, distinct self-verification commands 2.03→2.53 during training; agent-written checks correlate with +4.2 pp pass rate (95% CI: 1.8–6.6, task-level bootstrap). Baselines are the model's own initial policy rather than competing environment pipelines — a notable weakness: no comparison against training on SWE-rebench V2, R2E-Gym, or SWE-smith data. Tested at a mid scale (5.5k tasks, one ~frontier-candidate model), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel element is the combination of behavioral-specification extraction and reference-execution-grounded test oracles requiring no development artifacts, plus the agent-rollout-based verifier auditing (leakage probes and FN/FP solution reviews). The training recipe (GRPO, binary test rewards) is standard; the idea of synthesizing tests to validate solutions builds on CodeT and AceCoder; the filtering philosophy extends known oracle-problem concerns into an operational pipeline. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for scale (1k/3k/5k) and quality (5k filtered vs 8k unfiltered with identical training config, evaluated over the same checkpoint range), which is the paper's strongest methodological asset. Execution consistency is checked with 6 fresh containers per task. However: no multiple seeds or error bars for the five headline benchmark numbers; the behavioral-analysis CIs are bootstrap-based, but the main results have no uncertainty quantification. No code, dataset, or model release URL is stated anywhere in the paper — a major reproducibility gap for a paper whose contribution is a pipeline and dataset. Concerns: (i) the only trained model is the authors' own MiMo-V2.5, so generality across base models is untested; (ii) the paper evaluates against the initial policy only, never against alternative data sources, so the claim that source-derived tasks are the right substrate is supported only by absolute gains; (iii) the frontier model used for rollout-outcome filtering is unnamed, obscuring cost and potential train/test contamination; (iv) the authors state they verified the training set is disjoint from all five benchmarks, which addresses Goodhart-style contamination. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a pipeline that is built, run, and evaluated end-to-end, plus a dataset artifact). - Practical: Yes in principle — the pipeline uses general-purpose agents and containerized environments on standard infrastructure, but no artifact is released, so reproduction requires rebuilding it from the paper's description. - Efficient: Not stated — the paper never reports the agent compute, API cost, or wall-clock time to construct environments, though the ~75% rejection funnel implies substantial per-task agent spend. - Effective: Yes for the stated goal — consistent gains on five held-out, disjoint benchmarks spanning four task families, plus behavioral evidence of generalization, go beyond a single proxy. - Scalable: Only claimed via the 1k→3k→5.5k trend, which is a genuine measured trend but covers well under 10× the tested scale; cost of the agentic construction funnel at 100× is unexamined. Deliverable: a dataset and methodology in paper form; no software artifact, library, or released model checkpoint is mentioned. Strengths: - Removing all development-artifact dependencies (issues, PRs, commits, tests, docs) is a real advance in task-supply decoupling, substantiated by the Table 1 comparison showing 23-language coverage versus 1–20 for seven prior pipelines. - The 5k-filtered-beats-8k-unfiltered result is a clean, well-controlled experiment (identical training configuration and checkpoint range) that quantifies the value of verifier quality — a finding the field routinely asserts but rarely measures. - The post-rollout filtering suite (adversarial leakage probes, FN/FP solution audits against a reviewing agent, mixed-outcome retention) operationalizes the test-oracle problem into a concrete, executable quality gate; this is the most transferable technical content. - Behavioral analysis connecting RL to more exploration and self-verification, with a measured +4.2 pp (CI 1.8–6.6) association between agent-written checks and success, adds mechanistic evidence beyond benchmark deltas. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that all-pass/all-fail rollout outcomes are ambiguous ("do not reveal the cause" — could be difficulty or defects), and that filtering may therefore discard hard-but-valid tasks. They also implicitly bound their claims by noting the ambiguity of leakage filtering and by carefully scoping conclusions to the tested model and benchmarks. They do not include a dedicated limitations section; limitation discussion is distributed and brief, which slightly understates rather than confronts scope boundaries. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No cross-model validation: only MiMo-V2.5 is trained, so it is unknown whether the gains reflect the environments or a favorable interaction with the authors' own model; a second open-weight base model would materially strengthen the claim. - No data-source baseline: the paper never trains on an equal-sized pool from SWE-rebench V2, R2E-Gym, or SWE-smith, so the central claim — that source code is a better foundation than development artifacts — is supported by absolute improvements only, not by a head-to-head comparison. - No per-stage ablation of the filtering funnel: the 8k-vs-5k comparison bundles environment cleaning, execution consistency, and all three post-rollout filters into one condition, so the marginal value of each filter is unknown. - No release of the dataset, pipeline code, or constructed environments despite the dataset being the paper's principal artifact; "5,545 tasks" cannot be independently inspected. - The construction and filtering agents' identity, scale, and cost are undisclosed, making the pipeline's economics and reproducibility unverifiable. - Reward-hacking dynamics: with agent-authored tests and adversarial filtering, residual verifier imperfection is likely; the paper does not measure the false-positive rate of the final retained verifiers (only that flagged tasks were removed). Bottom Line: For practitioners building coding-RL data flywheels, this is one of the more substantive recent contributions — the artifact-free task construction and rollout-based verifier auditing are worth adopting regardless of model choice — but the absence of released data/code, a data-source baseline, and multi-model validation means it establishes a promising direction rather than a settled result.
