Knowledge-Graph-Augmented Chronos-2 for HEC-RAS Surrogate Forecasting

E Holmberg, E Ioup, M Abdelguerfi · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces KG-Chronos-2, a surrogate forecasting system that couples a frozen Chronos-2 time-series foundation model with a hydraulic knowledge graph (graph-conditioned historical retrieval and input-aligned residual correction) to predict 24-hour water-surface elevation fields from HEC-RAS simulations. - Why it's important: Numerical HEC-RAS time stepping is computationally expensive, and fast surrogates for near-term river forecasting would let practitioners bypass the solver over the forecast horizon; the paper targets whether foundation models plus project knowledge beat locally trained hydraulic surrogates. - How it does it: It forecasts low-rank WSE increments with frozen Chronos-2 over a PCA latent space, fuses the decoded trajectory with graph-conditioned historical analogs retrieved from a 2008 source simulation, and applies a lead-specific ridge correction gated by out-of-fold improvement, all anchored to the exact current WSE field. - The good: A direct paired hierarchical-bootstrap comparison against frozen Chronos-2 (10,000 replicates) shows a statistically supported 14.13% event-balanced RMSE reduction (difference −0.040643, 95% CI [−0.075177, −0.016317]) on the same frozen backbone, cleanly isolating the knowledge-coupling layer's value. - The missing: All evaluation is on two events (2002, 2011) from the same HEC-RAS project and geometry used for development, the authors themselves revisited these events during development, and the planned Moirai baseline failed to run — so transfer to new projects, geometries, or events is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in physics-solver surrogating and retrieval-augmented time-series forecasting who want a concrete, honestly-evaluated recipe for adapting frozen foundation models to a hydraulic domain; skippable for general ML readers since the techniques are domain-specific recombinations.

Rigor (60) shows real statistical care (10,000-replicate hierarchical bootstrap, seed-variance baselines) but only two evaluation events make the bootstrap fragile, and there is no component ablation of the KG layer. Resilience (58) drops under the closed evaluation lineage of self-overlapping authorship and the extreme-error tradeoff versus persistence. Problem & Motivation: HEC-RAS computes river hydraulics (water-surface elevation, WSE) from project geometry, cross sections, structures, and boundary conditions via numerical time stepping, which is expensive; data-driven surrogates can predict the next 24 hours of WSE at 4,675 cross sections from an available state history and prescribed inputs, bypassing the solver. Prior approaches in this line of work are locally trained neural operators (recurrent GeoFNO) or equation-informed networks; the gap addressed is whether a pretrained time-series foundation model, connected to native hydraulic project knowledge (reach relationships, hydraulic attributes, input schedules), improves on both frozen baselines and locally trained temporal/graph-recurrent surrogates in a "warm-start state continuation" setting. Key Idea: Decompose forecasting into (a) a frozen temporal predictor over a latent PCA representation of WSE increments with exact-state decoding (the current field bypasses the latent bottleneck, preserving full state fidelity), and (b) a project-knowledge layer — reach graph, 14 static hydraulic descriptors, and input-to-reach mappings — that selects historical analog windows and drives a gated per-lead ridge residual correction, so all project-specific learning concentrates outside the pretrained weights. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Frozen Chronos-2 forecasting: hourly WSE increments are standardized by a diagonal scale matrix, projected via incremental PCA onto K=256 loadings; one multivariate task with 512 increments is submitted per origin, and the latent median forecast is decoded back and integrated from the exact current field (Eqs. 1–3). (2) Graph-conditioned retrieval: a reach graph (71 reaches, 58 directed adjacency entries, hydraulically reweighted by a Gaussian kernel over 14 standardized descriptors per Eq. 4) conditions an 8-nearest-neighbor Euclidean search over 2,353 source-simulation origins with 8 state descriptors per reach; inverse-distance-weighted analog increments, scaled by an activity-ratio clipped to [0.5, 2], are integrated into an analog forecast fused with the Chronos forecast via per-reach coefficients α_r (Eq. 5). (3) Input-aligned residual correction: cross-correlation over lags 0–168h aligns seven input channels to receiving reaches; a 35-feature ridge model per lead predicts mean reach error, applied through a source-calibrated gate (Eq. 8) with global scale η=0.75, active on 27.35% of reach–lead pairs. Critical design decisions: exact-state anchoring (justified by construction and ablatable), frozen backbone (justified by the shared-backbone comparison design), and fixed calibration gates applied unmodified at evaluation (acknowledged as potentially optimistic). Evaluation uses 64 fixed 24-hour windows (32 each from 2011 and 2002 simulations), event-balanced RMSE averaged over two events, and a hierarchical event/window bootstrap for the paired Chronos comparison. Key Results: KG-Chronos-2 achieves event-balanced RMSE 0.246970 in native WSE units — the lowest of six systems — versus frozen Chronos-2 at 0.287613 (−14.13%), hydraulic DCRNN-style at 0.349729±0.0125 over three seeds (−29.38%), recurrent GeoFNO at 0.408510 (−39.54%), residual LSTM at 0.483055±0.005266, and persistence at 0.492611 (−49.87%). The paired bootstrap interval for the KG-minus-Chronos difference is [−0.075177, −0.016317]; active-window RMSE is 0.351510 vs. 0.431725 for frozen Chronos (−18.58%, CI [−0.161499, −0.018025]), and lead-24 RMSE is 0.434783 vs. 0.493318 (−11.87%). Notably, a pretrained frozen Chronos-2 beats the locally trained DCRNN-style model by 17.76% and GeoFNO by ~30%, an instructive finding in itself; the LSTM barely beats persistence on RMSE (−1.94%) while worsening MAE. The authors report mean per-event maximum absolute errors of 18.20 (KG) vs. 17.49 (persistence), revealing a large extreme-error tradeoff hidden by aggregate RMSE. The planned Moirai baseline failed during environment creation and is excluded — six, not seven, systems completed. The benchmark is a single HEC-RAS project at standard scale (122M WSE values, 8,737 hourly frames per event), not a stress test. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (KG-Chronos-2: project-structured retrieval plus gated residual correction wrapped around a frozen foundation model) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a frozen time-series foundation model outperforming locally trained hydraulic surrogates on this task). The ingredients — Chronos-2, PCA increment representations, k-NN analog retrieval, ridge correction — are standard; the genuine novelty is the domain-specific coupling of native HEC-RAS project records (reach graph, hydraulic descriptors, input-to-reach mappings) to a frozen predictor, which is a competent, well-motivated recombination rather than a new algorithmic primitive. The closely related Rangaraj et al. (KDD '26) also retrieve-augments Chronos for water levels, so the conceptual move is incremental. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: a direct paired bootstrap against the shared-backbone frozen Chronos-2 isolates the knowledge layer's contribution; three training seeds with reported standard deviations for LSTM and DCRNN-style; the residual LSTM ablates the shared latent representation; exact-state decoding is ablatable against Chronos by construction. Weaknesses: only two evaluation events, so the bootstrap's resampling units are few and intervals are conditional on the fixed procedure; no component-wise ablation of retrieval vs. input-correction vs. gating (the authors admit this); no significance tests for the DCRNN/GeoFNO comparisons;KG-Chronos-2 itself is a single run with multiple tuned hyperparameters (increment multiplier, α_r, input weight, ridge penalty, η, gates) selected on source validation. The authors candidly disclose that upstream fitted quantities leak across folds and that gate calibration may be optimistic, and that they revisited the 2002/2011 events during development — a Goodhart risk on the reused benchmark. Reproducibility: code excerpts, saved outputs, hashes, and environment versions (PyTorch 2.11.0, chronos-forecasting 2.3.1, RTX PRO 6000) are documented, but independent reproduction additionally requires the simulation HDFs, fitted objects, checkpoints, and the exact Chronos weight revision; no public code/data release URL is stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — a built forecasting pipeline on a fixed project). - Practical: Runs on a single workstation-class GPU (RTX PRO 6000) with an open-source Chronos-2 package, though inference requires one multivariate task per origin with 512×256 inputs. - Efficient: Not directly measured — no wall-clock or FLOP comparison against HEC-RAS itself or against the learned baselines is reported; the authors state a matched continuation-runtime study is needed. - Effective: The evidence shows lower RMSE/MAE/active/final-lead error than all completed baselines on the fixed benchmark, but extreme errors (max absolute ~18 native units) and unresolved physical-unit/datum verification mean hydraulic reliability is only proxied. - Scalable: Untested beyond one project with 4,675 cross sections and shared geometry; behavior on new geometries, missing states, or uncertain inputs is unexamined. Deliverable: paper plus an internal pipeline (saved run artifacts, source excerpts, hashes); no public library, CLI, dataset, or trained model release is stated. Strengths: - Clean experimental design: all six systems predict identical targets over identical windows on shared geometry, and the frozen-Chronos-vs-KG contrast cleanly attributes the measured gain to the knowledge-coupling layer rather than to the temporal model. - Statistical care unusual for domain surrogating: hierarchical event/window bootstrap with 10,000 replicates, seed-standard deviations for stochastic baselines, and explicit conditioning statements on the resampling procedure. - The counter-intuitive headline finding — a frozen, zero-hydraulic-knowledge foundation model beats purpose-built recurrent/operator surrogates by 17.76% — is itself valuable evidence for the field. - Unusually candid failure reporting: the Moirai run's environment-creation failure is preserved in the record, and the extreme-error tradeoff vs. persistence is disclosed rather than buried. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) all results describe a fixed, reused, same-geometry benchmark with two events and overlapping histories, and an untouched event or project would strengthen transfer evidence; (2) they revisited the 2002/2011 events during development, unadjusted exploratory comparisons constrain inference, and fold-leakage in gate calibration can make it optimistic; (3) the method assumes exact full-domain WSE history and prescribed inputs, approximate reach/station connectivity, and only seven matched input channels; (4) physical-unit conversion and datum remain unresolved, and no conservation or local extreme-error diagnostics are provided; (5) matched-input and matched-capacity ablations, and a runtime comparison, are needed to attribute gains and quantify savings. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' own admissions: (1) no runtime/throughput numbers at all — the central motivation (bypassing expensive numerical time stepping) is never quantified, so the practical payoff is asserted, not demonstrated; (2) the KG contribution conflates three additions (prescribed-input alignment, graph-conditioned retrieval, residual correction) with no component ablation, so the knowledge-graph framing could be doing little work relative to simple retrieval plus regression; (3) the bootstrap treats only two events, making the "95% interval" fragile — event-level variability cannot be estimated from E=2; (4) all baselines were fit by the authors on this benchmark (the GeoFNO is a reimplementation/replay), so no independent, externally validated hydraulic surrogate is included; (5) the extreme-error disclosure (max abs ~18) suggests tail behavior may be worse than persistence with no distributional diagnostics offered; (6) prior self-referential work (refs [2], [8], [9], all with overlapping authorship) forms a closed evaluation lineage on the same project data, which a reviewer should weigh when interpreting absolute numbers. Bottom Line: A carefully executed, unusually honest domain study that convincingly shows project-knowledge coupling improves a frozen foundation model on one fixed HEC-RAS benchmark — practitioners in hydraulic surrogate modeling should read it for the recipe and the frozen-model-beats-specialist finding, but the missing runtime evidence, two-event evaluation, and closed data lineage mean its conclusions should be treated as promising rather than established.

Bellman Policy Optimization (24 ▲ )

Zhuoqing Song, Haotian Xu, Xikun Zhang, Lidong Bing · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 23 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO), a critic-free policy-gradient loss for RLVR that replaces GRPO's token-level importance-sampling ratio with a smoothed ratio of complementary token probabilities, derived from a provably equivalent trajectory-level reformulation of Policy Mirror Descent. - Why it's important: RLVR for LLM reasoning is bottlenecked by policy-loss design choices; avoiding learned value models (critics) removes a major memory/compute cost and a known source of estimation error in large-scale reasoning training. - How it does it: Using the Bellman equations for terminal rewards, token-level advantages telescope along a response into (terminal reward minus initial value), turning PMD's per-state objective into a trajectory-level squared-residual objective whose gradient contains a mismatch-correction weight ω = (1+ε−μ)/(1+ε−π) instead of an importance ratio. - The good: The paper proves (Theorem 1, with a clean martingale argument in Appendix A.1) that the trajectory-level objective has the same unique optimal solution as PMD on states reachable under the rollout policy, and BPO beats four recent, well-tuned baselines (CISPO by 3.1 pp, DPPO by 4.1 pp, GSPO by 7.0 pp, GRPO-ClipHigher by 11.0 pp) under controlled, identical training settings on a 30B model. - The missing: All headline results come from a single model family (Qwen3), a single training dataset (DAPO-Math-17k English), apparently a single seed, and are reported at the checkpoint selected by peak AIME24–26 accuracy — the same benchmarks used for evaluation — with no error bars, no significance tests, and no code release stated. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or tune RLVR training pipelines and want a theoretically grounded alternative to PPO-style clipping; skip it if you need evidence beyond one model family and one math domain, which the paper does not provide.

Problem & Motivation: In RLVR for LLMs, outcome-level verifiable rewards are assigned to whole responses, so all tokens in a response share one advantage. The dominant critic-free method, GRPO, applies PPO-style clipping with token-level importance ratios, and its variants (GSPO, CISPO, DPPO) trade stability and performance in different ways. The alternative lineage — Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) — offers a principled per-state update with a KL trust region, but applying it to autoregressive generation naively requires action-value estimates at every intermediate token state, which means training a critic (extra memory/compute) or relying on inaccurate learned values on reasoning tasks. The gap is: can one recover the PMD update exactly without any intermediate value estimation? Practitioners training reasoning models with verifiable rewards have this problem. Key Idea: Telescope the Bellman equations along a sampled trajectory: because intermediate rewards are zero and transitions are deterministic, the sum of token-level advantages collapses to R(x,y) − V^μ(x). Substituting this into the PMD optimality condition yields a trajectory-level squared-residual objective (Eq. 18) whose only value-related quantity is the initial value V^μ(x) = expected reward for the prompt, which is directly estimable as the group mean reward. When the PMD solution π+ satisfies the per-token optimality condition, the residual δ(x,y;π+,μ) vanishes, so minimizing expected squared residual recovers PMD without critics. The practical loss then falls out by linearizing the residual, group-normalizing (which recovers the GRPO advantage Â_i), and approximating the full reverse KL with binary KL — the last step producing the distinctive gradient multiplier (1−μ)/(1−π), smoothed into ω_t = (1+ε−μ)/(1+ε−π). Methodology: The pipeline has a theoretical phase and an approximation phase. (1) Instantiate PMD with the rollout-policy advantage A^μ as f(s,y), giving the exponential-form update π+(y|s) ∝ μ(y|s)exp(ηA^μ(s,y)) at each state. (2) Rewrite the optimality condition to eliminate the state-dependent partition function (using Σ_y μ(y|s)A^μ(s,y) = 0), sum the per-token residuals along the trajectory, and apply the Bellman telescoping identity to obtain the critic-free objective: min_π E[φ(x)·δ(x,y;π,μ)²/(2η)] with δ = η(R − V^μ(x)) − Σ_t [log(π/μ) + KL(μ‖π)]. Theorem 1 proves unique-optimal-solution equivalence via a martingale argument: token-level residuals have zero conditional expectation under μ, so an almost-surely zero terminal sum forces every token-level residual to zero on reachable states. (3) Practical loss: linearize the squared residual around π=μ; estimate V^μ(x) by the group mean reward and set φ(x) = 1/std(group rewards), which recovers GRPO's Â_i; replace full reverse KL with binary KL (a lower bound on full KL), whose gradient combines with ∇log π into the exact identity (1−μ)/(1−π)·∇log π; apply additive smoothing (ε=0.1), a cap C=3.0, and GRPO-style asymmetric clipping masks on ω. Critical design decisions: (a) replacing the importance ratio with the complement ratio ω — justified by derivation but changes the off-policy correction semantics, and the linearization discards the second-order residual term; (b) binary KL approximation of full KL — a lower bound introduced by DPPO, cheap (no full-vocabulary logits) but approximate; (c) best-checkpoint selection on the evaluation benchmarks. Decisions (a) and (b) are partially justified by the theory plus ablations; (c) is a reporting concern, not a method choice. Key Results: On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base trained 400 steps on English DAPO-Math-17k (256 prompts/batch, 16 responses/prompt, 16384-token max length, R3 rollout-router replay), BPO reaches peak Avg@32 Pass@1 of 57.4% AIME24 / 41.0% AIME25 / 53.0% AIME26 (50.5% average), versus GRPO-ClipHigher 39.5%, GSPO 43.5%, CISPO 47.4%, DPPO 46.4% — gains of 3.1–11.0 percentage points, with BPO best on all three benchmarks. At end of training (step 400), BPO averages 49.4% vs 45.5% for DPPO, the strongest final baseline. Baselines are current (2025–2026 methods) with hyperparameters taken from published configurations and only the policy loss varied — a genuinely controlled comparison. Ablations on Qwen3-4B-Base (1000 steps) show BPO is insensitive to ε ∈ {0.05–0.3} (24.1–25.8% avg, all above GRPO's 20.5%) and to C ∈ {2.0–4.0} (25.3–25.8%). The evaluated scale is standard for academic RLVR experiments (single 30B MoE model, 400 steps); no stress-scale runs are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. Genuinely novel: the critic-free trajectory-level reformulation of advantage-based PMD with a formal equivalence proof, and the resulting ω = (1+ε−μ)/(1+ε−π) weight replacing the importance ratio. Standard recombination: the binary KL approximation is borrowed from DPPO, group-normalized advantages and asymmetric masking from GRPO/DAPO, and the likelihood-ratio value reparameterization builds on DPO-lineage prior work [11, 23–25]; the empirical gain is a new finding but obtained by combining these pieces in a new derivation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present for the two BPO-specific hyperparameters (ε and C) on a 4B model, and they demonstrate low sensitivity — the strongest robustness evidence in the paper. However, there is no ablation isolating the core claim (ω vs. plain importance ratio is the comparison, but no decomposition of which approximation step — linearization, binary KL, smoothing — costs how much), no multiple seeds, no error bars, and no significance tests; a 3.1-point margin over CISPO on Avg@32 with 30 questions per AIME could plausibly fall within seed noise. Hyperparameters for the 30B main run use defaults (ε=0.1, C=3.0), which is fair. No code, data, or model weights release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) the headline checkpoint is selected by peak mean accuracy on AIME24–26 — the same benchmarks reported in Table 1 — an optimistic-selection bias that inflates all methods' numbers but especially the margin; (2) single model family, single training set, single task domain (math); (3) the theory guarantees equivalence for the exact objective, not the approximated practical loss, so the theorem does not directly certify the algorithm actually run. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a THEORETICAL core result). - Practical: Yes — BPO is a drop-in policy-loss change requiring no critic model, no full-vocabulary logits (binary KL), and runs on standard RLVR infrastructure; the compared setup implies similar hardware to GRPO. - Efficient: Cheaper per token than methods needing value models; gradient computation needs both μ and π token probabilities, comparable to GRPO's importance ratios, and avoids the full reverse-KL cost of the exact objective. - Effective: Evidence supports it on math reasoning with one model family and controlled comparisons; the 3.1-point margin over the strongest baseline is less certain than the 11-point margin over GRPO due to absent variance estimates. - Scalable: Not tested beyond one 30B model and 400 training steps; the authors do not claim scale, and behavior over long training horizons (where clipping-path methods often diverge) is unverified beyond the 1000-step 4B ablations. Artifact: stops at paper form — no library, CLI, or released weights are mentioned. Strengths: - The Bellman telescoping argument that converts per-state PMD into a trajectory-level objective is a genuinely clean formulation, and the martingale-based necessity proof (Appendix A.1) is complete and non-trivial — most critic-free LLM-RL methods lack any equivalence guarantee of this kind. - The derivation transparently accounts for every approximation between the exact objective and the practical loss (linearization, group estimation, binary KL, smoothing, masking), so a reader can trace exactly where the guarantee is spent. - The controlled experimental protocol — identical settings except the policy loss, baseline hyperparameters taken from published configurations, BPO using untuned defaults — is more careful than typical policy-loss papers. - Hyperparameter ablations (Tables 2–3) show a wide stable region (0.5-point spread over C ∈ [2,4]), which supports the numerical-stability motivation for the smoothing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper does not include an explicit limitations section. It implicitly scopes the theory to terminal rewards, deterministic transitions, and states reachable under the rollout policy, and it presents the practical loss as an approximation chain rather than the proven object. It does not directly confront the single-seed/single-family evidence base or the best-checkpoint selection procedure. This is a credibility negative relative to the paper's otherwise careful style. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Checkpoint selection on the evaluation benchmarks (AIME24–26) creates optimistic bias for every method, and the relative ranking — the paper's central claim — is not validated on held-out benchmarks (e.g., MATH-500, GSM8K, or non-math verifiable tasks). - Single seed, no variance reporting; the 3.1-point margin over CISPO is the weakest link and could be seed noise given ~30-question AIME subsets. - No ablation decomposing the contribution of the mismatch-correction weight vs. simply removing the importance ratio (e.g., a plain REINFORCE-style −Â log π baseline) to confirm ω itself, rather than the masking/normalization stack, drives the gain. - The equivalence theorem covers the exact objective; no analysis quantifies the error introduced by the linearization or by binary KL (only that binary KL lower-bounds full KL), so the theorem's connection to the algorithm actually run is looser than the abstract implies. - Only dense/terminal-reward math tasks with binary verifiers; generalization to partial/process rewards, longer horizons, or agentic settings is untested. - No code release stated, which limits verification of the controlled-comparison claim. Bottom Line: For anyone engineering RLVR training loops this is worth reading — it is one of the few critic-free policy losses with a real optimality-equivalence theorem and a controlled win over four recent baselines — but the single-family, single-seed, eval-selected evidence means the 3-point margins should be treated as promising rather than settled, and the theoretical reformulation is the durable contribution.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses a reproducibility and interpretation crisis in LLM evaluation: a benchmark dataset name no longer specifies what was measured. The reported number depends on prompt templates, few-shot policy, answer extraction, decoding parameters, judge configuration, sandbox setup, timeout policy, and aggregation rules — none of which are conveyed by the benchmark name. Practitioners who build leaderboards, model developers who write evaluation appendices, and researchers who compare agent systems all face the same gap: two groups can run "MMLU" or "SWE-bench" and measure different things. Prior framings treated harnesses as implementation details of individual systems (LM Evaluation Harness, HELM, OpenCompass, Inspect, SWE-bench, BFCL); no prior work, in the authors' view, treats the harness layer itself as a coherent research object with a shared taxonomy, common failure modes, and reporting standards. The gap the survey closes is conceptual unification, not a missing technique. Key Idea: The central insight is that the harness is the executable definition of the evaluation and that the decisive analytical variable is the system boundary being measured: a benchmark-harness score characterizes a model endpoint under a prompt/inference/scorer contract; an agent-harness score characterizes a full system (model + scaffold + memory + tools + retry policy + environment); a tool-use score characterizes an interface contract (retrieval, selection, argument formatting, abstention, multi-turn state). Once this distinction is made explicit, most apparent comparability between published numbers dissolves, and the paper's reporting agenda (cite task version, harness version, scaffold, retry budget, trace policy, run date) follows naturally. Methodology: This is a position/survey paper with no algorithmic pipeline. The method is conceptual: (1) the authors construct a seven-layer stack of harness responsibilities (task registry, prompt specification, model access/inference, execution/environment, scoring, provenance, public comparison); (2) they map roughly 75 cited systems and benchmarks onto three harness families via tables specifying each family's system-under-test, execution contract, representative systems, and main risks; (3) they analyze six-plus failure modes (benchmark-name ambiguity, answer extraction as hidden modeling, scaffold effects, schema sensitivity, oracle brittleness, judge bias, temporal drift/contamination) and map each to family-specific causes in Table 7; (4) they propose a reporting agenda including a minimal six-item reporting bundle, "task cards" for executable benchmarks, portable trace formats, benchmark maintenance as research, and configurable model/scaffold boundaries in future harnesses. Not stated: any systematic search or inclusion protocol for the literature covered, any quantitative validation of the taxonomy, and any case study applying the checklist to existing published results. Critical design decisions — e.g., that tool-use harnesses deserve a separate family rather than being a subtype of agent harnesses, and that scoring authority should be decomposed per oracle type — are argued by example but not stress-tested against counterexamples. Key Results: Not stated. The paper reports no experiments, measurements, or quantitative outcomes — appropriately so for a survey, but this means the central empirical claim ("the same benchmark name under different harnesses measures different things") is supported by worked examples and references to prior systems rather than by the authors' own controlled demonstrations. The closest things to results are the taxonomy tables (Tables 1–8), the stem map of systems from SQuAD (2016) through MCP-Bench (2025), and the failure-mode matrix in Table 7. The cited evidence base (SWE-bench, WebArena, BFCL, MT-Bench, StableToolBench, SWE-bench Verified, etc.) is current and high-quality, but the paper's contribution over those sources is synthesis, not new data. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (treating harnesses as the primary object of LLM evaluation and classifying them by measured system boundary) plus a partial NEW TAXONOMY/position contribution. The constituent observations — prompt sensitivity, judge bias, scaffold effects, benchmark contamination, oracle brittleness — are individually well-documented in the primary literature (several of which the paper cites); what is genuinely new is the unified framing of the harness as a citable measurement contract, the three-family separation with the boundary argument, and the family-specific failure-mode matrix. The engineering systems discussed (LM Evaluation Harness, Inspect, etc.) are not the authors' contributions. Rigor & Reproducibility: Not applicable in the conventional sense: there are no ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests because there are no experiments. The paper is internally disciplined — claims are consistently attributed to specific cited systems, and the taxonomy tables are explicit about what each family measures. Methodological concerns a reviewer should flag: (1) no stated literature-selection methodology, so coverage breadth is unverifiable and possibly biased toward well-known systems; (2) the paper's central empirical premise is never demonstrated with the authors' own controlled comparison (e.g., the same model scored under two harness configurations); (3) no released artifact (checklist template, trace schema, or repository) accompanies the reporting agenda, so the proposed standard exists only as prose; (4) it is a non-peer-reviewed preprint (Preprints.org, posted September 2026, doi 10.20944/preprints202609.0236.v1). The reference list is current through 2025/2026, including ICML 2025 BFCL and two 2026 OpenAI items, which supports currency but places some load on not-yet-peer-reviewed sources. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual synthesis/position paper with no primary experimental claim; closest matching profile). - Sound: The argument is internally consistent and every normative claim is anchored to a named prior system, but the taxonomy's boundary cases (e.g., coding harnesses, judge harnesses, model-report stacks) are acknowledged as bridges rather than resolved formally. - General: The framework plausibly covers the full span of LLM evaluation infrastructure from static datasets (SQuAD, GLUE) to MCP-based agent tooling, which is a broad and realistic scope; generality beyond LLMs (e.g., to multimodal or non-LLM agent evaluation) is not addressed. - Tight: Not applicable — there are no bounds; the closest analogue is whether the three-family partition is exhaustive, and the paper concedes bridge cases (code execution, preference judging) sit between families. - Implementable: The deliverable is directly actionable as prose — the six-item reporting bundle (Table 8) and task-card specification could be adopted by leaderboard maintainers tomorrow — but no software artifact, schema, or checklist template is released; the work stops at paper form. Strengths: 1. The system-boundary argument (model endpoint vs. model+scaffold system vs. tool interface) is a genuinely clarifying analytical lens that reorganizes a fragmented literature into one decision: what object did the score measure? 2. Table 7's family-specific decomposition of failure modes is a real intellectual contribution — showing that "oracle brittleness" or "state leakage" is a different defect with a different fix in benchmark, agent, and tool-use harnesses is the kind of synthesis that changes how practitioners debug evaluations. 3. The seven-layer stack (Figure 2) and stem map (Figure 4) give the field usable coordinates, tracing the progression from dataset runners (LM Evaluation Harness) to evidence-producing infrastructure (HELM, Inspect) to environment experiments (SWE-bench, WebArena, TAU-bench). 4. The reporting agenda (citable measurement contracts, task cards, portable traces, maintenance-as-research) is concrete and forward-looking, and correctly identifies trace portability as the missing substrate for harness research. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the three families overlap (bridge cases in Section 4.4), that the taxonomy categories can shift as tasks become interactive or judge-scored (Table 1 caption), and that the survey does not rank models — it maps infrastructure. They also concede that judge harnesses "require their own reporting discipline" rather than being dismissed, and that repaired benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified can themselves lose diagnostic value. The limitations are confronted directly where stated, which is a credibility positive. However, the authors do not state the survey's own scope limits: no inclusion criteria for the literature, no discussion of how representative the ~75 covered systems are, and no acknowledgment that the proposed reporting standards impose real compliance costs on benchmark maintainers. Analyst-Identified Gaps: 1. The central claim is never demonstrated: the paper argues that harness choices change scores but runs no controlled experiment (e.g., one model under two parsers, two oracle configurations, or two scaffolds) — the strongest possible evidence for the thesis was one pipeline away and is left to citations. 2. No competitor synthesis is engaged: the survey does not position itself against prior surveys of LLM evaluation (e.g., surveys of LLM-as-a-judge or agent evaluation), so the reader cannot tell what fraction of the content is genuinely new framing versus reorganization of known material. 3. No validation of the reporting agenda: the six-item bundle and task-card proposal are untested — would adopting them actually resolve cross-lab non-comparability, and at what cost? The authors do not report any attempt to apply the checklist retroactively to a sample of published results to quantify how often current papers would fail it (a dogs-not-barking omission). 4. Normative recommendations outrun evidence: claims like "leaderboards that do not describe a maintenance policy are snapshots, not instruments" are reasonable but asserted, not shown to predict leaderboard decay. 5. Minor editorial red flags: the affiliation block includes medical/clinical institutions unrelated to the topic, and several references are dated 2026 relative to a September 2026 posting — neither is disqualifying but both warrant attention in peer review. Bottom Line: For anyone who runs leaderboards, maintains agent benchmarks, or writes model evaluation reports, this is a useful and well-organized synthesis that supplies vocabulary and a reporting checklist the field currently lacks — but it argues rather than measures, so readers wanting quantitative proof that harness variation moves scores, or a reusable artifact, will need to look elsewhere or build it themselves.

Problem & Motivation: Builders of K–12 AI tutoring systems — and the researchers training open alternatives to closed products — currently must choose between models good at exam-style problem solving (e.g., Confucius3-Math) and models aimed at tutoring dialogue (e.g., EduChat), with training mixtures organized by data source or subject rather than by the capability each example is meant to teach. The paper argues this is a data-design problem: a short answer, a prerequisite relation, a misconception diagnosis, and a Socratic hint supervise conflicting response behaviors, and mixing them without explicit capability targets obscures the intended response policy. Prior data-centric work (LIMA, Deita, LESS) and curriculum-structured educational data (K12-KGraph, EDUMATH) each address only part of this, leaving no open model whose training mixture and evaluation jointly cover the full learning–teaching loop. Key Idea: The single transferable insight is capability-oriented mixture construction with behavior-explicit instructions: label every training example with one of four educational capabilities, budget selection in supervised-response tokens (not example counts) per fine-grained task bucket so long tutoring dialogues and short hints compete on equal footing, and attach a task-specific pedagogical system instruction (20 templates, following LearnLM's pedagogical instruction following) so one model can learn that a problem-solving response should reveal the answer while a scaffolding response should deliberately withhold it. The token-budgeted selection is the most original piece; the rest is a competent assembly of known data-filtering techniques. Methodology: The pipeline has six stages. (1) Sources (100+ datasets) are mapped to the four-capability taxonomy plus a general-instruction component, each example assigned one primary capability and partitioned into fine-grained task buckets. (2) Deterministic cleaning: deduplication, schema validation, answer-reference consistency checks, K–12 relevance filtering, image-availability verification, and removal of overlap with the final evaluation sets — reducing the pool from ~1.34M to 870,711. (3) LLM-assisted auditing with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 assigns 0–100 usability scores and keep/rewrite/remove actions with capability-specific rubrics; rewrites are re-audited — leaving 440,100. (4) Preliminary k-center greedy selection over BGE-M3 embeddings compresses overrepresented sources (e.g., RACE 60,180 → 5,000), then GPT-5.6-Terra scores 1–5 on task-specific dimensions with minimum thresholds (stricter for correctness/validity/grounding) — leaving 121,318. (5) Token-budgeted k-center greedy selection within each bucket yields 60,951 education-specific examples (~12.0M supervised response tokens). (6) Each example receives exactly one of 20 pedagogical system-instruction templates; 9,048 general-purpose examples (DataFlow-Instruct-10K, Tulu-3-SFT-mixture, MathV360K) are added for a final 69,999-example / 15.96M-token corpus. Models are full-parameter SFT'd on Qwen3.5-4B/9B and Qwen3.8-27B bases via LLaMA-Factory (lr 5e-6, 3 epochs, 32,768 sequence length, bf16, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3). Critical design decisions: the four-capability taxonomy (motivated but not validated against alternatives), token- rather than example-count budgeting (sensible but unjustified quantitatively), and the instruction-assignment scheme (borrowed directly from LearnLM). No stage-level ablation justifies any of these choices. Key Results: OmniEdu-27B reaches 63.12% EM / 76.69% F1 on K12-Bench (best overall; base: 52.11%/73.48%), 85.89% on MathFish (best), 86.95% MaC on EDUMATH (second to Kimi-K3's 90.00%), 94.87% full-rate on GAOKAO-Bench, 69.52% on EXAMS-V, and 57.76% on MDK12-Bench (open-question correctness rising 62.08% → 78.77%). Tutoring gains are largest: MathTutorBench Scaffold win rate jumps from 20.42% to 75.79% (4B), 14.00% to 75.26% (9B), 57.16% to 78.74% (27B); LongTutor Evidence average rises from 36.80% to 78.20% (27B), with the best Teaching average of 3.02 among evaluated models (Claude-Opus-5: 2.72). General capability is retained or slightly improved (MMMU-Pro 64.97% → 67.98% at 27B; GPQA-Diamond 74.24% → 77.78%). Baselines include open educational models (Confucius3-Math-14B, MuduoLLM-14B, three EduChat variants — all consistently weak, e.g., ≤5.23% EM on K12-Bench for Confucius3-Math) and five frontier proprietary models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude-Opus-5, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3), which are current and strong. Evaluation spans 9 educational benchmarks plus 3 general diagnostics — standard academic benchmarks rather than stress-scale tests. Notably, proprietary models score near-random on some scaffolding settings (GPT-5.4: 6.32% Scaffold win rate), which the paper does not investigate. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (a released, capability-labeled 70K educational instruction corpus with provenance metadata) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (capability-balanced supervision yields cross-scale gains on tutoring and curriculum grounding without general-capability loss). The genuinely novel elements are the token-budgeted diversity selection and the four-capability taxonomy as an organizing principle for educational data; the pipeline stages otherwise combine established techniques (k-center greedy selection, LLM-as-judge filtering à la AlpaGasus/Deita, LearnLM's pedagogical instruction following), and SFT on a Qwen base is standard. No new training algorithm is proposed. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paired base-vs-SFT comparison at three scales is a genuine strength and cleanly isolates the training-mixture effect. However: no ablations isolate which pipeline stages or mixture components matter; no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported (fine-tuning variance alone could matter at the reported margins, e.g., 85.89% vs 85.40% MathFish); and two different proprietary LLMs serve as auditor and quality judge without judge-validation experiments. Code, the dataset, and all three model weights are publicly released (github.com/haolpku/Omni-Edu; huggingface.co/datasets/lhpku20010120/Omni-Edu and model pages). Methodological concerns: (1) several training sources are name-variants of evaluation benchmarks — LongTutor-Synthetic/Silver/Gold (3,862 examples), MathFish (3,581), TutorBench-v6 (3,492), MathTutor-v6 (2,899), OATutor-v6 — while the paper simultaneously evaluates on LongTutor, MathFish, TutorBench, and MathTutorBench; the decontamination claim covers "overlap with our final evaluation set" but the provenance naming demands explicit documentation of how synthetic/silver variants relate to the test sets, and this is the single largest validity risk; (2) K12-KGraph, a benchmark from the same authors (ref. 17), is both a training source and an evaluation (K12-Bench) source; (3) some tutoring metrics appear to be LLM- or human-judged win rates with no judge-reliability detail in the excerpt. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained and evaluated models). Practical: Yes — 4B–27B full-parameter SFT on commodity multi-GPU hardware with a released recipe; inference matches any Qwen-compatible deployment. Efficient: The corpus is deliberately small (70K examples / 15.96M tokens, ~3 epochs), so tuning cost is modest relative to typical SFT runs; the pipeline's use of two very large proprietary judge models is the main cost and a reproducibility liability. Effective: The evidence shows improvements on curated educational benchmarks including tutoring-judged behaviors, but no classroom study, no real-learner outcome, and no human-tutor comparison — effectiveness is demonstrated on proxies only. Scalable: Not tested beyond 27B and 70K examples; the authors claim the data design generalizes but provide no scaling experiment. The work delivers concrete artifacts: three fine-tuned model weights, the dataset, and pipeline code — not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The four-capability taxonomy gives education data construction an explicit, reusable vocabulary that connects subject accuracy to curriculum structure, diagnosis, and pedagogy — a real conceptual contribution to data design, not just data collection. (2) Token-budgeted bucket-wise diversity selection is a concrete, generalizable trick for mixtures spanning response lengths that differ by an order of magnitude. (3) The paired base/SFT evaluation at three scales, across nine educational benchmarks plus general-capability controls, is unusually thorough for a data-centric report and credibly attributes gains to the mixture rather than to scale. (4) Full release of weights, data, and provenance/audit metadata supports genuine reproduction of the mixture. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper acknowledges that knowledge-state diagnosis remains hard (LongTutor diagnosis accuracy ~54% at best, which it calls out directly), that gains vary across MMMU-Pro disciplines and benchmark subsets, and that frontier proprietary models retain advantages on some exam-style evaluations. It does not include an explicit limitations section in the provided text; the acknowledgments it does make are direct rather than minimized, but the contamination-adjacent data naming is not discussed as a risk. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The training-data provenance names overlapping evaluation benchmarks (LongTutor-*, MathFish, TutorBench-v6, MathTutor-v6) are unexplained; if any synthetic or silver variant derives from the benchmark's training split, the headline tutoring and curriculum numbers could be inflated — the paper must show the decontamination was benchmark-test-set-specific. (2) No ablation against a source-organized or size-matched random mixture, so the central claim — that capability-orientation (rather than curation alone) drives the gains — is asserted, not measured. (3) The near-zero scaffolding scores of GPT-5.4/GPT-5.6-Sol and Confucius3-Math's 0.00% on MathFish suggest format or protocol mismatches that could flatter the comparison; no format-invariance check is reported. (4) No human evaluation with actual students or teachers, despite the framing around real learning–teaching loops. (5) The 27B base is named "Qwen3.8-27B" while the 4B/9B bases are "Qwen3.5" — an unexplained inconsistency worth verifying. (6) Both judge models (Qwen3.5-122B for auditing, GPT-5.6-Terra for scoring) are used without any agreement or bias analysis, and the Qwen-family auditor fine-tunes Qwen-family models, a possible self-preference channel. Bottom Line: For practitioners building open educational models, this is a useful and unusually well-released data-centric recipe whose tutoring gains look real at the base-vs-SFT level, but the unexplained overlap between training-source names and evaluation benchmarks, plus the absence of any mixture ablation, means the central design claim should be treated as promising rather than established until independent replication.

#66 — Moderately Innovative (56)

Learning Long-Horizon LLM Agents from Demonstrations via Test-Time Generative Verifiers

X Zhang, M Hong · openreview.net · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes a dual-use framework for expert demonstrations: the same demonstration set trains both an SFT reference policy and a turn-level generative verifier, which then guides the frozen policy at inference time via turn-level truncated rejection sampling. - Why it's important: Long-horizon LLM agents suffer from sparse, delayed rewards that make RL expensive and unstable, while behavior cloning alone suffers from exposure bias; this offers a way to squeeze more agent performance out of a fixed demonstration set without online policy optimization. - How it does it: Candidate state-action-observation transitions are labeled as positive if they match the expert action and negative otherwise, a generative verifier is GRPO-trained on these labels, and at test time actions are resampled until the verifier accepts one (majority vote fallback after N tries). - The good: On ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B, SFT+RS@5 reaches 96.4% in-domain and 95.5% out-of-domain success (vs. 86.1%/86.5% for GiGPO) while cutting average interaction cost from 92.4/113.8 steps (Pass@5) to 28.9/32.2 at H=50. - The missing: The verifier's actual precision/recall is never measured, there is no ablation isolating verifier quality or the negative-sampling scheme, and code is not stated as released; on SearchQA the verifier-guided method is actually beaten by plain majority voting (36.24 vs. 37.50 EM) and wins only on tool-call cost. - Read it or not: Read it if you build multi-turn LLM agents and care about the demonstration-efficiency vs. RL-cost trade-off or test-time scaling for agents; skip it if you want a general-purpose process reward model validated beyond two text benchmarks.

Novelty (65) for the demonstration-derived turn-level label construction is real but modest, and Resilience (55) is weakened by the SearchQA accuracy loss to plain majority voting and the un-foregrounded negative 3B OOD result. Completeness (58) is further dented by self-distilled rather than genuine 'expert' demonstrations. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*52 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*40 = 56.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners training LLM agents for long-horizon interactive tasks (household text games, search-augmented QA, web navigation) face a supervision dilemma. SFT/behavior cloning on expert trajectories is cheap but degrades under exposure bias once the agent drifts off the demonstration distribution. RL fixes this in principle but requires costly online environment interaction (each turn may trigger API calls or real-world execution) and struggles with credit assignment under sparse terminal rewards. Expert demonstrations are typically consumed exactly once (to fit the policy via SFT) and then discarded. The gap this paper targets: extract a second source of supervision — turn-level action quality — from the same demonstrations, without human step annotation or Monte Carlo rollout labeling, and use it to improve the agent at test time rather than through further weight updates. Key Idea: Treat the expert demonstration set twice: (1) as behavior-cloning data for a reference policy, and (2) as a source of turn-level verifier labels — at each expert state, the expert transition is a positive example and transitions sampled from the frozen policy are negatives — so a generative verifier can act as the potential function exp(Q/β) in a KL-regularized policy-improvement step, approximating policy improvement purely at inference time through rejection sampling. This sidesteps the two known bottlenecks of process reward models: human step-level annotation and policy-dependent MC-rollout labeling (whose labels can be spuriously positive when a strong policy self-corrects). Methodology: Three stages. (i) Behavior cloning: SFT maximizes log-likelihood of expert actions, yielding π_ref. (ii) Verifier data collection and training: for each expert state s_h, the authors sample K candidate actions from π_ref, execute all of them to obtain observations, label the expert transition as 1 and sampled transitions as 0, then GRPO-train a generative verifier (Qwen base, reasoning then a \boxed{Correct/Wrong} judgment) with reward R = 0.15·R_format + 0.85·R_accuracy. (iii) Test-time scaling: truncated turn-level rejection sampling — sample candidate actions from the frozen SFT policy (up to N per turn), execute each to get its observation, query the verifier, execute the first accepted action; if all N are rejected, fall back to majority vote among the N candidates. The framing is the KL-regularized per-step policy improvement π* ∝ π_ref·exp(Q/β). The theory section analyzes environment interaction cost under a stationarity assumption (constant turn-level success probability p; verifier TPR/FPR independent of state): Proposition 1 gives accepted-action correctness p·TPR/(p·TPR+(1−p)·FPR) and expected cost 1/α; Proposition 2 shows rejection sampling always costs less than BoN under the same per-turn budget N (ratio (1−(1−α)^N)/(Nα) < 1); Proposition 3, under the all-steps-must-be-correct trajectory model, gives cost ratio ≈ α^(H−1)/TPR^H, which shrinks with horizon when the verifier is accurate. Critical design decisions: (a) treating all non-expert sampled actions as negatives (justified only by assuming demonstrations are optimal — explicitly acknowledged as an assumption); (b) executing every candidate to obtain its observation before verification, which the cost analysis counts as an interaction; (c) majority-vote fallback to bound worst-case cost (reasonable, though it dilutes verifier guidance). Key Results: ALFWorld (6 task types, ID and OOD splits, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B, 3 seeds, H=50): 1.5B SFT+RS@5 achieves 96.4% ID / 95.5% OOD success, vs. SFT Pass@5 at 96.4%/94.5%, GiGPO Pass@1 at 86.1%/86.5%, and GRPO Pass@1 at 73.3%/68.7%; interaction cost at H=50 drops to 28.9 (ID) and 32.2 (OOD) steps vs. 92.4/113.8 for Pass@5 — roughly a 3.2–3.5× reduction, claimed as "up to 4×". For the 3B model, RS@5 gives 96.4% ID but only 90.3% OOD — below SFT Pass@5's 93.7% OOD, a result the paper does not foreground. Turn-MV@K underperforms Pass@1 on several tasks, supporting the claim that naive aggregation fails in long horizons. SearchQA (HotpotQA in-domain; TriviaQA, PopQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue, Bamboogle out-of-domain; Qwen2.5-3B; RL baselines' numbers taken from a prior paper, marked *): SFT alone averages 32.05 EM vs. 29.77 for the best RL baseline (GRPO); SFT+MV@8 reaches 37.50 EM while verifier-guided RS@8 reaches 36.24 EM but with fewer tool calls (8.85 vs. 12.25). Surprising findings: SFT+Pass@K alone already beats both RL baselines on both benchmarks, and the theory's efficiency advantage of rejection sampling over BoN holds empirically in interaction cost. Baselines (GiGPO, GRPO, MT-PPO/MT-GRPO) are current and reasonably strong for 2025–2026; the tested scale is small models (1.5B–3B) on two text-based benchmarks. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (turn-level generative verifier trained from demonstration contrast without human annotation or MC rollouts, applied via test-time rejection sampling) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (demonstrations alone, used this way, beat RL post-training on these agent benchmarks at 1.5B–3B scale). The individual ingredients are standard — generative reward models, GRPO, rejection sampling, KL-regularized policy improvement — and the closest relatives are IRL-without-policy-optimization and the authors' own prior work on inference-time policy iteration (Zhang et al., 2025b;c); the genuinely new part is the demonstration-derived turn-level label construction plus the cost analysis showing turn-level rejection sampling dominates trajectory-level BoN as horizon grows. Rigor & Reproducibility: Results are averaged over 3 random seeds with standard deviations reported in ALFWorld tables, which is above the field's floor. Ablations are weak: there is no ablation over the number of negative samples K, no measurement of verifier TPR/FPR on held-out data (the two quantities the entire theory depends on), no comparison against an external PRM baseline (e.g., Web-Shepherd, cited but not compared), and no SFT+verifier-guided-beam-search or scalar-reward-model comparison. The SearchQA RL numbers are imported from a prior paper rather than re-run, a mild comparability risk. Methodological concerns: the verifier is developed and evaluated on the same two benchmarks; the negative-labeling scheme assumes demonstration optimality, which holds by construction in ALFWorld (all tasks solvable) but is only proxy-verified in SearchQA where "expert" trajectories are self-generated by Qwen2.5-32B and filtered by answer correctness; and the 3B OOD ALFWorld result (RS@5 90.3% < Pass@5 93.7%) contradicts the headline narrative for the larger model. No code, data, or model release URL is stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a lightweight THEORETICAL component under strong assumptions). - Practical: Yes — Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B models on standard hardware, though inference-time rejection sampling multiplies policy forward passes and requires environment rollback after executing rejected candidates. - Efficient: Favorable vs. Pass@K in environment interactions (28.9 vs. 92.4 steps ID at H=50) and vs. RL in total training interaction cost, but the verifier adds per-candidate LLM calls whose compute cost is not reported. - Effective: Mixed — clearly effective on ALFWorld, but on SearchQA it is a cost-efficiency play, not an accuracy win (MV@8 beats RS@8 37.50 vs. 36.24 EM), so it does not fully solve accuracy improvement on the tool-use task. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — beyond 3B parameters, beyond two text environments, and beyond H=50 horizons are untested; the theory suggests the advantage grows with H, but state-dependent verifier quality (violating Assumption 1) could erode it. Deliverable: stops at paper form — no library, CLI, dataset, or trained weights are stated as released. Strengths: (1) The negative-label construction — sample candidate actions at expert states and label them against the executed expert transition — is a clean, annotation-free way to get turn-level supervision that avoids the known policy-dependence pathology of MC-rollout PRM labeling. (2) The cost analysis correctly identifies the structural reason turn-level rejection sampling beats trajectory-level BoN in long horizons (local correction compounds vs. whole-trajectory resampling), and Proposition 3's α^(H−1)/TPR^H ratio makes the horizon dependence explicit. (3) The empirical efficiency result is concrete and well-plotted: near-identical success rates at 3–3.5× lower interaction cost on ALFWorld, directly relevant to anyone paying per environment step. (4) Honest framing of the method as inference-time policy improvement rather than claiming a new training algorithm. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly flag that Assumption 1 (stationary turn-level success probability and state-independent verifier TPR/FPR) is adopted "only for analytical clarity" and that real quantities are state-dependent, making the closed-form comparison an approximation. They also acknowledge that demonstrations are assumed to follow an optimal behavioral strategy — an assumption that strictly holds in ALFWorld but is only approximate elsewhere. They do not discuss the SearchQA accuracy shortfall of RS vs. MV beyond the efficiency trade-off, nor the 3B OOD result. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The verifier's operating characteristics (TPR/FPR) — the load-bearing parameters of all three propositions — are never empirically estimated, so the gap between the theoretical model and the deployed system is unquantified. (2) Executing each candidate action to obtain its observation before verification presupposes reversible or resettable environments; in real web, API, or robotics settings where actions have irreversible side effects, the method's applicability shrinks sharply and this cost/feasibility issue is unexamined. (3) No comparison to process reward model baselines or to a simple scalar verifier trained on the same data, so the "generative" choice is unvalidated. (4) The SearchQA "expert" data is distilled from Qwen2.5-32B outputs filtered by answer match — this is self-distillation, not expert demonstration, which weakens the optimality assumption and the claim of using demonstrations as the supervision source. (5) Both benchmarks are text-only with cheap, deterministic feedback; generalization to visually grounded or partially observable environments is extrapolated, not shown. (6) The best OOD result (95.5%) comes only from the 1.5B model; the 3B model shows no OOD gain from the verifier, suggesting the method's benefit may shrink with base-model capability — a scaling trend the paper leaves unexplored. Bottom Line: A practitioner building multi-turn LLM agents on simulated, resettable environments should read this for a concrete and well-costed alternative to agent RL at small scale, but the missing verifier diagnostics, absent code release, two-benchmark evaluation, and the SearchQA accuracy tie mean it is a strong proof of concept rather than yet a replacement for RL or mature PRM pipelines.

WanPE: Towards Cinematic Prompt Enhancement for Modern Text-to-Video Generation (25 ▲ )

Yubo Zhu, Yawen Shao, Ziyun Dai, Zixun Fang, Kai Zhu, Siyang Sun, Haolan Xue, Chuxin Wang, Tingyu Weng, Jingming Luo, Chen Shi, Lianghua Huang, Yufeng Ai, Yuzheng Wang, Wenyuan Zhang, Yu Shang, Yuxiang Bao, Zoubin Bi, Jie Xiao, Jinbo Xing, Jiaxing Zhao, Chongyang Zhong, Hengjian Chen, Chenwei Xie, Akide Liu, Zhehan Kan, Yu Liu, Wei Zhai, Sheng Zhong, Wei Tong · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WanPE, a 397B-parameter prompt enhancer trained on 1.05M real-world videos that converts user requests into shot-by-shot cinematic plans (camera, lighting, dialogue, audio, timing) for modern text-to-video generators, plus WanPEval, a 249-request human-annotated benchmark. - Why it's important: As video generators stretch to 30 seconds with strong instruction following, the prompt becomes the production blueprint; a mismatch between synthetic rewriting-style prompts and the video-grounded caption distribution generators were trained on directly costs video quality, and this work claims the largest gains precisely where it hurts most (50.86-point preference jump at 30 seconds). - How it does it: The core trick is reversed supervision construction — caption a real video into a hierarchical cinematic condition, then reconstruct a natural user request from it via an LLM, so SFT targets come from the video-grounded caption distribution rather than LLM rewriting — followed by GRPO with a nine-dimensional LLM-judged semantic-consistency reward. - The good: The controlled comparison showing reverse-constructed SFT beats matched forward rewriting by 10.37–14.69 points in expert preference (49.86 vs. 39.49/35.17 overall S) is the cleanest evidence that the distribution-alignment argument, not just more detail, drives the gains. - The missing: The 30-second arena — where the headline 50.86-point claim lives — is evaluated only against a single competitor (Seedance 2.5), the semantic-consistency reward is produced by the same class of LLM judge used during training (circularity risk), and no code, weights, or data release is stated. - Read it or not: Read it if you build T2V pipelines or work on prompt optimization, for the reverse-construction idea and the duration-stratified evaluation protocol; skip it if you want open artifacts or scale-independent findings, since everything is tied to Wan3.0 and unreleased 397B-scale training.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners of text-to-video generation face a conditioning mismatch: commercial generators like Wan3.0 are trained on video-grounded captions, but prompt enhancers produce synthetic forward-rewritten text from user requests. Earlier, weak instruction-following generators only benefited from cosmetic detail enrichment; with generators now synthesizing 30-second multi-shot video with camera, lighting, dialogue, and audio control, the prompt must plan an entire production — coordinating actions, camera choreography, editing pace, and sound across temporally ordered shots. Two open problems: (i) learning how cinematic elements are jointly organized across shots, in the distribution the generator actually expects, and (ii) preserving every user-specified constraint (subjects, dialogue, bindings, event order) across the full plan without omission, alteration, or temporal contradiction. Key Idea: Reverse the supervision construction direction. Instead of expanding a user request forward into a richer prompt (which yields a synthetic rewriting distribution), caption a curated real-world video into a hierarchical video-level-plus-shot-level cinematic condition y, then use an LLM (gpt-5.4 with a 2K-request human-written demonstration pool) to reconstruct a natural user request x from y, guaranteeing y ∈ Ysem(x). This aligns the enhancer's output distribution with the video-grounded caption distribution p_vg the downstream generator was trained on, formalized as minimizing KL to p_vg restricted to semantically valid outputs. Semantic fidelity is then reinforced with SC-GRPO: GRPO with a text-only reward from Qwen3.7-Max scoring nine dimensions (style, subjects, actions, dialogue, sound, camera, lighting, spatial relations, scene), penalizing omissions, alterations, wrong subject–attribute and speaker–dialogue bindings, ordering errors, and cross-shot conflicts. Methodology: Three-stage pipeline. (1) Data and reverse SFT: ~1.05M clips (≤30 s, ten content categories) are filtered for technical/visual/motion quality; a multimodal captioner f_cap produces category-adaptive hierarchical targets y_i (video-level summary + timestamped shot-level descriptions covering composition, subjects, actions, lighting, camera, transitions, dialogue, music, sound); captions pass structural and video-consistency checks; gpt-5.4 reconstructs x_i from y_i with few-shot human demonstrations; the enhancer is trained with negative log-likelihood L_SFT. (2) SC-GRPO: ~15K prompts (human-written diverse requests plus hard cases where SFT-enhanced videos failed human inspection); for each x, G samples are scored by the nine-dimension reward, standardized into group-relative advantages, and optimized with clipped PPO-style updates plus KL penalty to the frozen SFT reference (standard DeepSeekMath-style GRPO). (3) Evaluation: WanPEval (249 requests, 5/10/15/30 s, intent/scene/shot granularity, seven categories) with text-level semantic scoring and ~11K blind pairwise expert video assessments (60 film-domain experts, randomized order, four-outcome judgments), aggregated into preference scores S and Bradley–Terry scores with both-good/both-poor as ties. Critical design decisions: reverse construction (justified by the ablation in §3.2), LLM-judged reward with severity-graded penalties (convenient but self-referential), and format adaptation via GPT-5.4 for cross-generator transfer (pragmatic but untested for loss introduced by the rewrite step). Key Results: WanPE-397B + Wan3.0 improves over raw prompts by +10.66/+16.28/+18.84 points in expert preference S at 5/10/15 seconds and +50.86 at 30 seconds (S from 9.38 to 60.24). On the 5–15 s subset it leads all evaluated commercial systems (overall S 50.61, BT 61.85), beating Seedance 2.0 (S 43.42), MiniMax-H3 (36.40), HappyHorse 1.1 (24.89), Kling 3.0 (20.80), and LTX-2.5 (17.30); at 30 s it scores 60.24 vs. Seedance 2.5's 59.76 (competitive, not dominant — Seedance 2.5 leads action and advertising). Reverse SFT (49.86) beats Forward Rewriting (39.49) and Forward-target SFT (35.17), ranking first in all seven categories. SC-GRPO raises semantic-consistency scores by 18.6–23.3 points across 4B–397B scales (e.g., 75.5→97.6 at 397B) and lifts downstream expert preference from 42.70 to 49.69. Format-adapted WanPE beats native enhancers on LTX-2.5-Base (+14.45 S) and MiniMax-H3-Base (+5.17 S). A surprising secondary finding: prompt enhancement matters more as duration grows — the raw-prompt baseline collapses at 30 s (S 9.38). Baselines are current commercial systems; the comparison is on the authors' own testbed with their own generator, tested at production scale (512 GPUs, 397B parameters) but only at 249 evaluation requests. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (video-grounded reverse pair construction for prompt-enhancement training) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (WanPEval with duration/granularity stratification and a documented expert pairwise protocol). GRPO, LLM-judged rewards, hierarchical video captioning, and SFT+RL post-training are all standard; the genuinely novel element is the reverse-construction trick that turns real videos into (request, cinematic-plan) pairs to fix the training–inference distribution mismatch — a clean, transferable formulation rather than a new algorithm. The reframing of prompt enhancement as 'cinematic planning' is a position claim built on this mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: reverse vs. forward supervision is isolated with two matched baselines (Forward Rewriting refined over 27 instruction versions; Forward-target SFT on identical settings), and SC-GRPO is ablated at four model scales with reward curves shown. Human evaluation is reasonably careful: 60 domain experts, anonymous randomized pairwise presentation, Bradley–Terry correction for opponent strength, lower/upper bounds reported per cell, and ~11K judgments. However: no code, model weights, data, or captioner details are stated as released (only a project page URL); no multiple-seed error bars for training runs; the semantic-consistency metric is computed by an LLM judge (gemini-3.1-pro-preview for evaluation, Qwen3.7-Max for the training reward) with no human validation of that judge's agreement; evaluation is exclusively on the authors' WanPEval and predominantly on the authors' own Wan3.0 generator; and the 30-second headline comparison includes only one opponent. Methodological concern: the reward model that defines the training objective also defines the primary text-level evaluation metric, inviting Goodhart-style optimization of the judge rather than of true fidelity. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — an industrial component of a commercial pipeline). - Practical: Inference requires a 4B–397B LLM in front of the generator; the 397B-A17B variant (17B active, MoE) is plausible for a large API provider but not for on-premise or small-team deployment. - Efficient: Training used 512 GPUs for a 397B model; per-request enhancement cost and latency versus cheaper forward rewriting are not reported. - Effective: Expert preference against current commercial systems supports effectiveness at 5–30 s, but the evidence is proxy-based (expert preference on the authors' testbed) and the 30 s claim rests on a single opponent. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 30 s or beyond WanPEval's 249 requests; cross-generator transfer is demonstrated for only two generators and requires an LLM-based format adaptation step whose information loss is unquantified. The paper ships as a paper plus project page; no software artifact, weights, or dataset release is stated. Strengths: (1) The reverse-construction insight is a real conceptual contribution — grounding prompt-enhancement supervision in realized cinematic structure rather than LLM rewriting — and the matched ablation (Table 2, Exp2) credibly isolates its effect from mere detail addition. (2) The formalization (Eq. 3–4: video-grounded distribution restricted to semantically valid outputs) gives the heuristic pipeline a precise target and makes the distribution-mismatch argument testable. (3) The evaluation protocol is above the bar for this literature: duration- and granularity-stratified requests, 60 film-domain experts, blind randomized pairs, Bradley–Terry correction, and published per-cell confidence intervals. (4) Scale sweep across 4B/9B/35B/397B with consistent SC-GRPO gains (+18.6 to +23.3 semantic points) supports that the recipe, not a one-off large-model effect, drives the improvement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper has no dedicated limitations section. Implicitly acknowledged boundaries: WanPE outputs must be format-adapted (via GPT-5.4) for non-Wan generators, and evaluation against Seedance 2.5 is confined to the 30-second subset while the 5–15 s subset excludes Seedance 2.5. The authors do not directly confront judge circularity, the single-generator dependence of most results, or the unreleased-artifact situation; treating limitations this lightly is a credibility negative. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Reward/evaluation circularity: Qwen3.7-Max defines the SC-GRPO reward and the same metric family (with gemini-3.1-pro-preview) defines the headline semantic-consistency numbers, with no human-verified agreement study of either judge. (2) The 30-second result — the paper's most dramatic claim — compares against exactly one competitor on the authors' own testbed and generator; 'remains competitive with Seedance 2.5' is a much weaker statement than the 5–15 s leadership claim, and per-category numbers (Seedance 2.5 wins action at 68.18 vs. 50.00 and advertising at 81.25 vs. 75.00) complicate the aggregate. (3) Cross-generator transfer uses a lossy LLM format conversion whose effect is never ablated, and only two transfer targets exist. (4) WanPEval has 249 requests, is author-curated, and — while overlap with training data is excluded — both the training hard-case mining and the testbed were constructed by the same team with the same generator in the loop. (5) No cost analysis: a 397B enhancer per prompt is only justified if smaller variants show a clear quality cliff, and the 4B→397B preference spread (43.60→50.61 S) actually suggests 35B captures most of the gain at a fraction of cost — a comparison the authors report but do not discuss as a deployment recommendation. (6) '50.86 points' in the abstract describes the raw-prompt baseline gap at 30 s, not a win over a competitor; the framing invites over-reading. Bottom Line: For anyone engineering T2V prompt enhancement, the reverse-construction idea and the duration-stratified expert protocol are worth stealing, but the headline numbers are self-benchmarked, judge-in-the-loop, and unreleased — treat this as a strong industrial technical report with one transferable idea, not as reproducible evidence of general superiority.

Adaptive Preference Modeling via Explicit Indirect Relational Learning for Personalized Fashion Matching

S Liao, L Li, PY Mok · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces APCL, a recommendation framework that explicitly constructs indirect user–item and item–item relational views (via correlation sampling) and aligns them with direct relational views through a functional-view contrastive objective for personalized fashion complementary matching (top–bottom outfit completion). - Why it's important: Fashion e-commerce suffers from severe interaction sparsity (fast product turnover, cold-start items), so models that extract supervision from indirect relationships rather than direct interactions alone can recommend more reliably where data is thin. - How it does it: The core move is promoting indirect relations — co-occurrence-derived similar users and similar items — from implicit by-products of graph propagation into dedicated model views (IP, IC) that are trained to agree with the direct personalization (P) and compatibility (C) views via InfoNCE losses stacked on a BPR ranking loss. - The good: AUC of 0.9739 on IQON3000 and 0.9832 on Polyvore (top-as-given setting), a ~10% AUC improvement over the best reproduced baseline (CP-TransMatch, 0.8842/0.9001), supported by ablations showing each module contributes. - The missing: Three strong baselines (DGSR, TransRec+V, HMGL-OCM) are compared using numbers copied from their original papers under different protocols rather than reproduced, and the cold-start analysis only compares APCL against its own ablation, not against external baselines. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on multimodal/complementary recommendation and sparsity handling; practitioners seeking production-ready recommenders can skim it, as the evaluation is confined to small academic top–bottom outfit datasets.

Rigor (55) benefits from an unusually thorough six-component ablation and released code, but is reduced by mixed-protocol baseline comparisons (three baselines copied from papers under different preprocessing), no seed variance reporting, self-referential cold-start evaluation, and preprint status. Completeness (60) is a positive — limitations are confronted directly and published numbers are cleanly separated from reproduced ones.
