Problem & Motivation: Personalized fashion complementary recommendation — given a user and a garment, recommend a matching garment that is both outfit-compatible and aligned with the user's taste — must jointly model two signals (personalization and compatibility) under three handicaps: highly sparse interactions (fast-fashion turnover means most items accumulate few interactions), inherently multimodal product data (images, text, attributes), and the fact that many useful signals are indirect (similar users' choices, co-occurring items). Existing graph-based methods (NGCF, LightGCN) capture indirect higher-order relations only implicitly through message passing, entangling preference and compatibility signals in one latent space; co-occurrence methods use coarse frequency statistics. The authors target the gap of making indirect relations explicit, separable, and directly optimizable. Key Idea: Turn indirect relationships into explicit first-class views. Instead of relying on graph propagation, APCL pre-computes correlated users/items via a normalized co-occurrence similarity (C_ij = W_ij / sqrt(|N(i)||N(j)|)), samples top-K neighbors, gathers their positively-interacted items, and aggregates these into dedicated Indirect Personalization (IP) and Indirect Compatibility (IC) representations. A secondary idea — "functional-view" contrastive learning — then aligns direct↔indirect representations within each functional space (P↔IP, C↔IC) using InfoNCE, contrasting relational roles rather than modalities or augmentations. Methodology: The pipeline has four scoring modules plus an optimization scheme. (1) C module: CLIP-extracted visual/textual features of the given and candidate garments pass through modality-specific MLP+BatchNorm encoders; compatibility score s_c is a π-weighted combination of per-modality cosine similarities. (2) P module: BPR-style scoring — cosine of learnable ID embeddings plus user/item biases, plus modality-specific user preference factors (v_p_u, w_p_u) against encoded candidate features, giving s_p = s_u + π·s_v_p + (1−π)·s_w_p. (3) IP/IC modules: correlation sampling (5 steps: binary co-interaction matrix → normalized similarity → ranking → top-K neighbors → cross-attention selection of n related items) followed by a dual-pathway multimodal refiner — 1D convolution + attention pooling for visual features, a 2-head transformer + mean–max pooling for textual features. (4) Optimization: final score p_r = s_p + s_c (additive, not a trade-off), trained with L = γ1·L_BPR + γ2·(L_CL-1 + L_CL-2), where the two InfoNCE losses align direct and indirect representations per modality and per functional view. Critical design decisions: (a) additive rather than competing personalization/compatibility scores — motivated but not ablated against a learned combination; (b) explicit neighbor construction instead of graph propagation — the central claim, justified by interpretability arguments; (c) Conv1D for visual vs. transformer for textual in the refiner — asserted from modality priors, not empirically compared to the alternative assignment. A complexity analysis gives O(BD² + BKL + BnD² + Bn²D) per batch. Key Results: On IQON3000 (3,236 users, 142,737 garments, 216,791 samples) and Polyvore-519 (519 users, 33,107 garments, 49,440 samples), restricted to one-top/one-bottom outfits, with CLIP features and metrics AUC, HR@10, NDCG@10, MRR@10. Top-as-given: APCL achieves AUC 0.9739 / HR@10 0.9509 (IQON3000) and 0.9832 / 0.8999 (Polyvore), vs. best reproduced baseline CP-TransMatch at 0.8842 / 0.8789 and 0.9001 / 0.8573 (claimed improvements 10.1% and 9.2% AUC). Bottom-as-given (sparser): AUC 0.9016 / NDCG@10 0.7992 (IQON3000) and 0.7855 / 0.3302 (Polyvore), with NDCG improvements of 71.4% and 65.7% over CP-TransMatch — surprisingly large. HMGL-OCM's published AUC (0.9458 / 0.9372) is higher than CP-TransMatch's but still below APCL, though under a non-reproducible protocol. Ablations show removing the AP (indirect) module costs 2.9–5.7 AUC points and removing CL costs 2.0–7.3 points; removing the P module is catastrophic on IQON3000 (AUC 0.6654 vs 0.9739, top-as-given), showing the ID-embedding component carries most signal there. Long-tail analysis across interaction-frequency buckets ([0,2], (2,5], (5,10], (10,]) shows APCL leads in all buckets, with most samples in [0,2]. Hyperparameter sensitivity (temperature t ∈ [1,5] optimal; equal BPR/CL weighting optimal) is mild. Datasets are small/standard — no stress-scale testing. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an element of NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely novel piece is the reframing of indirect relations as explicit, dedicated learning views aligned via "functional-view" contrastive objectives (P↔IP, C↔IC) rather than implicit graph propagation — a conceptual distinction, though the ingredients (co-occurrence similarity dating to item-based CF 2001, attention pooling, transformers, InfoNCE, BPR, CLIP features) are all standard and the combination is incremental in mechanism. The empirical finding that relational-view alignment beats cross-modality alignment is the most interesting non-obvious result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and cover all six components (visual, textual, AP, CL, P, C) across both datasets and both directions — this is the paper's strongest rigor feature. A cross-modality-CL vs. functional-view-CL comparison directly tests the core claim. The authors describe a uniform grid-search tuning protocol, standardized preprocessing/seeds/optimizer across reimplemented baselines, and mention paired t-tests against second-best results, but no error bars, seed counts, or significance tables appear in the provided text. Code is released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/APCL-05BD; data are public benchmarks. Methodological concerns: (1) three baselines (DGSR, TransRec+V, HMGL-OCM) are compared via numbers copied from original publications under different preprocessing — a mixed-protocol comparison the authors at least flag transparently; (2) the claimed "10.1% improvement" is against the best reproduced baseline, while the strongest published number (HMGL-OCM) is only ~3% behind in AUC; (3) the cold-start and long-tail experiments compare APCL mainly against its own ablation rather than the full baseline suite; (4) large NDCG gains (65–71%) in the bottom-as-given setting warrant scrutiny of evaluation-protocol alignment. This is an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored artifact — released code). Practical: Yes — the model runs on standard hardware with modest components (MLPs, 2-head transformer, K neighbors); no GPU-scale requirements stated. Efficient: The authors report O(BD² + BKL + BnD² + Bn²D) time and O(|U|D + |R|D + ED² + BLD + BnD) memory, claiming near-linear scaling, but provide no wall-clock or memory measurements against baselines. Effective: Evidence supports the proxy task (AUC/HR/NDCG on held-out outfit triplets) convincingly, but there is no online A/B test or user study to show real-world recommendation quality. Scalable: Only claimed via complexity analysis; the largest test is 3,236 users / ~217K samples — two orders of magnitude below production e-commerce scale, and the O(BKL) co-occurrence precomputation cost at web scale is unexamined. Deliverable: released code (anonymous repo), no trained model weights or library mentioned. Strengths: (1) A clean conceptual contribution — promoting indirect relations from implicit propagation by-products to explicit, separately-optimizable views — that is easy to state, easy to reconstruct, and directly testable. (2) The functional-view vs. cross-modality contrastive comparison (Figure 6) is a well-designed experiment that tests the paper's distinctive claim rather than just aggregating tricks. (3) The ablation table is unusually thorough (six variants × two datasets × two directions × four metrics) and reveals an interesting asymmetry (the P module dominates on IQON3000 while visual features dominate on Polyvore). (4) Transparent handling of unreproducible baselines — published numbers are clearly separated from reproduced ones. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state three: (1) evaluation is restricted to top–bottom pairwise matching, excluding multi-category outfits; (2) the method depends on the availability of meaningful correlated users/products and may lose its advantage in extremely sparse regimes where such correlations vanish; (3) explicit relational construction adds computational overhead over simpler models. They confront these directly in the Discussion and Conclusion rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The cold-start experiment (Figure 9) only compares APCL against its own CL-ablated variant — the headline cold-start claim is never tested against external baselines. (2) The additive fusion p = s_p + s_c is never compared against learned or weighted fusion, leaving the "personalization and compatibility are not contradictory" claim only weakly tested. (3) No statistical reporting (seed variance, confidence intervals) despite mentioning t-tests. (4) The correlation-sampling similarity (cosine-normalized co-occurrence) is essentially 2001-era item-based CF; the paper does not compare against a simple kNN-CF + deep model hybrid, so the incremental value of the explicit machinery over cheap neighborhood heuristics feeding the same refiner is unquantified. (5) The direction-dependent result asymmetry (huge bottom-as-given gains) is noted but not explained mechanistically. (6) All experiments use one outfit category pair and one feature extractor (CLIP); sensitivity to the backbone is untested. Bottom Line: A solid, honestly-reported preprint whose explicit-indirect-relational-view framing is a genuine, testable idea for sparsity-robust complementary recommendation, but whose evidence base (small academic datasets, partially copied baselines, self-referential cold-start evaluation) means a practitioner should read it for the formulation and ablation insights, not as proof of production readiness.

#69 — Moderately Innovative (55)

SECO: Towards Code Compaction for Simulink via Verified Equivalence Extraction

Z Yu, Z Su, Y Yang, H Qiu, R Wang, Y Jiang… · suzcpp.github.io · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds SECO, a post-generation code compaction framework that uses LLMs to identify semantically equivalent code segments in Simulink-generated C code and admits a rewrite only after SMT-based equivalence checking confirms it. - Why it's important: Simulink-generated code ships on memory-constrained safety-critical controllers (automotive, aerospace), where every saved byte reduces silicon cost, and existing pattern-based merging misses structurally different but semantically equivalent code. - How it does it: It augments generated code with subsystem-boundary comments and constant parameterization so the LLM can reason at model level, then uses CBMC to verify input-output equivalence of a generated shared function against candidate segments, discarding anything unverified. - The good: The soundness-first design is validated end-to-end on real hardware across ARM, TriCore, and RISC-V, showing a 38.2% average assembly size reduction versus Simulink Embedded Coder/Frodo/SalSSA under -Oz with only 1.0% average runtime overhead. - The missing: Evaluation covers only 10 benchmark models (two from the authors' own industrial pipeline), there are no error bars or multi-seed runs despite LLM nondeterminism, and CBMC's floating-point semantics versus target-hardware behavior is never analyzed. - Read it or not: Worth reading for embedded-tooling and LLM-for-systems researchers who want a concrete template for pairing LLM proposals with formal verification gates; general PL/compilation readers can skip it, as the verification machinery (harness + CBMC) is standard.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building safety-critical embedded systems with model-based development deploy Simulink-generated code on resource-constrained microcontrollers, where code size drives memory footprint, chip area, and unit cost. Existing compaction is brittle: Simulink Embedded Coder merges only syntactically identical subsystems (same blocks, parameters, and configurations), and IR-level tools like SalSSA (LLVM SSA function merging) rely on structural similarity that fails when segments deviate from predefined patterns. Compiler approaches are also tied to specific IRs and cannot port across heterogeneous toolchains (e.g., GCC for TriCore vs. LLVM flows). LLMs could reason semantically, but they hallucinate plausible-but-wrong rewrites and offer no correctness guarantee, which is disqualifying for safety-critical deployment. Key Idea: Use Simulink model semantics as the partitioning context that makes LLM-guided candidate identification reliable, while never trusting the LLM: every candidate rewrite is admitted only if an SMT-backed equivalence check (via CBMC harnesses) proves semantic or contextual equivalence, and only if pre-compilation confirms an actual size win. The paper formalizes this as contextual equivalence (Definition 2) with a soundness corollary for extraction under a fixed context of segment-local constants. Methodology: Three phases. (1) Optimization-Aided Generation: Simulink Embedded Coder generates the reference C code; a custom parser extracts model semantics from the model's .xml files; the code is augmented by embedding subsystem-boundary comments (subsystem embedding) and replacing hardcoded constants with parameters via a parameterization map; a dataflow graph over blocks is built. (2) LLM-Assisted Extraction: an equivalence extraction agent (few-shot prompted with equivalence/counterexamples) proposes candidate segments and shared functions at two granularity levels (subsystem-level or free segments); a constraint checking agent validates format specifications (void return, pointer outputs, local variable scoping) and iteratively repairs syntax using compiler diagnostics up to COMPILE_ITER=3 attempts. (3) Semantic Equivalence Checking: candidate segments are mapped to the dataflow graph to derive input/output/local parameters, harness functions and harness files with output assertions are synthesized, and CBMC/Z3 verifies equivalence with a 300s timeout; failures produce compressed counterexample feedback to the extraction agent (VERIFY_ITER=3), after which candidates are discarded. Finally, pre-compilation of original vs. rewritten code retains only size-reducing rewrites. Critical design decisions: (a) subsystem embedding as LLM context — justified by an ablation showing variants without it reduce less code; (b) conservative discard on verification timeout — justified by the safety-critical setting but sacrifices completeness; (c) restricting extraction to loop-free segments inside loop bodies — stated in Discussion as what keeps CBMC tractable, a scope-limiting but sensible choice. Key Results: On 10 Simulink models (129–1,440 blocks, cyclomatic complexity 4–54) from SLNET and industrial pipelines, compiled with -Oz and deployed on ARM Cortex-A72, Infineon TriCore TC387, and XuanTie C906: SECO reduces assembly code size by 5.6%–90.7% versus Simulink Embedded Coder and Frodo, and by 5.6%–45.7% versus SalSSA on ARM. Table II per-model averages report 25.4% (SECO-4o) and 31.3% (SECO-5) reduction vs. Simulink, 61.0%/64.1% vs. Frodo, 21.5%/26.2% vs. SalSSA; the headline 38.2% figure appears to be aggregated across all four LLM backends (Table V reports 37.9%–42.5% vs. Simulink across backends). Runtime overhead vs. Simulink averages 0.6% (SECO-4o) and 1.4% (SECO-5) over 100,000-iteration executions; SECO is 18% faster than Frodo and, on the RAC model, 1.0%–1.3% faster than Simulink with 60.7% fewer L1-dcache-loads (120M vs. 305M, via perf). Extraction success rate (ES/(ES+DS)) is 86.5% (SECO-4o) and 94.0% (SECO-5). Ablation shows disabling subsystem embedding (SECO-*w) reduces gains on most models — SECO-4ow achieves zero reduction on OHC. Sensitivity study over four backends (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Claude-Opus-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) shows success rates of 84.1%–94.3% and offline costs of 95.1s–417.8s and 8,012–18,209 tokens per model. Baselines are reasonable: Simulink Embedded Coder is the production tool, SalSSA (PLDI 2020) is the strongest function-merging representative, Frodo is the authors' prior DAC'24 work; SalSSA could only run on ARM due to its LLVM-IR dependency. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is using Simulink model-level semantics (subsystem boundaries, constant parameterization) as an LLM-partitioning context for equivalence extraction, wrapped in a formally verified admit/discard loop — a formulation not present in prior generator- or compiler-level compaction. The individual ingredients (LLM agents with feedback loops, harness-based CBMC equivalence checking, function merging, pre-compile profitability filtering) are standard techniques composed competently for a new setting; the theoretical frame (semantic/contextual equivalence, Corollary 1) is a straightforward restatement. Rigor & Reproducibility: The ablation isolating subsystem embedding (RQ4) and the four-backend sensitivity study (RQ5) are genuine strengths, and per-phase timing/token breakdowns are reported. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests appear anywhere, despite LLM inference being stochastic — a notable omission since per-model size deltas between SECO-4o and SECO-5 are sometimes zero or a few bytes. Two of ten benchmarks come from the authors' own industrial pipelines (their prior Mercury/Knight work), and Frodo is the authors' own prior tool, so baseline provenance is partially self-referential. The artifact is stated to be public at https://github.com/YzhDDDing/SECO, which supports reproducibility. A methodological concern: soundness rests on CBMC's floating-point semantics exactly matching target hardware behavior (rounding, NaN handling, compiler FP flags), which the paper neither discusses nor tests; a verified-equivalent rewrite could still diverge on hardware if these semantics differ. Also, SalSSA is evaluated only via Clang on ARM while TriCore/RISC-V use GCC, so cross-toolchain comparisons on those platforms are Simulink-vs-SECO only (the authors do acknowledge this compiler-choice rationale in Discussion). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — a 24K-line C++/Python framework). Practical: Yes — runs on a single desktop (AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, 32GB RAM) with LLM APIs plus standard tools (GCC/Clang, CBMC). Efficient: Offline cost of 95–418 seconds and 8K–18K tokens per model is cheap for a build-time optimization; deployed-code cost is ≤1.4% average runtime overhead. Effective: The evidence supports the stated problem on the tested models — verified rewrites yield real measured size reductions on real hardware — though the 1.0% average overhead means some models trade time for space rather than winning both. Scalable: Untested beyond 1,440-block models; the 300s CBMC timeout already discards candidates with complex floating-point control flow, so scaling to larger or FP-heavy models likely increases the discard rate rather than breaking correctness. The work delivers a software artifact (GitHub repository with code and experimental results), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The soundness-gated LLM architecture is the right pattern for applying LLMs in safety-critical contexts — the case study of a rejected candidate (LLM produced Abs*c instead of Abs+c) concretely demonstrates the verification layer catching a real hallucination. (2) The subsystem-embedding idea is a genuinely clever bridge: it injects model-level structure lost during code generation, and the ablation (SECO-4ow failing entirely on OHC, and SECO-4o beating SECO-5w on most models) credibly shows the semantic context matters more than LLM capacity. (3) Evaluation breadth is above average for this area: three real embedded architectures, three baseline systems, runtime measured on-device over 100,000 iterations, plus a perf-based microarchitectural explanation (cache locality) for a counter-intuitive speedup. (4) The Discussion honestly maps out bounded-checking scope (loop-free segments only, state variables handled via explicit read/write splitting) rather than overclaiming generality. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: verification incompleteness (complex candidates time out at 300s and are conservatively discarded, sacrificing completeness for soundness); small runtime overhead from function calls and context preservation; platform dependence confined to the pre-compile analysis step (new targets need cross-toolchains); extension to other MDD tools (SCADE, Ptolemy-II) requiring new parsers; and per-backend trade-offs where stronger LLMs cost more tokens and time. These are confronted directly and quantified, which is a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge the FP-semantics question, LLM nondeterminism, or benchmark provenance issues. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Floating-point soundness gap: CBMC's SMT-based float reasoning must match target-architecture and compiler FP behavior (rounding modes, -ffast-math absence, FMA contraction) for the soundness guarantee to hold on-device; the paper deploys on hardware but never cross-checks verified equivalence against on-device behavior beyond aggregate timing — a silent assumption in a safety-critical pitch. (2) Statistical fragility: single runs, no seeds/variance, and a headline number (38.2%) that does not match the per-backend table averages (25.4%–42.5% vs. Simulink depending on the table), making the exact aggregation behind the headline unclear. (3) Small, partially self-sourced benchmark set (10 models; 2 from authors' industrial pipeline; Frodo is authors' own tool) with no external Simulink corpus coverage. (4) SalSSA (2020) is the only academic compiler-level baseline; no comparison against HyFM (2021), MergeFunctions, or binary-level tools like RollBin cited in their own related work. (5) The contextual-equivalence soundness corollary assumes the context c carries no side effects, but the formal justification that LLM-proposed segments never alias global state beyond what the harness captures rests on the Discussion's engineering argument, not on a checked property. (6) Hallucinated-but-equivalent-but-unprofitable rewrites are filtered by pre-compilation, yet the paper does not report how often verified rewrites fail the profitability filter, which limits understanding of where the pipeline loses yield. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing Simulink-based embedded development gains a concrete, verified, artifact-backed tool worth trying — the LLM-plus-formal-verification gating pattern alone is worth study — but the narrow benchmark set, missing statistical rigor, and unexamined floating-point semantics mean the reported 38.2% number should be treated as promising rather than settled, and the formal verification community has stronger pure function-merging alternatives if Simulink semantics are not in play.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a category-aware post-training framework for repository-level SWE agents that partitions tasks into three repository-domain categories, trains same-origin category experts via alternating agentic RL and self-repair SFT (Refresh–Repair–Expand), and consolidates them into one 27B model through label-routed multi-teacher on-policy distillation with ReLU-gated reward extrapolation. - Why it's important: Joint RL on heterogeneous SWE tasks exhibits a "category see-saw" — aggregate resolution improves while some task categories regress — and hidden category regressions cannot be diagnosed or fixed from a single pooled score. - How it does it: A hierarchical evidence-grounded labeler (SWE Labeler) maps tasks to a coarse A/B/C category partition that drives separate expert training streams, mastery-aware replay of verifier-approved self-trajectories, and per-task teacher routing during distillation — with no external teacher model supplying trajectories or action targets. - The good: The final integrated policy is evaluated across three rounds on two benchmarks and beats both Pooled RL and Balanced RL in aggregate and in every category: 58.04% on Pro-618 (+5.39 pp over the 52.64% base; +2.54 over Pooled RL) and 59.00% on SWE-bench Multilingual (+2.78 over base). - The missing: The authors explicitly state that no ablation isolates the contribution of individual components (RRE, replay choices, routing granularity, extrapolation gate, λ=1.25), so the framework is validated only as an indivisible whole against two joint-RL baselines. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building SWE or other agentic post-training pipelines who care about multi-capability training dynamics and expert consolidation; skippable if you only want a new RL algorithm, since Agentic-miniRL is a competent assembly of existing ideas (MiniRL, RLOO, K1-in-reward).

Problem & Motivation: Teams post-training LLM agents for repository-level software engineering train one shared policy on a pooled mixture of tasks that differ materially in trajectory length, reward variance, and skill demands (bug fixes, cross-module changes, build repairs, security patches). Under finite sampling and update budgets, pooled RL can improve some task groups at the expense of others while a single aggregate metric conceals the redistribution — the "category see-saw." Prior work either pools data (SWE-RL, SWE-Gym, SWE-Master), decomposes the inference workflow into stages (Agentless, SWE-Fixer, AutoCodeRover), or splits-and-fuses experts across conventional domain boundaries (Branch-Train-Merge, MOPD, ExOPD). No prior work, by the authors' account, partitions tasks within the single SWE domain into observable categories, trains category experts, and integrates them into one deployable policy. Key Idea: The core move is to treat a within-domain task taxonomy (not a domain boundary) as the axis of specialization: an evidence-grounded labeling system assigns each executable task a Repository Domain L1 label, a deterministic rule coarsens 18 domain families into three routable categories (A: service/data/security; B: user-facing applications; C: systems/tooling/runtimes), and this same category map drives (i) separate expert RL pools, (ii) mastery-adaptive data selection inside a Refresh–Repair–Expand loop, and (iii) label-routed teacher selection during multi-teacher on-policy distillation. The ReLU gate on the extrapolation term — keeping only tokens where the teacher exceeds the reference policy — is the specific trick that converts a signed, canceling residual into a systematically nonnegative learning signal. Methodology: Four stages. (1) Task construction: ~32K executable candidates from merged PRs and issues, with leakage checks, deduplication, gold-patch fail-to-pass/pass-to-pass validation, and Docker-based environments (RepoLaunch); combined with a four-language slice of SWE-rebench V2 to form the 6,723-task training corpus. (2) SWE Labeler: an LLM-based (Qwen3.7-max) two-stage hierarchical annotator producing 26 Task Type L1/119 L2 and 21 Domain L1/108 L2 labels plus three 4-level scale axes; every L2 label is a decision record (authoritative source, e.g., CWE/ISO 14764, operational rule, positive signals, boundary notes). (3) Expert training: each category expert starts from the same Qwen3.6-27B base and alternates Agentic-miniRL (RLOO with G=8 rollouts, K1 log-ratio placed in the reward path before return-to-go, clipped importance-weight behavior correction, sign-aware proximal mask, turn-aware loss reduction over assistant turns) with Repair SFT on its own verifier-approved successful trajectories, quota-allocated by current 4-rollout mastery estimates; between RL rounds the policy probes an expanded pool of previously omitted base-zero/base-one instances. (4) Integration: the student, re-initialized from the base, generates on-policy trajectories; per-task routed teachers supply an advantage A = Σ_k m_k(x)[−d_t,k + (λ_k−1)·max(e_t,k, 0)] with λ_k=1.25, clipped to [−5,5], optimized by vanilla policy gradient with the turn-aware reduction; environment reward is not used in the student loss. Critical design decisions: RLOO over mean-centered GRPO (justified analytically — it restores the (G−1)/G advantage shrinkage for rare successes), K1-in-reward over K3-as-loss (citing prior gradient-bias analysis), and same-origin teachers (justified by shared tokenization/interface, though the authors admit same-origin teachers may add too little signal). A detailed anti-hacking protocol (repository sanitization, deferred test injection, fresh-sandbox replay, trajectory auditing for external answer retrieval) protects reward integrity. Key Results: On Pro-618 (an audit-filtered 618-instance subset of SWE-bench Pro, categories 221/201/196), the final MOPD policy achieves 58.04% ± 0.20 mean resolution vs. 52.64% base, 55.50% ± 0.46 Pooled RL, and 55.34% ± 0.92 Balanced RL — a category-wise Pareto improvement with per-category lifts of +3.32/+2.65/+1.53 over Pooled RL. The three pre-integration experts reach 59.58%/58.87%/57.48% on their target categories (+7.84/+4.48/+5.61 over base), and MOPD recovers 80.8%/111.1%/84.8% of those gains. On SWE-bench Multilingual (300 tasks, SWE-agent scaffold), MOPD reaches 59.00% vs. 56.22% base and 57.00% Balanced RL, though the paired bootstrap 95% CI versus Balanced RL ([−0.78, 4.78]) crosses zero. Balanced RL, using only 1,548 of 6,723 tasks, matches Pooled RL overall (+2.70 vs +2.86 pp) but does not reduce the see-saw gap, motivating the expert route. Instance-level diagnostics show 30.3% of 2,769 training records regress during initial RL despite category-mean gains of 4.60–7.26 pp; Repair SFT recovers 61–73% of regressed records that received repair examples. Baselines (Pooled RL, Balanced RL) are the authors' own implementations under an identical Agentic-miniRL recipe rather than published external systems; scale is a standard 27B model on ~6.7K tasks — real but not stress-scale. A notable honest finding: minimum category gain (G_sim) and aggregate gain trade off, and MOPD's SSG (0.63) is slightly worse than Pooled RL's (0.54). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (partially) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the intra-domain category-expert specialization-and-integration setting for repository-level SWE, the RRE policy-adaptive frontier loop with mastery-refreshed self-repair, the SWE Labeler artifact, and the empirical demonstration that balancing mixture proportions does not resolve the see-saw. The RL and distillation machinery is a competent combination of existing components — MiniRL, RLOO, K1-in-reward, MOPD (Ma et al., 2026), and ExOPD extrapolation (Yang et al., 2026), the latter two adopted nearly as-is with the ReLU gate as the modification. Rigor & Reproducibility: Three-round evaluations with population standard deviations are reported for endpoint comparisons; paired instance-bootstrap 95% CIs appear only for Multilingual Full differences (and the vs.-Balanced interval includes zero). Training uses a single seed (42) per configuration with no multi-seed variance. Ablations are absent by the authors' own admission — no component isolation of RRE stages, replay quotas, routing granularity, λ, or the ReLU gate. Checkpoint selection on Pro-618 makes it partially a development benchmark, though final models are also evaluated on held-out Multilingual; only two of three Multilingual comparisons are statistically clean. The Pro-618 exclusion of 113 instances is documented against public audit artifacts with an explicit accounting table — a credibility positive, though it means headline numbers are not comparable to other SWE-bench Pro reports. No public code, data, or model release URL is stated in the provided text. Reward-hacking defenses are unusually thorough for this literature. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with executable evaluation; no formal claims). Practical: Requires 27B-class models with 64 devices for RL (32 train + 32 vLLM inference), per-task sandboxes with 4 CPUs/16 GiB, and 131K-token contexts — feasible for well-resourced labs, not commodity hardware. Efficient: Substantially more expensive than pooled RL (three expert pipelines × two RL phases + two SFT phases, plus K+1 frozen teacher forwards during distillation); the authors concede the compute overhead. Effective: Evidence supports the stated goal on two benchmarks with per-category wins, but expert-gain recovery is incomplete (80.8% on category A) and hard routing leaves multi-category tasks mis-served. Scalable: Not tested beyond three categories and one base model; behavior at 10× categories or data is unexamined and the authors note best K may vary. The work delivers a framework and (implicitly) trained model weights internal to Alibaba; no reusable artifact release is stated in the provided text. Strengths: - The see-saw diagnosis is genuinely informative: decomposing pooled-RL gains into G_sim and an SSG metric, with a table interpreting their joint movements, turns a vague multi-task interference concern into a measurable quantity — and the Balanced RL control shows data rebalancing alone does not fix it. - Instance-level mastery tracking (30.3% of training records regress under initial RL; 61–73% of repaired regressed records recover) is a level of diagnostic granularity rarely reported in SWE-agent papers, and it directly motivates each RRE component. - The reward-integrity protocol (git-history sanitization, deferred test injection, fresh-sandbox patch replay, trajectory auditing for external fix retrieval) addresses documented failure modes in executable SWE training that most contemporaneous work ignores. - Teacher-free expert development (RL first, self-repair from verifier-approved own rollouts) removes the dependence on a stronger external trajectory teacher that most SWE post-training pipelines require. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: hard one-to-one routing ignores multi-category tasks; training multiple experts plus teacher forwards adds substantial compute and best K is unknown; same-origin teachers may be too similar or too distant for stable integration; test-driven rewards can invite hacking or reflect brittle specifications and their controls do not eliminate pretraining memorization; results on Pro-618 do not generalize to the full unexecuted Pro set; and — explicitly — the experiments evaluate the complete framework and do not isolate component contributions, with single-run category trajectories confounded by evaluation variability. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section; the missing-ablation admission is unusually candid. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline comparison lacks any external baseline: no published SWE post-training system (SWE-RL, SWE-Gym, SWE-Master) is run under the same scaffold, so the +2.54 pp win is only over the authors' own pooled/balanced variants of the same recipe. - The MOPD integration is never compared against cheaper consolidation alternatives (parameter merging, Branch-Train-Merge, simple expert-weight averaging), so the reader cannot tell whether routing-based distillation is necessary or merely sufficient. - Only three coarse categories from one routing axis are tested; the richer 227-label taxonomy is built but never used for specialization, leaving the central design's granularity choice unvalidated. - The Multilingual result versus Balanced RL is not statistically significant (CI includes zero), yet the abstract-level narrative reports it as an improvement alongside Pro-618. - Category B contains only 516 instances and Multilingual B only 25, so per-category conclusions rest on thin strata; and the balanced-control comparison (1,548 vs. 6,723 tasks) confounds mixture balance with total data volume. - Teacher quality attribution is circular in one respect: experts are selected by target-category Pro-618 scores and then evaluated on those same category subsets used for selection. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic RL pipelines for heterogeneous coding tasks will gain a concrete, well-diagnosed template — category-aware expert streams plus routed on-policy distillation — that demonstrably beats its own pooled baseline on two benchmarks, but the absence of external baselines, ablations, and released artifacts means its components should be treated as a promising recipe to replicate rather than a validated optimum.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WorldCrafter, a camera-controllable autoregressive video world model that compresses historical observations into a fixed-budget, pose-queryable implicit 3D-aware memory, improving revisit consistency and camera-control accuracy during minute-scale interactive exploration. - Why it's important: Real-time interactive world models forget scenes once content leaves the context window, so revisited regions are regenerated inconsistently — a core blocker for using video world models as persistent, explorable environments. - How it does it: A memory encoder initialized from a pretrained novel-view-synthesis representation (LagerNVS) maps retrieved history latents into a compact 3D-aware representation, from which a pose-guided readout module extracts a fixed set of target-view-specific tokens that condition the video DiT via self-attention — no depth estimation or warping. - The good: The strongest evidence is the ablation-backed revisit-consistency gain: WorldCrafter reaches 0.255 LPIPS / 18.016 PSNR on matched first-visit/revisit frames versus 0.487 / 14.050 for the best of 8 baselines (Lyra 2.0), and each memory-design choice is individually ablated. - The missing: All quantitative evaluation runs on the authors' own curated 145-image benchmark with no public benchmark, no released code or weights mentioned, and a mixed evaluation protocol where some baselines run full-step and others distilled. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building memory mechanisms into video world models — the implicit-memory-vs-spatial-memory comparison and 21.7× memory-processing speedup are directly relevant — but skip it if you need reproducible artifacts, since none appear to be released.

Problem & Motivation: Interactive video world models (e.g., Genie-3-style systems, camera-controllable streaming video diffusion) let users explore generated environments by moving a camera, but they must remember scenes observed minutes earlier so revisits look consistent. Existing memory solutions each fail in a distinct way: full-history attention is computationally prohibitive; frame-retrieval/context memory covers too few views; explicit spatial memories (depth estimation + warping toward target views, as in Lyra 2.0, Alaya-EVOKE, Matrix-Game 3.5) provide geometric alignment but overconstrain dynamics and cost ~1.35 s/chunk in depth+warping; geometry-pretrained implicit encoders (VGGT-based, e.g., CineScene, GIM-World) prioritize geometric prediction over the appearance fidelity needed to visually reproduce a previously seen scene. The paper targets anyone building long-horizon, camera-controlled world models that need both dynamic content and faithful recall. Key Idea: Reuse a pretrained latent novel-view-synthesis representation (LagerNVS) as the memory space — because NVS training forces the encoder to preserve both geometry and appearance across views — and let the requested future viewpoint shape which information is compressed into the generator's fixed token budget via a pose-guided readout, rather than leaving the DiT attention to search an uncompressed or view-agnostic memory. Joint optimization of encoder, readout, and DiT lets the memory co-adapt to the generator's token space. Methodology: The system is a chunk-wise autoregressive latent video diffusion model (flow matching, DiT initialized from Helios-base) conditioned on [M; z_r; z_t]: memory tokens M, a recent-context window z_r, and the noisy current chunk z_t, plus UCPE-based parallel camera-attention (PRoPE-style relative pose encoding, zero-initialized, applied only to the noisy tokens). Pipeline per rollout step: (1) max-coverage retrieval greedily selects k−1 history latent frames whose joint field of view best covers the upcoming trajectory (plus the latest frame); (2) the memory encoder Φ (LagerNVS-initialized, latent patch embedding, relative camera tokens) maps selected latents to representation tokens R; (3) a readout module (LagerNVS decoder layers + projections) queries R with sampled target poses C_q to emit a fixed-size M (token count equal to 4 full frames); (4) the DiT denoises the chunk, which is appended to history. Training is 4 staged phases: window adaptation (760K OSP videos, 5K iters), camera-branch training with frozen DiT (46K videos), memory-encoder warm-up, and joint encoder+readout+DiT+camera training with a final 1K-iteration synthetic (MIND) adaptation. Real-time interaction comes from pyramid distribution-matching distillation (3 resolutions × 2 steps) with a hybrid trick: a high-noise model distilled with synthetic data handles subject-following while a low-noise model distilled without it performs the last step to avoid smeared textures; WorldCrafter-fast reaches 16 fps on 4 GPUs. Critical design decisions — pose-guided over pose-free readout, joint over frozen encoder optimization, max-coverage over similarity-based retrieval — are each justified by controlled ablations (Table 4, Figure 5). Key Results: On the authors' curated benchmark (145 images from HappyOyster, Project Genie, web sources, and GPT-Image2; 83 dynamic / 62 static scenes; 5 metric trajectories each = 725 videos of 528–1,648 frames with closed-loop revisits, resized to 640×384): revisit consistency of MEt3R 0.166 / LPIPS 0.255 / PSNR 18.016 / SSIM 0.517 (WorldCrafter) and 0.129 / 0.186 / 20.868 / 0.616 (WorldCrafter-fast), versus the strongest baseline Lyra 2.0 at 0.334 / 0.487 / 14.050 / 0.390 — a stated 47.6% relative improvement over the strongest baseline. Camera control: lowest RotErr (13.536°), TransErr (1.475), CamMC (1.546) among 9 methods; the distilled variant drops to third (18.251° RotErr). VBench custom-input mode: best overall score 81.910 (vs. 81.406 Alaya-EVOKE, 80.841 SANA-WM), best in 5 of 8 dimensions. Ablations show context memory degrades MEt3R to 0.382, frozen encoder to 0.227, pose-free readout to 0.251, and similarity-based retrieval to 0.213. Memory processing costs 0.062 s/chunk (0.049 s encode + 0.013 s readout) versus 1.346 s for depth estimation + warping — a 21.7× reduction. Baselines are recent (2025–2026) camera-controllable world models and appear current; notably WorldCrafter-fast beats the full-precision baselines on revisit consistency, an unusual and slightly counter-intuitive result the authors do not dig into. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (implicit 3D-aware memory with pose-guided readout for video world models) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (appearance-preserving NVS representations transfer better to world-model memory than geometry-estimation representations, and joint encoder-generator optimization materially outperforms a frozen encoder). The surrounding machinery — flow-matching DiT, chunk-wise autoregression, UCPE/PRoPE camera conditioning, DMD distillation, FramePack-style context — is a competent combination of existing techniques; the genuinely new element is repurposing a latent-NVS encoder as a jointly-trained, pose-queried memory interface and the max-coverage retrieval scheme. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a genuine strength: four single-factor variants (context memory, frozen encoder, pose-free readout, similarity retrieval) under matched training, inference, and token budgets, plus latency measurements and a revisit-interval sweep showing the memory advantage widens with horizon. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; all metrics come from the authors' own newly curated benchmark (Goodhart risk — the method is developed and evaluated on the same data distribution, and the benchmark is not stated as public); baselines are evaluated under heterogeneous conditions (full-step with refiner for SANA-WM, full-step for Lyra 2.0 and HY-WorldPlay, distilled for the rest), which complicates fair comparison; camera-pose ground truth for evaluation relies on VGGT-Ω estimation rather than known poses for all settings. No code, weights, or benchmark release is mentioned — only a project page (drexubery.github.io/WorldCrafter). The work is an arXiv preprint, so results are not yet peer-reviewed, and the paper originates from an industrial lab (Tencent ARC Lab) with several baseline systems from other companies evaluated by the authors. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — a real-time interactive demo). Practical: Yes in principle — 16 fps on a 4-GPU machine for the distilled model, though the GPU type is unstated and the base model's speed is not given. Efficient: Memory processing is 21.7× cheaper than depth-based spatial memory (0.062 s vs 1.346 s per chunk at 640×384), but per-chunk history re-encoding adds latency the authors themselves flag. Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem on the authors' proxy — matched-frame revisit metrics and estimated-pose camera error — not user studies or physical-consistency tests in a deployed product. Scalable: Untested beyond ~1,648-frame trajectories and 640×384 resolution; the fixed k=9-frame encoder input means memory capacity does not grow with horizon, and behavior at 10× longer explorations is claimed only qualitatively. The work stops at paper form plus a project page; no reusable artifact is documented as released. Strengths: (1) The memory-space choice is a real insight with a falsifiable rationale — NVS pretraining demands appearance-and-geometry preservation, unlike geometry-estimator pretraining — and the ablation against context memory (MEt3R 0.166 vs 0.382) directly tests it. (2) The pose-guided readout reframes memory as budget allocation under a fixed token constraint, and the pose-free ablation (MEt3R 0.251 vs 0.166) confirms the allocation argument rather than just capacity. (3) The efficiency analysis is unusually concrete: per-component latency breakdown showing the 21.7× cost reduction over depth+warping pipelines. (4) The hybrid distillation split (high-noise model with synthetic data for subject-following, low-noise model without it for texture fidelity) is a practical, well-motivated solution to a real distillation trade-off. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that consistency can still break along particularly complex or extended trajectories, and that re-encoding history at every chunk incurs extra latency; they propose an autoregressive streaming memory encoder as future work. These are stated plainly in the Discussion without minimization, which is credible — but the acknowledgment is brief and no failure cases are shown quantitatively. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The evaluation benchmark is self-curated and not stated to be public, so the headline numbers cannot be independently checked and the method was tuned on its own test distribution. (2) The revisit-consistency protocol compares generated revisits to generated first-visits — a model could score well by globally reducing drift or smoothing detail, and the PSNR/LPIPS/MEt3R agreement does not rule out fidelity loss; a visual-quality-per-scene-detail check is missing. (3) Baseline conditions are inconsistent (some full-step, some distilled), so the claim that WorldCrafter-fast outperforms full-precision baselines on memory may partly reflect evaluation asymmetry. (4) The memory encoder sees at most 9 frames (~2–3 chunks of history); behavior when the relevant observation falls outside this selection window — e.g., a subject seen once, 50 chunks ago — is central to the motivation (Figure 1c shows it qualitatively) but is never isolated quantitatively against retrieval failure. (5) All camera ground truth for evaluation comes from VGGT-Ω pose estimation, which could bias camera-error metrics toward methods whose generations are VGGT-friendly. (6) Training scale is modest (thousands of iterations per stage) and the data-mixture effects (synthetic vs. real) are described anecdotally ("smeared textures") without measurement. Bottom Line: A practitioner building long-horizon, camera-controlled world models should read this for the concrete evidence that jointly-trained NVS-derived implicit memories beat both context retrieval and depth-warping spatial memory on cost and revisit consistency — but should treat the absolute numbers as unverified until an independent reproduction exists, since everything rests on a private benchmark with no released artifacts.

TL;DR - What it does: This MSc thesis (partially published at RecSys '25) introduces a pre-processing step that uses LLM-generated user profiles to filter "out-of-character" items from a user's history before running the ACCENT influence-based counterfactual explanation framework, and proposes two new popularity-alignment metrics (PDS and EPD) to diagnose the problem. - Why it's important: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) in recommenders can be formally valid yet feel arbitrary to users when they cite atypical items, undermining the trust that explanations exist to build; this is the first systematic study of popularity bias inside the CFE generation process itself. - How it does it: The method greedily removes history items whose deletion most perturbs an LLM-written natural-language user profile (embedded via SBERT), then feeds the filtered history to ACCENT, so influence-based counterfactuals can no longer cite the misaligned items. - The good: The most credible finding is a bidirectional correction effect on MovieLens 1M: LLM-8B filtering cuts PDS for blockbuster users from 18.36 to 6.26 and for niche users from 7.12 to 5.30, while explanation size, coverage, and surrogate necessity/sufficiency stay roughly unchanged — and it is the only variant with a statistically significant gain over ACCENT (EPD 0.014 vs. 0.017, p < 0.05). - The missing: Only one result in the entire study is statistically significant, evaluation is restricted to 736 extreme users with histories capped at 100 interactions on a single recommender (NeuMF) and a single CFE framework, and all "alignment" evidence is offline proxy metrics — no user study is run. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in explainable recommender systems who care about bias in explanation pipelines and want the PDS/EPD metrics and the misalignment diagnosis; practitioners seeking deployable explanation methods can skip it given the cost and the thin, single-metric significance.

Problem & Motivation: Users of recommender systems increasingly demand explanations, and counterfactual explanations — "you were recommended X because you liked A and B; otherwise you'd have seen Y" — are empirically preferred by users over generic transparency statements. The Rashomon effect means many valid counterfactual sets exist for one recommendation, and the thesis argues the chosen set should match the user's perceived preferences, not just formal criteria. Its specific concern is that influence-function-based CFE methods like ACCENT (SIGIR '21) inherit popularity bias: popular items have disproportionate training leverage and hence high influence scores, so CFE sets skew toward blockbusters for niche-oriented users (and vice versa). Prior work on CFE selection addressed proximity or diversity, not user-alignment, and no prior metric quantified popularity misalignment of explanations. The gap closed is the absence of any diagnosis or mitigation of bias in the explanation layer as distinct from the recommendation layer. Key Idea: Measure how much removing each history item changes a semantic representation of the user — either a sum of SBERT item embeddings or, better, an embedding of a 300-word LLM-written preference profile — and pre-filter the items whose removal most perturbs that profile, so that ACCENT's influence-based search operates only on items consistent with the user's self-perceived taste. The LLM acts as a cheap semantic judge of "does this item belong to this user?", which popularity-blind influence scores cannot do. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) train a NeuMF recommender (embedding size 16, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-3) on 80% of interactions; (2) build a user profile — embedding variant: e_u = Σ SBERT(item metadata); LLM variant: t_u = LLM(concatenated item descriptions), then e_u = SBERT(t_u); (3) run a greedy algorithm for n iterations, at each step removing the candidate item whose deletion maximizes cosine dissimilarity between the current profile and the profile built without it (the LLM variant regenerates the full textual profile per candidate, costing O(n·s·T_LLM) LLM calls); (4) run ACCENT — which extends Koh & Liang influence functions to item-pair score gaps and sums per-point influences until removal of set Z flips the rec/rec* ranking — on the filtered history H_u \ τ_u. Evaluation uses two proposed metrics: Popularity Distribution Similarity (χ² distance between binned popularity histograms of history items vs. counterfactual items) and Expected Popularity Deviation (per-user squared difference of mean popularity, averaged). Validity is assessed via surrogate-model necessity/sufficiency (Watson et al. framework), counterfactual set size, LLM-extracted aspect overlap, and coverage. Critical design decisions: greedy rather than exhaustive subset search (justified by factorial blowup, but greedy is known to be suboptimal); pre-processing rather than modifying ACCENT's objective (simple, framework-agnostic, but cannot repair deeper misalignment); using the same embedding model for both variants (mxbai-embed-large-v1), which keeps the comparison controlled. The n-item filter size is left as a hyperparameter (n=5 on ML-1M, n=1 on Amazon) without a sensitivity study. Key Results: Tested on MovieLens 1M (6,040 users, 3,952 items, 1,000,209 interactions, 4.19% density) and Amazon VideoGames 5-core (94,761 users, 25,612 items, 814,587 interactions, 0.03% density), on 736 users: the 250 most niche and 250 most blockbuster users per dataset, capped at ≤100 history interactions. RQ1: ACCENT is systematically misaligned — on ML-1M, PDS is 7.12 (niche) and 18.36 (blockbuster) versus the random-removal augmentation's 7.38/7.93, and on Amazon 3.54/14.29. RQ2: LLM-8B augmentation yields the most consistent alignment gains (ML-1M blockbuster PDS 18.36→6.26; niche 7.12→5.30; Amazon blockbuster 14.29→6.06), with a bidirectional correction — counterfactuals move toward popular items for blockbuster users and away for niche users. Embedding-based filtering wins only for ML-1M niche users (PDS 2.42). Notably, the simple top-influential (FIA-score) removal baseline achieves the lowest EPD on both datasets for both groups, arguably a stronger result than the LLM method on that metric. RQ3: 8B (Qwen3, quantized Q3_K_S) outperforms 4B (Gemma3) — e.g., ML-1M blockbuster PDS 10.39→6.26 — and the 4B model exhibited instruction-following failures including hallucinated summaries and mid-response language switches. Validity is preserved: mean CF set size 1.32 vs. 1.35 (ML-1M), aspect overlap 0.207 vs. 0.189, coverage 78.8% vs. 80.2% (Amazon 72.7% vs. 72.9%). Only one comparison is statistically significant: overall EPD on ML-1M, LLM-8B vs. ACCENT (0.014 vs. 0.017, p < 0.05). Scale is modest — a single small recommender, ≤100-item histories, ~500 users per dataset — i.e., standard benchmark scale with extreme-user subsampling, not stress-scale. A surprising unexplained anomaly: reported nDCG@10 of 1.303 on ML-1M exceeds the metric's theoretical maximum of 1. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first quantification of popularity misalignment in influence-based CFEs, via two new metrics — PDS and EPD are NEW FORMULATION contributions at metric level) plus NEW METHOD (LLM-profile-based history filtering as a CFE pre-processing step). The mechanism itself — greedy item removal scored by cosine similarity of SBERT embeddings — is a standard combination of known components (LLM profiling, Sentence-BERT, greedy search, off-the-shelf ACCENT) applied to a new problem setting; the genuinely new element is the diagnosis that influence scores inherit popularity bias and the demonstration that semantic filtering corrects it bidirectionally. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partially present: multiple filtering strategies (embedding, LLM-4B, LLM-8B, top-influential, top-popular, random) are compared against ACCENT and direct set-construction baselines, which is a reasonable ablation space, but the filter size n is not swept and no per-component ablation of the LLM prompt is given. Statistical testing is minimal — exactly one significance test is reported; no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed runs are given for the NeuMF training or the stochastic LLM outputs. Code is released at https://github.com/ahasami/llm-augmented-cfs, forked from the public ACCENT codebase; no dataset splits or model weights beyond what the repo contains are mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation is confined to the authors' own extreme-user construction on two datasets, neither of which was used for method development in a circular way, but only one recommender and one CFE framework are tested; (2) the aspect-overlap evaluation uses the DeepSeek v3 API while the method itself uses an LLM, creating an LLM-judges-LLM circularity risk; (3) validity is measured through a lightweight surrogate classifier rather than the retraining-based counterfactual proximity ACCENT's original evaluation used, so fidelity claims are proxy-based; (4) the nDCG@10 = 1.303 value on ML-1M is mathematically impossible for exact nDCG and is not discussed, suggesting a reporting or metric-definition error; (5) the 4B-vs-8B "size" comparison confounds model family (Gemma3 vs. Qwen3) with scale. The thesis is a preprint-stage MSc thesis with one peer-reviewed RecSys '25 short paper covering part of it; the RecSys portion carries higher confidence than the thesis-only material. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — released code). - Practical: Yes — all components (NeuMF, SBERT, quantized 4B/8B open-weight LLMs) run on commodity single-GPU hardware, though the LLM filter needs 10–15 seconds per profile query. - Efficient: Poorly — the LLM variant costs O(n·s·T_LLM) LLM calls per user (queries scale with filter size × history length), which is why users with >100 interactions were excluded; the embedding variant is O(n·d·s) and cheap. - Effective: Partially — alignment improves on a popularity proxy (one significant EPD result), but the paper does not show users actually perceive or value the corrected explanations, and the stronger EPD baseline (top-influential removal) undercuts the necessity of an LLM. - Scalable: Not tested — 736 curated users with ≤100-item histories is far below production scale, and the authors themselves concede the runtime "might limit scalability to large-scale or real-time applications"; no experiment supports scaling claims. Deliverable: a released code repository implementing the filtering pipeline plus reusable PDS/EPD metrics; no trained models or packaged library. Strengths: - The core diagnosis is genuine and new: influence-based CFEs systematically surface popularity-biased items, quantified with two concrete, reusable metrics (PDS via χ² distance; per-user EPD), applied to 736 extreme users across two contrasting datasets (dense vs. extremely sparse). - The bidirectional correction finding — the LLM filter pushes explanations toward popularity for blockbuster users and away for niche users, rather than toward a global average — is a non-obvious result that distinguishes semantic filtering from any fixed popularity heuristic. - Honest baseline design: the top-influential (FIA-score) ablation is reported even though it beats the LLM method on EPD for both datasets, and the paper acknowledges that random augmentation on Amazon outperforms everything on PDS due to sparsity artifacts. - The validity-preservation analysis (set size, coverage, surrogate necessity/sufficiency before and after filtering) directly checks that alignment gains do not come at the cost of causal fidelity, which many explanation papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront: data sparsity (Amazon's ~4-item histories make profile inference unreliable); LLM hallucination and inconsistency, including that some individual users may receive worse explanations; the philosophical tension of using an opaque LLM to produce transparent explanations; high computational cost (full O(n·s·T_LLM) complexity analysis in §7.4); reduced coverage with a proposed fallback to raw ACCENT; and the fact that most gains are small in absolute terms, with only one significant result, requiring user studies to establish practical significance. This is a credibility positive — limitations are stated candidly and not minimized. They also correctly flag in future work that the misalignment may originate in the popularity-biased NeuMF recommender rather than ACCENT itself, and that only the popularity axis of alignment was evaluated. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The comparison of Gemma3-4B vs. Qwen3-8B conflates parameter count with model family, training data, and quantization; the RQ3 conclusion "bigger is better" is not supported by a controlled size ablation within one family. - The nDCG@10 of 1.303 on ML-1M exceeds the metric's range and is never explained or corrected — a red flag for the correctness of the evaluation harness or the negative-sampling procedure that goes unexamined. - Necessity/sufficiency are computed with a surrogate classifier rather than retraining, yet are presented as evidence of preserved "causal validity"; the surrogate's own fidelity to the NeuMF is never validated. - The aspect-overlap metric relies on an LLM judge (DeepSeek v3) while the method itself injects LLM-written profiles, so any improvement in aspect overlap could partly reflect shared LLM biases rather than genuine user-alignment gains. - No experiment isolates whether the misalignment stems from the recommender or ACCENT (acknowledged as future work), and no debiased recommender is tried — so the central causal claim about the source of misalignment rests on argument, not measurement. - Only users at the niche/blockbuster extremes are evaluated; behavior on the 60% "diverse" majority, who are the bulk of real traffic, is unknown. - The filter size n (5 for ML-1M, 1 for Amazon) is chosen without justification or sensitivity analysis, and the interaction between n and the alignment/validity trade-off is unexplored. Bottom Line: A readable, honest, and diagnostically valuable thesis that establishes popularity misalignment in influence-based CFEs and contributes reusable metrics, but with one statistically significant result, proxy-only fidelity evaluation, and a costly filter beaten on one of its two metrics by a trivial baseline, it is a promising workshop-to-short-paper contribution rather than a must-read — researchers extending bias-aware explainability should read it for the diagnosis and metrics, practitioners should wait for the user studies and scalability work.

Qwen-Planner-Agent: A Closed-Loop AI-for-AI Framework for Real-World Mobile Planner Agents (9 ▲ )

Tingyu Qu, Weigao Sun, Yuecheng Liu, Yucheng Zhao, Yi Zhu, Yifeng Ding, Qiyi Wang, Sihan Cao, Pengkun Jiao, Hanlei Xie, Xiongwei Wu, Qichao Wang, Haodong Zhang, Jiajun Liu, Yuhao Wang, Yuqing Xie, Junpeng Zhao, Long Chen, Ming Ma, Sihan Yang, Ziwang Zhao, Yanhao Jia, Liangquan Gong, Feida Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Steven Hoi · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Qwen-Planner-Agent, a 27B/35B-A3B Planner Model plus runtime Harness system for mobile planning tasks, built through a closed-loop "AI-for-AI" development framework that converts execution feedback into new training data, reward scheduling, and Harness revisions. - Why it's important: Real-device mobile-agent development is bottlenecked by costly, hard-to-parallelize device interaction, and long-horizon mobile tasks (cross-app coordination, state tracking, recovery) remain unreliable for frontier LLMs; a feedback-driven lifecycle attacks both the data-scale and reliability problems. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a shared action-feedback-verification contract connecting three loops — an agent-driven data flywheel, hybrid-environment online agentic RL with Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) that reweights efficiency rewards only for success-saturated trajectory groups, and alternating model-training / LLM-edited-Harness refinement cycles. - The good: The advantage-calibration analysis is genuinely quantitative: the paper derives that GRPO-style normalization restores unit-scale advantages to efficiency-only signals even with a small efficiency weight (λ_eff = 0.1), and ablations show full CARE cuts output tokens by 32.5% at comparable training accuracy while calibration-free CARE trades accuracy for brevity. - The missing: The headline benchmark (MobilePA-Bench) is authored by the same team, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and no code, data, or model weights are released — so the frontier-beating margin (77.05% vs. 76.84% for GPT 6 Astra) cannot be independently verified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building agentic RL pipelines or agent scaffolds, particularly for the CARE normalization analysis and the model–harness co-evolution ablations (+5.83/+8.98 pp on internal/MCPMark), but the framework-level "AI-for-AI" framing is largely packaging around competent, known techniques.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building mobile agents face two coupled problems: complex long-horizon tasks (multi-app dependencies, changing state, failure recovery, completion verification) strain agent reliability, and real-device interaction is expensive and hard to parallelize, limiting how much development and evaluation data can be produced. Prior mobile-agent training (DigiRL, MobileRL, Mobile-R1, PhoneBuddy) mostly uses fixed reward designs and single-environment backends, and treats the runtime scaffold (memory, skills, tool exposure) as static rather than co-adapted with the model. The paper targets researchers and product teams who need to train and iterate on real-world planner agents at scale without per-task human trajectory authoring. Key Idea: The single transferable insight is competence-conditioned learning-signal scheduling: rather than a fixed reward, classify each rollout group by its success rate and switch the auxiliary reward (progress shaping → outcome consolidation → efficiency refinement) and the advantage normalization anchor as the policy's competence on that task grows. The supporting derivation shows why the efficiency stage needs a calibration floor — within-group normalization of a success-saturated group reduces the advantage to approximately −(e_i − ē)/σ_e regardless of λ_eff, so small efficiency differences acquire unit-scale influence unless the normalization denominator is floored at σ_anchor = √(p_high(1 − p_high)). Methodology: The pipeline has three phases under a common POMDP-style formulation (policy sees observations through a Harness context function H_η, acts from a structured typed action space, and a task verifier V produces outcomes from execution evidence ξ not necessarily visible to the policy). (i) AI for Data: LLM task-construction agents emit executable task specifications with completion criteria; rollouts run against three backends — programmatic sandboxes, LLM-simulated environments, and selective real-device sessions — and curation separates completion verification from learning-suitability checks, with human gates before each data release; development-set failures drive down-sampling of mastered tasks, up-weighting of unstable ones, and construction of new coverage tasks. (ii) AI for Training: supervised cold start with turn-level error masking (cross-entropy over unmasked, non-erroneous turns, Eq. 4), then online agentic RL on GRPO-style clipped group-relative objectives (Eq. 10) with CARE's three reward regimes (Eq. 5) and advantage calibration (Eq. 9); an LLM controller reconfigures (λ_prog, λ_eff, p_low, p_high) every N updates from training statistics and held-out validation metrics. (iii) AI for Harness: a runtime with a Scenario Adapter (tool-conditioned Skill guidance), Persistent Memory Manager (user model / episodic / curated long-term / prospective memory with provenance and supersession semantics), and Executor; co-evolution alternates RL under fixed Harness configuration η^(k) with LLM-based editing of η from held-out development feedback (Eq. 12), all updates human-reviewed and versioned. Critical design decisions: the hybrid environment allocation (justified by fidelity/cost trade-offs, though no quantified comparison of backend fidelity is given), the separate-normalization alternative from GDPO is explicitly rejected with a ranking-preservation argument (well-justified), and the bounded LLM reward controller (plausible but unvalidated against simple alternatives like grid search or bandit tuning). Key Results: On MobilePA-Bench (1,700+ executable tasks, 200+ tools, 13 domains), Qwen-Planner-Agent 27B scores 77.05% Overall, above GPT 6 Astra (76.84%), Claude Opus 5 (75.71%), and all other evaluated closed/open systems; its base model started at 67.22% (a +9.83 pp gain). The 35B-A3B variant reaches 69.91% from a 54.90% base. Estimated output cost is $2.41 per 1,000 tasks (thinking tokens included) versus $3.06–$67.76 for the commercial comparison set — though this covers output tokens only. With the checkpoint fixed, the Harness adds 5.15 pp on 27B (71.90→77.05) and 5.12 pp on 35B-A3B. CARE reduces output tokens 32.5% versus vanilla RL at matched training accuracy; without advantage calibration, outputs shorten but accuracy drops materially. Co-evolution over 4/3 iterations lifts a separate 27B checkpoint from 82.67→88.50 on MobilePA-Internal and 38.00→46.98 on MCPMark, exceeding harness-only baselines (84.23 / 42.26). Long-history memory: the Harness lifts 27B BEAM-10M from 21.99% to 67.24% and BEAM-1M from 40.12% to 73.71%, versus best direct-context results of 25.64% and 54.84% and officially-reported Mem0 results of 48.60% and 64.10%; gains on short-history benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, BEAM-100K) are near-zero, with some pairs regressing. General agentic evaluations improve on 6/7 (35B-A3B) and 5/7 (27B) of Claw-Eval, BFCL-v4, MCP-Atlas, Tau-3, Toolathlon, SWE-Multilingual, SWE-Pro, with small drops on MMLU-Redux, C-Eval, IFEval (e.g., 27B average 90.05→89.70). Baselines are current frontier systems, which is a strength, though scores for closed models are self-run by the authors. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (CARE, specifically the success-derived normalization anchor — the derivation of Eq. 7–8 is the sharpest technical contribution) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the full Model+Harness system and hybrid environment infrastructure); the closed-loop AI-for-AI framing is a NEW FORMULATION at the systems level but mostly a reorganization of known ingredients (self-instruct-style data flywheels, GRPO-style RL, LLM-edited scaffolds à la OPRO/TextGrad, external memory à la MemGPT/Mem0). The genuinely new part is the advantage-calibration analysis and the demonstrated harness/model alternating refinement; the rest is competent composition of existing techniques in the mobile setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: CARE vs. vanilla RL vs. CARE-without-calibration (Figure 6), Harness contribution under fixed checkpoints (Table 1 paired rows), and staged co-evolution vs. model-only vs. model+harness (Table 2, Figure 7). However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and the 77.05% vs. 76.84% headline margin is well within plausible run-to-run variance. No code, data, or model weights are released (a project page URL exists but release of artifacts is not stated). Methodological concerns: MobilePA-Bench was created by the same author group (reference [11] shares authors), creating a Goodhart risk even though final evaluation is claimed separate from development sets; MobilePA-Internal is explicitly internal and unauditable; closed-model baselines were run by the authors under unspecified prompting/harness-matching conditions; Mem0 long-memory numbers are cited from official reports rather than re-run. The cost comparison excludes input tokens and Harness processing, which flatters the system relative to API-priced baselines. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — the Harness is a built, deployed runtime). - Practical: The 27B and 35B-A3B planners are trainable on multi-GPU clusters (Roll + Megatron-Core + vLLM stack); the memory-augmented Harness runs at inference time, but real-device backends and the LLM-simulator add operational dependencies beyond commodity hardware. - Efficient: Output-token cost of $2.41/1K tasks is the lowest in the compared set, and CARE's 32.5% token reduction compounds this; input-side and Harness overhead costs are not reported. - Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem on mobile benchmarks and transfers partially to MCPMark and general agentic suites, but all evaluations are on benchmarks or internal sets — no real-user deployment metrics are given. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the reported model sizes and benchmark scales; the co-evolution loop is claimed as a pathway to continued improvement but only 3–4 iterations are shown, and long-run stability of LLM-edited harnesses is unexamined. The work delivers a described (not released) system: trained planner checkpoints, a Harness runtime, and a training infrastructure; no library or dataset artifact is publicly delivered. Strengths: - The CARE advantage-calibration derivation (Eqs. 7–9) is a real analytical contribution: it identifies a concrete failure mode of GRPO normalization under reward composition (efficiency signals regaining unit advantage scale in saturated groups) and fixes it with a principled anchor, validated by the ablation where calibration-free CARE degrades accuracy. - The model–harness co-evolution ablation is cleanly designed — model-only vs. model+harness vs. alternating refinement, with development-set feedback excluded from training — and shows gains beyond harness alone on both mobile (+5.83 pp) and non-mobile (MCPMark, +8.98 pp) tasks. - Long-memory evaluation is honest about trade-offs: the paper reports near-zero or negative harness gains on short-history benchmarks and concentrates claims on BEAM-500K/1M/10M where gains are large (e.g., 21.99→67.24 at 10M). - Deployment realism: structured action interfaces rather than pixel-level GUI control, explicit memory provenance/supersession semantics, and human-gated update pipelines reflect a serious engineering posture. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that simulated and real-device feedback are not treated as equally reliable; that LLM-simulated environment responses require validation; that harness revisions and data releases remain human-gated and no candidate update is autonomously applied to serving systems; that the framework is presented "as a development pathway rather than claiming that sustained autonomous co-evolution has already been established"; that co-evolution results are on a separate 27B checkpoint with a development set rather than an independent final test; and that future work must reduce manual intervention in data refinement and harness updates. These are stated directly and constitute a credibility positive — the authors do not overclaim autonomy. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: single-run numbers throughout, with a 0.21 pp margin over the strongest baseline presented as a first-place ranking. - MobilePA-Bench provenance: the primary benchmark and the system come from the same team; independent reproduction or third-party benchmark confirmation is absent. - Closed-model baselines are self-run; the paper does not report prompting, scaffolds, or retry budgets used for competitors, so comparability of the frontier comparison is unverifiable. - The LLM-based CARE controller is never compared against trivial alternatives (fixed thresholds, random or grid-searched φ), so its contribution over simple schedule tuning is unknown. - Hybrid-environment allocation is described qualitatively; no measurement of how often LLM-simulated backends produce invalid trajectories or how much real-device data was actually used. - The $2.41/1K cost figure omits input tokens and Harness compute, which is precisely where memory retrieval and skill loading costs accumulate — the comparison is favorable by construction. - Privacy section (2.5.3) mixes implemented controls with normative "should" statements (user-level access enforcement depends on "trusted upstream services"), leaving the actual security posture unclear. - General-capability regressions on MMLU-Redux/C-Eval/IFEval are small but consistently negative; no mitigation analysis is offered. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic RL or agent scaffolds gains concrete, transferable value — especially the advantage-calibration analysis and the staged co-evolution evidence — but should treat the headline benchmark ranking as an unverified, vendor-adjacent result and look to independent reproductions before accepting the frontier comparison.
