MintAct: A Unified Visual Agent for Digital Environments (12 ▲ )

Mingfei Gao, Rui Tian, Haiming Gang, Bohan Zhai, Le Zhang, Yuanzheng Gong, Di Feng, Ege Özsoy, Kaixin Ma, Vishwesh Kirthivasan, Oğuzhan Fatih Kar, Roman Bachmann, Anders Boesen Lindbo Larsen, Afshin Dehghan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MintAct, a family of 2B/4B/8B vision-language agents (fine-tuned from Qwen3-VL-Instruct) that unifies UI grounding, multi-step navigation across mobile, desktop, and web, and visual tool use in a single set of weights, together with an asynchronous multi-domain RL training framework. - Why it's important: Serving and maintaining separate specialist models per digital-agent domain is impractical at the compact sizes needed for on-device deployment, so the paper targets the cost and engineering burden of fragmented agent stacks. - How it does it: The core move is a multi-stage recipe (high-res single-step SFT → low-res multi-step SFT on balanced domain mixtures → per-domain RL specialists distilled back via rejection-sampling fine-tuning → joint asynchronous RL) combined with prompt-conditioned action sets and explicit per-domain quota control that prevents fast environments from dominating the training mixture. - The good: A single MintAct-8B reaches 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified, 67.0 on AndroidWorld, 74.7 on Weblica, and 24.5 on MM-ToolSandBox — matching or beating size-matched per-domain specialists and competitive public models, with an unusually thorough ablation table per training stage. - The missing: Joint RL covers only mobile and desktop (not web or tool use), RL task pools are drawn from the same environments as evaluation benchmarks (OSWorld, AndroidWorld), no seeds/error bars are reported, and no code or weights release is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building GUI/tool-use agents or agentic RL infrastructure, since the four-mechanism treatment of asynchronous mixed-domain RL (quota, backpressure, dual-clip surrogate, truncated importance sampling) and the synthetic-environment transfer results are directly reusable; skip it if you only want a novel modeling technique — the architecture and RL objective are assembled from known parts.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building digital assistants currently maintain separate specialized models for UI grounding, mobile navigation, desktop control, web navigation, and visual tool use, because each domain differs in observation space, action space, data sources, and executable environments. The authors argue this fragmentation is costly to serve and scale, especially at compact on-device sizes, and that naive merging of action sets or data lets domains interfere and erodes per-domain quality. A secondary, less-discussed problem is infrastructural: online RL for these agents requires heterogeneous environment backends that are slow, noisy, and produce long multimodal trajectories, and naive asynchronous mixing lets the realized training distribution drift toward whichever domain executes fastest. The paper addresses both the modeling question (can one model unify domains without loss?) and the systems question (how to train stably across domains asynchronously). Key Idea: The central insight is that unification can be achieved through interface design and data control rather than architecture changes: (i) a shared observation space of raw screenshots with pixel coordinates normalized across all domains, (ii) prompt-conditioned action sets, where each domain's actions and tools are exposed via a domain-specific system prompt instead of merging action spaces, and (iii) explicit balanced mixing of domains in both SFT and RL. On the systems side, the key trick for joint asynchronous RL is admission control at the point of consumption — per-domain quotas on a shared trajectory queue plus quota-normalized backpressure to pause fast domains' producers — paired with a dual-clip surrogate for staleness and truncated importance sampling for trainer/inference engine mismatch. Methodology: The pipeline is a four-stage recipe on top of Qwen3-VL-Instruct. (1) High-resolution single-step SFT on public grounding datasets (GroundCUA, MolmoPoint, GUI-Odyssey, AndroidControl) at up to 2,116,800 pixels per image. (2) Low-resolution multi-step SFT on ~177.7k environment trajectories (42.7k mobile, 23.5k desktop, 51.7k web, 59.8k VTU), up/down-sampled to a 25%:25%:25%:25% mixture, using an append-only multi-turn format for KV-cache reuse; a tool-registry-aware segmentation scheme with loss masking handles dynamic tool discovery in VTU trajectories. (3) One RL specialist per domain, distilled back into one model via rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT) on ~90k judge-filtered successful trajectories. (4) Joint agentic asynchronous RL on mobile + desktop using GRPO-style group-relative advantages without std normalization, DAPO-style online filtering of uniform-outcome groups, environment-failure masking, a dual-clip surrogate (ε_lo=0.2, ε_hi=0.28, c=3), and one-sided truncated importance sampling (C=2) — with no KL anchor and no entropy bonus. Infrastructure components (rollouter on SGLang, environment manager with per-backend pools, Megatron trainer, bounded FIFO message queue with disk offloading of images, periodic weight sync every K=5 steps) are described at implementation depth. Critical design decisions: prompt-conditioned action sets (well-justified by ablation showing specialists don't beat the joint model); append-only context for RL-friendly prefixes (justified by engineering argument, not ablated); coarse credit assignment for dynamic-tool segments by assigning trajectory reward to the last segment only (acknowledged as an approximation). A synthetic-environment flywheel (~16,300 tasks over 3,348 forked OS-style environments generated by coding agents) is additionally explored for RL and SFT. Key Results: All numbers are single-run point estimates without error bars. MintAct-8B: 80.8 MMBench-GUI, 93.7 ScreenSpot-v2, 56.6 UI-Vision, 64.5 OSWorld-G, 71.0 AndroidControl, 67.0 AndroidWorld, 48.9 OSWorld-Verified, 74.7 Weblica, 39.1 Online-Mind2Web, 24.5 MM-ToolSandBox. Gains over the Qwen3-VL-8B base are large (AndroidWorld 47.6→67.0, OSWorld-Verified 33.9→48.9, MM-ToolSandBox 3.1→24.5). Against baselines: MintAct-8B exceeds EvoCUA-8B on OSWorld-Verified (48.9 vs 46.1), WEBLICA-8B on Weblica (74.7 vs 70.6), but trails MAI-UI-8B on AndroidWorld (67.0 vs 70.7); baselines are recent (2025–2026 era) and strong where reported. The ablations are the most valuable evidence: two SFT stages are complementary (stage 1 alone scores 9.4 on OSWorld-Verified; stage 2 alone drops UI-Vision to 25.0); RFT lifts AndroidWorld from 44.8→55.7 (2B) and 53.5→62.4 (4B); joint RL exceeds single-domain RL specialists on average (Nav. Avg. 55.9 vs 54.1/54.3) and transfers to web without web RL data (Weblica 57.5→60.8). Synthetic-environment RL transfers to unseen real benchmarks: training purely in synthetic environments lifts AndroidWorld 47.6→60.3 and iOSWorld 2.3→18.8 from the base model, though real in-domain RL is still better (AndroidWorld 66.7 vs 59.8). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the unified agent family and its asynchronous multi-domain RL infrastructure) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a single small model can match per-domain specialists across grounding, three navigation domains, and tool use simultaneously). The individual ingredients — asynchronous RL frameworks (AReaL, Magistral, SkyRL-Agent, AsyncWebRL), GRPO/DAPO objectives, rejection-sampling distillation, synthetic web environments (Weblica) — are all existing; the genuinely new elements are the per-domain quota + backpressure mechanisms for controlling cross-domain training composition in asynchronous RL, and the empirical demonstration that unification without per-domain regression is achievable at 2B–8B scale. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a systems paper: per-stage SFT ablation (Table 5), specialists-vs-joint for SFT, RFT, and RL (Tables 4, 6, 7), and a synthetic-environment ablation (Table 8), each across all three model scales. Hyperparameters for SFT and RL are published in appendices, including system prompts. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any comparison; several margins (e.g., MintAct-8B 67.0 vs RL-mobile 67.8 on AndroidWorld; grounding shifts within ~1 point) are within plausible run-to-run noise. Training task pools are drawn from OSWorld and AndroidWorld, the same environments used for evaluation (OSWorld-Verified, AndroidWorld), which is a train/eval overlap concern the paper does not discuss — in-domain RL gains may partly reflect task familiarity. Rewards are assigned by a VLM-as-judge, a self-reported signal whose accuracy is never validated against human judgment. No code, weights, or data release is mentioned anywhere. Hyperparameters reveal the joint-RL mixture is 25% mobile / 75% desktop, while the data pipeline elsewhere emphasizes 25/25 balance — a distribution choice that is not justified or ablated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (models trained and evaluated; infrastructure built and run, though not deployed to external users). - Practical: Models are 2B–8B, explicitly sized for on-device use, but the training stack (200+ desktop environment instances, 4 trainer + 12 rollouter nodes, separate Linux cluster) is beyond academic-scale resources; inference cost is not stated. - Efficient: The async framework's motivation is GPU utilization under slow GUI environments, but no throughput numbers, GPU-hours, or wall-clock training costs are reported. - Effective: Evidence covers all claimed capabilities on standard public benchmarks with size-matched specialists as the key control; effectiveness on tasks the RL judge may grade leniently remains unverified. - Scalable: Joint RL is tested on only two of four domains at ~3k+3k tasks; scaling to all domains is explicitly claimed as future work, and the 250-step RL budget is short relative to the infrastructure described. The work delivers trained model artifacts and an internal infrastructure description; no public artifact release is stated, so as published it stops at paper form. Strengths: (1) The clearest evidence in the paper is the specialists-vs-unified control: at every pipeline stage and all three scales, a single jointly-trained model matches or exceeds specialists trained on individual domains (e.g., joint RL Nav. Avg. 55.9 vs 54.1 mobile-specialist and 54.3 desktop-specialist), which directly tests the paper's central claim rather than merely showing aggregate gains. (2) The four-mechanism analysis of joint asynchronous RL — separating the staleness gap (dual-clip surrogate) from the engine gap (truncated importance sampling), and separating mixture drift (quota) from wasted generation (backpressure) — is a crisp, transferable systems contribution with each mechanism tied to a specific failure mode. (3) The synthetic-environment experiments provide a clean transfer result (synthetic-only training lifts iOSWorld 2.3→18.8 with zero real iOS exposure) that meaningfully de-risks synthetic environments as a data source. (4) The tool-registry-aware trajectory segmentation with segment-specific loss masking is a concrete, reusable solution to a real problem in SFT over dynamic-tool trajectories. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: joint RL covers only mobile and desktop, and extending to all domains is resource-intensive and left to future work; appending every screenshot to context causes rapidly growing memory use and motivates context management; navigation and tool use remain 'largely a separate capability' rather than a policy that automatically switches between them; on-device/server-side collaboration is unexplored; and the function-calling formulation with dynamic tool registries forces coarse, segment-level credit assignment (trajectory-level reward on the last segment), which they call an approximation and explicitly contrast with more principled alternatives. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Train/eval overlap: RL task pools are curated from OSWorld and AndroidWorld, which are also evaluation benchmarks (OSWorld-Verified, AndroidWorld); the paper never reports held-out-task performance on these benchmarks or discusses contamination. (2) No validation of the VLM-judge reward: all RL and RFT data filtering rests on an unquantified judge, and both benchmark scoring and synthetic-environment RL use the same judge methodology, so systematic judge errors would be invisible. (3) Single runs with no variance reporting, despite several headline margins of 1–3 points. (4) The 75/25 mobile/desktop RL mixture contradicts the paper's own 'balanced mixing' principle and is unexplained. (5) The joint-RL claim of 'matching or exceeding per-domain specialists' is nuanced by Table 7: RL-joint trails RL-mobile on AndroidWorld (66.7 vs 67.8) and RL-desktop on OSWorld-Verified (48.3 vs 49.2), so the average-level superiority rests on web transfer — a framing the text glosses over. (6) VTU joint RL is absent (only ~800 RL scenarios, and VTU stays flat at the SFT level in joint runs), so the 'unified agent' claim is strongest for navigation and weakest for tool use at the RL stage. (7) No throughput or cost measurements for the async infrastructure despite it being a headline contribution. Bottom Line: A practitioner building compact GUI or tool-use agents gains concrete, reusable value here — the unification-without-regression result, the quota/backpressure recipe for mixed-domain async RL, and the synthetic-environment transfer evidence are things few other papers document at this depth — but the missing release of code and weights, the train/eval overlap, and single-run reporting mean the exact numbers should be treated as vendor self-reports rather than reproducible baselines, and the newer unified-agent releases it cites (e.g., UltraCUA, MAI-UI) cover adjacent ground.

MATCH: Model-Aware Tool Learning with Curriculum Scheduling and Hierarchically Gated Rewards

S Liu, H Yin, L Liu, Z Chen, Y Zhao, F Huang · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MATCH, a closed-loop reinforcement-learning framework for tool-calling LLMs that couples a policy-adaptive curriculum scheduler (MACL) with a hierarchically gated tool-call reward (HTGR) applied to GRPO training. - Why it's important: RL-based tool learning currently wastes training on samples that are too easy or too hard as the policy improves, and additive rewards give credit to argument choices for a wrongly selected tool, so fixing both targets real inefficiency and reward-hacking in agent training. - How it does it: MACL maintains a per-sample difficulty estimate (1 − smoothed reward) that is refreshed online from the same HTGR reward groups used for GRPO, selecting samples near the moving mean difficulty plus a top-k pool of harder cases; HTGR awards tool-name, argument-key, and argument-value credit only when all prerequisite levels are correct. - The good: The ablation table is the most credible element — removing either component degrades API-Bank overall accuracy by 5.5–7.4 points (72.19% → 64.82–66.67%), and removing both drops 11.7 points, matching the ToolRL-reward/full-data configuration almost exactly. - The missing: No statistical reliability is reported — no seeds, error bars, or significance tests on any result, and no code release, while the headline margin (7.20 points on API-Bank, 2.62 on BFCL V3) comes from single runs on a 4,000-example training set shared with the closest baseline. - Read it or not: Read it if you are actively designing RL rewards or curricula for tool-calling agents and want a concrete, well-ablated recipe; skip it if you want new theory, large-scale evidence, or reproduction-ready artifacts.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is dragged down by Novelty (48) and Impact (35): both contributions are modest modifications of existing machinery (ToolSample's filtering, ToolRL's additive reward), and no artifact of any kind is released. Rigor (58) is the paper's relative strength — unusually thorough ablations including initialization, gating, and weight-sensitivity studies with a prespecified default — but the complete absence of seeds, error bars, or significance tests undermines the 0.31–2.62-point margins that carry several claims. Non-Obviousness (50): the credit-leakage observation is crisp but predictable once stated. Completeness (55) and Resilience (52) are reduced by the missing limitations section, the unexplained SFT400+GRPO collapse on BFCL Multi Turn, and the missing uniform-sampling control. Weighted composite: 0.20*48 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*50 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*52 + 0.10*35 = 51.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training LLMs to invoke external APIs via RL face two failure modes the paper identifies. First, curriculum/dynamic-sampling methods (e.g., ToolSample) use fixed reward-statistic thresholds to define "informative" samples, but sample difficulty is policy-dependent: as the policy improves, the difficulty distribution shifts and a static selection band drifts off the informative region (illustrated in Figure 2 over 14 epochs). Second, fine-grained rewards (e.g., ToolRL) sum tool-name, argument-key, and argument-value scores additively, so a response with a wrong tool name still collects argument-level credit when arguments coincidentally match the reference — a credit-leakage problem. The work targets practitioners doing GRPO-style post-training for function calling, evaluated on API-Bank and BFCL V3. Key Idea: Two symmetrical fixes bound into one loop: (1) define sample difficulty as 1 − smoothed reward and let that estimate co-evolve with the policy — each epoch select samples within ε_band of the current mean difficulty (the capability boundary) plus a top-k fraction of harder samples; (2) gate the reward hierarchically so argument-key and argument-value credit is granted only when the tool name is correct, making the reward dense but leakage-free. The same HTGR reward groups simultaneously drive the GRPO update and MACL's difficulty refresh, which is what makes the loop "closed." Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Offline difficulty initialization: N=128 stochastic rollouts of the initial policy per sample yield exact-match accuracy α_i, from which d_i^(0) = 1 − α_i; exact match is deliberately used here because the pre-RL policy is not yet aligned with HTGR scores. (2) Online difficulty refresh: for each selected sample, the M=4 GRPO rollout rewards are mean-normalized to [0,1] using HTGR's known reward bounds and folded into an exponential moving average (η-hyperparameter); unselected samples keep their prior estimate. (3) Curriculum selection and update: the mean difficulty μ_t over the full dataset serves as the capability boundary; the training subset is the boundary band {|d_i − μ_t| ≤ ε_band} union a top-k hard subset drawn from above-mean samples (fraction r_hard = 0.3), then standard GRPO (clipped surrogate, actor-side KL with β=0.001) runs on this subset with an unmodified objective. HTGR decomposes reward as R = λ·R_fmt + R_tool, where R_tool scores each reference call via a pairwise gated score (w_n + w_k + w_θ increments, default 0.4/0.3/0.3) only for same-name predictions, greedily matched for multi-call outputs, normalized by the number of reference calls. Critical design decisions: difficulty derived from reward rather than static attributes (justified by Figure 2's drift analysis and the initialization ablation in Table 3, where rollout init beats constant/random init by 4–6.4 points, mostly on L3); gating rather than weighting the hierarchy (Table 3 shows Full HTGR at 72.19% vs Name-only at 64.15%); and retaining a top-k hard subset rather than pure boundary sampling (Figure 5: removing it collapses L3 from 62.60% to 43.51%). All three are ablated, which is more than most papers in this subarea do. Key Results: On the same 4,000-example ToolRL training set (ToolACE + Hammer + xLAM), with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct trained on 4×A800 via veRL, MATCH reaches 72.19% overall on API-Bank and 62.87% on BFCL V3. Against the strongest baseline, ToolSample, that is +7.20 and +2.62 points overall; against ToolRL, +7.87 and +5.14. The largest gain is API-Bank L3 (62.60% vs 39.69% for ToolSample, +22.91), and on BFCL V3 Multi Turn (22.63% vs 18.50%). SFT baselines are weak (SFT400 at 50.59% API-Bank overall; SFT4k at 47.07%), and the raw backbone sits at 62.48%/41.97%. Backbone generalization (Table 5) shows MATCH beating the ToolRL numbers reported by Qian et al. across Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B and Llama-3.2-3B, though on 1.5B the margin is only 0.67 points (63.82% vs 63.15%). Baselines are current (Tool-N1, ToolRL, ToolSample are all 2025 work) and trained on identical data, which strengthens comparability. Reference rows include GPT-4-turbo (72.43% API-Bank), which MATCH edges out by 0.24 points in-house but is excluded from best/second-best annotation. Tested scale is standard academic (7B models, 4k samples) — not stress-scale. Notably, SFT400+GRPO yields 0.00–0.25% on BFCL Multi Turn, an unexplained collapse the paper does not discuss. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (incremental) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new elements are the policy-co-evolving difficulty estimate driving curriculum selection and the prerequisite-gated decomposition of the tool-call reward; both are well-motivated and ablated. However, each is a modest modification of existing machinery — MACL is a moving-average variant of ToolSample's reward-statistic filtering plus classic proximal-curriculum theory (Tzannetos et al.), and HTGR is ToolRL's additive decomposition with a tool-name gate — applied within standard GRPO. The closed-loop coupling of reward and scheduling is the most distinctive framing but is architecturally trivial (the same reward tensor feeds both). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the paper's strength: component removal (Table 2), difficulty-initialization alternatives (Table 3), reward-hierarchy truncation, weight-allocation sensitivity (Table 4, spanning 69.32–72.50% with the default within 0.31 of the best), scheduling hyperparameter sweeps (ε_band, r_hard, both peaking at 0.3), and four sampling-strategy comparisons. The authors also explicitly state the default weights were fixed before the sensitivity analysis, a credibility positive. Weaknesses: no seeds, error bars, or variance reporting anywhere despite single-run deltas of 0.3–2 points being interpreted in the weight analysis; no code or model release is mentioned; backbone generalization (Table 5) reuses ToolRL's published numbers rather than re-running ToolRL under identical settings, introducing a reproduction caveat the authors acknowledge; and the training set originates from ToolRL while the closest baseline (ToolSample) comparison relies on the authors' own reproductions. No Goodhart-style train-on-test contamination is apparent (API-Bank/BFCL are evaluation-only), but the training data's provenance from a baseline paper's suite warrants noting. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Yes — 7B backbones trained on 4×A800 GPUs with veRL, all commodity hardware within reach of any lab running GRPO. - Efficient: The offline initialization costs N=128 rollouts per sample (≈512k generations for 4k samples), and per-epoch cost is bounded by the curriculum subset; no wall-clock or FLOP comparison against full-data or ToolSample training is reported, so the efficiency claim relative to baselines is unevaluated. - Effective: The evidence (two benchmarks, four backbones, component ablations) supports improved tool-call accuracy on single-step decomposed trajectories, but multi-turn training is decomposed into single steps, so end-to-end agent behavior is only proxied. - Scalable: Untested beyond 7B/4k-sample scale; the difficulty-refresh mechanism requires a full-dataset difficulty mean each epoch and EMAs over sparse (unselected samples never refresh) estimates, whose behavior at 100× data or with much larger models is only claimed, not shown. The paper stops at paper form — no library, CLI, dataset, or checkpoint artifact is mentioned. Strengths: - The credit-leakage observation is crisp and the gating fix is minimal and correct: argument correctness for a wrong tool genuinely has no execution semantics, and Figure 1's motivating example makes the failure concrete. - The closed-loop framing — the same reward tensor serving both the GRPO advantage and the difficulty refresh — is a clean unification that avoids a separate difficulty model or extra rollouts. - The ablation that removing the top-k hard subset collapses L3 accuracy from 62.60% to 43.51% is a genuinely informative finding: near-boundary sampling alone starves the capability boundary from expanding. - The weight-sensitivity analysis with a prespecified default, openly showing the default is 0.31 points below the best tested allocation, is an unusually honest reporting practice. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - The paper implicitly acknowledges limited scale by testing only up to 7B and only two benchmarks, but never states scope boundaries or failure modes explicitly — there is no limitations section or paragraph. - It does acknowledge (in the RQ5 setup) that Table 5 baseline numbers come from ToolRL's paper under a different setting, making cross-table comparisons inexact, and that the 7B ToolRL row differs from their in-house reproduction. - The absence of an explicit limitations discussion is a mild credibility negative; nothing is minimized because nothing is confronted directly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No seed variance or significance testing: the 2.62-point BFCL V3 margin over ToolSample and the 0.31–0.67-point margins in Tables 4–5 are well within plausible single-run noise for GRPO, which is notoriously high-variance. - The difficulty-refresh loop only updates selected samples, so unselected samples' difficulty estimates go stale; the paper never quantifies how stale estimates distort μ_t, the very quantity the band is centered on. - Multi-turn performance (22.63% BFCL MT) remains low in absolute terms and training decomposes trajectories into single steps, so the reported gains may not transfer to genuine multi-turn agentic execution; the L3 +22.91 jump is dramatic and would benefit from qualitative analysis of what changes. - The SFT400+GRPO baseline scoring 0.00–0.25% on BFCL Multi Turn is a red flag for the shared training/eval pipeline that goes unexamined. - No comparison against simpler alternatives to MACL, such as uniform random sampling with the same per-epoch subset budget, which would isolate whether the gain comes from curriculum structure or merely from reduced sample volume per epoch. Bottom Line: A competent, well-ablated incremental contribution — a gated reward and an adaptive band are sensible fixes that demonstrably matter on two standard benchmarks — but the absence of variance reporting, code, and scale makes it a useful recipe for agent-training practitioners rather than a landmark result; those needing a single reference should read it alongside ToolSample and ToolRL, which cover much of the same ground.

VideoGen-Agent: Reinforcing Video Generation Agents (35 ▲ )

Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, Yuhui Zhang, Yaohui Zhang, Zihao Lin, Kaituo Feng, Suozhi Huang, Xiangyi Li, Yu Li, Chunyuan Li, Shilong Liu, Mengdi Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 22 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VideoGen-Agent, a multimodal agent (built on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) trained via SFT then multitask GRPO reinforcement learning to orchestrate external search, simulation, generation, and verification tools for video generation across six task categories, plus VABench, a held-out 600-prompt benchmark. - Why it's important: Current text-to-video models fail on prompts requiring post-training knowledge, named-entity identity preservation, physical consistency, or ordered multi-phase events — failures that block practical uses like product demos, education, and film pre-visualization. - How it does it: A shared policy learns category-specific tool workflows through teacher-distilled SFT trajectories followed by RL with a hybrid reward (0.1 format + 0.5 VLM-judged video quality + 0.4 tool-use correctness) and per-task advantage normalization. - The good: The strongest evidence is the tool-upgrade experiment: swapping in stronger generation tools raises the VABench score from 75.6 to 86.1 with the agent policy frozen, showing learned tool-use strategies transfer to backends unseen during training, and ablations cleanly attribute gains to SFT (+9.7 over zero-shot) and RL (+6.4 over SFT). - The missing: The evaluation judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro with category-specific rubrics) is the same model and rubric used as the RL training reward, and VABench is the authors' own benchmark, so the headline numbers carry a self-evaluation/Goodhart risk that no independent third-party benchmark or judge mitigates. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in agentic RL for generative models and video-generation practitioners deciding between fine-tuning generators versus wrapping them with trained agents; skippable if you only need another leaderboard on existing T2V benchmarks.

Problem & Motivation: Video diffusion models produce visually plausible clips but often fail prompts that demand (a) procedural knowledge of specialized actions (e.g., a specific Tai Chi form), (b) visual identity preservation for named people/characters/landmarks, (c) physically consistent motion under given initial conditions, (d) compositional multi-subject scenes, or (e) temporally ordered multi-phase events. Because this knowledge is not in the generator's weights, prompting alone cannot fix it. Prior agentic approaches (VISTA, Newton, AutoMV, etc.) target single objectives; nobody has trained one agent to select and compose the right tool for heterogeneous requirements. The work targets practitioners building video-generation pipelines for content creation, education, and pre-visualization. Key Idea: Train a single shared policy, via SFT on teacher trajectories followed by multitask GRPO, to follow category-conditioned tool workflows, where the reward jointly scores tool-call validity, task-appropriate tool use (verified via output-utilization checks, not just call counting), and final video quality, with a second per-task advantage normalization (following AgentRL) equalizing learning signal across categories. A common tool interface lets the trained policy plug into upgraded generation backends without retraining. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Data: Claude Opus 4.7 generates 24K prompts (4K per category), deliberately simplified on non-target dimensions; Gemini 3.1 Pro or Claude Opus 4.7 act as teacher agents producing tool-use trajectories (16K for SFT, 8K prompts reserved for RL). (2) SFT: next-token prediction on 16K teacher trajectories; failed action spans are masked from the loss but kept in context so recovery actions still supervise. (3) RL: GRPO with n=6 rollouts per prompt, asymmetric clipping (ε_lo=0.2, ε_hi=0.28), β_KL=10^-3 toward the SFT reference; only agent-emitted tokens receive the policy gradient, tool responses are context. The reward R = 0.1·R_format + 0.5·R_vlm + 0.4·R_tool; group-relative advantages are re-normalized per task category within the global batch. The toolbox spans augmentation (web text search, image search, a custom impulse-based rigid-body/SPH simulator), generation (T2V, I2V, R2V, motion-conditioned M2V), and verification (Grounding DINO 1.5, Depth Anything V2). Three design decisions: (i) fixing category-specific default workflows (justified as guidance for a shared 8B policy, though it risks teaching workflow imitation rather than genuine tool selection); (ii) the 0.4 tool-use reward weight (ablation-supported — removing it costs 4.4 points, more than removing the VLM reward); (iii) separate toolsets for training vs. evaluation (a deliberate and well-justified extensibility probe). Key Results: On VABench (600 held-out prompts, 100 per category, scored by Gemini 3.1 Pro with the training rubrics): VideoGen-Agent with Toolset 1 (Seedance 1.0 Pro Fast + Wan 2.1-VACE-1.3B generation tools) scores 75.6 overall versus 56.5 for its base generator Seedance 1.0 Pro Fast (+19.1) and 73.2 for Seedance 2.0, the strongest standalone baseline. With Toolset 2 (Seedance 2.0 Fast, Wan 2.1-VACE-14B), the frozen policy reaches 86.1, best in all six categories (e.g., Multi-Shot 94.6, Procedural Knowledge 92.1 vs. Seedance 2.0's 78.0). Ablations: prompt rewriting 57.3, zero-shot tool use 59.5, SFT 69.2, RL 75.6; removing the tool reward → 71.2, removing the VLM reward → 73.3; single-task RL reaches 76.3 (+0.7 over multitask). Human preference: 84.3% for VideoGen-Agent-Toolset 2 over Seedance 2.0 across 100 pairs rated by 4 raters. Judge-human agreement: 92.0% over 600 pairs, but only 72% on Procedural Knowledge (88–100% elsewhere). Baselines include current proprietary models (Kling 3.0, Hailuo 2.0, Seedance 1.0/2.0) and open-source ones (CogVideoX-5B, Mochi-1, HunyuanVideo-13B, Wan2.1-T2V-14B), so the baseline set is current. Tested at benchmark scale only (single 600-prompt evaluation); no latency, cost, or wall-clock numbers are reported despite multi-step agentic rollouts. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel element is multitask agentic RL for video generation — extending SFT+GRPO tool-use training (established for search/QA in Search-R1, and for images in Gen-Searcher) to a setting where the reward must evaluate generated visual content across six heterogeneous capability categories, plus the tool-upgrade transfer experiment. The GRPO objective, teacher-distilled SFT, and individual tools (search, Grounding DINO, Wan-VACE, physics simulation) are all standard components; the contribution is their combination and the multitask reward/normalization scheme applied to video generation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: training stages (vanilla → prompt rewriting → zero-shot → SFT → RL), reward components (VLM, tool), and single-task vs. multitask RL — this is above average for ablation coverage. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; single-task vs. multitask differs by only 0.7 points with no variance estimate. The judge-agreement study (92.0% overall, per-category breakdown, comparison against GPT-4o and Qwen3-VL-235B) is a credibility positive, but the 72% agreement on Procedural Knowledge undercuts the largest headline gain (+14.1 over Seedance 2.0 in that category). Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluation judge is the same model with the same rubrics used as the RL reward — the agent is literally optimized against the test metric; (2) VABench is the authors' own benchmark, not a standard external one; (3) Toolset 2 contains Seedance 2.0, so the 86.1 vs. Seedance 2.0 comparison is partially a tool-identity confound (the 75.6 vs. 73.2 Toolset-1 comparison is the cleaner one); (4) prompt construction and RL-failure exclusion criteria (trajectories failing due to tool errors are dropped) could bias optimization toward easy prompts. A project homepage exists (andyca111.github.io/VideoGen_Agent); no code, data, or model-weight release is explicitly stated in the text, though the physics simulator source is said to be in supplementary material. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with benchmark and human evaluations). - Practical: Runs on 8×H200 GPUs for the 8B policy plus 8 more for tool serving, but depends on proprietary APIs (Claude, Gemini, Bing, Seedance) — no fully local deployment path is shown. - Efficient: Not evaluated — no inference latency or dollar cost per video is reported, a notable omission for an agent that makes many sequential generator calls per prompt. - Effective: Evidence supports the claim on the authors' benchmark and 100 human-rated pairs, but effectiveness is measured with the training judge, so real-world prompt faithfulness is only proxied. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the six training categories; the extensibility experiments (robotic action-to-video pipeline, unseen task combinations like a named character performing a specialized action) are qualitative/illustrative rather than quantitative at 10× scale. The work delivers a trained 8B agent policy and a 600-prompt benchmark; no public code/model release is confirmed in the text. Strengths: - The tool-upgrade experiment (75.6 → 86.1 with a frozen policy and unseen generation backends) is the paper's most convincing and least common result: it demonstrates that learned tool-use behavior, not generator quality, accounts for the agentic gain, and that the framework composes with future generator improvements. - The tool-use reward verifies functional utilization of tool outputs (e.g., that a retrieved image path actually feeds the R2V call, that simulation flow conditions the M2V call) rather than rewarding tool-call counts — a design detail most agentic-RL papers skip. - Honest ablation ladder that separates prompt rewriting (+0.8) from zero-shot tool access (+3.0) from SFT (+9.7) from RL (+6.4), plus reward-component ablations, giving a credible attribution story. - Constructing a 24K trajectory dataset across six capability categories where none existed is a substantial data contribution that others can reuse. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the system is limited by generation-tool quality and latency, the coverage of verification feedback (Grounding DINO only checks generic common-noun subjects — the system prompt itself forbids using it for named entities, processes, or simulation outputs), and the six-task training boundary. They also acknowledge in the case study that stance-level errors persist in Procedural Knowledge generation despite correct retrieval (the Seedance 1.0 variant produces a horse stance instead of the empty stance). They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive; the limitation section is short but accurate to what the experiments show. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Reward/test-metric circularity: Gemini 3.1 Pro with the training rubrics serves as both the RL reward and the VABench evaluator. RL is known to exploit judge weaknesses, and no evaluation on an independent benchmark (e.g., T2V-CompBench, SeqBench — both cited in related work) is provided. - The Toolset-2 headline (86.1) partially measures Seedance 2.0 against itself; a cleaner presentation would foreground the Toolset-1 delta, and a Toolset-2 ablation with the vanilla policy given Seedance 2.0 directly (prompt-rewriting + Seedance 2.0 single-pass) is missing. - Compute/cost asymmetry with baselines: the agent makes multiple sequential generator calls per prompt (simulation, retrieval, multi-segment generation, verification, regeneration) while baselines are single-pass; no latency or cost normalization is reported. - No variance reporting: the multitask vs. single-task comparison (75.6 vs. 76.3) and all category-level deltas lack seeds or confidence intervals, and with 100 prompts per category, single-point differences of a few points may not be significant. - Human evaluation is thin relative to the claims: 100 pairs, 4 raters, one comparison (Toolset 2 vs. Seedance 2.0); no human evaluation for the Toolset-1 configuration or per-training-stage comparison. - The RL failure-exclusion rule (dropping trajectories that fail from external tool errors) is a selection filter whose effect on the learned policy is not analyzed. Bottom Line: This is currently the strongest documented demonstration that agentic RL can teach a small policy to orchestrate heterogeneous tools for video generation and that the skill transfers across generator upgrades — a practitioner in video generation or agentic RL should read it, while discounting the absolute VABench numbers for judge-training circularity and waiting for independent reproduction on external benchmarks.

From Pattern Recognizers to Personalized Companions: A Survey of Large Language Models in Mental Health (15 ▲ )

He Hu, Yucheng Zhou, Qianning Wang, Yingjian Zou, Chiyuan Ma, Juzheng Si, Jianzhuang Liu, Zitong Yu, Laizhong Cui, Fei Ma, Qi Tian · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 23 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This survey organizes the fragmented literature on LLMs in mental health around a three-phase evolutionary thesis — Phase I: passive Information Tools/Pattern Recognizers for detection; Phase II: stateless Empathetic Conversationalists for single-session dialogue; Phase III (frontier): stateful, longitudinal, personalized agents with Profile, Memory, Reasoning, Planning, and Tool Use modules. - Why it's important: Mental healthcare faces chronic access barriers (resource scarcity, cost, stigma, privacy), and the field's literature is growing so fast and so fragmented that researchers and clinicians lack a coherent map of where the technology stands and what the credible next steps are. - How it does it: It imposes an explicit operational taxonomy (interaction granularity, user-state modeling, cross-session persistence, personalization, memory, autonomy) and then reviews adaptation methods (pre-training, SFT/PEFT, RL alignment), inference-time strategies (prompting, CoT, RAG), multimodality, agent architectures, ~80 datasets, and evaluation benchmarks through that lens. - The good: It is unusually candid for a survey about evidentiary weakness — Table VII shows almost no system has clinical validation with real patients, and the paper argues LLM-as-a-Judge is only a partial proxy (moderate Cohen's κ agreement) rather than clinical assessment. - The missing: As a survey it runs no experiments, and the Phase III narrative is built largely from synthetic-data systems whose own structural-fidelity problems (documented in the survey) undermine the very longitudinal claims the framework highlights. - Read it or not: Worth reading for NLP/agent researchers entering mental health or for clinicians wanting a structured map of the technical landscape; skip if you already know the Phase I/II literature and only need the agent-architecture frontier.

Problem & Motivation: Mental health conditions (depression, anxiety, loneliness) are rising globally while traditional care is constrained by limited clinician capacity, high cost, stigma, and privacy concerns, leaving many people without timely support. LLMs promise scalable support, but the research corpus — spanning social-media detection, fine-tuned counseling chatbots, multimodal assessment, and agent systems — has grown without a unifying narrative. Prior surveys target narrower slices (social-media disorder detection, single-session psychotherapy dialogue, or broad generative-AI scoping reviews), so the paper's gap is contextualization: a framework that lets a reader place any given system on a developmental trajectory and see what is missing to reach clinically meaningful support. Key Idea: The organizing insight is a three-phase evolutionary thesis with explicit operational criteria (Table I): systems differ along interaction granularity (single-turn → multi-turn → longitudinal), user-state modeling (none → session → persistent), memory (none → context → long-term), and autonomy (reactive → interactive → goal-directed). The corollary claim is that the Phase I→II transition was driven by training and inference techniques (SFT, RLHF-style alignment, CoT, RAG), while the Phase II→III transition requires an architectural shift — stateful cognitive agents with Profile/Memory/Reasoning/Planning/Tool modules — rather than better conversational models per se. Methodology: This is a narrative/systematic survey, not an empirical study; its "method" is the taxonomy plus coverage. It curates papers (mainly from ACL Anthology, PubMed, arXiv, Web of Science) satisfying two inclusion rules — involves LLMs and targets a mental-health task — and reports the field's growth (Figure 1, with psychotherapy at roughly 58% of surveyed papers, diagnosis ~25%, education ~9%, assistance ~8%). Coverage proceeds: (1) application pillars (assessment/diagnosis against DSM-5/ICD-11 and instruments like PHQ-9/GAD-7; therapeutic intervention; education via virtual patients; clinician assistance); (2) adaptation techniques — domain pre-training (ProMind-LLM), SFT (full vs. PEFT/LoRA/QLoRA), RL alignment (DPO/KTO/ORPO, GRPO as in Psyche-R1), inference-time prompting/CoT/RAG, and multimodal fusion; (3) agent architecture with five modules (Profile, Memory — including Ebbinghaus-inspired forgetting and cognitive-distortion tracking — Reasoning, Planning, Tool Use); (4) five dataset tables spanning detection corpora (e.g., RSDD, 116,484 Reddit users; UMD, 1,556,194 posts; SWDD, 4,854,421 Weibo posts), dialogue corpora (ESConv 1,053 dialogs / 14.1 turns; SoulChatCorpus 2,300,248 entries), multimodal resources (AVEC series, MODMA, D-vlog), and a synthesis-paradigm taxonomy (dialogue-level → cognitive-level → personalized-realism-level); (5) a three-tier evaluation metric hierarchy (automated surface metrics → semantic/dialogue quality → clinical/relational attributes like empathy, therapeutic alliance, safety) and proposed Phase III evaluation dimensions (longitudinal consistency, escalation behavior, crisis handling, therapeutic alliance, grounded in CTRS/PANAS/WAI instruments). Critical design decision: the phase taxonomy is imposed analytically, not derived from a formal literature search protocol (no PRISMA-style methodology, no stated paper counts per section), so its comprehensiveness claim rests on the authors' curation judgment. Key Results: As a survey there are no headline model results. The quantitative outputs are: the paper-count trend (Figure 1, rapid growth 2021–2025 across four application categories); the application distribution (~58% psychotherapy, ~25% diagnosis, ~9% education, ~8% assistance); five resource tables cataloguing ~80 datasets with sizes, languages (English, Chinese, plus Korean, Japanese, Persian, Spanish), and tasks; a metric-attribute table mapping evaluation attributes to studies; and Table VII, a validation-settings matrix for 14 representative systems (ChatCounselor through TheraMind) showing expert, clinical, and automatic evaluation — where the clinical column is essentially empty, i.e., almost none of the surveyed systems have been validated with real patient populations. The paper's substantive "findings" are syntheses: (a) synthetic data now dominates Phase II/III resources but exhibits distributional shift, smoothed emotional dynamics, and cultural homogenization versus real therapy transcripts; (b) automated safety metrics do not translate into clinically appropriate behavior (false reassurance, delayed escalation); (c) BLEU/ROUGE/F1 correlate poorly with therapeutic quality; (d) LLM-as-a-Judge shows only moderate agreement with human raters. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the three-phase operational taxonomy with per-criteria distinctions) plus a synthesis contribution — it is primarily a survey, not a new method or dataset. Genuinely novel is the explicit operationalization of the phase boundaries (Table I) and the proposed four-dimension, instrument-grounded evaluation protocol for longitudinal agents (longitudinal consistency, escalation, crisis handling, therapeutic alliance tied to CTRS/PANAS/WAI). Everything else — the coverage of SFT/PEFT/RL/RAG/multimodal techniques, the dataset tables, the agent module decomposition (Profile/Memory/Reasoning/Planning/Tools) — is a competent organization of existing ideas; the agent-module framing is borrowed from the general LLM-agent literature and applied to this domain. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, seeds, or significance tests apply (no experiments). Reproducibility of the survey itself is limited: no systematic-search protocol (no keyword list, date range beyond "consistent set of search keywords," no PRISMA flow, no inter-curator agreement), which weakens the "comprehensive" and "more comprehensive than prior surveys" claims. The curated resource collection is released at a project repository (Awesome-Mental-Health-LLMs), which is a concrete artifact and the main reproducibility asset. The arXiv preprint is dated September 2026 (v1, arXiv:2609.25186) and appears formatted for an IEEE venue; it is not stated as peer-reviewed, so treat the synthesis as preprint-stage. Methodological concerns: (1) several cited works carry 2026 arXiv/venue dates, suggesting heavy reliance on very fresh, unreviewed material; (2) at least one surveyed system (TheraMind, ref [18]) shares authors with the survey, and PsyLLM (ref [17]) is also by overlapping authors — self-citation shaping the Phase III narrative is a conflict-of-interest flag; (3) the phase taxonomy is a categorization the authors apply, and boundary cases (e.g., datasets labeled "semi-real") are not adjudicated with stated criteria. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL-adjacent survey — no system is built or run; the deliverable is the taxonomy, the dataset/benchmark inventory, and the repository artifact. Practical: Not applicable to a method; the curated repository is freely available and browseable. Efficient: Not applicable; the survey consolidates resources, which itself saves curation effort for newcomers. Effective: The taxonomy is effective as a narrative device and the evaluation-gap analysis (Table VII) is evidence-backed, but the Phase III roadmap is aspirational — the paper itself shows the field lacks clinical-outcome evidence. Scalable: Not applicable; the framework will face strain as the corpus grows since inclusion criteria are informal. Deliverable: a paper plus a public resource collection (Awesome-Mental-Health-LLMs); no library, model, or dataset of its own beyond the curation. Strengths: - The operational phase taxonomy (Table I) is genuinely useful: it converts a vague evolutionary story into checkable criteria (persistence, memory, autonomy) that can be applied to any new system, enabling the thematic grouping this summary feeds. - The evaluation-gap analysis is honest and specific: Table VII's near-empty "clinical" column, the critique of LLM-as-a-Judge calibration, and the proposed CTRS/WAI-grounded trajectory-level evaluation protocol constitute a real research agenda, not boilerplate future work. - The dataset synthesis taxonomy (dialogue-level → cognitive-level → personalized-realism-level, Figure 5) paired with the cited evidence on synthetic data's structural-fidelity failures (smoothed emotional arcs, distributional shift, echo-chamber effects) is a sharp, well-sourced contribution to an under-discussed problem. - Coverage breadth is real: ~80 catalogued resources across five tables, spanning seven languages and text/audio/video/physiology modalities, with consistent per-resource fields (source, task, size, turns, open-source status). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly confront: (1) multimodal cue ambiguity — non-verbal signals are context-dependent, systems overfit dataset artifacts, and spurious correlations (lighting, background) undermine clinical validity; (2) synthetic-data risks — distributional mismatch, echo chambers, cultural homogenization, lack of longitudinal coherence; (3) SFT's double-edged nature — bias amplification and out-of-distribution degradation; (4) evaluation deficiencies — automatic metrics correlate poorly with therapeutic quality, LLM-judges show limited expert agreement, and almost no real-world clinical validation exists, attributed to ethical/legal/privacy constraints on RCTs; (5) safety-metric gaming — "safe-looking" outputs that are clinically inappropriate (false reassurance, delayed escalation). This directness is a credibility positive; the authors do not minimize the field's evidentiary weakness. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No systematic review methodology is described; "comprehensive" coverage is asserted, not demonstrated via a reproducible search protocol, so the survey's completeness is unverifiable. - Overlapping authorship with surveyed systems (PsyLLM, TheraMind) is not disclosed as a potential bias in the Phase III framing or the Table VII validation analysis. - The three-phase thesis is presented as an observed trajectory but risks being a prescriptive narrative: borderline works that mix phases (e.g., a fine-tuned model with RAG memory but single-session evaluation) have no assigned place, and no inter-rater check on phase assignment is reported. - The proposed Phase III evaluation protocol (longitudinal consistency, escalation, crisis handling, alliance) is never instantiated as a concrete benchmark or applied to even one existing system — the roadmap stops at proposal. - Safety and efficacy of Phase III agents are discussed almost entirely from the NLP literature; clinical-informatics and human-subjects perspectives on harm (dependency, privacy of longitudinal memory, regulatory status as a medical device) receive little treatment relative to the risk the paper itself implies. - Quantitative claims in Figure 1 (category percentages) lack the underlying paper list counts in the text, preventing verification of the growth trend's composition. Bottom Line: For anyone entering LLM-for-mental-health research, this is currently one of the most useful maps of the territory — the taxonomy, dataset inventory, and brutally honest evaluation-gap analysis justify reading it — but it is a preprint synthesis with informal methodology and no empirical contribution, so it complements rather than replaces the primary literature, and its Phase III optimism should be tempered by its own evidence that clinical validation is nearly absent.

TL;DR - What it does: This Master's thesis reports a live-production deployment study of four LLM-based agents for taxi request handling at Portuguese dispatcher Geolink lda. — a structured multi-model WhatsApp agent (WAH), a fully conversational WhatsApp agent (WAC), a keyword-based Whisper voice-detection layer on an existing IVR (Napoleão expansion), and a Realtime-GPT voice agent (RTN) — and measures their operational viability in real dispatch traffic. - Why it's important: Taxi dispatch is a low-latency, safety-critical, multi-channel service where offline benchmarks do not predict production behavior; very few papers evaluate LLM agents on live customer traffic where hallucinated tool calls cause real dispatch errors. - How it does it: The thesis contrasts two architectural poles under identical production conditions — narrow, structured agents that use LLMs only for intent classification/routing with tool-grounded commitments and explicit human-in-the-loop escalation, versus end-to-end conversational agents with many tools and full autonomy. - The good: The negative result is the most credible finding: the broad-scope WAC agent (13 tools, 5 tool groups, GPT 4.1-mini) failed live testing due to hallucinated tool calls, misparameterisation, and message loops, while the narrow-scope RTN agent (3 tools) reached a 53% service rate in the same model class — a clean within-site demonstration of the reliability–flexibility trade-off. - The missing: Key success claims lack quantitative baselines — the claim that WAH's 65% completion rate is "comparable to the human operator rate" is asserted without a number, and there are no ablations, significance tests, or error bars anywhere. - Read it or not: Practitioners deploying LLM agents in high-stakes, low-latency phone/messaging services will find the failure-mode taxonomy and the scoped-vs-conversational comparison genuinely useful; researchers seeking controlled experiments or new methods can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: Taxi dispatch services receive requests through voice calls and messaging platforms, where telephony adds band-limited audio, packet loss, barge-ins, and disfluent speech, and text messages are informal and ambiguous. Dispatch operators need fast, reliable intake of pickup, destination, time, and constraints; errors (wrong pickup, false booking confirmation) carry real operational cost. Prior work evaluates task-oriented dialogue systems on annotated benchmarks (JGA, slot F1), which the thesis argues fails to predict live performance. The gap addressed is empirical: which LLM agent architectures (structured intent-routing vs. fully conversational; local vs. cloud vs. real-time streaming) are actually deployable in production, what failure modes emerge in live traffic, and whether human-in-the-loop escalation can absorb errors without overwhelming operators. The work builds on a predecessor master's thesis (Ribeiro, Taxi-Link/Napoleão IVR) that used history-based pickup prediction with DTMF confirmation. Key Idea: The core insight is that architectural scope, not raw model capability, determines production viability: constrain the agent to a few tools, a fixed candidate set of pickup locations, and tool-grounded commitments (never confirm an action without a successful API response), and route all residual uncertainty to human operators — this outperforms full conversational autonomy given models available at viable cost and latency. This is an evaluation finding rather than a new algorithmic technique; the thesis itself does not claim a novel method. Methodology: Four agents were implemented and incrementally deployed in live Geolink dispatch traffic (~4,000 taxis, 30 fleets): (1) WAH — a two-step intent classifier over a locally deployed, quantized Qwen3:30B (fast/simple) and Gemma-4-31B-Heretic (complex/ambiguous) pair, routing into four intents (Show/No-Show, Cancellation, Taxi Request, Location Message) and executing pre-existing templated WhatsApp flows, with operator override via a centralized web chat interface; (2) WAC — GPT 4.1-mini as full conversational orchestrator with 13 tools across 5 groups (booking, coverage/FAQ, handoff, conversation control, status/history), a seven-part system prompt (identity, guardrails, booking workflow, tools/escalation, communication, ground facts, examples), and structured JSON output for message type/body; (3) Napoleão expansion — a local Whisper model transcribing a fixed-length recording after a prompt tone, thresholded confidence over two keywords ("taxi"/"operador") with fallback to operator, integrated into the Asterisk PBX; (4) RTN — OpenAI Realtime-GPT v1 connected via SIP through Asterisk, with three tools (Book Taxi Trip restricted to the caller's five most frequent pickup addresses, Hang Up Call, Redirect Call) and a procedural prompt enforcing a fixed question order. No objective function or learning procedure is involved; evaluation is via operational metrics (completion rate, handoff rate/reason, satisfaction, failure-mode frequency) over live traffic. Design decisions favoring scope limitation and HITL are argued from the literature review but not ablated. Key Results: WAH (3-month rollout to all WhatsApp traffic, 2 months of comparison data): 65% service completion rate (described as comparable to the pre-deployment human-operator rate, for which no figure is given), 4.79/5 average satisfaction from a post-service star survey, steady growth in conversations/users/services, with initial growth attributed partly to a publicity drive. Napoleão voice expansion (1-month test, all Napoleão users): 14% of interactions used voice — 1% voice-activated taxi, 5% voice-activated operator, 9% fallback (6% user error/silence, 3% interpretation errors); manual review found voice users predominantly older adults. RTN (1 week, one fleet queue, 100+ calls): 53% service rate, 21% redirect rate, 26% user hangup (mostly immediately after first contact); hallucinations were rare and mostly caught by fallback, except one case where the agent fabricated tool results and claimed a booking succeeded. WAC (planned 1-week test, ended early): unrecoverable hallucinated tool calls, wrong tool parameters, and message loops despite prompt iteration; judged infeasible at current model capability/cost. Notable qualitative finding: Realtime-GPT drifts from European to Brazilian Portuguese mid-conversation, persisting through prompting iterations. Baselines are limited to the pre-deployment system (WAH) and internal comparisons; no external baselines exist for a production-only study. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (with elements of NEW SYSTEM/TOOL). Genuinely novel is the paired live-traffic A/B of structured-vs-conversational agent architectures in the same dispatch environment and the quantified failure-mode evidence that tool count and scope, not model identity, predict reliability (WAC with 13 tools failed; RTN with 3 tools succeeded on the same model class). The individual components — Ollama-served quantized Qwen/Gemma, GPT 4.1-mini function calling, Whisper keyword spotting, Realtime-GPT over SIP, HITL escalation — are standard combinations of existing ideas applied to taxi dispatch; the literature review is competent but the methods are not new. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations isolate which components matter (e.g., single vs. dual local models in WAH; the effect of the five-location restriction on RTN's hallucination rate is asserted, not tested). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests — understandable for single-run live deployments, but the RTN test covers only ~100 calls over one week and the WAC failure is a single trial of one configuration (GPT 4.1-mini, 13 tools) with one prompt iteration history. The claim that WAH's 65% matches human-operator performance is unsubstantiated by a reported number. Evaluation confounds are partially acknowledged: WAH growth coincided with a publicity drive. No code, data, prompts (explicitly excluded), or model weights are released. Test formats and durations were shaped by Geolink's operational availability, so the experiments are opportunistic rather than designed; the thesis is transparent about this, which raises confidence in honesty but limits inferential strength. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (live-deployment systems study; also SYSTEMS in that working agents were left in service). - Practical: Yes — runs on a custom RTX 5090 PC and a Dell Pro Max GB10 (128 GB unified memory) for local models, plus commercially available OpenAI APIs; no exotic infrastructure required. - Efficient: Local quantized models and Whisper keep operational cost low (<0.5 s transcription latency); the WAC agent showed that broader capability at acceptable cost/latency is exactly what is not yet efficient. - Effective: Effectiveness is shown on the real problem (live dispatch traffic, real bookings, retained-in-service WAH and Napoleão expansions), though satisfaction is a single self-selected star rating and RTN sentiment is manual qualitative review. - Scalable: Not tested — single operator site, ~100 RTN calls, one fleet queue; the authors do not claim multi-site or 10× scale, and manual intracall review would not scale. The work delivers deployed production artifacts (four agents, an operator web dashboard, Asterisk/SIP integrations) rather than a released library or dataset; nothing public is shipped. Strengths: - Rare negative-result evidence from live production: the WAC failure (hallucinated tool calls, loops, refusal to self-escalate) is documented concretely and contrasted against RTN's scoped design, giving the reliability–flexibility trade-off empirical teeth rather than anecdote. - Multi-channel, multi-architecture comparison under identical operational conditions (same dispatch backend, same operator fallback layer), which most LLM-agent papers lack entirely. - Careful treatment of telephony-specific failure modes (ASR confidence, endpointing, PT-PT vs. BR-PT drift) grounded in the spoken-dialogue literature (Bohus & Rudnicky, PARADISE, grounding theory) rather than imported chatbot assumptions. - Honest accounting of confounds (publicity drive, short test windows, manual review) and of the fact that results may be model-generation-specific. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that all deployments occurred in a single operator environment (Geolink) with a specific user base and fleet system; that audio-based agents required manual intracall review, constraining analysis scale; that RTN and WAC test windows were short (WAC ended early due to failure severity); and that the model landscape shifted mid-study (two new OpenAI realtime models released after testing). They confront these limitations directly and frame the WAC/RTN architectures as scaffolding for stronger future models — a credible, non-defensive treatment. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline WAH comparison ("65%, comparable to the human operator rate") is never backed by the baseline number, satisfaction survey response rate, or any control for call mix/difficulty — the thesis itself (citing ACQIs) notes that containment metrics must be controlled for difficulty, but no such control is reported. - WAC's failure is attributed to model capability, but tool count (13), prompt design, and WhatsApp message-latency patterns are confounds; a scoped variant of WAC (e.g., 5 tools) was never tried, so the "scope, not capability" conclusion rests on the WAH-vs-RTN contrast across different channels and models. - The RTN hallucination-rate claim ("extremely low" due to few tools) is not quantified — no hallucinations-per-call figure, no comparison with WAC's rate on a common metric. - No measurement of operator-side workload or handoff quality (e.g., time-to-resolution after escalation, escalation appropriateness), despite the thesis's own literature review arguing these are essential HITL metrics. - User satisfaction is measured only for WAH via a post-service prompt susceptible to selection bias; RTN sentiment is informal manual review. - The 26% RTN hangup rate signals an acceptability problem that is noted but not analyzed beyond user discomfort with AI. - No code, prompts, or evaluation protocol are released, and the single-site, Portuguese-language setting limits external validity. Bottom Line: A practitioner considering LLM agents for voice or messaging automation in a safety-critical dispatch business will gain more from this thesis's concrete live-traffic failure modes and its scoped-vs-conversational comparison than from most benchmark papers in the TOD literature, but researchers should treat it as a well-documented single-site case study rather than controlled evidence.

Ovis-Embedding: Pushing the Frontiers of Universal Omni-Modal Embeddings (20 ▲ )

Ovis-Embedding Team · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 23 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Ovis-Embedding, a family of universal embedding models (3B omni-modal; 2B/9B vision-language) initialized directly from natively multimodal understanding backbones (Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3.5) and trained with a four-stage recipe to support any-to-any retrieval across text, image, video, audio, and interleaved inputs. - Why it's important: Retrieval repositories now mix modalities (audio queries matching video tutorials, PDF diagrams, service records), and existing embedders bolt audio onto vision-language models after the fact, producing geometry learned without acoustic inputs — this work argues the fix is to start from a backbone that already fused all modalities. - How it does it: Strip the generative head from a Qwen-Omni understanding model, pool the last non-padding hidden state as the embedding (no projection head), then train in four stages: LoRA-restrained contrastive pretraining with focal-weighted InfoNCE plus KL distillation from expert teachers, full-parameter finetuning with homogeneous-source (single-dataset) micro-batches for harder in-batch negatives, annealing distillation with student-confidence-adaptive KL weights, and post-hoc hybrid PCA + residual adapters for elastic embedding widths. - The good: Ovis-Embedding-Omni-3B scores 58.46 on MMEB-v3, beating the 8B Tianmu-Emb-Uni by 5.19 points and ranking first on the aggregate of all six modality groups (image 77.55, video 64.99, VisDoc 78.26, text 47.15, audio 50.08, agent 45.52), with a 23.45-point margin on the out-of-distribution VisDoc-OOD subset. - The missing: Most training-recipe components (focal loss, homogeneous sampling, distillation weights, LoRA-vs-full-parameter) are supported only by qualitative claims — no ablation tables are presented — and MAEB/MVEB ranks are self-computed by inserting locally run scores into a leaderboard snapshot rather than from official submission. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building multimodal/omni-modal retrieval systems who want the current recipe frontier and a strong open model; skippable for readers seeking rigorous component-level evidence, since the recipe is a competent assembly of known techniques (focal loss, distillation, Matryoshka-style adapters) applied to a new backbone choice.

Resilience (42) is similarly weak — the leaderboard rankings and recipe claims would likely not survive official submissions and adversarial scrutiny of the undisclosed distillation teachers. Novelty (58) is real but narrow (native omni-modal initialization vs. audio-retrofit), and Impact (62) depends entirely on promised, unverified open-source artifacts.
